are also the legislative "mystery tours" (Esser) which do not emanate from 
conflicts which are to be anticipated or about to be fought out but which 
instead fix certain states through a political act of will — states which 
ideally are expected not to produce conflict but approval and obedience. 
It is problematic that such pre-decided conflicts lack the tension and the 
uncertainty which motivate the generalization of law. Subjects of conflict 
of this kind are arbitrarily specifiable but are ultimately interpreted merely 
as artefacts of politically regulated power towards binding decisions — and 
not as a tried and tested restriction of expectations. The problem has served 
as an impetus for forced "democratization" of politics. It has brought us 
the (unfortunately posed) question of the political legitimation of law-
making, a question which has given rise to a substantial body of literature. 
The theoretical approach proposed here seeks a fundamentally different 
solution. Only by interpreting the unity and the characteristic function of 
the legal system in the context of the functional differentiation of the legal 
system can one discern why and how law (similarly to money but in a 
quite different manner) is "exploited" in the political system in a manner 
quite alien to its function, without any consideration for its specific regener-
ation capacity. 
This discussion of the unity and function of the legal system provides 
an opportunity to examine a striking new development in the study of law, 
a completely new kind of critique of law which has recently been much 
debated at congresses and conferences as well as in literature. The critique 
of law is of course as old as differentiated forms of law (see above all Nörr, 
1970). The fact that no law can satisfy all wishes has always been vexing 
and has kept the search for remedies and redresses going. In the hands of 
people, lawyers and courts, law is obviously not what it should be. 
Following the invention of printing in the 16th century, criticism of the 
complexity of law — which could now so to speak be read by all and was 
therefore public — also came into its own. This discussion continued into 
the 18th century and revolved around the open question of whether redress 
was more likely to come from the authority of the legislator — which 
then, to be consistent, would have to forbid the quoting of the opinions 
of jurists in court — or from the systematizing logic of the dogmatism of 
law.40 This criticism remains embedded in a sceptical-realistic world view 
and therefore, like the legal system itself, is not fully differentiated. "Giacche 
liti, giudizi ed avvocati ci han da essere finche durera il mondo ne rimedio 
e facilmente da sperare a certi inevitabili difetti della giurisprudenza" 
(Muratori, 1958: 119). 
40 See for example Muratori (1742, quoted from the Milan edition, 1958: 111 f.), which 
proposes an option for reason and against authority. Here it does not even occur to 
the author to deny that legislation can be a means of clarifying and simplifying law, 
whereas today the precise opposite is true. 

30 
Niklas Luhmann 
Today a completely different kind of world view and a completely 
different kind of criticism of law are becoming prevalent, though they have 
not yet found a valid formulation. On the one hand, they activate human 
rights movements in the sphere of communicatively concentrated inter-
nationality, championing the cause of all structurally underprivileged people 
without any consideration of legal-technical feasibility. On the other hand, 
they complain about "too much of a good thing" — in the legal sphere, 
for example, about the "juridification of life", about excessive use of 
legistu<.η which is in itself positive, about rationality defects and the 
disastrous effects of affluence. Yet they are unable to identify a criterion 
or a limit at which the desirable is transformed into the detrimental. This 
criticism operates a double bind — rejecting what it is not yet willing to 
give up and at the same time making demands the legal-technical realization 
of which would terrify them. 
The discussion of "delegalization" — a concept originated in the United 
States — provides a good example of this.41 Delegalization is concerned 
partly with shifting specific aspects of law into other areas, for example 
replacing court decisions by the amicable persuasion of arbitration; and 
partly with the related prospect of excluding entire areas of life from the 
sphere of law. The appeal of this program resides not least in the fact that 
no distinction is made between alternatives to specific legal institutions 
and the law itself.42 However if one bears in mind the unity and function 
of the legal system, one is obliged to reflect on how delegalized alternatives 
propose to implement their schemes for the anticipation and avoidance of 
litigation, which brings us back to the question of law, a question merely 
"repressed". The question of law invariably forces its way back, unless it 
is argued that one must accept the arbitrariness of those in power43 or the 
moral pressures of well-meaning fellow citizens. 
A critique of law which merely objects to an excess of regulation and 
does not consider the conflict aspect of law poses the problem incorrectly. 
It criticizes the political use of law, the extent of such use, perhaps also 
the contents of such laws. But this still leaves open the question of whether 
and how the legal system itself as a closed, self-referential reproduction 
unit can exist side by side with a money economy and welfare state 
policies in modern conditions. If one does not differentiate between the 
corresponding system references, one will in some circumstances fail to 
recognize important development tendencies in law, such as the trends 
41 See the highly critical account by Abel (1980). 
42 The title of the last-mentioned work underlines that such a distinction can be conceived 
and formulated. 
43 Abel (1980: 407) rightly stresses that: "delegalization presupposes that the people or 
entities that interact outside formal legal institutions are roughly equal in political 
power, wealth and social status".

towards social engineering and the instrumentalization of law; nor will 
one be able to understand Max Weber's skepticism about the social-
eudaemonistic tendencies in law which were beginning to emerge in his 
time. 
However, it is equally false to regard conflict regulation as the sole 
function of law. It is indisputably the case that many conflicts have been 
shifted out of the sphere of law.44 From this perspective, law does in fact 
enter into competition with other, functionally equivalent possibilities. But 
the actual use of these alternatives means a renunciation of motives, 
occasions and situations for the establishment and reproduction of law. 
Conflicts are then no longer used to generalize expectations but are regarded 
as conflicts only in ad hoc fashion and are eliminated whenever possible. 
In order to advance beyond the present unsatisfactory discussion of 
subjects such as legalization, the plethora of laws, bureaucratization, the 
formulation and complexity of law, we must first recall the connection of 
a fully autopoietic constitution of social subsystems with the principle 
of functional social differentiation. Functional specification, whatever its 
evolutionary advantages and further potential may be, seems to be the ideal 
starting point for the full differentiation of subsystems, i.e., a principle for 
which there is no equivalent in the respective environments of the systems 
(including the intra-societal environment). The function system, although 
it uses and reproduces social communication and remains capable of connec-
tion with the environment, is, so to speak, free to constitute unity on its 
own account, to communicate closure and openness, to create the structures 
necessary for this purpose and to coordinate all this with its own function. 
In other words, we argue that an empirically ascertainable connection 
exists between the principle of differentiation of the social system and 
the form in which subsystems in society differentiate themselves as self-
referentially closed and as open to the environment. It is a question here 
of two sides of one and the same process of social differentiation, which 
is simply the making possible of a form of communication of closure and 
openness which is characteristic of subsystems. For the legal system this 
means the differentiation of a connection between normative closure and 
cognitive openness. Here that which serves as a contrafactual norm is, in 
the process of social evolution, increasingly pointed to the function of law. 
The critique of law is therefore essentially a critique of social differentiation. 
This leads to a large number of related questions requiring further 
analysis which can only be outlined here. Perhaps the most interesting is 
the question of whether an upper tolerance level for complexity exists 
beyond which the specific legal symbiosis of normative and cognitive 
44 Some motives working in this direction are discussed in Aubert (1983: 134 ff.), above 
all: avoidance of the all-or-nothing risk, saving of time and money, elimination of 
publicity, external control, possible loss of standing. 

32 
Niklas Luhmann 
orientations no longer functions. One indicator here is that the development 
of logic and of the empirical sciences in the past hundred years has raised 
doubts about the scientific character of jurisprudence. Closely related to this 
is the question of whether jurists can continue to base their understanding of 
the law and their interpretations on consequence orientation where it is 
possible to find out what the possibilities of prognosis are.45 It is equally 
important to ascertain the significance of similar treatment of similar cases 
and disparate treatment of disparate cases and of the legal doctrine which 
is designed to deal with these questions, when on the one hand legislation 
rigorously specifies and incessantly changes legal questions, and on the 
other hand the causal perspective of social engineering — because of 
differences between the relevant factors — makes it practically impossible 
to compare cases. The reversal of the conflict perspective discussed above 
(in part VI) must also be taken into consideration: if it is no longer a 
question of deciding what expectations (tested against what generalizations) 
can be maintained in the event of conflict, if instead conflicts decided in 
advance are created in order to append regulations to them which have 
legal validity, then it must be assumed that the response to this will be a 
profound change in the conception of law — although at present no 
empirical indicators are available for the registering of such change. 
The common denominator for all these different problems may lie in 
the fact that the evolution of the social system makes possible the establish-
ment of a highly improbable order, an order which is full of preconditions. 
The combination of normative closure and cognitive openness discussed 
above is one of these improbabilities. It is probable that such contradictory 
attitudes of expectation will ruin one another. Very specific conditionings 
are required in order to guarantee separability and compatibility, and given 
the rapid pace of social change these conditionings rapidly lose their 
credibility. Every reference to the validity of conditions of validity finally 
becomes suspect simply by the fact of being used as an argument. All 
that remains is the demand for continuous adjustment of law to social 
development while maintaining the regenerative capacity of normativity. 
Law which is adaptive, responsive and capable of learning must avoid the 
discrediting of its own normativity or else it will reduce itself to being an 
instrument of bureaucratic implementations of political power. 
What the new critique has taken up appears to be this immanent 
improbability, which emerges all the more clearly as political demands on

law increase. Given the complexity of the facts, prognoses are difficult, as

describes itself remain a matter of crucial importance. And here advances 
and improvements can be made on the basis of interdisciplinary theoretical 
developments and an emergent sociological theory of society.

The Law of Law 
F R A N 9 0 I S E W A L D 
Paris 
It is a fact that there is no (positive) law without a law of law; no law 
without a principle, an instance of reflexion, whereby the law thinks about 
itself. 
This reflexivity corresponds, firstly, to a logical need. The proof was 
given by Kelsen: a norm is legal only on condition that it derives from a 
norm that is itself legal (Kelsen, 1962: 255 cf.). The law presupposes itself; 
it necessarily precedes itself. The fact that the law has no origin assignable 
to a fact is a fact which characterizes the law as law. In consequence, any 
positive legal norm presupposes another one that confers its legality on it. 
The idea of a single legal norm has no meaning. Similarly, for Ferdinand 
de Saussure, the idea of an isolated signifier has no meaning (de Saussure, 
1955: 155). 
This idea of law's preceding itself expresses the transcendental nature of 
the law. Kelsen was not the first to enunciate it. Aristotle had already 
shown the need for it; and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, after invalidating the 
sociological thesis that would identify law with social constraint, explains 
in Book I of the Social Contract 
how it is impossible to derive a legal 
relationship from any fact whatever, in particular from the fact of power. 
The fiction of the social contract is, as Althusser has shown, caught up in 
the difficulty that what gives value to the act of entering into the contract 
depends on the contract itself (Althusser, 1967), and social contract and 
fundamental norm do nothing but describe the need for a law of law. They 
are two formulations of the same problem, that of the law's necessary 
precedence over itself. 
Social contract and fundamental norm refer back to two different imagin-
ary legal entities, two ways of conceiving of the question of principle. 
These images, which it is difficult to do without — Kant would have 
called this schematism of the understanding — can lead to error by inducing 
consideration of the validity of the thesis on the basis of the actual 
possibility of the image proposed: the validity of the social contract will 
be made to depend on its material existence; the fundamental norm is 
imagined as a single norm. A careful reading will seek to dig out the 

The Law of Law 
37 
rational core from the forms in which it is conceived. It is in fact not 
necessary for this principle of reflexiveness of law to be bound up with 
any particular legal act. It is a logical need, which many acts may meet. It 
is more of a principle of validation, or more exactly a principle of interpreta-
tion. "The experience of codified legal systems shows how the same legal 
text, the same article of a code, may through time, with transformations 
of "the Law", come to found two differing norms. The norm, then, is not 
the article of the code or the text of the law; it is not even their meaning, 
but something that depends on and refers back to the normative instance, 
namely the law of law. 
As we know, it was traditionally in the element of "natural law" that 
this reflection of law on itself took place. It is typical of present-day 
legal experience that the idea of natural law has become impossible or 
impracticable for us. The idea of natural law is something that we no 
longer understand; it has become alien to us. But this does not ipso facto 
imply that a legal order can live without a body for reflecting on itself. 
Our impossibility of formulating a natural law anew raises more problems 
than it solves. It confronts us with the need to formulate this element of 
law reflecting on itself outside the form of natural law. And all the time 
we know that if this function is not fulfilled, law will evaporate into a 
pure exercise in legality, in power or in constraint. 
Thus, law presents itself as having a twofold, divided structure. This 
structure defines the framework of any possible legal experience. Legal 
systems may vary and may differentiate in the course of history — and 
they have certainly not failed to do so — but these variations cannot affect 
the twofold, divided structure of the legal experience. Better, when one 
legal system or order succeeds to another, this presupposes not merely a 
difference in the norms and their content, in the architecture of the system, 
but also in the reflexive body that gives the new law its legal value. If 
norms change from one system to another, this cannot in the last analysis 
come from anything but what gives normative value to the norms of 
positive law. Thus, it is the contemporary experience of French law that 
it is not necessary to change the Code — specifically, the Civil Code — in 
order to change the law. Transformations in the normative instance are 
sufficient. Between the norm and its interpretation there is, then, a solid 
bond and a reciprocity: the one changes along with the other. Describing 
a real system cannot mean describing merely certain practices of positive 
law, but the bond that they form along with their interpreting body. 
This structure of the legal experience may no doubt be described in 
terms of autopoiesis or of self-referential system. But there is nothing 
necessary about that. If autopoiesis describes only this, it does no more 
than repeat in new words something that is very well known. It teaches 
us nothing, tells us nothing new. Autopoiesis theory can be of interest 
only in so far as it offers some special way of understanding the law's 

38 
Francois Ewald 
reflection on itself. Moreover, autopoiesis can only be a special case of 
something that ought to be described in a more general vocabulary, of 
which autopoiesis proposes only one particular modality. 
To describe the element of reflexivity of law, I propose to speak of a 
rule of judgement 
(Ewald, 1986 b). Legislation, doctrine and case law are all 
practices of legal judgement. Their articulation, distribution and mutual 
competence depend on the type of rationality that this legal judgement 
obeys. This type of rationality defines, for a particular legal order, the 
economy of its "juris-diction". The rule of judgement is not a rule laid 
down by a body, but is what regulates the judgement of all bodies; 
accordingly, not something that one applies, but something whereby one 
judges. It is one of the characteristics of the practice of legal judgement 
that the rule of judgement must constantly be made explicit. Statute, 
doctrine and case law derive from it and express it; but it can never be 
reduced to these. It is a sort of necessary ideal on the basis of which legal 
practices reflect the constraint that binds them, their unity and their 
systematicity. Constantly reformulated, it never ceases to depart from itself 
through the judgements that express it. 
The doctrine of autopoiesis is one way of formulating this problem of 
the rule of judgement, of the law of law. It is quite a problem whether 
this law is internal to the legal system associated with it, whose reflexive 
instance it is, or external to it. It would no doubt be truer to say that the 
rule of judgement is that whereby a legal system closed round its own 
order comes into contact with its exterior: what one in general calls the 
social. Either one thing or the other must be: either the doctrine of 
autopoiesis is the theory of law that does not claim to deal with it except 
from outside. It is then nothing but the application to law of the theory 
of autopoietic systems. In this case, like deontic logic or legal linguistics, 
it runs the risk of saying as much about law as a system as it fails to say 
about law as practice. In this case, it will have to abandon its pretension 
to be an adequate element of reflection of legal practices. The law spoken 
about in autopoiesis will then be an abstract law, a philosopher's or 
sociologist's law, a law with the characteristic of being all the more 
loquacious the more indifferent it is to the practitioner. In this case, I 
repeat, the doctrine of autopoiesis is less a theory of law than systems 
theory applied to law. There is liable to be as much relationship between 
the law it discusses and law as it is practised as there is between the dog 
as a barking animal and as a constellation in the heavens. As such, it does 
not interest me — or not any more than does systems theory. 
But if I have understood rightly, this position of externality is not tenable 
for the doctrine of autopoiesis. The observer forms part of the observation, 
and the observation, that which is objectivized about the object, depends 
on the place that the observed offers the observer. The doctrine of auto-
poiesis derives its competence from its particularity. From this point of 

The Law of Law 
39 
view, the position of autopoiesis with respect to law is similar to that 
which Kelsen's Pure Theory occupied. To be sure, the Pure Theory claimed 
to be a "science" of law external to its object. It nevertheless did have 
legislative value (and claims) with respect to the law. This is the approach 
from which I wish to appraise the theses of autopoiesis. 
I. Columbus' Egg 
Autopoiesis, first of all, is presented as a theory of law that is both post-
Kelsen and post-sociological. The theory of law in the 20th century has 
been characterized by the radical split between these two viewpoints, the 
external one (of the sociology of law) and the internal one (of the Pure 
Theory) each of them maintaining profoundly antagonistic relationships, 
each laying claim to exclusivity. The theory of law appeared to be more 
conservative, while sociology claimed to be critical. This division has 
become untenable: Kelsenian positivism does not make it possible to think, 
from a legal viewpoint, about the difference between legal systems; at the 
same time, and for the same reasons as those that made the shortcomings 
of positivism felt, the critical project that inspired sociology has largely 
lost its force. Who today would dare claim to wish the end of law? The 
dream today is of synthesis, of reconciliation of the two points of view, 
internal and external: of the construction of a theory that would be both 
a sociology of law, and the converse. 
Autopoiesis proposes one way of reconciling the two points of view 
which, by contrast with certain sociological attempts, does not seek to 
reconcile the irreconcilable: the transcendental (the legal) and the empirical 
(the sociology of legal practices). This desire for reconciliation implies in 
both formulations that the law is a social system, a differentiated social 
subsystem, reproducing itself autonomously, more specifically autopoieti-
cally. It is the notion of system, in fact of logic, that allows, without 
contradiction, the conception of the articulation of the law as a closed 
system and the social. It favors the transcendental over the empirical, 
though without any constant. Kant would be more at home in it than 
Gurvitch. 
Autopoiesis is indisputably the daughter of Kelsen's Pure Theory. Kel-
sen's reversal is familiar: whereas hitherto the philosophy of law sought 
outside positive law, and mostly as its foundation, for the principle of its 
legality and validity (the one entailing the other), Kelsen, in an inaugural 
gesture unheard of in legal tradition posited that the legality (and the 
validity) of the legal system could be based only on its own positiveness.1 
1 Though the premises might be found in Pascal's 
Pensees. 

40 
Francis Ewald 
Far from the positivity of a legal order having to be explained by any 
recourse whatever to a legitimating body, the very fact of the law's 
positivity was given explanatory value. The law was a foundation for law. 
Ipso facto, 
the project of giving a "foundation" to law lost its meaning. 
The law did not have to be explained, but analyzed. And a given legal 
system could accept no other instance of judgement than itself. It could 
be judged only by its own standard. For us, Kelsen's reversal marks the 
legal experience's entry into the age of modernity. It is the one we are still 
in. Autopoiesis itself finds the condition of its possibility in Kelsen's 
gesture. It follows him, and it does not break with him. 
One cannot stress enough how dramatic Kelsen's gesture could (and 
can) be. This is, by the way, what those theoreticians of law that claim to 
make it a "science" most lack: the awareness that the history of the law 
has the form of a drama, that it is intertwined with the dramas of the 
reason that mark the history of the West. The law, Kelsen posits, is founded 
on nothing other than its own positivity. The proposition had more than 
merely theoretical value. It was implicit in it that it was no longer possible 
to found law on anything external, whether a natural law, an ideal society, 
a notion of justice or a doctrine of the rights of man. Underlying Kelsen's 
thesis is a formidable crisis, the depth of which is adequately indicated by 
the Great War and the laceration of Europe. Kelsen's thesis fitted into the 
growing awareness that continuing to found law upon a doctrine of justice 
could only end by particularizing it and therefore destroying it. Justice, 
the Rights of Man, everything in which the possibility of agreement, the 
hope of universality, had been placed, was instead revealed as a factor of 
unending war. At the very moment when the doctrines of natural law, on 
which since Aristotle the possibility of law had been based, were revealing 
themselves as destructive of law through their very affirmation, Kelsen, 
through the positivist position, saved the Western experience of law. At 
the very moment when the isms — historicism, sociologism, in short the 
relativism of the human sciences — were walling up any doctrine of natural 
law in the particularism of its particularity, Kelsen showed that a law was 
nevertheless possible, on condition that it be forearmed against any attempt 
to found the law upon any natural law whatsoever. 
Autopoiesis is fundamentally following up Kelsen's gesture. To be sure, 
it rejects the hypothesis of the fundamental norm in favor of the idea of 
an interaction, of a correlation, of some solidarity among norms. But this 
is a secondary proposition by comparison with the reconfirmed thesis that 
law can have no other reference than itself. Certainly, from Kelsen to 
Luhmann the idea of system is not the same, but this is secondary in regard 
to the thesis of the transcendental nature of legality, and to the idea of 
the necessary self-reference. Kelsen's positivism gives law an existence 
indifferent to time, to history and to the conflict of values fought out 
there. Autopoiesis confirms law in its existence without taking on the now 

The Law of Law 
41 
condemned form of natural law. As an autopoietic system, the law is again 
sheltered from the storm, indifferent to time, able to reproduce itself 
indefinitely. All very suited for reassuring an epoch that still comes out in 
a cold sweat at the idea that it might have been able to take as a desirable 
goal the death of law. 
Autopoiesis thus fits into the tradition of sociological reflection upon 
law. At the end of the 19th century, at least in the continental countries, 
thinking about law was generally pursued as a critique of the old jusnatural-
ist positions. The law was henceforth to be social. Jurists had the dream 
that the human sciences, sociology in particular, could supply them with 
rules that would allow legal judgement to be always adequate to the 
norms that society continually secretes. Thanks to sociology, society could, 
predominantly through the mouth of judges, perpetually judge itself. The 
State would wither away into civil society, and civil society would dissolve 
into the social. But they had to cry off. The project was realizable only on 
condition that the human sciences became scientific. As we know, they 
will never achieve that. In particular, one must be aware that, even if they 
did become more scientific, they would still be incapable of supplying the 
desired rule of judgement. Firstly, of course, because knowledge of what 
is gives little indication as to duty. Yet legal judgement always has a goal: 
the rule of judgement expresses a policy of law that no science, even 
political science, can supply it with. But also because, in principle, the 
human sciences relativize everything they touch, themselves more than 
anything. Articulating the rule of judgement around the human sciences 
could lead only to depriving it of the necessary objectivity. In short, the 
project of sociology of law would itself lead to the ruin of law. 
That does not mean that the project should be given up. But instead of 
its being carried on chiefly by jurists, it should be by sociologists. There 
begins the era of sociological theories of law, the last epigones of the 
jusnaturalist doctrines. Except that society has replaced nature and at the 
same time positive intention has been transformed into a practice of 
denunciation. The jusnaturalist doctrines sought for the conditions on 
which the law could be just; the sociological doctrines repeat ad 
nauseam, 
in more or less radical forms, that the law is unjust, that its legitimacy is 
deceptive. That it is never there except to hide relationships of force and 
domination that underlie it. Like the jusnaturalist doctrines, the sociological 
and critical theories of law are underlain by the same desire for justice, for 
judging the positive law in the name of justice. 
While in recent times the critical passion seems to have deserted the 
sociologies of law, they remain firmly attached to the idea that the law is 
fundamentally social. There is a proposition there that is so obvious that 
one cannot see how to get round it. The idea is to find this foundation of 
law, which can no longer be sought for in philosophy, in some sociology. 
That is what gives sociology its competence: being responsible for supply-

42 
Francois Ewald 
ing the theory of law as a social phenomenon, it would at the same time 
be for it to state the truth of law. But it is constantly haunted by the 
Kelsenian cleavages and prohibitions: How could a sociology of law, 
despite everything, grasp law "from within"? How could sociology in some 
way divest itself of its own conditions of possibility? That seems today to 
be the great problem of the sociology of law. 
The sociology of law is in crisis. Autopoiesis is its chance, come to give 
it restored youth. Autopoiesis reconciles the internal and external points 
of view in the study of law, in more rigorous fashion than those types of 
discourse in which theory would consist in juxtaposing the discourse of 
legal doctrine's reflection of the transformations of law with the more 
ideological than sociological one carried on by social philosophers about 
social change.2 Luhmann's doctrine of the act of communication, his thesis 
of the closure of the legal order as a normative order and of its openness 
as a cognitive order, allow, without contradiction and without raising 
immediate logical and epistemological impossibilities, the conception of a 
way of thinking about the articulation of law and society. It would have 
to do, not with any social causality, any play of reflection, but with a 
cognitive strategy. Communication would take place, and would have to 
see itself, in terms of rationality, which would, as it were, be the medium, 
the interface, between law and society. This solution has the merit of 
respecting the viewpoint of the actors, of not reducing their will to an 
unconscious logic perceptible only by the scholar, and of not being reduc-
tive for law. 
Thus, autopoiesis may appear as a kind of Columbus' egg in the order 
of the theory of law. It would simultaneously allow one to transcend and 
to conserve the split between the pure theory and sociology; it would 
complement one by the other and ultimately reunite them. It would be the 
theory that was needed. All these virtues should at any rate assure it of 
immediate and lasting success. All the more so because, being bound up 
with the philosophy of autonomy and self-organization, it presents itself 
as a theory that at the same time allows reconciliation of the affirmation 
of the individual and his creative power with his belonging to a group 
whose solidarities make him what he is. 
II. Autopoiesis: A Theory of Social Law 
This is the pointer to the combination of circumstances that gives auto-
poiesis its chance, that defines the program it has to accomplish. For 
autopoiesis as yet exists only at the stage of program. One may very well 
2 Ost (1983) is typical of this type of discussion. 

The Law of Law 
43 
suspect it will always remain only at the program stage. Perhaps observation 
of legal systems will bring about an enrichment of the theory of autopoietic 
systems. But it may be suspected that, conversely, the theory of autopoietic 
systems may be of slight help in dealing with the issues raised by law at 
our own point in time. 
That there is no place for a meta-law, no more than, as Jacques Lacan 
says, there is any possibility of a meta-language, is a thesis that will no 
doubt be accepted by the autopoiesis school. The class of all classes is itself 
a class. What else does the hypothesis of self-reference state but that the 
knowledge of the object is never anything but the way in which the object 
itself reflects upon itself? There is no theory that does not have its place. 
And the thesis of autopoiesis is that any theory has to associate with its 
statements their conditions for being stated. In a word, in the very act of 
asserting its validity autopoiesis declares itself to be a particular theory. 
The doctrine of autopoiesis may be a particularly broad and general theory, 
capable of incorporating any other theory as particular; but that very fact 
designates it as particular. The consequence of this position is that the 
doctrine of autopoiesis cannot, if it is not to annihilate itself, count as a 
theory of law in general. Its validity does not depend on its being a truer 
theory than others (from its point of view true and false are not good 
criteria for distinguishing one theory from another), but merely more 
"profitable" at a particular point in time. The doctrine of autopoiesis can 
take its validity only from its performance in our own current legal 
position. It has no value in itself. It is in relation to the self-regulation of 
contemporary legal practice that it should be evaluated. 
I propose to designate our own legal position today as that of social law 
(Ewald, 1986 a). By "social law" I do not mean only the legal disciplines 
that deal with work and social security. Social law cannot be defined by 
the objects it deals with, but instead by what makes these objects capable 
of legal treatment. Social law designates a certain technique, a certain way 
of laying down law, articulated round a certain type of legal rationality, a 
type of juris-diction. If law exists only as system (and here it is of 
little moment whether it be an autopoietic system or not), this systemic 
character — which is in fact always particular, the way norms are produced, 
generated and articulated with each other — defines a type of jurisdiction. 
That is simultaneously the way of thinking about the question of the 
sources of law, the relationships between fact and law, and the question of 
the criterion of legality. The law is not bound up with any one type of 
jurisdiction. On the contrary, these may vary and be transformed, giving 
birth and reality to different legal systems. What is called in France "civil 
law" refers to a certain type of jurisdiction. A type of jurisdiction, a system 
of law, thus always has a reflexive character: it includes not only a certain 
normative content, a set of special rules depending on the criterion of 
legality peculiar to the legal system considered, a way of practicing legal 

44 
Frangois Ewald 
judgement, whether in the form of syllogistic deduction or in the more 
"flexible" forms such as a balance of interests, but also a body of doctrine 
through which the whole set of these practices are reflected and regulated, 
ensuring, in an expression of Maurice Hauriou's, their own "policing" 
(Hariou, 1926: 52). 
What is it that characterizes social law? Firstly, that it is no longer 
reflected in any natural law, in any reference whatever to nature. Nature 
has been succeeded by society. It is not certain that this is "better"; in any 
case, it is certainly no truer. The fact is that we have lost the possibility 
of referring to nature, whether Aristotle's ontological nature or Kant's 
human nature. Classical natural law found its condition of possibility in 
that which made possible a knowledge of nature as ontology and theology; 
modern natural law in that which made physics possible as science. Social 
law, for its part, appears in the same epistemological act as makes possible 
the human sciences. 
Along with nature, there also falls the reference to the universal. The 
society objectivized by sociology is characterized by it firstly by being 
divided into associated and opposed interests, with a multiplicity of special 
strategies arranged around the principle of the specificity of their own 
calculation. And man in the human sciences loses transcendental power 
and is reduced to the ineradicable particularity of his conditioning. The 
social space is henceforth constituted in such a manner as to accept nothing 
external to itself, and on the other hand to be animated by perpetual 
movement. Nothing can any longer claim identity for itself. Everything 
changes, unceasingly. The social bond can no longer have the form of an 
original contract, whose terms would be invariable; these terms can only 
be continually negotiated and renegotiated. Moreover, it is no longer 
necessary to make the assumption of a contract. Men are bound to them-
selves, through a network of solidarity on which they depend and from 
which they draw their identity. 
The consequence of this epistemological position is that it ruins the 
possibility of the universal. Values are only ever particular, and any value 
seeking to take on universality would ipso facto be denounced for seeking 
to dominate. The way in which the developing countries find themselves 
constrained, in order to assert their identity, to denounce the particularity 
of a principle so obvious for us as pacta sunt servanda exemplifies this issue. 
The present day is marked by the end of the way of articulating the 
universal and the particular which the theoreticians of modern natural law, 
from Grotius to Kant, were able to formulate: anyone today seeking to 
base a doctrine of the Rights of Man on a theory of natural law would 
ipso facto invalidate it. The present situation is marked by the fact that 
those values that might hitherto have seemed the most unequivocal have 
become problematic and are the object of division and conflict as to their 
interpretation. In short, what had right into the 19th century remained the 

The Law of Law 
45 
basis for the possibility of law — a doctrine of justice, of natural rights 
and duties — has in our present situation become the principle of its own 
destruction. 
With social law, the demand for justice has become a threat to the law. 
This is the irreducible problem any philosophy of law has today to face. 
It is one of the paradoxes of social law that the reference that it originally 
took contains its own destruction. Hence the need, assumed by Kelsen, to 
think about law without justice. Positivism is the theory of social law; the 
only theory that makes it possible as law. This has no doubt not been 
sufficiently stressed: the Pure Theory is the theory of law in the epoch of 
social law. 
The second characteristic of social law, of the jurisdiction of social law, 
is that it is a law that must find the conditions for its own possibility, for 
the objectivity of its rule of judgement, within itself. It cannot be within 
a doctrine of natural law, as we have just seen; nor in the legislator's will. 
Both because the latter, sociologically, always proclaims itself particular: it 
is never more than the will of a majority, the expression of a social group 
that has (for better or worse) secured a position of domination. Thus, 
the legislator's will, no longer subject to a transcendental reference and 
proclaiming itself to be a particular will, cannot yet be treated as legal 
unless it becomes bound by rules, by a law, specifically by a law of law, 
which must itself be social. Where then, in the new situation, is one to 
find the conditions for formulating a law capable of limiting the henceforth 
omnipotent will of the legislator? 
I pointed out just now how jurists had become aware of sociology's 
inability to supply them with the regulatory principle they were seeking. 
There have been other theoretical attempts: the Germans, perhaps already 
on the path of autopoiesis, advocated the self-limitation of the State. This 
solution clearly offered few guarantees, since only the State had the power 
to self-limit itself (cf. Duguit, 1924: 644). The search was then made from 
the angle of comparative law for the formulation of a "common law of 
humanity" (civilized humanity, implicitly) (cf. Saleilles, 1900). One can 
imagine the difficulty of the endeavor in the situation following the First 
World War, marked as we too well know by the formation of the totalitarian 
States. The solution could only be positivist, though it seems apparent that 
positivism states itself to be radically incapable of giving it. Did not Kelsen 
himself state that "any content can be legal" (Kelsen, 1962)? In these 
circumstances, one can understand how the formation of the jurisdiction 
of social law might have seemed threatening to law, encouraging impossible 
endeavors to reformulate a natural law, the premises of which were now 
being sought for in St. Thomas.3 
3 The first series of Archives de pbilosophie du droit et de sociologie juridique, from 1931 to 
the war, is ample evidence of this "return" to St. Thomas. 

46 
Francois Ewald 
It was for practice to find the solution that the theory had been unable 
to supply. It is particularly interesting in the autopoietic perspective: it is, 
namely, the practice of the general principles of law. At the international 
level, the practice was invented to make the Nuremberg Tribunal possible. 
What had to be judged were crimes against humanity, a charge formulated 
specially for the case, in breach of the right of man whereby "no one may 
be punished except according to a law established and formulated prior to 
the offense" (Article 8 of the "Declaration of the Rights of Man and 
Citizen", 26 August 1789). Accordingly, the accusation, till then unformu-
lated, had in some way to subsist in a latent state, consubstantial with the 
existence of humanity itself. The rule had not been invented for the needs 
of the case; it merely rendered explicit a "principle", more or less as Prince 
Charming awakens Snow White, who has been waiting only for him in 
order to be what she is. An operation of this kind inevitably rebounded 
upon the framework of domestic law. To maintain the legal tradition 
trampled underfoot during the war, lo and behold, there were discovered, 
even in the absence of texts and in the lacunae of law, principles in the 
name of which even the acts of the legislator could be condemned. The 
practice has since considerably developed, particularly with the setting up 
of Supreme Courts with the responsibility of verifying the constitutionality 
of the laws. In my vocabulary, the practice of general principles is character-
istic of the jurisdiction of social law; it is the way in which the law of law 
is formulated there. 
The general principles of law cannot be confused with the text of the 
Declarations of Rights. Firstly, because the first characteristic of principles 
is that they are not formulated in a text. The judge "discovers" them in 
the silence of the law — they are like the white space between the lines. 
But above all, it is because the principles do not refer to any natural law, 
since they do not rest on any philosophical doctrine. The general principles 
of law have no other support than the positive practices of law themselves. 
They are neither superior nor anterior to law. They are law itself, reflecting 
on itself on the basis of its own tradition. They are not timeless. They do 
not remain identical to themselves. Their power lies on the contrary in the 
flexibility of their identity, their stability, their mobility. The general 
principles of law are a way for the law to bind itself, to preserve its identity 
while being receptive to change. By the general principles of law, the 
positive law binds itself only to itself, to its own positivity. Thus, one 
discovers how there may in practice be, in the positivity of law itself, the 
possibility of a law of law. Thus, with the practice of the general principles 
of law, one enters the phase of critical positivism, of a positivism that finds 
within itself the conditions of its own internal critique. It is in the form 
of the general principles of law that the essential reflexivity of law is 
practiced in the epoch of social law. 

The Law of Law 
47 
I imagine that the proponents of autopoiesis will see in the general 
principles of law a remarkably autopoietic practice. Perhaps it is. But if it 
is, this also has the effect of particularizing the doctrine. For this practice 
of the general principles of law is absolutely not a practice of law itself, 
but only of the particular law that social law is. What in France is called 
"droit civil" (civil law) cannot have any kind of practice such as that of 
general principles. It characterizes only a certain type of jurisdiction and 
not all possible jurisdiction. 
III. The Tautological Condemnation 
Let us accept that autopoiesis finds its validity as a theory of social law. I 
wish in closing to consider two further points. Firstly, whether autopoiesis 
may be anything other than a theory of social law, whether it may be valid 
as a general theory of law; secondly, whether autopoiesis may be the venue 
that social law needs for its own regulation. Is autopoiesis capable of 
playing a role similar to the one the Pure Theory was able to play at its 
time with respect to the positive practices of law? In short, can autopoiesis 
be the mode of reflection of law upon itself that a critical positivism would 
be? 
The autopoiesis approach formulates, in new language, what Aristotle 
showed, very long ago, in his Politics. Our legal tradition begins with 
Aristotle, when he introduces the distinction between legal justice and 
particular justice (Villey, 1978: 55). That is to say when he distinguishes 
law and legality. Aristotle explains that while legal justice is bound up with 
respect for the law, particular justice is bound up with the principle of 
equality: a judgement is not legal, is not a just judgement, unless it treats 
equals as equals. The problem is as follows: if one starts from individuals — 
and one can only start from individuals, since it is the existence of a rule 
of justice alone that makes community possible — there is no possibility 
for men ever to agree on a rule, on a common measure, that would enable 
them to treat themselves from the viewpoint of equality. In fact, says 
Aristotle, "Everyone is a bad judge of himself', everyone tends to assert 
what distinguishes himself from others — a specific difference which is 
never relative except to one criterion — as being an overall superiority. 
Moreover, how could one judge oneself well in one's relationship to others 
as long as there existed no reference for this judgement, no rule recognized 
as objective (Aristotle, Politics, III 1280 a)? This is the problem of law: if 
one abandons the Platonic position that reciprocates and identifies right 
and law, law and legality, law and commandment, for an approach that 
seeks to generate the rule of law from individuals themselves, one is 
confronted with insurmountable difficulties. The rule of justice, the com-
mon measure, is possible only on condition of supposing itself itself. Its 

48 
Fran5ois Ewald 
supposed presence is necessary in order to get out of a solipsism which 
would otherwise be radical. 
Aristotle states that if there is no logical solution to the problem of the 
origin of law and of the objectivity of judgement by oneself of oneself 
and of others, this problem nevertheless is given a practical solution, 
demonstrated by the actual existence of communities (Aristotle, Nicomachean 
Ethics, Book V, Chapt. V). He gives the example of money. Nobody ever 
decided on the value of goods and of merchandise; the practice of com-
merce, however, the existence of money, are there to prove that the problem 
of the common measure does have a practical solution. In saying this, 
Aristotle is stating that the question of the origin or foundation of law has 
no meaning, no possible solution; law is always presupposed (if it exists); 
there is no law that does not precede itself. 
Thus, Aristotle defined what is and will remain the problem of law in 
the Western tradition: the problem of the objectivity of judgement by 
oneself of oneself, the problem of the common measure, the problem of 
just judgement. This position had two consequences. The first is that it 
posed the question of law as a critical question in relation to legality. Law 
is not on the side of power, of constraint, of commandment; it states no 
rule of conduct. That is part of legality. Law is, on the contrary, the 
question asked of legality, in some sense of any possible legality: on what 
conditions is a legality legal? On what condition can a legality, in a given 
historical situation, for a particular community, act as a common measure? 
Law does not, properly speaking, designate any normative content; it is 
the critical question asked of legality, the venue in which the question is 
raised of the objectivity of judgement, that is of a common measure. This 
Aristotelian position on law radically distinguishes it from morality, from 
the problems of good and evil, of what ought to be done or not; it makes 
a problem of logic, or better, a problem of transcendental logic. 
No doubt, the fact that in our legal experience we have acquired the 
habit of linking the problem of the objectivity of judgement with the 
question of sovereignty and the legislator's will as the general will has led 
to a confusion of law and legality, and to making the very existence of a 
legality into the sign of the existence of law. But this is at the cost of 
making it impossible to distinguish, for instance, between Western law and 
so-called socialist law. If the West is characterized by maintaining the 
question of law as a critical question asked of legality, socialist "law", 
which rejects the question, is in fact nothing but pure and simple legality, 
legality without law. In practice, while law and legality are confounded in 
the rule of law, law and legality answer two different questions which it 
is important to distinguish. If the problem of legality is: Here is what you 
must do, then the problem of law can be formulated: Here is how you 
will be judged. 

The Law of Law 
49 
In the second place, the Aristotelian position on law leads to concluding 
that the Law does not exist, because the conditions for the objectivity of 
judgement 
by oneself of oneself cannot remain identical to themselves 
throughout history. The particularity of legal systems and legal experiences 
refers back to a necessity of law itself. There is no meaning in trying to 
speak of law in general; it is a necessary consequence of the autopoiesis of 
law. Autopoiesis has no meaning as a theory of law unless it is speaking 
about a particular legal system. It has meaning only as a theory of social 
law. The autopoietic position necessarily leads it to limiting itself. 
I now come to my second question: Does autopoiesis supply an adequate 
theory of social law? Is it capable of being that element of reflection of 
law upon itself that will enable it to answer the question of the objectivity 
of judgement and thus might serve it as a guiding principle? Can autopoiesis 
act as a critique of the legality of social law? 
To the very extent that autopoiesis seeks to develop in the traditional 
form of a theory of law, it will render itself incapable of fulfilling that role. 
The situation of social law in fact prohibits the law of law from taking on 
the form of a theory. The problem that social law poses to the philosophy 
of law is to know how objectivity of judgement is possible that does not 
espouse a form of universality. It has in fact been seen that in the situation 
of social law any universal statement immediately proclaims itself as particu-
lar. An objectivity without universality? This may well seem a theoretical 
impossibility. And autopoiesis, which remains a theory, is constrained, 
faced with this problem, to seek the solution in a sort of exacerbated 
formalism, in a logic that can do nothing but apply itself to devoiding 
itself of all content. For it knows very well that any content would 
immediately invalidate it. On the one hand, autopoiesis finds in the situation 
of social law the conditions for its possibility and validity; but because it 
wants to be theory, it dissolves its particularity instead of laying claim to 
it, in an empty schematism which it sees itself constrained to indefinitely 
repeat. Because it wishes to take on the form of theory, autopoiesis is 
condemned to the indefinite circularity of a formulation that refers back 
to its own statement which itself refers back to its statement, as in the 
famous paradox of Epimenides the Cretan. It is unceasingly condemned to 
affirm A = A, because Α φ A. This may well remind one of certain images 
of the Hegelian consciousness, sustaining themselves indefinitely on the 
giddiness of their own idealism. 
How can one do anything else, one will ask? Must one abandon the idea 
that there is no law in a law of law, the thesis of the self-reflexivity of law? 
Certainly not, since it is constitutive of our legal experience. One should 
merely understand that in the epoch of social law, it cannot take the form 
of theory. Specifically, in the age of social law, the philosophy of law must 
conceive of itself and develop in a critical form, that is, a resolutely 
atheoretical one.
