Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
HUBERT ROTTLEUTHNER 
Berlin 
When concepts, models, approaches, perspectives, paradigms or theories 
of one discipline are taken over in other areas of knowledge and transferred 
to other disciplines, the original source may be termed a leading discipline. 
In the history of science there have been times when some disciplines 
seemed especially favored in their capacity to supply others from their 
stock. In the 19th century, for instance, biology would have to be counted 
among the candidates for the leading discipline, especially after Darwin. 
At least as we may see it today, such concepts as development, evolution, 
struggle, life and organism found broad transdisciplinary distribution, 
originating in biological contexts. 
From the point of view of sociology of knowledge (and therefore also 
history of science) the process of transferring elements of knowledge from 
one objectively delimited area to another is an instructive phenomenon, 
which also involves some methodological subtleties. When are borrowings 
from one discipline made by another? What internal problems are to be over-
come by introducing external elements? What advance in knowledge is hoped 
for, and what subsidiary problems result? How exactly does the transfer mech-
anism function? In what circumstances does it become apparent that there 
has merely been a chasing of pretty pictures, a following of fashion? 
I should like to start by briefly explaining the sense in which I use the terms 
metaphor and scientific metaphorism to characterize this transfer process. I 
shall then explore the use of biological metaphors in legal thought in the 19th 
century, using as examples the terms "organism" and "development". It will 
be necessary to clarify what is at all "biological" about these concepts. 
Finally, I should like to draw some conclusions from the 19th century 
debate for attempts at a revival of biological concepts in more recent legal 
theories. 
Metaphor 
In line with the Greek etymology, by metaphor I shall mean in the 
following a transfer, particularly of concepts. In German the term usually 

98 
Hubert Rottleuthner 
denotes an expression involving an image. This is not the sense I wish to 
use, even though pictorial elements are ubiquitous in transfers from biology, 
for instance, in the well-known comparisons of the state — or the church — 
to the individual person, with head, body and individual organs. Concepts 
of germination, flowering, growth, withering of flowers, trees, etc., or 
individual cells, belong here, as do the well-worn analogies between the 
stages of life (ontogenesis) and changes and cycles of state forms, ages of 
the world, or phylogenesis1. 
Since ancient times the attitude towards metaphors (even in the non-
pictorial sense) seems always to have been ambivalent. On the one hand, 
the unsuitable, inadequate aspect of every transfer is warned against, but 
on the other the fertility and originality of metaphors are praised: they 
allow description of a well-known object in another light, the description 
of something as something else (e. g., state as an organism). Skepticism is 
always appropriate; a number of stages of it can be characterized: 
(1) What field or what discipline does the expression come from? 
(2) What questions was it introduced there to solve; in what theoretical 
context and with what consequences? 
(3) What characteristic meaning and what intension does it have in its area 
of origin? 
(4) To what set of other objects (extension) of other disciplines is the term 
transferred; to solve what problems, and in what theoretical context? 
(5) What original characteristics of meaning remain conserved, which 
change, and which become irrelevant? 
(6) In the new field, the new theoretical context, does the metaphor 
facilitate the solution of major problems, or is it merely a new fa^on 
de 
parier? 
I. Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought in the 19th Century2 
1. Biological Metaphors 
In speaking of biological metaphors, I am presupposing that there is a 
delimited area of origin, the discipline of biology, from which a transfer to

other spheres takes place. The candidates mentioned above — development,

of general concepts which are given different uses in the various disciplines, 
but are those that have acquired their specific meaning in the original area, 
in the leading discipline, biology, and have thus been transferred to other 
areas. What, then, is originally biological about these concepts? 
In the history of the disciplines, the first irritating point is that the term 
"biology" appears for the first time only around 1800 — specifically, in 
C. F. Burdach (1777 — 1847) Propädeutik %um Studium der gesammten 
Heilkunst. 
Ein Leitfaden akademischer 
Vorlesungen. Under biology, he brings together 
morphology, physiology and psychology. The term is then found in 1802, 
in both G. R. Treviranus and J. B. Lamarck. It apparently was taken over 
from the latter by Auguste Comte (1839), as a term for a science that 
studies the relationships between organism and environment (Ballauf, 1971; 
see also Lepenies, 1976: 29). The idea of a "developmental history of 
nature" (Kant 1790) was alien to it until the 19th century. What we bring 
together today under biology was treated in Comte's time and the period 
before 1800 as part of natural history (Historia Naturalis). Its procedure 
was to collect and describe, and it covered roughly zoology, geology, 
meteorology, hydrography and botany3 as well as mineralogy, physical 
geography, paleontology, comparative morphology, and biogeography. Not 
only natural history but also parts of natural philosophy comprised what 
we now know as biology4. At the end of the 18th century, to be sure, a 
growing interdependence of the various disciplines can be noted, but a 
clear demarcation of biology from geology (the paleontological study of 
fossils), study of the earth and countries (biogeography) or medicine 
(anatomy, morphology, embryology) had not yet taken place. One can 
agree with W. Lefevre (1984) that the formation of biology as an independ-
ent discipline became possible only with Darwin's theory of descent — the 
theory that integrated all the subdisciplines. The mere study of orders in 
natural history was fused into a theoretical (which in the 19th century means 
historical) science. Simultaneously with Darwin's theory of evolution, an 
antivitalist, mechanistic physiology was differentiated out (cf. Mendelsohn, 
1974 and see also his earlier survey, 1964). 
This tricky situation, which from the start makes it hard to speak of 
biological metaphors (without running the danger of slipping over into areas 
of medicine, geology, etc.), can be clarified by an examination of the two 
concepts whose use in 19th century legal thought I should like to go into 
in more detail: the concepts of organism and development.

2. Organism 
Comparisons of state, society, church or other collectives with the individ-
ual, his body and his physical and spiritual attributes are age-old5. It would, 
however, be only at the price of blindness to the history of concepts that 
one could treat these as "organic" conceptions. It is only much later that 
the terms "organic" and "organism" appear within the spheres of meaning 
in which we understand these terms today: the oppositions organic/inor-
ganic and organic/mechanical were established only towards the end of the 
18th century. Thus, for instance, van Krieken (1873), in his historical 
description of organic theories of the state, draws a distinction between an 
unconsciously organic period and a consciously organic one (the latter 
since Fichte and Schelling, with the explicit use of the terms; previously 
there was only the metaphor of the body politic). Until the early 18th 
century the old instrumental conception of organ (= organori) still prevailed. 
The body with its organs was understood more as a machine (on models 
of circuits, pumps and levers). The term "organism" probably first appears 
in G. E. Stahl (Theoria medica vera 1708) in a medical context, in place of 
the older terms corpus organicum or organized body (cf. Dohrn-van Rossum, 
1978: 559; Ballauf, 1984: col. 1331). 
By 1800 the use of the term "organism" seems to be established, but not 
only in areas that we would later assign to the fields of biology. The definitions 
given by Kant to natural products as "organized beings" (Kant, 1790: § 65) 
were generally extended beyond the spectrum of plant, animal and human 
being, to refer to spiritual and moral organisms in which the parts are alterna-
tely cause and effect, operate through their relation to the whole, and the 
whole is an end in itself. It is not the reference to the biological sphere, but 
the formal categories of part and whole, cause and effect, means and end that 
allow the ubiquitous use of the concept of organism — from the definition 
of the state as "objective organism of freedom" (Schelling, 1803: 547) up to 
the mechanistic metaphors of, for instance, Saint-Simon, who called society 
"une veritable machine organisee"6. 
As regards use of the metaphor of organism in the 19th century, one 
must be careful to ask how far references to natural objects understood 
biologically are in fact being made7. It cannot be taken as a matter of 
course that the term "organism" always implies a biological metaphor.

3. Development 
The same is true of the concept of development. We link it with biology 
because theories of the development of life, especially Darwin's theory of 
evolution, seem to us to form its core. The German word Entwicklung (or 
Entwickelung) first appears, as a literal translation of evolutio in 1645 in Philip 
von Zesen (cf. Wieland, 1975, and for the sequel, also Zimmermann, 1953; 
Weyand, 1972), with the meaning of the unfolding of something (a knot, 
a role of manuscript, a package). Beginning in the early 18th century the 
term was also applied to mental phenomena: ideas, concepts, thoughts, 
etc., which are developed (more or less in the sense of explicated). It spread 
first of all in poetics, and only then into areas which we would today 
regard as biology and medicine. In the context of embryology, it was used 
both by proponents of preformation theory and by supporters of epigenesis. 
Ontogenesis is portrayed as the development of characteristics already laid 
down in the germ, whether pre-formed or requiring the mediation of a 
formative drive (nisus formativus, 
C. F. Wolf, Theoria generations, 
1759). On 
the assumption of the constancy of species, this could only mean eternal 
recurrence. In the last third of the 18th century the term is also applied to 
the political and social area. Images from the organic world of animals and 
plants, as well as comparisons with the stages of life, were frequently used 
to clarify historical developments. In this way, the two terms that interest 
us were finally combined in the topos of organic development. Here it is again 
of importance for our context that at least by the time of Hegel the concept 
of development had become detached from the (pre-)biological debate. 
My summary is therefore rather sobering: neither organism nor develop-
ment can be regarded as originally biological concepts. This is not only 
because of the lack of integration of the biological disciplines around 1800, 
but also simply because of the fact that both concepts already appeared in 
Meyer, 1969: 134). It is uncertain whether this is also true for Spencer's basic law of 
differentiation and integration: "Spencer spoke of reciprocity (Wechselwirkung) as he 
showed that biology borrowed the concept of division of labor from sociology in 
order to return it in an enriched form. Reciprocity signifies the transfer of a concept 
from one scientific discipline to another and then back into the original discipline." 
(Lepenies, 1976: 172; for what Spencer said cf. Spencer, 1873/1961: 305: "The services 
of the two sciences are, indeed, reciprocal.") — The point, however, would be to 
work out more specifically those characteristics taken over from the biological area 
and any new ones that might have been added. Without that, a critique of the 
metaphor of the organism which asserts that organic systems are of essentially higher 
structural invariance than social systems, with the former integrated through life and 
the latter through meaning, is simplistic. Such a critique ignores the fact that the 
metaphor was also used to encompass the rationality and meaningfulness of life, 
including social life. Cf. Luhmann, 1971 a: 11; 1971 b: 92 ff.; 1971 c: 372; also Canguil-
hem, 1981; Hirst, 1973; Lepenies 1976: 169 ff.; and as long ago as 1905, Gumplowicz: 
393 ff. 

102 
Hubert Rottleuthner 
quite a few other areas too. The use of both terms in legal thought does 
not therefore support the conclusion that a biological metaphor is being 
used. To show this, one would have to find out whether individual authors 
really had a biological area of origin in mind. I regard such proof as 
possible only in the rarest of cases. It seems rather that the terms organism 
and development were "on every lip", ubiquitously used, without thought 
for any "origin". 
However — and despite this sobering fact, this thesis can allow us to 
soar again 
both concepts apparently went through a biologization in 
the second half of the 19th century: on the one hand as a result of Darwin's 
theory of evolution, which in the decades following 1860 dominated 
thinking about development through the principles of divergence and 
variation, selection based on the struggle for existence, and reproductive 
isolation (prevention of backcrossing); on the other, through advances in 
microbiology. At this latter level, the attempt was made to find the 
particular mechanisms of variation and inheritance, which Darwin's theory 
had only asserted at a macro-level. From microbiology arose a view of the 
structure of the organism, in the specific sense of an association of cells.% 
To the extent that the reference is made to these findings and concepts in 
other disciplines, for instance in legal science, which interests us, one may 
very well speak of the use of biological metaphors. 
4. "Organism" and "Organic" in 19th Century Legal Thought 
Thus, if I nevertheless seek below to sketch the use of the concepts of 
organism and development in legal thought throughout the whole 19th 
century, this can only be with the goal of picking out the process of 
biologization of the metaphors. I shall confine myself here to a few 
prominent authors who must again stand as representatives of the major 
trend9. 
"Organic" is a favorite word of the historical school, applied to all 
possible types of phenomena and contexts, including developments. In 
Savigny it is clear that no comparison between the legal and biological 
spheres is meant thereby; instead, language, its formation and its continual 
elaboration, provide the pattern for the emergence and development of 
law. "This organic connection of law with the being and character of the 
people is also preserved through time, and is in that too to be compared

215).

to language" (Savigny, 1814: 77). The law allegedly develops, unfolds itself 
organically "from inner force and necessity, independently of chance and 
individual will"10. 
In the first editions of his work on the Spirit of Roman Law (1852; 2nd 
ed., 1869), Jhering still shares Savigny's critical attitude to the shaping 
power of legislation. Silently transferring Schelling's definition of the state 
as "objective organism of human freedom" to the law (Jhering, 1852: 25), 
he defines the latter further: 
[t]here is no external aggregate of arbitrary definitions ... that owes its origin to the 
thinking of the legislator, but like the language of a people, an internally complete 
product of history, ... Human intention and calculation admittedly has its part in 
forming it; but it finds more than it creates ... The pressure of life has driven law 
and its institutions ahead, and maintains it in persistent external reality. The form 
impressed on it by the mentality of the people and its whole way of life is what every 
legislative thought and will finds before it, and cannot tamper with, without itself 
becoming a disgrace. (Jhering, 1852: 26) 
To be sure, he clearly sees the references to nature in the characterization 
of law as an organism: "in using this picture, we are ascribing to law the 
characteristics of a natural product, that is, unity in diversity, individuality, 
growth from inside outwards, etc." (1852: 26). But then, employing the 
distinction between anatomy (observation of structure) and physiology 
(observation of function), he moves increasingly into a medical metaphor, 
denoting the legal institutions as the "skeleton of the law" (1852: 36), or 
speaking of the heart, blood, arteries or pulse of the legal organism (1852: 
44). 
A closer, extremely laborious reading of Jhering's major works will 
show that his organism metaphors are used inconsistently11. Jhering is in 
fact the top metaphorician in 19th century legal thinking. He takes his 
comparisons from every possible discipline. To be sure, his multi-discipli-
nary metaphors feed on organism analogies too; but at the same time, a 
rich catch is taken from the fields of medicine, chemistry, linguistics, 
mechanics, geometry, aesthetics, architecture, gardening, etc. Against the 
background of this burgeoning metaphorism, his use of the terms organic/ 
organism looks rather arbitrary.

Here he refers to van Krieken's monograph: "what cannot be defined is

Van Krieken's work (1873) has central importance in my strategy of 
argumentation; it is in fact an attempt to take the treatment of the state as 
organism seriously as a scientific, biological metaphor. 
In the original (!) technical [in the sense of terminus technicus, H. R.] application to 
scientific areas, the concept linked with the term organism covered everything that 
was equipped with organs of sense perception, or was otherwise alive — animals and 
plants — which were strictly distinguished from a third 'kingdom', that of the 
inanimate or inorganic bodies (van Krieken, 1873: 125). 
He understands the concept of organism no longer in terms of the formal 
categories of whole and part, but according to the model of the cell (1873: 
124 ff.) with its characteristics of nourishment, movement and multiplica-
tion12. One might also think that this strict biologization of the organic 
metaphor had simultaneously brought about the end of its usefulness (as 
in Jhering). The irony of the development of the organism metaphor, 
however, lies precisely in the fact that — after van Krieken and in explicit 
debate with him — an author appears who wishes to use this metaphor in 
complete seriousness·. Otto Gierke (1841 — 1921; from 1911, Otto von Gierke). 
In an early work (Gierke, 1874), published only one year after the appear-
ance of van Krieken's work, Gierke discussed his argument. I wish to go 
into this argument and Gierke's later elaboration of the organism metaphor 
in rather more detail, because Gierke was aware of the methodological 
traps of a conceptual transfer and carried out the individual steps in it in 
a fairly precise fashion. 
Gierke first of all rejects the restriction to a scientific concept of the 
organism. What was primarily involved was a "general human conception 
of the natural being" (Gierke, 1874: 71). The specifically scientific concept 
was insignificant (1874: 73). In our context, this is already a central point: 
Gierke understands organism not as a concept metaphorized from one 
particular discipline into another, but as a more or less trans-disciplinary 
concept — though one that was initially related — extensionally — to a

"organized beings", through the categories of whole/part, end (in itself)/means, cause/ 
effect (or interaction), and the more substantive definitions of characteristics like 
irritability, sensitivity (A. v. Haller), contractivity, irritability, sensitivity (J. C. Blumen-

self-multiplication, self-shaping, heredity, self-regulation (W. Roux), up to A. Port-
mann's internality and self-representation in appearance, of which metabolism, preser-
vation, regulation, multiplication and development are subordinate parts. On this, cf. 
Ballauf, 1984; Lefevre, 1984: 182.

particular area of reality ("natural living being"). Intensionally, however, 
one was in no way bound to the meaning involved in a particular discipline. 
The concept of organism had in the meantime become a terminus 
technicus 
in legal theory and legal doctrine which still bore the traces of its "pictorial 
origin", though these should not be a source of irritation. After all, this 
was true also of such terms as body, corporation or organization. There 
were superordinate, common characteristics of an organism applicable both 
to the individual human being and to the state. Expressed in terms of 
theory of meaning, partial identity of intension with difference of extension 
is thus being asserted13. It would, however, be inappropriate to draw 
conclusions from known characteristics of the individual human organism 
to unknown characteristics of the state. 
Following this restriction to a number of common characteristics, the 
conclusion is no longer difficult. The organism is to be understood not 
only as a natural product; in speaking of social formations in this way, one 
does so in the sense of a higher spiritual organism. 
In a longish passage which I reproduce below, Gierke sets out the stages, 
starting from a specific constitutional approach, which suggested the use 
of the concept of organism. It becomes clear that the common features of 
meaning are reduced to the model of whole and part. 
Deeper reflection on the nature of the state led to the idea that the state was a 
compound unit, the specific life of which did not coincide with the life of any of its 
parts. This idea provided a new and special perspective on all political relationships 
which had not yet been distinguished from other legal relationships. An invisible 
mode of being that did not coincide with any person nor any set of persons had to 
be conceived of as a real being and introduced into the law as a subject; the individual 
person, relationships with the state, had to be thought of, not as otherwise a whole 
complete in itself, but as part of a whole, particular parts or sub-complexes of the 
whole had to be thought of as vehicles of various activities of life in each of which 
nevertheless the unity of the whole effectively showed itself; the task of public law 
had to be understood, in contrast to private law which mediates between coordinated 
individuals, as that of giving rules for the internal life of a compound unit, for the 
relationships between a whole and its parts. ... Those characteristics of natural beings 
that relate to the existence of a living unit as distinct from the sum of its parts and 
to the activation of this unit through differentiated sub-complexes were picked out 
and applied to the formation and elaboration of the concept of 'organism', abstracted 
from any particular living being. The concept of 'organism' in this sense was then 
applied also to the state, of which all those characteristics were true in the same way 
(Gierke, 1874: 71 f.). 
With the specification of the legal and pragmatic problems, the concept of 
organism suddenly becomes distinct. In Gierke the point is first of all to

grasp the essence, the reality, of human communities and associations (such 
as state, church, municipality, cooperative) (on this cf. especially Gierke, 
1902). Specifically arguing against the "atomistic and mechanistic" construc-
tion of the legal person and that of the state as a legal person, against the 
fiction of these as a mere locus of ascription, Gierke asserted the specific 
reality of associations as social organisms. He distinguishes between the 
individual organism of the individual person, which was the element for 
the private-law view and could not be analyzed into component parts, and 
the compound total or collective organism, the internal structure of which 
was of interest from the viewpoint of "social law". (The concept of social 
law is introduced by Gierke via that of the social organism, as its object 
area). 
Gierke is clear about the problems of a comparison between natural and 
social organisms: 
Properly understood, the comparison says nothing more than that in the social body 
we recognise a living unit of a whole made up of parts, as otherwise observed only 
in natural living beings. We do not forget that the internal structure of a whole whose 
parts are people must have characteristics for which nature offers no examples; that 
here there is a mental connection, produced and shaped, activated and dissolved, 
through psychically motivated action; that here the realm of natural science ends and 
the realm of the science of mind begins. But we regard the social whole, like the 
individual organism, as a living thing, and assign the community, like the individual 
being, to the generic term of living being. The pictorial features accompanying and 
going beyond this arise partly from the need for clarity and partly from linguistic 
compulsion. All advances in thought have come about through the use of images. 
Even our most abstract concepts are born of images. In science too we ought to 
make use of images, as long as we remain aware of that and do not take the image 
for the thing. However, as long as we have available to denote the thing itself only 
terms whose shaping as images is not yet complete, we must endeavour to separate 
the conceptual content from the pictorial admixture (Gierke, 1902: 18 f.). 
Nevertheless, a comparison always remains a mere aid to knowledge. It can clarify, 
but not explain. If it is used to draw conclusions from the correspondence of some 
characteristics to otherwise unperceivable correspondence of the things compared in 
other characteristics, then it becomes a source of error. The organic theory has not 
kept itself free of such excesses. Among them is the anthropomorphic representation 
of the state (1902: 16). 
From this conception of the organism, i. e., above all from the consideration 
of the legal person in its internal structure (internal relationship) and its 
relation to other (legal) persons, quite specific practical consequences are 
alleged to arise (on this cf. Gierke, 1895), in respect to: 
— the systematic building up of the legal order (e. g., the separation of 
private law from "social" law ( = constitutional law), associational law; 
or in general, norms for the internal life of the community); 
— individual legal concepts; 
— decision of particular questions (constitution; membership; foundation 
as a collective act, not as contract; incorporation/disincorporation; 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
107 
organization; organ (representation); competences; procedures; legal 
capacity; accountability of the legal person). 
The example of Gierke shows that the metaphor of organism was losing 
the arbitrariness it had in legal thinking in the first half of the 19th century, 
to the extent that it can be adduced to describe a specifically legal problem 
or phenomenon: primarily the internal structure of legal persons, but also 
collective labor relationships. It also appears, however, that the metaphor 
is no longer enough for the constructive solution of the problems. For 
instance, to decide whether and how the accountability of a legal person 
is to be construed, the metaphor has no longer any part to play. Here other 
preferences seem to enter in, which use the concept of organism only for 
the sake of appearances. (I shall go further into this below). 
5. Legal Development in the 19th Century — Biological Metaphor? 
In this context the point is not to summarize theories of legal development 
in the 19th century — the century of its flowering and ripening, to use 
another couple of metaphors (cf. Stein, 1980; Rottleuthner, 1986 a; 1986 b). 
It is instead much more to the point to follow the traces of biological or 
at least natural models in evolutionary thinking about law in the first half 
of the 19th century and clarify to what extent a "biologizing" influence 
came from Darwin's theory of evolution. 
Despite Hegel's use of many pictorial images to clarify processes of 
development or unfolding (germ, bud, flower, etc.), there can hardly be 
an author who has so decisively denied natural determinacy in human 
history, the history of reason. The historical world is gradually permeated 
by the objective reason of the world spirit; the historical process constitutes 
an "advance in the consciousness of freedom" — and the law is for Hegel 
the outstanding indicator of the stage of freedom reached, which must also 
always be reflected in consciousness. Starting from Hegel, an interesting 
line in theories of legal development can be followed through the 19th 
century, linking the efforts at a universal history of law. The term appears in 
Hegel's pupil Eduard Gans (1824), who sought to systematize written 
material available from high cultures, in his case on the law of inheritance. 
Subsequently, the information base for a theory of the development of law 
shifts more and more into ethnographical reports on preliterate societies, 
the so-called natural peoples14. This certainly brings an element of nature 
into consideration; but at the same time, the traditional expression "natural 
14 This shift has recently been repeated by U. Wesel (1985). Like the earlier critique of 
the historical school of law, with its limitation to Roman and German sources, he 
warns that the current history of law neglects or entirely ignores the "early forms" 
of law in preliterate, non-European societies, which have for some time been dealt 
with in ethnology and cultural anthropology, entirely cut off from legal history. 

108 
Hubert Rottleuthner 
history" shifts in meaning: this set of disciplines, previously merely system-
atizing and descriptive, is dynamicized (cf. Lepenies, 1976). History is no 
longer a narrative, a report, but a developmental process linking up nature 
and society with each other. The now prevailing perception of the "natural 
historical method" clearly adopts a monistic program: to trace the same 
developmental regularities in both nature and society. 
Particular honor in the effort to construct a universal history of law, in 
addition to Bastian (1860), Hildebrand (1894), Leist (1892), Waitz (1859 ff.) 
et al., goes especially to the Bremen judge Albert Hermann Post, who was 
extremely productive (cf. Post, 1867; 1872; 1876; 1878; 1880/81; 1884; 
1891). He aimed at making jurisprudence scientific through application of 
the comparative method and by linking it up with the natural sciences. 
The comparative sciences (for him linguistics, comparative religion and 
ethnology) are seen by him as natural sciences "which discover natural 
laws in the history of peoples" (Post, 1872: 2). The bases of his world view 
nevertheless shift over time from Kant, via Schopenhauer, a mechanistic 
philosophy, and Darwinism to the world soul15. 
The universal history of law finds its culmination in the Hegelian Josef 
Kohler (Kohler, 1915), who, to be sure, seems to return to a type of 
rational monism. 
Even if we can find aspects of nature in the post-Hegelian tradition of 
a universal history of law — stress on natural peoples, scientific monism, 
dynamicization of natural history — an explicit reference to biology is 
nevertheless absent. The explanation for its absence may lie in the fact that 
another discipline of natural history had become the vehicle of the idea of 
development, though today we hardly associate it with it: geology, especially 
in its paleontological and stratigraphical branches. Geology was at any rate 
the discipline that broke the narrow biblical time scale (of around 6000 
years) and first opened a broad time dimension for developmental pro-

Law, which appeared in 1861, i.e., two years after Darwin's Origin, has

If by any means we can determine the early forms of jural conceptions, they will be

the earth are to the geologist. They contain, potentially, all the forms in which law

Our top metaphorician, Jhering, of course also uses this kind of geological 
metaphor, even as late as 1877 in his Der Zweck im Recht·. 
It is the task of science, in relation to the formation of the earth's crust as to the 
history of formation of law, to reconstruct the actual processes (Jhering, 1877: 344; 
cf. his earlier statement, 1865: 4—5). 
The influence of geology on Charles Darwin, communicated especially 
through Charles Lyell (geologist and lawyer) is well known17. 
Let us, however, turn to the impetus given to developmental thinking 
in the 19th century by Darwin's own theory of evolution. In the legal area 
it seems above all to have been the metaphor of struggle which was brushed 
up through this, though it was of course much older. It no doubt inspired 
the title of Jhering's well-known work (Der Kampf urn's Recht, 1872), or 
at least helped it to gain very wide distribution (cf. Wieacker, 1973 a/b; 
Pleister, 1982: 358 ff.). It seems to have penetrated even into the ramifica-
tions of dogmatics. Rainer Schröder (1984: 340 ff.) has shown that through 
the honorific interpretation of the concept of struggle the Supreme Court 
of the Reich declared admissible in economic and commercial conflict 
means otherwise inadmissible in civil law. 
From the point of view of metaphor, it is an interesting fact that the 
discovery of the struggle for existence as the mechanism of natural selection 
came from Darwin's reading of Malthus' An Essay on the Principle 
of 
Population (1798) — at least according to Darwin's report on his Malthus 
experience of October 1838 (Darwin 1876: 100—01). The later return 
transfer of natural selection to the social sphere thus constituted a meta-
metaphor18. 
Terms associated with development theory, like evolution, struggle, 
natural selection, survival of the fittest (Spencer, 1873/1961), and the 
biological, reductive category of race, were used extremely loosely towards 
the end of the 19th century even in legal and constitutional theory, by

to denote all forms of struggle among social units, whether internationally 
or within a state such as the Dual Monarchy. The professor of German 
law in Lausanne, Ludwig Kuhlenbeck (1905), was even clearer with his 
thesis that race and blood were the decisive factors in the development of 
peoples (1905: 115). In his application of "biological principles" to state 
and society, there emerges an ugly mixture of racism, cultural elitism and 
anti-socialism. Against the influx of inferior race elements, which for him 
at the time meant against "polonization", he suggested restricted legal 
status for those not "of the people" (1905: 124-25; 204-05). The extremely

so deeply has it sunk as a leading discipline — to the "conscious study of 
life", and he sees this all within a Christian framework. 
This loose treatment of biological metaphors — like the use of the 
concepts of organism and development in the pre-biological phase of the 
first half of the 19th century — might be explained by the political 
ambitions of the various authors. Among the activist Social Darwinists 
there are authors who do not transfer the theory of descent fatalistically 
back to society as a theory of decadence (the decline of humanity through 
increasing race mixture), but instead advocate social selection and "race 
hygiene", and oppose measures of social policy for the weak as dangerous 
softness. It seems clear to me that such people were seeking to disguise 
their political objectives in reputable biological terms (cf. Mann, 1973; 
Marten, 1983). I should like to conclude these historical observations by 
exploring in greater detail the political significance of my two central 
concepts — organism and development — with their semantic satellites. 
6. The Political Ambivalence of the Concepts of Development and 
Organism 
The concepts of organism and development are linked by their ambivalent 
and therefore broad political applicability. Development can easily be linked 
with dynamism and progress, with directions and goals of development, 
19 If they can at all be clearly delimited, in view of the spreading of the theory of descent 
as a world view by Ernst Haeckel et al. 
20 Vol. 1 had the subtitle: "Also on the question of the reconciliation of the struggles 
of our two great political parties of right and left, led astray by the assumptions of 
the a priori false post-classical legal schools, in private, public, religious and social 
areas". 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
111 
which recall the ideals of perfectibility of the 18th century. But "develop-
ment" was also linked — specifically in the historical school — with the 
aspect of objectivity, a context which was remote from the deliberate, goal-
directed action of men. The forces or regularities of development act 
inevitably. History cannot be made. This is the strategy employed against 
the social contract theories of the 18th century. To be sure — and this 
complicates application to a higher level — neither version can unambigu-
ously be assigned to political camps (right/left, conservative/progressive, 
bourgeois/socialist, etc.). After all, Marx's theory also stresses the "objective 
laws" of historical development, their natural character. The proletariat 
and its vanguard have at most better insight into the necessities (and the 
good fortune that the laws of history are on their side). On the other hand, 
it is precisely the racist-oriented Social Darwinists that regard control of 
the development of population and therefore of society as possible through 
measures of race hygiene. The survival of the fittest, the struggle for 
existence, can be controlled not only through the abolition of social policy 
measures which keep the weak and unfit alive, but also through deliberate 
selection (ranging from psychological tests to immigration quotas to bans 
on marriage and programs of sterilization and ultimately of extermination). 
There is a similar ambivalence about the organism metaphor in political 
contexts (cf. Böckenförde, 1978: 592 ff.; 602 ff.; 610). On the one hand, it 
can be used against interventions by the sovereign state; there is no 
sovereign that is external to the whole. The comprehensive view makes all 
into parts dependent on each other. The whole lives only in its parts, and 
can persist only through their balanced, organic relationship. On the other 
hand, there were always endeavors to designate individual parts as top or 
center as against other political, subordinate parts (how could the sovereign 
monarch otherwise be integrated as an "organ"?), or quite simply (for 
instance in Gierke, 1902) the priority of the whole over the individual 
parts was asserted — whatever "the whole" embodied. 
In the organism there is on the one hand a promise of the self-organiza-
tion of all parts into a living whole21, but at the same time the whole 
represents an organic, natural context, the mystification of a totality free 
of all contradiction. This ambivalence is also shared by the counter-
metaphor of the machine. It awakens the association of feasibility, of the

preserving it, thereby itself preserved; the citizen acts likewise towards the state ... if 
every part of every citizen only preserves himself in the position prescribed for him 
by the whole, then precisely thereby he preserves his part of the whole; and precisely 
by the fact that the whole preserves every part in this position, it returns to itself,

II. A Recent Case: Autopoiesis in Law 
From the viewpoint of political applicability, recent attempts at using 
biological concepts and findings in the legal area can be classified quite 
simply: as an attempt at using scientific metaphors to bolster endeavors at 
breaking down or pushing back government regulation, which are them-
selves based on a critique of the (alleged) increasing legalization and 
shortcomings in legislative control. This may be true both of the borrow-
ings from ethology and of those from sociobiology, which itself uses 
genetic metaphors24, as well as for the variants of autopoiesis that interest 
us here. The motto "from planning to evolution" (Luhmann, 1985 a) shows 
this clearly. Of course, merely to consider the social problematic that set 
them in motion would not do justice to the methodological efforts and 
personal objectives of the authors. I think, though, that one can accept a 
little injustice in order to cull the first fruits of the historical discussion in

Part 1 for the present-day debate. The program "From planning to evolu-

efforts of the young Hegel (cf. fn. 23) and then of Savigny and other 
representatives of the historical school of law, with their critique of the 
old regime and their advocacy of the "inner forces of organic development". 
The use of organic and evolutionary metaphors against the legislator is 
then repeated in the second half of the 19th century, particularly in Herbert 
Spencer's critique of contemporary social legislation. I suspect that similar 
arguments were used in the period after the First World War, too, against 
the new thrust of intervention, but I have been unable to go into further 
detail in this context. 
1. Lessons from History 
What can be derived for our present discussion from these historical 
findings is a fervent request to the autopoiesis thinkers: 
(1) At least to attempt to give dates and places in talking about historical 
developments, "new" forms of social organization and regulation or the 
peculiarities of "present" circumstances (where is the point of development 
at which "the legal system reaches autopoietic closure" (Teubner, infra: 
232)?25 This has the simple advantage that others too can understand and 
evaluate what is in each case being claimed. We are all autopoietic creatures 
for a certain period, but the closure of our intellectual system need not make 
us into autistic creatures, talking at cross purposes with no comprehension. 
(2) Once the claim of newness of the social phenomena has been clarified 
this would also make more plausible the discussion of the newness of the 
theoretical treatment. Otherwise things are made too easy for those who, 
with historial flair, could show that everything was there already anyway. 
What, then, is the gain in knowledge, in the face of presumably new 
problems, from introducing the concept of autopoiesis into legal thinking, 
by comparison, for instance, with that of organism? 
A related lesson from the historical part above, connects the political 
implications of these theories to their substantive aspect. I have learned 
from Otto Gierke that the advantage of metaphorical use of terms lies in 
25 Teubner and Willke (1984) is full of unspecified temporal assertions; if any dating is 
done, it is astonishing: "In the economy, a considerable degree of complexity was 
developed even early in the 19th century" (1984: 11). "With the positivization of law, 
the time horizon (at latest since the world economic crisis and the Keynesian revolu-
tion) ... was shifted into a future that is in principle open and manipulable" (1984: 
10). — One could also hold that the legal system became autopoietic at the moment 
when it separated from other social subsystems, as it did perhaps from religion and

the extent to which they can be applied to the solution of specific problems. 
Gierke at any rate assumed that he had through the concept of organism 
opened up better understanding of the legal person, of the state, of 
associations, etc., with their inner structure. What then are the specific 
problems that the concept of an autopoietic system can help illuminate? I 
can see four areas: 
(1) The interpretation of the legal system as an autopoietic system might 
explicate a concept of law which would enable hitherto disparate elements 
of legal theory to be integrated or seen in another light, thereby leading 
to fruitful questioning. 
(2) Besides this more conceptual field, autopoiesis seems to be adduced 
particularly for explaining the use of law to give direction to social 
change; for explaining the limits of social control by legal measures and 
for specifying the requirements for the knowledge required for control. 
(3) The concept of autopoiesis can be applied in the context of evolutionary 
theory. The old discussion of social and legal change can be reinterpreted. 
(4) Finally, there are efforts — similar to Gierke's — towards a reformula-
tion of fundamental legal concepts such as the state, association, enter-
prise, market, contract, obligation, etc. (cf. Teubner, 1985). In what 
follows I will not pursue this aspect. 
2. The Legal System as An Autopoietic System 
An autopoietic system is defined as a system that produces and reproduces 
its own elements through their interaction (Varela/Maturana/Uribe, 1974: 
187); a system with autopoietic organization is in turn defined as "a unity 
defined by a network for producing components which: 
1) take part recursively in the same network for producing components 
that also produces these components, and; 
2) establish the production network as a unit in the space in which the 
components are located" (Maturana, 1982: 158; also in Zeleny (ed.), 
1981: 21), 
or: 
A unity realized through a closed organization of production processes 
such that: 
(a) the same organization of processes is generated through the interac-
tion of their own products (components); and 
(b) a topological boundary emerges as a result of the same constitutive 
processes (Zeleny, 1981: 6). 
The stress is on organizational closure and on the recursive, self-referen-
tial process of self-reproduction. Mention is also made of "basic circularity" 
(Maturana, 1982). 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
115 
To explain the metaphorical usage in the legal area a few methodological 
explanations need to be inserted: the definitions of an autopoietic system 
are couched very formally, in the sense that the area of origin is no 
longer recognizable (on the origins in the problem of colour perception, 
interpretation of the nervous system and retinal organization, cf. Maturana, 
1982: 88 ff.), and in such a way that the concept could without further ado 
be used transdisciplinarily. The originally constitutive elements of meaning 
referring to the nervous system and the individual cell are rejected. Auto-
poiesis becomes a "universal human notion". There is, here, from the 
methodological point of view, a repetition even among the biological 
inventors of autopoieisis of what had taken place between van Krieken 
and Gierke. While van Krieken had referred to the specifically biological 
meaning of "organism", Gierke deliberately detached the concept from this 
context (though still relating it to "natural beings", while our biologists 
of autopoiesis do not seem to be entirely agreed whether they should 
confine themselves to living systems). 
However, the fact that the concept of autopoiesis was already formalized 
by its inventors does not by itself make it possible to see in it a continuation 
of the old organic analogy. The early divesting of its biological connotations 
may even have contributed to its extension26. The painful drawback is only 
that in new areas of application the meaning of the individual components 
of the concept must be re-established — without, for instance, establishing 
links to the cell model. Scientific specialization has gone so far that the 
wealth of knowledge on the structure and function of a cell can no longer 
meaningfully be transferred into other areas of knowledge (before the 
explosion of microbiology van Krieken was still able to speak simply of 
nutrition, movement and multiplication; see p. 104 above). Metaphors can 
no longer be formed except at an entirely abstract level, with the conse-
quence that every transfer into another discipline requires entirely new 
meanings to be established. 
It is then proper to ask what advantage is supposed to distinguish 
the metaphor of autopoiesis in comparison with (non-biological) formal 
concepts of organism which work with the relationship of whole and part 
(and not with those of cell theory of around 1850). Luhmann (1984: 27) 
asserts that the paradigm of whole and part would have to accommodate 
inexplicable properties, notably properties of a hierarchical summit27.

auto?) After all, such expressions as system and life world trip much more readily off

"Only then and thereby can such a product (i. e., an organized and self-

product of nature is "closed" insofar as it contains "in itself and its potential 
a relationship to ends." (Kant, 1790: § 65) 
Difficulties might perhaps arise for autopoiesis supporters from the 
translations of the causal terms (cause, effect, causality). Since on all the 
evidence they do not give the concept of causality much value, especially 
that of "linear causality", it should be stressed that Kant is speaking of 
mutual causation and of an "intrinsic causality". 
The distinction between linear causality and circular/recursive causality 
is given particular emphasis by the autopoieticists, who readily appeal to 
von Foerster (1984). He introduces the concept of causality in the context 
of the discussion of "trivial machines", characterized by a deterministic 
connection between input and output (where input apparently is understood 
as a sufficient condition). He then briefly explains the theory of recursive 
functions, without reintroducing the concept of causality in that connection. 
The mark of a recursive function is that the same operation is continually 
utilized in a given situation. Today one can perform this version of 
Nietzsche's "eternal recurrence", for example, by repeatedly pressing the 
square root button on a pocket calculator. This image of monotonous 
stupidity probably is the appropriate metaphor for historicity as it is 
understood by autopoiesis.29 
My comparison above shows that the central terms cannot be entirely 
uninterpretable signs: otherwise such a "translation" would not be possible. 
The interesting characteristics are, however, so diluted that in every applica-
tion, whether in the biological or legal area, a specification must first take 
place. What happens, then, when a theoretician climbs down from the thin 
air of autopoiesis to the soil of law? It sounds more or less like this. 
The legal system consists, as do its elements, of legal acts (or legal 
communications). The "basic circularity" of the legal system too, the 
circular process of self-referential elements, can be seen in the recursive 
production of legal acts — by legal acts. "No legally relevant event can 
derive its normativity from the environment of the system. In this respect, 
it remains dependent on the self-generating connection of legal elements 
and on the limits of this connection" (Luhmann, supra: 20). The self-
referential closure of the legal system is produced in a circular relationship 
goal than that which used to exist generally in Germany: a great variety and particular-
ity in the parts, but a common legal basis for the whole, which continuously reminded 
every German tribe of its indissoluble unity." (Savigny 1814: 42 —43).

between legal decisions and normative rules (Luhmann, supra: 21—22; 
Teubner, 1984 a: 295 — 96). This basic circularity of law is held to be the 
foundation of legal autonomy, of law as an autopoietic system. 
This suggests some questions inspired by legal theory: Can legal acts be 
the only basic elements of a legal system? If there is a basic circularity 
between legal decisions and normative rules, it would seem that the 
elements of a legal system must be both legal acts and legal rules. For legal 
rules are in themselves not legal acts. Only their adoption, formulation, 
application, violation, implementation, etc. are legal acts. 
The definition of a legal act as any communication that alters the legal 
situation is misleading.30 Luhmann defines the "elementary unit" of a legal 
system as that which alters the legal situation, but elsewhere as that which 
gives rise to legal consequences (Luhmann, supra: 16 ff.). Kelsen already 
had said with respect to this: 
The Pure Theory of Law defines the concept of the legal act as follows: A legal act 
is an act by means of which a legal norm is issued (figuratively speaking, "created") 
or applied. Moreover, the Pure Theory claims that an act is a law-creating or law-
applying act only if it corresponds to the norms that govern the creation and 
application of the law within the legal system, that is, only if the act in question is 
based on the legal system. That the law governs its own creation and application is 
a characteristic of the normative order as a dynamic system (Kelsen, 1952: 200). 
In saying this, Kelsen gives a different formulation to that which Luhmann 
and Teubner denominate as the "self-referential closure of the legal system." 
Legal norms can only come into valid existence on the ground of other 
valid legal norms. There is no creatio ex nihilo. There also cannot be a naked 
transfer of moral conceptions or political goals into legal norms. Rather, 
there are procedural and jurisdictional legal norms that regulate the coming 
into existence of valid legal norms. 
Of course, this method of closed validation cannot be used by Kelsen — 
nor by the autopoieticists — to describe the origin of a "primal constitu-
tion". As is well known, in order to solve this problem and to reach an 
end in the hierarchy of norms, Kelsen hypothetically introduced a basic 
norm, which says that adopted, effective norms should be followed (Kelsen, 
1960: 219). The basic norm, alleged to be the ultimate ground of validity, lays 
down adoption and effectiveness as conditions of validity — as (hypothetical) 
preconditions for the bindingness of the (adopted and effective) norms. 
Luhmann asserts that by breaking off the justification of validity Kelsen 
was seeking to avoid circularity; but that validity is circular (Luhmann, 
1985 a: 115): "Decisions are legally valid only on the basis of normative 
rules because normative rules are valid only when implemented by deci-
30 Teubner (infra: *15*); here acts are also described as "self-descriptions of communica-
tions". There may well be an act of describing, but acts are not (self-) descriptions. 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
119 
sions."31 But this is true only, Kelsen might reply, if we presuppose a 
norm that declares efficient implementation to be a condition of validity. 
(Admittedly, this does not solve the well-known problem of whether a 
legal norm is valid after it has been duly enacted but before its first 
application.) 
Hart's distinction between primary and secondary rules is perhaps more 
suitable for describing the self-organization of law. According to Hart, a 
complete legal system exists only if (when?) there are not only primary 
rules which — as duty-imposing rules — are indistinguishable from moral 
norms, but also further rules that lay down what is to be regarded as a 
valid legal norm, how legal changes are validly to be brought about and 
who is competent in what procedure to apply the valid legal norms, and 
with what powers. 
What gain in knowledge does autopoietic terminology bring by contrast? 
I think that instead a vague concept of production or constitution (obfus-
cated as in Marx's exegesis of the early '70s) is used to cover up situations 
which have in the meantime been somewhat illuminated in legal theoretical 
debate. What, for instance, is to be understood by "produce" in a statement 
such as: "positivity of law means that exclusively the internal reference 
context constantly produces new norms" (Teubner and Willke, 1984: 20)? 
Perhaps another aspect ought to be understood by the self-constitution 
of the legal system. In legal theory some norms are assigned a constitutive 
role (as distinct from a regulatory one). Particular social circumstances are 
brought into being only through the application and observance of legal 
norms. A legal person, a board of directors, the President of the United 
States, are formations that could arise only on the basis of norms. They 
are not natural formations with whose existence legal consequences might 
be bound up, which trigger off legal consequences; instead they exist — 
as "institutional facts" — only if legally specified conditions are met. 
Legal norms may be constitutive in a further sense: Not only for acts, 
circumstances, position etc., but for particular descriptions 
of action. The 
description of an action as a particular act (including legal act), for instance, 
the fact that the killing of another can be described as murder, is something 
of which legal norms are also constitutive. The legal norm does not 
constitute or produce the act itself (John Smith stays dead), but without 
it the specifically legal nature of the description of the act would not be 
possible. 
The fact that a particular act becomes legally relevant in the environment 
of the legal system is itself a decision within the legal system: namely to 
31 In a comparable German version it is as follows: "Gesetze gelten als Normen nur, 
weil vorgesehen ist (?), daß sie in Entscheidungen angewandt werden, so wie diese 
Entscheidungen Situationen nur normieren können, weil dies in Gesetzen vorgesehen 
ist." (Luhmann, 1983: 140). 

120 
Hubert Rottleuthner 
assimilate the description of the act to the statutory definition in a norm. 
By contrast with normative closure, Luhmann sees in this an aspect of 
cognitive openness of the legal system: through programming it is making 
itself dependent on facts in the environment (Luhmann, supra: 20). In 
Kelsen's terminology, one might speak here of a "cognitively open" condi-
tion of validity, as distinct from a (normative) ground of validity. 
Why should all these various aspects be denoted by the term "self-
production of the legal system"? 
According to Luhmann (e.g., supra: 15 — 16, 25 — 26) the fundamental 
distinction (coding) of a legal system is the dichotomy between legal and 
illegal (Recht/Unrecht). The closure and unity of the legal system is 
constituted by it. But if a system must be provided with a yes-no code, 
why shouldn't the legal system be based on the distinction between legal 
and non-legal, while "wrong" would be considered part of the "legal"? 
The question about the unity (closure) of the legal system is connected to 
the question of the ultimate unit (element) of the legal system, since there 
are not only acts of norm-observance and of norm-application, whose 
negation consists in violating a legal norm ("wrong"), but also acts which 
do not give rise to any legal consequence — for one thing, there are acts 
that are legally irrelevant, but there are others, of particular interest, that 
signify an unsuccessful effort to create "institutional facts". The incorrect 
official form has been filled out, a person who is under age has signed the 
contract, at the ceremony the "yes" refuses to be uttered. Such failures of 
constitutive legal acts are legally relevant but manifest no wrong. Thus, 
several distinctions can be offered: right — wrong, legally relevant — 
legally irrelevant, successful legal acts (behavior which gives rise to legal 
consequences) — unsuccessful legal acts. Which distinction is basic, which 
derivative? Or do they all stand in a basic-circular relationship? 
3. Control Problems of An Autopoietic Legal System 
If the legal system, the political system and the various other social systems 
(economy, family, education etc.) all constitute autopoietic systems for 
themselves, how can they then be brought into relationship with each other? 
Specifically, as regards the traditional themes of political programming of 
legal processes for directing, controlling or influencing social processes: 
— How is this procedure described in autopoietic frames of reference? 
— How is the efficiency of the legal system explained? 
— How is its inefficiency explained? 
— What suggestions are made to explain the regulatory capacities of the 
legal system (if deregulatory abstention is not preferred from the outset, 
which is not however the case for all autopoieticists)? 
The closure of an autopoietic system is not to be understood in the 
sense of autistic encapsulation. Different autopoietic systems can come into 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
121 
relationship with each other — but not "directly" or "immediately". The 
law cannot control social processes "directly", on the model of "linear 
causality" (Teubner, 1984 a: 298; 1984 b: 130), nor do such social systems 
react "directly" to legal programs. Instead, legal norms and decisions are 
supposed to be adopted in reference to a model of social reality as internal-
ized in the legal system: an internal representation (Teubner, 1984 a: 297). 
The autopoietic systems addressed might well be affected by and amendable 
by regulation, "but only within the limits of their reproductive organiza-
tion. Any external regulatory influence leading to a new internal introduc-
tion of the elements but not maintaining this self-reproducing organization 
is either irrelevant to the system or leads to its destabilization, going as far 
as the disintegration of the regulated system" (Teubner, 1984 b: 127) or to 
the social or political overloading of the legal system (to make the "regula-
tory trilemma" complete). The talk is then no longer of direct influence, 
control, regulation, etc.; but such terms are used as the "initiation" of 
mutual self-regulatory processes (Teubner, 1984 b: 128), modulation, im-
pingement, etc. 
The question is what has been gained by comparison with traditional 
effectiveness and implementation research, which after all also stresses the 
independence of the regulated area, under the theme of restrictive condi-
tions or of specific implementation structure? I at any rate see no difficulty 
in reformulating the "regulatory trilemma" without reference to autopoiesis 
and even making the analysis more sophisticated. 
Most of the theoretical interest about control by the autopoiesis support-
ers undoubtedly concerns shortcomings 
of control; as noted above, this 
interest feeds on the critique of the tension between an insufficiency of 
regulation and regulatory inefficiency. The stress is on the various condi-
tions for the self-organization of the various systems (political system, legal 
system, other social systems). The fact that these specific conditions are 
not adequately met explains the control shortcomings. 
I see the advantage of an autopoietic approach in its indication that the 
various areas differ through their differing structure and organization, 
which have to be suitably affected by a regulation. I have doubts, however, 
whether the autopoiesis concepts can say anything more detailed about the 
specific limits of controllability, about the specific structure and organiza-
tion of the various autopoietic systems — apart from the platitude that the 
"limits of their particular self-regulation" (Teubner, 1984 b: 128) are to be 
observed. "A regulation is successful only to the extent that it maintains 
the self-producing internal interaction of the elements in the regulating 
systems of law and politics and is at the same time compatible with self-
producing internal interactions in the regulated social system" (Teubner, 
1984 b: 128). This does not supply any criterion or define any boundary, 
but merely brings together general characteristics supposed to be relevant 
in decisions, explanations and prognoses. What is to be understood by 

122 
Hubert Rottleuthner 
these specifically in a case of application can no longer be said in the 
context of the autopoiesis concept. We are of course stimulated to such 
questions as: what is the difference in the type of "self-producing internal 
interaction" in the education system on the one hand and in the economic 
system on the other? But what do we have to know in order to be able 
to answer such a question? What is achieved if the systems-theoretical 
conceptualization is supplemented with the term "self-producing"? 
Things are similar with Gierke: the concept of organism seemed to him 
to be capable of defining the essence of associations and of the legal person. 
But it no longer answers such specific questions as standing to bring suit 
in court or the criminal accountability of a legal person. 
4. The Evolution of the Autopoietic Legal System 
However, things are not (yet) so specific with "autopoiesis". The classical 
themes of theoretical legal sociology are awaiting: besides the concept of 
law and the question of social change through law, there remains the 
question of the social conditions of legal change, of development of law. 
Just as in the autopoietic view from the legal system towards the system 
to be regulated one cannot speak of causal effect, direct influence, or 
immediate control and determination, so conversely one cannot speak of 
any direct dependency of legal change on social change or reflection of the 
economic base in the legal superstructure, etc. Attention is instead shifted 
towards the mechanisms of change internal to the law. "External mechan-
isms can only have a "modulating" effect on legal developments while the 
evolutionary primacy passes over to internal structural determination" 
(Teubner, infra: 232). 
But what has been gained there by comparison with theories that stress 
the "relative autonomy" of law and of legal development and have worked 
out the "mediations" in detail? I fear rather that the vague concept of 
production (see p. 232 above) might encourage notions of a law that begets 
law. Against this, recourse might be had to the critique already directed 
against the historical school of law with its model of development of inner 
forces in legal development. (At least it still had the spirit of the people 
as a substrate category.) And what is one to think of the specific emergency 
and amendment of legal norms, i. e., legislation, being described as follows: 
On the level of concrete interactions, particularly in the political system, legal norms 
can adequately be explained as the result of processes of power and decision-making 
by various interests and interest groups. Concerning these findings, the question arises 
as to whether and how far these legal norms represent functional solutions to social 
problems. At the same time, important interactions between these modes of explanation 
can be assumed. In particular, an analysis should be made of how far social structures 
and functions affect and delimit political strategies (Teubner, infra: 227 — 228). 

Biological Metaphors in Legal Thought 
123 
This surely cannot be even the penultimate word of an autopoietic theory 
of legislation.32 
In other respects, as far as evolutionary mechanisms are concerned, 
recourse is had to the old biological metaphor of variation, selection and 
stabilization (retention) (mostly following Luhmann, 1972; cf. Teubner and 
Willke, 1984: 2 4 - 2 5 ; Teubner, infra: 228). The autopoietic turn then 
consists of the internalization of these mechanisms (also called evolutionary 
functions).33 Again the advantage of the autopoietic perspective lies in the 
fact that its vanishing point is located in the internal processes of the legal 
system, where everything is possible in the law. But how this internal 
functioning is to be analyzed cannot be discussed in any more detail merely 
by using its formal categories. For further specification, interestingly, those 
three concepts are transported from other, Darwinian dimensions of biology 
as developmental mechanisms, and then of course require their specific 
legal interpretation (though the link to legal historical research is still very 
remote). 
The concept of an autopoietic system, precisely because of its formal 
character, has the advantage of being able to bring many very different 
aspects together. However, its level of abstraction dodges the niveau of 
legal sociological and legal theoretical research in particular fields. From 
its broad perspective they are all squashed up together. But the concept 
will be helpful to the extent that it brings relationships to light — once it 
has gone beyond the labor required to clarify the self-produced conceptual 
difficulties of the theory of self-production.

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal 
System 
HANS-GEORG DEGGAU 
Hannover 
Introduction 
If both society and its communicative subsystems are asserted to be auto-
poietic, two questions arise. What appearance does the autopoietic identity 
of the systems have, and how are their connections and their mutual 
relatedness to be defined? Since all social systems are supposed to consist 
of nothing other than communications, the autopoietic identity and the 
system connections must be derived from their communicative forms. If 
they are placed side by side as autonomous (in the sense of isolated) 
systems, then their connections can be arrived at only externally and ex 
post facto. 
Instead, I shall attempt in the first part to show how the autopoietic 
system-identity becomes accessible to definition only as something already 
defined — that is, one cannot begin in an indefinite manner from identity 
and difference — and what the initial communicative situation is. I shall 
set this out in more detail, in order on the basis of it to be able in the 
second part to look at whether and how the autopoietic final element is 
constituted as communication; for the elements of the communicative 
process must themselves produce the communicative "surplus" which 
specifies them as suitable for autopoietic communication. Some of these 
communicative elements will be looked at from that viewpoint. From this 
it will appear that the unity sought for cannot be found in the leading 
difference, the thematics or the possibilities of linkage, although these are 
conditions of autopoiesis. The latter is constituted only in the processes of 
self-description and in structures, through definite types of communicative 
linkage and system-specific, communicatively-generated contents. For the 
legal system this is conditionalized legal normativity. 
The relationship between the legal system and other communicative 
systems can thereby likewise be defined more closely, without any forcing: 
the legal system has possibilities of intervention because it is specialized in 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
129 
a structure that all the other systems also show. No system can exist without 
structures of expectation — and this is precisely what is congruently 
generalized by the legal system. The starting point for the analysis of 
system relationships is, then, to be sought in their communicative relations 
and differences. 
I. Aspects of the General Communication System as an Auto-
poietic System 
1. Identity and Basic Self-reference 
Autopoiesis refers to systems.1 Autopoietic systems are systems which 
reproduce themselves autopoietically. The "autopoietic process, which itself 
produces what makes it possible" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 223) defines the system 
as a unitary one. Its unity is neither the unity of the system, to be denoted 
through characteristics, nor that of its structures or elements. What makes 
its unity cannot be adequately understood ontologically in the sense of 
something given, or only as an academic construct, (Luhmann, 1984 a: 240; 
differently, Maturana, 1982: 264 — 65). It is neither an objective nor a 
subjective unity in the traditional sense (Luhmann, 1984 a: 240). Such 
correlations do not hold water in defining the unity of the system. Instead, 
the unity is defined by autopoiesis; that is, purely systemically, through the 
self-reference and circularity producible only by the system. These exist 
only in systemic processing itself and are describable only through it: they 
escape definition from outside. What functions as a unity, what is an 
element, what makes self-reference, follows only from the processing of 
the system itself. It is only from the relating of elements among themselves 
by the system that they acquire system character and the system acquires 
its unity. That means at the same time its closure, i.e. its autonomy, but 
not in the sense of autarchy or being in moral terms a law unto itself, but 
only as self-definition of its processing identity. 
The identity is, then, at this general level, determined exclusively by the 
system itself. This presupposes that the system exists already as a system, 
that it can determine itself; for were it undetermined, it could not determine 
itself as something more determined.2 This is the reason why recourse has 
1 The concept of system is applied below only to social systems.

is not definitio,

identity of the system cannot be seen as self-aware positing of the system by itself, 
on Fichte's model. The identity-producing reproduction of the system is not an act 
of consciousness or will. If we speak of a system as active, we usually presuppose 
consciousness, will, intention, etc. The elements of subject, consciousness and justifica-
