then to be had to considerations of evolutionary theory: for the description 
and explanation of the differentiated form of a system as system. 
The concept of differentiation refers to the process of continual re-
formation of differences. But differentiation as the formation of difference 
implies identity. All definition of identity, whether as observation or as 
process or otherwise, is possible only through difference. 
Both identity and difference must be referred to each other. Without 
such a linkage, no information can be derived either from the identity or 
from the difference. Difference is only conceivable through negation. 
Negation is only possible as negation of something. Difference and negation 
are relational concepts. Since identity does not exist without difference, 
identity itself must also be relational. 
This relation can be found only in relation to something.3 It is only as 
a relation of difference that it can supply information and be communicated. 
But the difference itself is not tangible or substantial. It is tied to the 
process. In order for the process to advance in time it cannot simply stop 
at the difference. As an aspect of the process which is itself to be understood 
as a processing of difference, the difference must be further processed. It 
is only through process that it constitutes meaning and provides the 
possibility of communications of linkage. This processing of difference 
presupposes identity and is constitutive of it. 
Differences do not exist in themselves. They are on the one hand possible 
only in relation to other differences and identities; on the other, they are 
due to the system, or observer, concerned. This in turn finds one of its 
conditions in the difference, without which it cannot be constituted. 
The question thus arises how the relationship between identity and 
difference can be defined concretely, that is, how does their relation appear, 
or more precisely, how does their difference appear? This relation between 
identity and difference is structured as a self-referential unity. 
The problem of mediation of identity and difference cannot be solved 
by putting pure identity at the beginning in order then to deduce all 
tion implied thereby (motives inter alia) are however not yet introduced at all initially. 
For the thesis is, even at the cost of an epistemological paradox, precisely to assert 
the autopoiesis of the system as a real process, independent of observation, which has 
no need of the aspects mentioned. The linguistic subjectivization of the system is to 
be understood as its material de-subjectivization. The autopoietic process is not simply 
a result of external observation, but should, according to Luhmann, be independent 
of this. 
3 If abstraction is made from the reference to something, then nothing is left but the 
identity and difference of the concepts of identity and difference, which are then, 
however, no longer distinguishable: absolute identity — absolute difference; for then 
identity must be identical with itself, because there is no longer any other possibility 
of identification. It must then, however, at the same time be identical with pure 
difference, which, as identical difference, no longer distinguishes itself from anything 
else. 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
131 
difference from it. Identity and difference must already be thought of as 
in reference to something. This is why Luhmann seeks to conceive of 
identity, and temporalize it from the outset as a differentiated unity, and 
thus already to incorporate the aspect of process in its constitution. He 
even asserts "the difference between identity and difference" as a "new 
guiding difference" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 26). This fundamental difference is 
understood self-referentially, whereby "unity can arise only through a 
relating operation" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 58). 
This "relating operation" is the basic operation of self-reference, which 
is conceivable only relationally. For the system elements, this is the "basal 
self-reference" (Luhmann, 1982: 369; 1984a: 600 f.).4 As pure self-reference 
it would lead no further, since therein the element refers to nothing else 
than itself. Instead, the element must as itself refer to something else, which 
it is not itself, but starting from which it can be grasped as itself. For this 
reason, "the unity of the element must be constituted as unity of identity and 
difference" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 370). 
The element is at the same time one for another. It incorporates this 
relation into itself. Its possibility is to be found in the reference structure, 
i. e., its meaningfulness. In reference, which is extremely selective, A cannot 
refer to A, but must refer to a non-A which itself in turn refers to A. 
The reference horizon is, as non-^4, therefore not the totality of all possible 
possibilities, but is system-specifically bound. A refers, not to everything 
else, but only to a possibility space set by the system itself, a selection set. 
The reference from A to non-^4 could otherwise not acquire the necessary 
self-referentiality, because a reference from non-^4 to A would be conceiv-
able only as infinite, opening up infinite selection spaces and no longer 
able to cope with linkage possibilities. 
The conditions of the autopoietic reproduction of systems have thereby 
been characterized in general terms; for communications which produce 
communications and are produced by them must, as elements of the 
communication process, show basic self-reference. Without this, which 
contains the continuation of the process in embryo, no new elements of 
the same type can proceed from those. It is only from this unity of the 
elements that the unity of the system proceeds — as on the other hand it 
is only this that engenders the unitariness of the elements. It is only this 
that testifies to the autopoiesis of the system and not only of the elements. I 
shall now clarify these general considerations further for the communication 
system of the whole of society. 
4 Here Luhmann distinguishes self-reference in relation to the elements as basic self-
reference — element/relation; in relation to the processes of the system as reflexivity — 
before/after; and in relation to the system itself as reflection — system/environment.

2. Society as Communicative System 
For Luhmann, society is a system of communications, not of actions 
(Luhmann, 1984 a: 60 f.). Action is constituted only through and in the 
communication process (Luhmann, 1984 a: 191). The element of the com-
munication process is the individual communication. This consists in the 
interplay of information, communication and understanding, so that the 
communication must "be seen as a three-part selection process" (Luhmann, 
1984 a: 194). For information, a code of behavior is chosen in which 
information is communicated. Through understanding, a unity of the 
communication process then arises: Β informs A through a communication; 
A understands this and can also distinguish between the two aspects. 
It follows from this "that communication is possible only as a 
self-referential 
process" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 194). For communication can only continue if 
it refers to other communication. In this continuation, it reproduces itself 
precisely through the fact of further communication. This "further" is 
possible exclusively as a reference to communication. From communication, 
it is only communication that can arise, nothing else. The impulses to 
communication, their contents, may be arbitrary. But they are communi-
cable only in the form of the tripartite selection that the communications 
system makes available. Therein lies its closure, if you will: the closure of 
its identical form. 
Communication as "processing of selection" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 194) 
always contains a meaning-reference. The dimension of meaning lies in the 
fact that all three aspects of communication are selective and each refer to 
something else. Meaning as "form of a surplus of references to further 
possibilities" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 93) compels meaningful selection. Commu-
nication is highly selective, and refers to a multiple reference horizon. The 
reference character is inherent in every communicative act. Through its 
own selections, it anticipates those of the continuation of communication. 
It thus offers possibilities of linkage. 
The possibilities of linkage are conditions for the possibility of continu-
ing communication. It is only as long as they are guaranteed that communi-
cation can go further. "The unity of the individual communication is, 
considered dynamically, nothing more than the capacity for linkage" 
(Luhmann, 1984 a: 204). It is only its unity that makes the formation of 
further differences possible.5 The need, just shown, for severe restriction 
of the linkage possibilities formed as self-reference is, as extremely high 
condensation of meaning, indispensable in order to make linkages transpar-
ent and operational, i.e., practicable (cf. Luhmann, 1984a: 140). 
5 The theory of autopoietic systems can therefore be understood in this respect as a 
working out of the conditions of possibility of autopoietic reproduction, which can 
be reduced to "possibilities of linkage". Cf. Luhmann (1984 a: 590). 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
133 
One of the most important mechanisms of such reduction of social 
complexity lies in communicative self-observation and self-description, 
through which alone the concept of action becomes possible. Through it, 
the communicative system controls itself. The self-description is preceded 
by self-observation in which the system applied a difference to itself. 
Observation is understood by Luhmann, following Spencer Brown, as 
distinction and denotation (Luhmann, 1984 a: 230). If the difference be-
tween system and environment is brought about by the system itself, then 
a distinction is present. Observation then consists in the fact that "within 
this distinction ... the system is denoted as originator of the communica-
tion" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 230); and by the system itself. This self-observation 
then becomes "self-description, when it produces semantic artefacts to 
which further communications can refer and with which the unity of the 
system is denoted" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 618). 
For communication, therefore, the individuated set of linkage possibili-
ties is defined not only generally through self-reference, but also through 
the selection of such self-referential self-descriptions. It is therefore true of 
social systems that they "can carry out their self-reproduction only with 
the help of self-observations and self-descriptions" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 230). 
For self-description is an abbreviated expression of attributed communica-
tion. Communication cannot in every one of its acts repeat the whole 
communication itself — though this too would be an (extreme) form of 
self-reference. For its continuation it requires such abbreviations that only 
itself can produce, which it attributes to the determination of linkages. 
Since at the same time every communication represents a highly selected 
selection, it becomes still further sharpened through the attribution. 
It is only this that constitutes action. This can be seen daily, for instance 
in the assignment of guilt, which can always be assigned differently. 
Through it, a particular process is constituted communicatively, is con-
structed and selected from among other possible attributions. Speaking 
generally, this makes available and guarantees possibilities of linkage, while 
at the same time "any amount of complexity is restricted through self-
simplification, which structures" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 234). Such self-simplifi-
cations, defined in the general communications system as actions, can be 
found in all communications systems. They result from self-observations, 
from communications about communications; they are fixed shortenings 
of sets of linking actions and attributions. It is through this self-reference 
too that the element identifies itself as itself and not itself. And it is only 
this that provides the possibility of a guarantee of continuation of the 
communicative process. The concomitant self-reference is a general expres-
sion of this, in so far as this concomitant relation means, or guarantees, 
the unity of the system and the elements, making "self-observation into a 
necessary component of autopoietic reproduction" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 64). 

134 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
But this too only points to the fact that the autopoietic element of the 
communication system is the individual communicative act. As such, it is 
initially not distinct from other communicative acts. It is possible only on 
the basis of communication, and makes further communication possible. 
That is its meaning. We shall therefore proceed to investigate whether, or 
how far, the communicative acts of the subsystems specify autopoietic 
closure or if their newly constituted unity is to be sought in something 
else. 
II. The Communicative Subsystems 
1. The Need for Their Differentiation 
Society is the total communicative system, with which no further communi-
cation is possible, for this would itself form part of society. The social 
subsystems that have differentiated are also meaningfully structured com-
munication systems, distinguished for an observer also by their function. 
Nevertheless, it cannot be asserted that their autopoiesis is oriented deliber-
ately towards their function. Instead, this takes place through the difference, 
constituted by the system itself, of its unity and difference: "functional 
orientation is certainly not a requirement for self-referential reproduction" 
(Luhmann, 1984 a: 406). 
In order for autopoietic subsystems to be distinguished from other 
subsystems and thereby also from the society as a whole, they must develop 
a system-specific autopoiesis which as communicative autopoiesis coincides 
with that of the whole of society, but which differentiates itself in its 
specific formation of unity. For the "mere participation in the autopoiesis 
of society" is not enough to make the partial systems into autopoietic 
systems proper (Luhmann, supra: 19). 
For autopoiesis, then, differences must be formed, which underlie the 
communications of the individual systems as intrinsic to the system. They 
must be different from communicative acts of society as a whole. They 
therefore require additional qualities through which they are specified and 
distinguished but also through which the subsystem is closed as identical 
and is reproduced. These special communicative acts should be neither 
produced nor producible by other systems. Because of the communicative 
character of all social systems, each communicative act must be qualified 
as such. Other characteristics, ontic or otherwise, cannot play any part 
here. This is because the subsystems "consist only of communications" 
(Luhmann, 1984 b: 311). Their specific unity-forming element can therefore 
likewise only be of a communicative nature. Luhmann's thesis that they 
"do not close themselves as communicative, do not distinguish themselves 
as communication systems from their environment" (Luhmann, 1984 b: 
311) therefore seems problematic. To be sure, it is true that the subsystems 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
135 
need "an intrinsic principle of constitution of unity, applying only to them, 
for which there is no correspondence in their environment" (Luhmann, 
1984 b: 311). But it must then be clarified in detail how this special unity 
is related to the communication process of the system and how the system 
is in a position to produce entirely new unities, not communicatively 
distinguished, which provide the basis for autopoiesis. The positing and 
the possibility of such emergent unities — e. g. payment for the economic 
system (Luhmann, 1984 b) — does not replace the analysis of these connec-
tions. 
I shall therefore seek out the starting point for locating the specification 
which leads to the formation of the autopoietic system element and which 
can, in my view, be only of a communicative nature. On the basis of some 
characteristics of communicative autopoiesis (guiding difference, thematics, 
self-description, possibility of linkage, structure), I shall examine whether 
a kind of communicative "surplus" can be found in them, out of which 
the elements of unity can be formed. If this is not the case, it must be 
made clear under what conditions the elements sought for can otherwise 
emerge. 
2. Conditions of Differences of the Subsystems and Their Autopoiesis 
Social evolutionary theory gives no adequate answer to the question, 
because it does not explain the logical and systematic conditions of the 
identity of a system. The evolutionary aspect will therefore not be explored 
here; instead I shall seek to show how on the basis of a communicative 
total system, communicative subsystems can be distinguished and how the 
general conditions of their autopoiesis appear. 
I think that differentiation is possible in many different ways. Among 
these I have selected five possibilities. A fundamental one is the guiding 
difference, which gives all system communication its relevance. It is also 
decisive for the thematics that the system can take up. Linkage possibilities 
provide the guarantee for the transition from one element to the next. Self-
descriptions emerge, through which the system gives itself expression. For 
continuation of the system, the formation of structures which are to be 
seen as structures of expectations is necessary.6 
The autopoietic process is not accessible directly as a real process, but 
is only open to observation; the observer's distinctions will presumably be 
different from those of the system. Accordingly, the general characterization 
6 In my view these descriptions are enough, at least for the definition of the legal 
system. I suspect, however, that this is on the one hand characteristic of the legal 
system, but on the other not sufficient for other systems. For the legal system can 
define its content as expectations, which is not possible for the other systems, at any 
rate in the form of the legal system.

Hans-Georg Deggau 
below of a subsystem can only be given from the standpoint of the observer. 
To link up with Part I, I shall orient this description towards the basic 
concepts of identity and difference. 
What follows abstractly for the differentiated subsystems then becomes 
concrete directly in the legal system. The aspects of this differentiation will 
be studied to find what the ultimate communicative element of the legal 
system is and how it is constituted. In doing this I shall analyze the aspects 
studied for their contribution to the autopoietic constitution of the legal 
system. Here I place particular value on the description of the emergence 
of the unity element from the communicative contexts. 
(a) Guiding Difference 
Through its orientation towards its guiding difference, the system refers 
itself to an identical difference. This serves to set its own limits, i. e., its 
identity; for it is on this basis that it always also distinguishes what belongs 
to it and what does not. The system thereby organizes its horizons of 
meaning and selection. Affirmative reference to itself becomes possible for 
it, as does definition of the negation, internal or external to the system — 
that is, the exclusions, the demarcations from other things as non-identical, 
non-belonging. All operations of the system must be oriented towards this 
in order to be system operations, but this also sets up an infinitely broad 
operational space. 
The guiding difference is a communicative difference. It is selective, and 
increases the further selection possibilities of the communicative process. 
Through the reference of communication to it, the system can communica-
tively distinguish what belongs to it. By reference to it, it may also reject 
communications. 
The guiding difference, while it thus defines the substantive framework 
of possible system identity, and thus also its information-processing possi-
bilities, says nothing about how the system, through processing, sets the 
boundaries, and what mechanisms it uses to maintain its identity. 
If these are, however, asserted autopoietically as autonomous, as a core 
of the autopoietic reproduction and closure of the system, it follows that 
the guiding difference can contribute only slightly. The specific unity that 
has to constitute the system if autopoiesis is to be possible does not result 
from it. While it can orient the general communicative process, it cannot 
constitute any communicative elements differing from other communicative 
acts but which are producible only through elements of the same type. 
The fundamental communicative difference of the legal system is that 
between right and wrong, legal and illegal, possibly just and unjust. These 
mutually exclusive pairs of values guide legal communication. It is on their 
bases that the relevance or irrelevance of communications is decided. It is 
only with reference to them that something is assessed as belonging to the 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
137 
system or not belonging to it. Thus, the legal system can do nothing with 
physical or chemical differences as such. They may however become 
relevant if they become essential to the evaluation of a legal consequence 
(thus, whether something is legal or illegal). 
Through the guiding difference, the legal system obtains an initial legal 
definition. It roughly indicates what the system is concerned with, and for 
what problems and complexes it has competence. The aesthetic guiding 
difference has, for instance, a different content from the legal one. This 
makes a difference from other subsystems possible.7 Linking communica-
tions are thus controlled through the fact that every contribution must 
justify the extent to which it contributes anything to the evaluation of 
"legal or illegal". 
But the concretization of the guiding difference in the legal system does 
not yield very much for the constitution of legal autopoiesis. It must be 
borne in mind that the ultimate communicative elements sought for have 
to be correlated with the guiding difference: they must not only be 
compatible with it but must themselves retain or permit the distinction 
between "legal and illegal". 
(b) 
Thematics 
The "universalization of possible relevances" attained through the guiding 
difference (Luhmann, supra: 17) is concretized and generalized communica-
tively through the possible themes. The system can thus take up themes 
and treat them in its own way. 
As system themes they are, however, accessible to the system only under 
the conditions of the guiding difference. Thematization, or change of 
theme, is also only possible in this way. How and whether a theme is taken 
up depends on the system itself. Thematics in each case deals with certain 
differences which are correlated with the difference of other themes, es-
pecially the guiding difference. The correlations open to a system take on 
their value only through its identity and thereby the difference from other 
systems. 
In the varying correlations of differences through which the system 
classifies, compares and relates, it also forms the procedures and modes 
7 The legal system can thereby be meaningfully asserted as divided into two areas: the 
general legal system has as its object the communications which refer, in normative 
or non-normative fashion, to the guiding difference between legal and illegal, and 
process further selections. To that extent, even everyday conversations about legal 
themes belong here. Binding changes in expectations of behavior are not meant to 
be, and are not, set off by this. By contrast, the legal system in the narrower sense 
is the system that processes normativity and changes expectations of comportment 
through congruent generalization, and is oriented to the concept of legal action as 
attributed communication. It includes both major and minor changes, legislative acts 
or declarations of intent.

which it uses to identify, grasp and describe itself. It is only the manipulation 
of differences (observation) that makes this possible; here the guiding 
difference is not sufficient, because it cannot grasp or express the complexity 
of the relationships, but merely represents a communicative principle 
of judgement. Through the manipulation of internal differences (self-
observation) the system must, for the possibility of continuing communica-
tion, develop fixed sets of links through which it distinguishes itself from 
other systems. This cannot however be achieved through thematics, yet 
thematics do determine the "accent" of the language, such that an observer 
can easily determine whether it is a lawyer, politician, artist or someone 
else who is talking. 
Thematics bring about further densification of the possibilities of com-
munication for the legal system as well. This does not mean that there is 
any conclusive canon of legal themes, but only that possible themes arise 
in the orientation around the guiding difference between legal and illegal. 
Thus, one can communicate legally about the guilt of an accused person 
or the justification of a dismissal, but not about sports results. These may 
take on legal significance only when reference to the guiding difference is 
made, for instance in the case of the prohibitions on drug use. 
In the context of the guiding difference, therefore, thematic restrictions 
serve only to break down insufficiently transparent complexes and to limit 
the system. Along with it, further differences are posited, which may be 
directed at other communications or at those of the system itself. Here 
too, however, no communicative surplus is visible that might lead to the 
constitution of autopoietic elements. The point in the thematizations is the 
structuring of the general communicative process as such, from which no 
sub-systemic autopoiesis can be developed. 
Thematic orientation and selection thus do not constitute communicative 
acts out of which autopoietic elements might crystallize. They do not give 
the communications any specific character: all of them have to be thematic 
because all communication already means thematic selection. 
(c) Linkage possibilities 
The systems consist of ephemeral, evanescent elements since the communi-
cative acts do not endure, as they are not arranged for exsitence over time. 
It is only if provision has been made for their successor or at least for a 
possibility of succession that the system can continue to exist. The possibil-
ity of self-continuation must exist at the moment of dissolution of an 
element; its possibilities of linkage must be maintained or realized. 
This happens because a communicative element is not something existing 
neutrally, only for itself, but understands itself in anticipation as selective 
and thereby as meaningful. It acquires its character as an element only in 
contexts of meaning, in regard to what selective possibilities there are. It 
defines itself by pointing beyond itself. 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
139 
It is in such references that its specifically communicative nature lies; 
the linkage possibilities that come under the above-mentioned conditions 
are at the same time possibilities of exclusion. They have specified them-
selves so far that in principle only similarly specified communications can 
follow from them. The understanding context of reference and meaning is 
made possible and is held up through the meaning structure of expectation. 
The linkage capacity of a communicative act can therefore be seen as the 
fundamental condition for the autopoietic process. But the linking up of 
a communication with other communications says nothing about its subsys-
tem specific character, since the point is precisely to establish the specificity 
of the element, which then must be capable of linkage vis-ä-vis other 
elements of the same type. What this specificity consists in, however, 
cannot be deduced from the general need for linkage capacity. 
Correspondingly, it is also true of the legal system that a legal communi-
cation can be followed by another communication only if it takes over the 
selections developed thus far. If it does not, it will bring the communication 
to date under a new guiding difference, thus leaving the legal system and 
possibly becoming incomprehensible. 
The linkage possibilities of the elements are, then, determined substan-
tively, through their selectivity and identity. The meaning which arises 
through and from differences here follows from the dense network of 
selections. That means, then, that only communications of law are com-
municable in the legal system, since only they offer possibilities of legal 
linkage. While this is a formulation of a general condition of legal auto-
poiesis, it does not follow from it how the element that is to meet this 
condition can be constituted. 
(d) 
Self-descriptions 
Observations are processes in which an identifiable distinction is drawn 
and described. If a system applies distinction and description to itself, it is 
a case of self-observation. In the communicative process this means that 
the information communicated refers to the communicative process itself. 
If such references take on a fixed semantic form, then it is a case of 
descriptions, or self-descriptions. Self-descriptions that have arisen freely 
in interaction systems must however develop further into structural pro-
visions that make linkage possible at any time with what has existed already, 
that is, the continuation of the communication. Large social subsystems 
cannot operate with only momentary self-descriptions. Instead, they must 
extend over time. 
Through self-descriptions, the system's reference to itself is expressed. 
They are therefore self-referential; for they refer to particular communica-
tive processes without which they would have no meaning — as, conversely, 
they reintroduce these into the system and give them meaning. 

140 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
The constituting and practice of communicative systems incorporate 
many of these self-descriptions operationally. 
They make possible a definite 
furtherance or continuation of the system. The unity of the self-descriptions 
as a communicative, semantically acquired body of self-observations always 
carries within it the anticipatory aspects of temporal synthesis. Such antici-
pations as identity selections and identity controls may take on normative 
character. Through them, the system may produce an identity norm, 
through an identical form of self-expectation. They can thus count as the 
system's conception of itself, whereby it measures itself and orients itself. 
It becomes the criterion of development and therefore also of the control 
of possible deviations. Through the self-descriptions, thus, differences are 
engendered, through which the system defines itself. To be sure, it is not 
the self-description, but can only be read off from it; but through the 
establishment of its own difference, the system also makes its identity 
accessible to itself, and makes its reformulation or transformation possible. 
The self-description of the systems seems to be a mechanism lying 
much closer to autopoiesis; for the self-descriptions can be produced and 
reproduced only communicatively, but meaningfully only through reference 
to an identical system. Along with the guiding difference and the thematiza-
tions, the self-descriptions, from their necessary orientation towards an 
identical system, thus take on a highly self-referential character. They 
presuppose identical networks and references within which they alone are 
meaningful. Their character of mutual reference shows their close systematic 
connection. 
But even this is not enough to produce the internal self-referential core 
of autopoiesis. It is incorrect to say that self-descriptions proceed only 
from self-descriptions and can produce only self-descriptions; for self-
descriptions also proceed from general communicative situations and acts. 
Certainly, what suggests itself is to study their role in autopoiesis. To that 
extent, it is true of the whole system of society that its communicative 
autopoiesis cannot manage to do without self-description.8 
This indicates mainly and primarily only the reference of the communica-
tion to past communication. It refers to it by denoting parts, individual 
acts or the whole of the communication that has taken place separately, 
and communicating about it. This orientation towards itself is essential: 
for control, for the possibility of continuation, for clearing up misunder-
standings, for correcting, for evaluating developments, for attribution 
(addressing), etc. 
Such references, which may have arisen interactionally and flow directly 
back into the communication, acquire consolidation that goes beyond the 
8 A particularly effective self-description of the system is the concept of action. It allows 
the summarizing of communicative structuring and at the same time assignment or 
attribution of major complexes. 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
141 
individual concrete reason for them and may take on significance for all 
communications in the system. They may then count as self-descriptions 
of the system because they keep on appearing as reference to self, and in 
them communicative positions oriented towards the guiding difference are 
formulated. 
In the legal system, with its thoroughly worked-out dogmatics, legal 
theory and legal philosophy, there are many self-descriptions which are 
independent of the particular individual communication (though of course 
reproducing themselves only through it), but usable in it. There is a range 
of linguistic artefacts available. It is through their connection and their use 
that the system defines itself. Only the legal system is in a position to 
change, modify, loosen or densify these self-descriptions and the legal 
structures (see below) connected with them. 
Self-descriptions structure the possible communications about law to a 
large extent. They define the possibilities of linkage. Their meaning as 
selection often consists precisely in the impossibility of particular connec-
tions. They prescribe, crudely or in detail, what is possible. It is only 
through reference to them that legal communication can be planned and, 
in certain circumstances, also be strategically carried out. 
A particularly usable and highly generalized self-description of the social 
system of society is represented by the concept of action. "Actions are 
constituted by processes of attribution. They arise from the attribution of 
selections ... to systems" (Luhmann, 1984a: 288). Action is thus to be 
understood not as "deed", but only as constituted through communication, 
as reference to communication, to communicative situations. To that extent, 
action is communicative. There is therefore an emergent social level of 
action, which is communicatively constituted. 
The concept of action makes it possible to find further differences in 
the communication network itself. Through the concept of communication 
as a threefold unity, differing material was already brought to unity: 
not only the selections, but also self and other as those involved. The 
communicative act allows their differences in reference to its unity to 
disappear. This does not however explain communication's possibility of 
continuation. The unity of the diverse must again be used to distinguish 
the diverse. This is brought about by the concept of action, since it assigns 
to self or other, as the communicators, particular selections. 
The concept of action is also a self-description of the legal system, but 
it acquires its specific definition only when the action is qualified as legal. 
Its reference to the identity of the system is however not enough if it is 
to be understood as autopoietic unity, unless it is still further qualified. 
For this, the action must be equipped with something that gives it further 
significance. This happens through the reflexive stressing of the basic self-
reference by applying the process of legal description of the world in its 
distinctions to itself. Whatever in the events of the world is denoted by 

142 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
the legal system as legal action or legal consequence can be once more 
applied to the denotative or descriptive process. In the self-description of 
the system, much is thus again treated as legal action or legal consequence. 
Through this, and through binding up with the conditions of law, an 
action becomes a legal action. The legal system not only denotes it in 
general as an action, but selects out certain actions. They are distinguished 
by appearing in the conditional form set by the legal system itself. This is 
a communicative form which has synthetic character, but is not specific as 
such for the legal system, since other systems use it too. 
But this simultaneously indicates the possibility of autopioetic reproduc-
tion. In the form of "if A then B", the first element is constituted as action 
or event, which can however also denote a cognitively recognizable legal 
position. The first elements in this relation are, then, elements that proceed 
from self-descriptions, qualified by their link with the following element 
as legal action or as legal event. As legal, they are characterized through 
their reference to the guiding difference of "right and wrong". 
If the legal consequence, however understood, is to be regarded as the 
apodosis part of the implication, then the autopoietic element sought for 
could, at least formally, possibly lie in the whole implication. For if the 
legal synthesis is the communicative quality through which communicative 
language is achieved (though this must be defined more precisely), then a 
communicative element would be constituted which could not be produced 
by other communicative contexts — and which would itself be possible 
only through linkage to communications of the same type. 
Apart from the specific legal character, to be sure, there should still be 
detailed study of who communicates where, when and how; for the 
emergence of these communicative elements is bound up with communica-
tive processes. The precondition is, therefore, again the breaking up of what 
has in the communicative act been brought to unity through attribution. 
Specifically: if A has been caused damage by Β, Β must compensate. This 
connection as such is of course of a legal nature, but its communication 
itself is not yet a legal autopoietic element. It can become this only if these 
implications are ranked in with other framework implications (when the 
judge has decided, the decision applies). These include procedures, trials, 
institutions, etc. 
But this depends precisely on what is to be understood as legal conse-
quence. If law is understood as congruently generalized expectation, then 
a legal consequence is a change in the position of expectations. If however 
the legal consequence can be formulated only with recourse to this, then 
it is to be looked at in the next section. 
Summarizing, it may therefore be said that it is through the legal self-
descriptions of the system — to which the legal concept of action is 
central — that communications refer to communications oriented towards 
"legal and illegal". Through their necessary self-reference, they restrict the 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
143 
possible communications much more than is done by the guiding difference 
or the thresholds of thematizations; for a kind of identical core is consti-
tuted, through the self-definition of the system as self-description. However, 
this is still not enough for autopoietic reproduction. 
An essential condition of the autopoietic closure of the communicative 
system is met only where there is a type of linkage which forms itself and 
excludes other linkages. The elements of the communicative process in 
which such syntheses take place must anticipate precisely such linkages in 
their self-reference. Additive, subtractive or logarithmic linkages are not 
possible in law. The type of linkage — though not yet typical of the legal 
system — is in principle that of implication. In it, certain communications 
are linked with others in the form of the "if-then". The protages of this 
implication are legal actions or legal events. The apodosis is the legal 
consequence. The autopoietic character of the legal implication lies then 
in the fact that it is only in linkage with such implications that other ones 
can be created; for only legal actions, legal events and legal consequences 
can be synthesised in it. Since this formal condition is however not yet 
enough, we shall now look at how the substantive conditions of the legal 
implication can be seen against the concept of structure of expectations. 
(e) Structures 
Structures conserve linkage possibilities. They are themselves selections 
oriented around identity, which make possible selections among the rela-
tions within them. They control the relationships between the elements of 
the system through time, by bridging the gap that has arisen from the 
ending of one element. 
This means that structure makes it possible for the system to maintain 
its existence and identity. The temporary bridging takes place through 
expectations. These guarantee the identity and identification possibility of 
the communicative elements of the social subsystem. For social structures 
are "nothing other ... than structures of expectation" (Luhmann, 1984a: 
397). 
It is only along them that the communicative process can move. Substan-
tively, they provide the guiding thread through time. Communication 
therefore acquires its identity essentially through the reference to expecta-
tions which are anticipatory ideas of how the communications will or 
ought to develop, i.e., it determines their possibilities of development. 
The disappointment of expectation makes everything classifiable that was 
not in line with the expectation. 
This generalization largely filters the possible successful communications. 
It thereby defines differences and negation. It is extremely intensified 
selection, which alone makes links possible. It also, therefore, provides the 
negation possibilities of the links themselves. This concreteness is necessary 

144 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
for the system. But it does not lie at the level of the distinction of "this 
or everything else". The totality formulae "A or not-A" or "A and not-
A" are, in their abstraction and simple juxtaposition of identity and 
negation, referred to everything possible, unusable. The limits of the system 
are defined precisely by the fact that the system itself controls its potential 
for negation. In the difference from other systems, through limit and 
difference, the system implies a high level of negation. The class of possible 
negations of the system is established by it itself "as the limitation of the 
quality and linkability of the elements" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 389). 
In general, then, structures are conditions without which autopoiesis 
cannot take place. They are to be met within all social systems, and 
therefore as such not specific to a system. The social structures formed 
through expectations can lead to the constitution of unities intrinsic to 
subsystems only if they are further condensed and become so highly 
selective that their potential for negation excludes everything except one 
single communicatively differentiated type of event. This is in my view 
the case with the legal system, where the expectation structures are so 
highly specialized and generalized that legal communications acquire a 
unitariness of their own. 
The analysis of further aspects such as conditioning or codification might 
clarify their role in the general communicative process. But they too 
provide no direct jumping-off point for the formation of subsystemic 
autopoiesis. What follows from this? 
The alternative that can be seen seems to be as follows: either the 
subsystems cannot differentiate themselves only through their communica-
tive processes, structures and elements; then their difference must lie in 
something else. If this something else is, however, not communication nor 
communicatively engendered, then it is rather hard to maintain the thesis 
that subsystems consist "only of communications". Or it can be shown 
that the elements that make the system's closure possible are after all 
communicatively generated; then the formation of their difference must 
be localizable and describable in the communicative process itself. The 
constitution of the ultimate communicative elements that engender auto-
poiesis and therefore identity and intersystemic differences is then a result 
of the communicative process itself. From it proceed emergent systems 
that show an autopoiesis of their own, that do not owe their specificity to 
their environment. 
The thesis to be worked out below and displayed in the case of the legal 
system is that the specific difference of the legal system proceeds from 
certain communicative operations that acquire their "content" from the 
system's structure. This content is the result of communicative handling of 
information and time, to the extent that expectations consist of anticipatory 
communications. The autopoiesis of the legal system is, then, the result of 
various aspects. Together, these form a context which could not maintain 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
145 
itself lastingly on a purely interactional level. It is only its institutionaliza-
tion and procedural consolidation that allow it to take on a form that goes 
beyond a system of interactions. For this, however, many kinds of structure 
are necessary. 
Among legal communications, individual ones can, in accordance with 
the system's self-description, be understood as legal actions. They are 
thereby distinguished by the system from other communications and differ-
entiated from them. Therein lie the communicative connections that make 
it possible to situate a legal communication, for instance, as a legal action 
in the legal system, and to deal with it as such. 
The self-reference of legal action is, like its system reference, only 
possible through time. Bridging structures whereby the linkage possibilities 
are concretely regulated and controlled make it possible for the legal system 
not to cease to exist with the cessation of the legal communication as legal 
action. They guarantee its possible continuation. For it is through structure 
that legal action as a past event is linked in time with its future, without 
this linkage depending on the duration of the event. On the contrary: it 
presupposes its end. It is in this linkage, however, that it shows its meaning. 
This legal meaning, the selection of legal action, is only possible on the 
basis of the legally meaningful situation of whoever sets the action going. 
The "action situation" is legally determined and defined. It is only legal 
structures that make it into what it is. The same is true of legal events. 
The legal consequence is the new position in regard to selection and 
expectation. 
As set out above, the system structures take the shape of expectations. 
For these are the general social form of the anticipatory synthesis in time 
through which the present is linked with the future, and thus through 
which the anticipation of action, its realization and its evaluation as a 
consequence become possible. Expectation anticipates in time what is 
expectable as possible. It refers to itself to the extent that the present is 
seen in the light of the expected, i. e., future, and the future in the light 
of the present. The end of the action, the termination of the event, is the 
condition for the possibility of linkage: the meaning of the action/event as 
simplified description in the meaning network of legal expectations makes 
the structure whereby there can be a passage from one event to the next. 
However, the law shows the peculiarity of becoming condensed along 
the expectation dimension. The distinction is drawn between cognitive and 
normative expectations (Luhmann, 1985). The difference is defined by their 
capacity to learn. Cognitive expectations are able to learn; normative 
expectations are not. The law numbers among the normative expectations 
since it retains the expectations even when they are disappointed. It sticks 
to them against the facts. By contrast, cognitive expectations change in the 
event of disappointment; they learn, they do not expect against the facts. 

146 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
It is only its normative character that makes the legal system possible as 
something autopoietic, since the connection between legal action and legal 
event is distinguished by its content as normative. The peculiarity of its 
communications as already worked out through the aspects discussed so 
far, takes on its definitive delimiting identity only through this. For while 
the descriptions thus far already permit the separation of the legal system 
from the social system, they were able to indicate only formally where the 
autopoietic reproduction was to be seen, and thus what reproduces itself 
specifically via the general reproduction. This surplus is characterized 
through conditionalized normativity. 
Without it, to be sure, the legal system can be separated from other 
systems and asserted as something specific. But these general differences 
are not enough to assert the possibility of autopoiesis instrinsic to the 
system. Rather, the specific difference must lie in something that cannot 
as such constitute itself by itself. For the legal system, we can denote this 
surplus as conditionalized 
legal normativity. 
For its character as legal normativ-
ity can be justified by no other system, nor given to its communications. 
Hence Luhmann's thesis: "The positivity of law is its autopoiesis" (supra: 
18) becomes understandable. Law can be produced or changed only through 
law, validity only through the valid. This constitutes its specifity. The 
closure lying therein — through which alone the closure of the system 
becomes possible — is defined by the connection of the legal action with 
the legal consequence: "it is nothing but legal communication that selects 
legal acts from the variety of social acts and events. One needs to extend 
this idea to legal procedure and legal doctrine. Both become self-referential 
when the legal discourse selects certain procedures and certain reality 
constructs as legal ones" (Teubner, infra: 224); mutatis mutandis, 
this is true 
of the legal event. The starting point is the expectations of comportment 
which are changed by the legal action or legal event as singled out, 
specialized legal communications — which is precisely what their specificity 
lies in.9 
The communicatively constituted difference of the autopoieticized legal 
system can then be summarized as follows: in the orientation around the 
guiding difference between "legal and illegal", this relationship forms 
mediated and linked self-descriptions of the system. These constitute a kind 
of self-referential core of the system. Since the latter then applies the basic 
distinctions of its description of the world (legal action/legal event — legal 
9 Other attempts at differentiation which point to force as the characteristic of the legal 
system, such as Luhmann, 1981: 138 ff., seem to be problematic; for it is not a further 
differential communicative element that is worked out, but an additional content that 
is asserted additively. Force must thus be justified as an act of the law, i. e., as action, 
i. e. as communication that is attributable to the legal system. Only then would it be 
adequate. 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
147 
consequence) to itself, through this communicative operation it emphasizes 
legal actions and legal consequences, gives them special significance. This 
becomes clear, however, only through the conditional form in which legal 
action and legal consequence are linked: the legal action becomes a condi-
tion of the legal consequence, and only through that becomes a legal 
action. This means that without legal actions/events there can be no legal 
consequences, and without legal consequences no legal actions/events. We 
thus have a legally organized type of linkage which makes it possible to 
relate legal communications of the same type to each other. Here the 
linkage of these communications of the same type through the traditional 
criteria of validity can be restricted severely to such ones (definition of the 
linkage capacity of a normative element by normativity). The emergence 
of (normative) legal consequences is then possible only in relation to and 
linkage with past normative communications. This, at least formally, meets 
one condition of autopoiesis. What gives the individual communications 
this rank, for instance the singling out of decisions, would have to be 
found from a precise analysis of the legal system. 
There is, however, still no exact description of what constitutes its "inner 
identity", namely the validity of particular communications. This lies in 
the expectation structure itself. Congruently generalized expectations which 
react with reluctance to learn from a case of disappointment are legally 
normative. To be grasped communicatively, this normativity requires a 
particular shape; not simply any formulation of expectations is legally 
normative. But since the objective type of linkage can be based only on 
linkages of the same type and these are all to be characterized substantively 
as normative, the constitution of the ultimate autopoietic element of the 
legal system is clear: only those communications which refer to other 
normative legal communications can be distinguished as autopoietic legal 
communications. The main link here is that the normative synthesis is itself 
normative, i. e., that there can be a progress only from validity to validity. 
This can no longer be established normatively externally, but is left up to 
the autopoietic process. 
III. Expectation Structure and "Priority" of the Legal System 
From all this there follows as a further thesis that the legal system has a 
certain "priority" over the other systems, to the extent that it densities a 
structure that can be encountered in all communication systems. For the 
peculiarity of the legal system lies in the fact that it has a particular type 
of expectation as its content: congruently generalized expectations. It 
therefore consists of the same stuff as the social structure as such, to the 
extent that it is expectation structure, and differentiates itself from the 
latter. Its specific difference lies in an area which essentially affects all 

148 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
subsystems: the difference of the legal system lies in the difference of its 
expectations. 
There follows, firstly, a certain structural closeness in subject of the legal 
system to the other social systems. Its own modelling of expectations 
concerns only their general character and is therefore potentially applicable 
in every system; for no system can entirely do without normative expecta-
tions. Even a system oriented towards the cognitive style of expectation 
expects in a normative fashion that there will be cognitive expectation, 
that is, that the cognitions acquired hitherto will continue to be applied. 
Expectations as temporal projections can be divided into cognitive and 
normative expectations (and corresponding combinations). Since further 
differentiations are not available, not more than a maximum of two subsys-
tems can be distinguished through this typology, to the extent that the 
specificity is seen in the relationship to the expectations. Accordingly, not 
every subsystem can be distinguished by a specific type of expectation. 
One of the two possible systems that can be distinguished only through 
expectation is the legal system, since it is a system of normative expectations. 
It regulates the generalized expectations in normative fashion; through its 
positivity it also regulates changes in such normative expectations. Its great 
closeness in subject to the expectations and the fact that it is to be 
understood as definition of the expectation structure, that it thus lays 
down what can or will be expected, that it actualizes extremely densified 
expectations, that it therefore congruently generalizes social expectations 
and thus creates normativity, distinguish it as a social subsystem and 
represent its characteristic feature. Its communications, to the extent that 
they belong to the internal legal circle, are therefore always aimed at 
normative expectation situations. Its peculiarity lies in a type of special 
expectations distinguished by the congruence of their objective, temporal 
and social generalization. This difference of the legal system testifies to its 
closeness to the other social systems. 
The structure of expectation that decks out an event with meaning and 
guarantees it possibilities of linkage applies to all social systems. Expecta-
tion means here not individual expectation, but system expectation, the 
expectation of the system in which it arises. To that extent, the legal system 
is distinguished by specialization in a structure that all social systems show. 
This is true also of systems that are in principle oriented towards a cognitive 
style of expectation; for exclusively cognitive expectations cannot be met 
with for the reason that they too always cognitively expect in normative 
fashion. 
If one therefore attempts to formulate the relationship of the legal system 
to the other social systems in this respect, it appears that the legal system 
can in principle be relevant for every other social system; it has only to 
structure expectations there, i. e. generalize them appropriately. The object 
of law is structures that all other systems also show. The converse is however 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
149 
not true.™ It is only this fact that makes the law's possibility of intervening in 
regulatory fashion in other systems plausible. At the same time, regulatory 
problems can be discerned here when, for instance, expectations are not 
generalizable or must be created anew by the legal system. 
From this there follows the specific relation of the legal system to the 
other systems: the legal system is assigned a priority in structuring expecta-
tions vis-a-vis the other systems. On the basis of its specific difference, it 
has at all times the possibility of determining the communicative processes 
of the other communication systems. Its power of modification of expecta-
tion, i. e., determination of departures from and comportment towards the 
expectations, allow it to "intervene". On the other hand, however, the 
legal system depends to an extent that needs closer definition on the 
provision of those social expectations that it takes, can take, or must take 
as an object. Without them it would not exist. 
The legal system is therefore a type of expectation-guiding system, which 
can structure others' expectations, its material. This cannot however be 
understood as an absolute regulatory claim of the legal system. It is 
therefore dependent only on a structural possibility whereby the legal 
system's relationship to other systems is characterized — which does not 
yet say anything about the possibility and reality of the realization of this 
possibility.11 
The legal system can, thus, take up or even produce expectations of 
other systems, i. e., incorporate "outside expectations" in legal shape into 
the autopoietic production and reproduction of expectations as legal action 
or consequence, that is, give other expectations legal quality. Communica-
tion and action in a system can thus become legal communication and legal 
action, as law. They are then distinguished as such by their normative 
character, without losing their character as communications of the other 
system. 
10 This thesis is pointed up here since certain final conclusions can be drawn from it. 
It is not however meant to say that there are no other correspondences between 
individual systems in other respects. All I am advocating is to seek common features, 
similarities or differences at the constitutional level of the systems themselves. This 
is true for instance of meaning, language etc. If differences are understood from this 
point of view, then possibilities of understanding can presumably be more easily 
established. 
11 This varies in differing respects. Since one cannot start from a zero point, but a 
certain measure of regulation has to be presupposed, the starting point for the object 
of regulation has to be regulatory intensity, regulatory level, regulatory extent. Social 
expectations often already incorporate the legally articulated expectations. Specifically, 
and not simply in the contra-position of autonomous systems, what has to be studied 
is where the centers of autopoietic reproduction lie, where the particular system 
closure is to be seen and how it is related to the internal expectation structures and 
those of the law. This seems to me also to be a starting point for an understanding 
of the implementation and control problem in general. 

150 
Hans-Georg Deggau 
From this, the following consequences can in my view be drawn. The 
thesis of the autonomy of the law and the other social subsystems is not 
questioned. Autopoietic reproduction takes place independently of whether 
the specific feature of the autopoiesis of a system is the closure of legal 
normativity or whether the principle is "payment for payment" (Luhmann, 
1984 b). In my view however, the legal system's relationship to the other 
systems is to be defined in a different way than for instance through 
equality or symmetry. Instead, there is a basic asymmetry in the relationship 
of the system structures. 
The legal system generalizes and specializes a structure, namely expecta-
tions, which is fundamental in all systems, since there is no system that 
could exist or reproduce itself without expectations, which is due to their 
temporal nature and that of their elements as ephemeral events. However, 
no converse relationship exists. The specificity of other systems does not consist 
in a special way of dealing with the expectations that underlie and structure 
the legal system. 
There follows a structural affinity of the legal system with the other 
systems because there is a structural identity: wherever expectations 
exist, they can be taken up by the legal system and modified, and 
defined in a generalized form. This points to the locus of the possible 
influence. System control through law takes place through the provision 
of generalizations of expectation, i. e., structural changes. Since, however, 
these do not define the systems solely and exclusively, for each system 
the internal relationship of the autopoietic closure to the structuring of 
expectation is to be clarified, before the possible starting point and 
point of application of the legal regulation can be adequately defined. 
Since this is not the case for the other systems, the structural aspect 
and the autopoiesis have to be correlated inside them. From this there 
follow the possible limits to regulation. 
On the other hand, however, the relationships of the other subsystems 
to the legal system have also to be analyzed. To the freedom of the 
legal system there corresponds its dependence on social expectations and 
on the political system. In other words, how are its dependencies in 
relationship to the other systems defined? What role do expectations 
play in this? The presumption is that the possible "regulatory 
contents" 
are to a certain extent provided by the situations to be regulated, which 
has to do with its formal character. This is not to be misunderstood 
to the effect that any content whatever in the legal system is already 
defined a priori. 
Since it can create new expectation situations, it is to 
a certain extent independent of them. Furthermore, it ought to be able 
to bring about pieces of social integration only if there already exists 
a social adequacy of the social system. It can, therefore, not produce 
social integration in its systematic conditions — even if these are 
understood only as indifference. Again, an analysis of the constitution 

The Communicative Autonomy of the Legal System 
151 
of the ultimate communicative autopoietic elements of the other systems 
would be important, because then the context in the communication 
space could in each case be determined specifically and in regard to the 
system communications.

The Autonomy of Law: Two Visions Compared 
RICHARD LEMPERT 
Ann Arbor 
Visions of Legal Autonomy 
During the past decade the effort to understand the place of the legal 
system in society has, in England and America, given rise to a renewed 
interest in the possibility of legal autonomy (Thompson, 1975; Balbus, 
1973; 1977; Trubek, 1977). More recently, on the continent of Europe, 
especially in Germany, scholars have focused on an apparently radical form 
of autonomy — embodied in the idea of an autopoietic system — in an 
effort to understand how law functions (Luhmann, 1985 d; Teubner, 1984). 
These two approaches to understanding the legal system paint pictures that 
have much in common, but they are differently developed; they are sup-
ported by different types of arguments and they are advanced at different 
levels of abstraction. 
The Anglo-American approach grows out of the empirical untenability 
of a crudely instrumental Marxism which posits that law is the barely 
disguised instrument by which one class dominates another in all things. 
The clearly redistributive elements of the modern welfare state as well as 
empirical studies of the treatment of rioters (Balbus, 1973), the enforcement 
of Draconian, class-based legislation (Thompson, 1975), and even the law 
of slavery (Genovese, 1972; Tushnett, 1975) have shown that the generation 
and application of legal norms cannot be explained solely — and sometimes 
can hardly be explained at all — by the class positions of involved groups 
and parties. It appears, in particular, that the legal system's own norms of 
procedure and substance have important implications for the way the law 
in the first instance affects the distribution of wealth and power between 
parties. The rediscovery of Pashukanis (1980) and theories building on his 
work (see e. g., Balbus, 1977, Stone, 1985) have shown that Marxist theories 
of social organization are not necessarily threatened by legal norms that 
take no explicit account of the class positions of those whose behavior will 
fall within the ambit of the law or by the application of legal norms without 
regard to the social class or other socio-economic attributes of the parties. 
Indeed, some have suggested that legal autonomy in this sense or even, 
on occasion, special sensitivity to the interests of the less privileged may 

The Autonomy of Law: Two Visions Compared 
153 
contribute to capitalist domination by giving a legitimacy to law which 
ultimately makes the masses easier to govern (Hay, 1975; Thompson, 1975; 
but see Hyde, 1983). 
The Continental interest in autopoiesis and its implications for legal 
autonomy grows, on the other hand, out of a larger concern with systems 
theory and what systems theory approaches imply for social systems. Its 
development, to date, is largely associated with the work of one man, 
Niklas Luhmann, but as the conference at which this paper was first 
presented attests, other Continental social theorists are becoming increas-
ingly attracted to it (see e.g., Teubner, 1984; infra). 
The vision of law as an autopoietic system is rooted, as I understand it, 
in the idea that society and its major subsystems may be profitably viewed 
as autopoietic systems, a perspective that is inspired by recent attempts to 
understand the integrity and functioning of biological systems. Autopoiesis 
implies a system which is completely closed in the sense that the constitutive 
elements of a system are all parts of it, and as such both reproduce and 
are reproduced by it. At the same time an autopoietic system is open to 
its environment in that the form in which the system reproduces itself 
takes account — in its own terms — of the behavior and activity that are 
ongoing in its environment. Put another way, environmental activity is 
not just or simply mediated by the system of interest (and in this respect 
autopoiesis is not just another open systems theory). Its implications are 
indirect as the system models the environment in its own terms (Teubner, 
1984), proceeding perhaps to reconstitute or even change itself on the basis 
of the systemic representation of environmental contingencies. Environ-
mental influences must be indirect because social meanings exist only within 
the context of social systems (Luhmann, 1985 b). In the case of law this 
involves — to use Luhmann's ambiguous and problematic language — a 
system which is at the same time normatively closed and cognitively open 
(Luhmann: 1985 d: 6, 7; 1985 c: 113; supra: 19 — 21; see also the discussion 
in this paper, infra: 178 — 182). An important implication is that the legal 
system takes cognizance of extra-legal activity only in its own terms — 
that is, only in terms of what is, according to law, legally relevant. 
Although the two visions of legal autonomy are not necessarily incompat-
ible, there are important differences between them. In part these differences 
reflect the fact that the Continental vision involves an abstraction (the legal 
system as a subsystem of social systems) of an abstraction (social systems 
as in some sense like biological systems), while the Anglo-American vision 
of legal autonomy is rooted in the failure of earlier theoretical visions to 
meet the test of reality.1 Thus, the Anglo-American vision is influenced by 
1 In addition to the crudely instrumentalist Marxist vision, there was the earlier 
formalistic vision which posited an autonomy so complete that legal action could be 
understood as a matter of common sense and logical analysis entirely on the law's 
own terms. This vision was destroyed forever when confronted with the common 
sense empiricism of the Realists.

Richard Lempert 
and tends to hew closely to empirical studies of the way in which legal 
power articulates with other sources of power in society. The Continental 
vision, on the other hand, tends to be abstract — developed by logic, 
analogy and a firm a priori theoretical commitment to a model rather than 
by examples or confrontation with empirical facts. To the extent that there 
is an empirical puzzle that motivates the Continental model, it is found 
largely in the widespread sense that there is a law-related crisis in the 
regulatory state and that current theories of law neither adequately capture 
the reasons for the crisis or (if there is no crisis) for the sense of crisis, 
nor provide any guidance for those who would better adapt the legal 
system to the demands the regulatory state places on it. 
A second difference between the Anglo-American and Continental per-
spectives on autonomy, which reflects the role that empirical studies have 
played in each, is that the Anglo-American approach seeks to abstract a 
theory of legal autonomy from the actual operations of the legal system in 
particular situations. This gives Anglo-American theories a somewhat static 
quality; so long as society is organized along essentially the same socio-
economic lines, the implications of autonomy for the legal system remain 
essentially the same. Autopoiesis in so far as it posits continual openness 
to the environment posits continual — albeit system dictated — responses 
to changes in environmental conditions, which means continual responses 
to changes in other subsystems of society and to changes in the encompass-
ing social system. Indeed, autopoietic systems exist only through their 
autopoiesis which implies constant reconstitution with concomitant "molec-
ular" changes. Thus, the Continental theory more than the American theory 
lends itself to the study of legal evolution or, more precisely, adaptation 
(Teubner, infra). 
A third difference is most curious. Although conflict theory, including 
modern Marxism, is generally regarded as the dominant response to func-
tionalist theories in sociology, a good deal of functionalism underlies the 
Anglo-American perspective on legal autonomy. This is, no doubt, in part 
because the theory has its genesis in the perceived failure of the conflict 
model — carried to an extreme — to explain legal behavior. Beyond this 
the idea of legal autonomy is tied to the ways law serves society. The 
predominant explanation of why something like the rule of law persists in 
modern capitalist societies — legitimacy — is functionalism in the service 
of a conflict perspective. 
The idea of autopoiesis on the other hand, although advanced by the 
leading modern functionalist, does not in itself suggest a functionalist 
justification for the autonomy the legal system enjoys. If the legal system 
is autopoietically organized it will enjoy the autonomy associated with 
autopoietic systems regardless of whether and what social functions it fills. 
It could hardly be otherwise. The legal system reconstitutes itself according 
to distinctly legal values rather than under the direct influence of the needs 
of some other system of society. Functionalism is brought in only by the 

The Autonomy of Law: Two Visions Compared 
155 
back door, so to speak. The legal system, Luhmann hypothesizes in another 
of the more problematic aspects of his theory, fulfills a distinct function 
in society relating to the management of disputes (Luhmann, 1985 c: 120; 
supra: 27 —29).2 It is, according to Luhmann, only because the legal system 
fills this particular function and fills it uniquely that it is and can be 
autopoietically organized. 
Given the basic convergence of two different perspectives on an idea of 
legal autonomy, together with the different sources of inspiration for the 
two perspectives, and the differences in the way the two theories have been 
advanced, it should be of interest and one hopes it will be instructive to 
confront one perspective with another. What I propose to do in this paper 
is to construct a theory of legal autonomy rooted in the Anglo-American 
perspective (although not derived from a concern for an empirically tenable 
Marxism).31 shall then turn to Luhmann's work on autopoiesis to examine 
ways in which the idea of autopoiesis accords or conflicts with the theory 
I develop and to contrast the theoretical adequacy of the two perspectives.4 
Before doing this, however, we must confront one more issue, namely the 
theoretical status of Luhmann's attempt to extend the ideal of autopoiesis 
from the living systems the term was coined to describe to social systems. 
Theory or Metaphor 
Some authors (e. g., Teubner, infra) suggest that the idea of autopoiesis as 
applied to social systems is essentially a metaphor. If it is only this, there

185) seems strained and unsatisfactory.

indicate the origins of the work that immediately inspired it, rather than to claim a 
special status for it. The theory I offer is neither the Anglo-American theory nor 
necessarily a typical representative of the theoretical perspectives developed by Anglo-

work of authors in the Anglo-American tradition, although tracing it to its roots it 
is the influence of a continental scholar, Max Weber, that predominates. The work of 
two liberal theorists, Nonet and Selznick (1978) also contributed in important ways

of autopoiesis is, however, not motivated by a desire to promote my own perspective,

and suggesting that my theory compares favorably to it. It is, I assume, understandable 
if I leave to others the task of pointing out weaknesses in my preferred theoretical 
position.
