Changing Paradigms in the Sociology of Law 
211 
that they are not uncontroversial is easily seen by considering some of the 
illustrative alternative positions which I have added to each of the axes 
which presently frame enquiry in this field. At the very least, mainstream 
work must justify the positions it takes. But the great merit of Luhmann's 
work in sociology of law is actually to collapse these axes into each other 
by showing how the extremes do in fact meet up (it is noteworthy, 
for example, that Kelsen can be seen as making both ontological and 
epistemological claims about the distinctiveness of law). What is more, 
Luhmann's approach is a positive one. It is not intended, as is so often 
the case, to demonstrate the impossibility of doing sociology of law but 
rather to create a theoretically justifiable starting-point 
for this field. If law, 
society and sociology are to be analytically distinguished for the purposes 
of developing sociology of law (and it is hard to see how this can be 
avoided) Luhmann offers us a model of how to justify this in theoretical 
terms rather than merely adopting pragmatic positions along the relevant 
axes. We can learn from the way he poses his theoretical questions even if 
we cannot always accept his answers. What Luhmann does is what all 
theorists in this field should do: he starts from the problem of how, where 
and why law, society and sociology actually become distinguished from each 
other. For Luhmann the differentiation of law and society is represented as 
the historical (evolutionary) outcome of the emergence of functionally 
differentiated societies. The "positivity" of law and its reproduction as an 
autopoietic system is then seen as a further historical stage of this evolution 
(although the theory is certainly presently unclear as to when this final 
stage was reached and how it is to be identified). It is this same attention 
to starting points which underlies Luhmann's (and Teubner's) attempts to 
offer a sociological explanation of law's reproduction in relation to the 
way one autopoietic system may understand another. 
The merit of Luhmann's framework can be assessed by examining it in 
relation to the recent critique of mainstream sociology of law coming from 
some members of the Critical Legal Studies Conference in the United States 
(see e. g., Gordon, 1984). It can be seen that Luhmann's approach provides 
a sociologically articulate anticipation of their attempt to deny the very 
possibility of the sociology of law. They focus on legal institutions and 
doctrine in an effort to show that law and politics cannot be distinguished. 
Luhmann's theory, however, includes an account of how and why these sub-
systems have different functions, and stresses exactly the "de-politici2ing" 
function of law. The Critical scholars reject the mainstream approach to 
investigating the relationship between "law" and "society" with the argu-
ment that law is in fact constitutive 
of society (see Figure 2). But Luhmann 
argues that this is going too far for, as Willke helpfully explains, this is to 
misunderstand functionally differentiated societies. Although law is indeed 
everywhere, it becomes both more and less relevant than in segmented or 
hierarchically organized societies. Though entering into all social action it 

212 
David Nelken 
does so as only one (separable) aspect of it. It follows that it is in truth 
possible to examine the relationship between law and other features of 
society (Willke, 1987). Interestingly enough Gordon himself does admit 
that Luhmann's work marks an advance on existing approaches in sociology 
of law. In his view, "Autopoiesis provides a more elaborate metaphor for 
the law-society relationship than the unexpressive, neo-Marxist notion of 
relative autonomy" (Gordon, 1985: 2).5 This is because in his opinion the 
latter idea is only a negative rather than a positive explanation of the nature 
of legal autonomy. By contrast to this, Lempert explained that this theory 
could be seen as a reaction against earlier Marxist theories of the economic 
determination of law (so that for him "relative autonomy" is used as a 
poor synonym for "partial autonomy"). In these terms, his Anglo-American 
perspective could therefore be seen as a doubly negative theory by compari-
son with Luhmann's starting point. 
Having argued for the value of Luhmann's framework and questions, 
why not go all the way and also accept his answers? Perhaps, as some 
contributors undoubtedly assume, the really interesting and important 
problems only arise in applying the theory and drawing out its practical 
and political implications. I cannot follow this route because I have too 
many reservations about Luhmann's claims concerning the actual relation-
ships between law and society and sociology, both where these derive from 
his general systems theory as well as from autopoiesis theory more narrowly. 
And it is precisely the practical implications which he (and others) derive 
from some of these hypothesized relationships which make me want to 
pause and re-examine their theoretical force. 
Let us consider first Luhmann's approach to the relationship between 
"law" and "society". It is hard to deny that this suffers from all the defects 
of the neo-Parsonian functionalist and evolutionary scheme in which it is 
embedded. Like Parsons, Luhmann is consciously engaged in a process of 
re-writing and synthesizing Durkheim's ideas about functional interdepend-
ence in modern society with Weber's theorems on social action, rationality 
and legitimacy. But Luhmann also introduces characteristically original 
elements into Parsonian theory. Just as systems theory was used to reformu-
late Weber's approach to the way organizations control themselves and 
their environment, so autopoiesis theory is invoked to revise the notion 
of internal functional differentiation derived from Dürkheim. Luhmann 
also breaks with Parsons' argument that law provides normative integration 
5 For a sophisticated recent attempt to use the idea of "relative autonomy" to provide 
a new starting point for sociology of law, see De Sousa Santos (1985). Although 
Marxist in conception, it has some similarity to Luhmann's approach perhaps because 
being influenced by Althusser it shares a common derivation from Parsons. But De 
Sousa Santos is explicitly concerned to integrate legal pluralism into this theory, which 
Luhmann in his Rechtsso^tologie 
was disposed to dismiss. 

Changing Paradigms in the Sociology of Law 
213 
for the social system (see Bredemeier, 1962), challenging the idea that such 
integration is necessary or possible. But his more complex (and not always 
clear) explanation of how the legal sub-system maintains congruent expecta-
tions in a society without a center is still recognizably Parsonian. 
The difficulties of this functionalist mode of explanation are familiar 
enough, and Luhmann tries to deal with some of them. He insists that it 
is always possible to find "functional equivalents", and indeed argues that 
sociological "enlightenment" lies in the discovery of functional equivalents. 
He even applies this insight to the debate over de-legalization and the 
increasing resort to lay forums and mediation, arguing that this does not 
necessarily indicate any reduction in the function of law itself even though 
the forums themselves may be changing. At other times, however, 
Luhmann's arguments about the way law must function do seem to assume 
that legal institutions themselves must keep to their functions without 
allowing for the possibility that these could and would be achieved regard-
less (see especially Luhmann, 1985 d). Nor is it obvious that the functions 
Luhmann attributes to the legal sub-system must actually be achieved. 
According to his theory it would often be sufficient if the impression was 
successfully given that they were being achieved. This applies especially to 
his arguments about the need for law to handle certain contentious problems 
on behalf of politics. Luhmann fails to take his own arguments to the 
conclusion that law needs only to conceal its "political" resolution of political 
choices, not actually behave non-politically. 
These weaknesses of functional explanation matter because Luhmann 
draws important practical and political conclusions from his analysis of 
law's functions, warning of the dangers of functional de-differentiation if 
law should come to resemble politics in its concern for attaining predictable 
consequences. Such apparently prescriptive theorizing may or may not be 
justifiable.6 But it is regrettable that his view of law's functions does lead 
him to dismiss the manifest evidence of law's efforts to achieve such 
"result-oriented" outcomes. As Lempert rightly notes, Luhmann's approach 
is hard to square with legislative initiatives. But even adjudicative decisions 
are shaped by "policy" considerations or "goal-reasoning" and debates over 
the justifications of specific types of decision-making such as sentencing 
do not make sense if it is assumed that they cannot be concerned with 
outcomes. Luhmann makes two points in reply. He argues that the "val-
idity" of these decisions is not called into question by their predictive 
inadequacy and that the level of consequentialist reasoning employed by 
the courts is often primitive. But this cannot dislodge the need to explain 
why courts make attempts at such reasoning (which may improve under 
the influence of external influences such as the "law and economics" 
6 See the attempt to defend Weber from accusations of similar charges in Brubaker 
(1984). 

214 
David Nelken 
movement). Luhmann's criticisms of law's departure from its functions 
echo arguments that are sometimes heard in American or German jurisprud-
ence and constitutional law theorizing. But it might be more sociologically 
profitable to show how and why legal institutions succeed in fusing such 
apparently incompatible functions as adjudication and regulation. It is not 
always easy to follow why Luhmann sees some tendencies as irreconcilable 
and at other times embraces them as evidence of the paradoxal requirements 
of modernity. For Luhmann "the critique of law is the critique of social 
differentiations", but this seems to owe more to his preference for delegated 
decision-making, conditional programs and the rest, than to any inherent 
requirements of modern development. And even he admits that his proposi-
tions would not apply to a centrally organized (socialist) state. 
There are also difficulties about understanding (let alone accepting) 
Luhmann's revisions of the way we should view the relationship between 
"law" and "sociology." As the previous discussion of consequentialist 
reasoning might have suggested, another way of thinking about law and 
consequential reasoning is in terms of the various overlapping and contrast-
ing discourses which interact with law and on which law relies (see e. g., 
Fitzpatrick, 1984; Garland, 1985; Nelken, 1987). But Luhmann's approach 
is quite different from that of Foucault even if it is just as sensitive in its 
own way to the reflexivity of knowledge and the contingent status of 
"truth" and "justice" (see Murphy, 1984). Autopoiesis theory carries impli-
cations for the very form and focus of theorizing (see e.g., Heller, infra 
and Hutter, 1987). Yet the standpoint from which Luhmann's sociology of 
law is written is still not clear. Luhmann insists that the social theory of 
law has an essential part to play in explaining to law the nature of its 
autopoiesis and its limits (see Luhmann, 1985, conclusion to second edi-
tion). But if "law" cannot work these matters out for itself, how is it able 
to understand when the explanation comes from outside? There are also 
other difficulties of interpretation. Luhmann claims that the nature of law's 
autopoiesis lies in its distinctive normative elements (which allow it to 
remain "cognitively open"). But it is at least as arguable that the boundaries 
of law's understanding are set by its idiosyncratic way of knowing and 
categorizing the social world (cf. Nelken, 1987). Thus law is not cognitively 
open. The distinction "legal/illegal", upon which Luhmann lays such stress, 
hardly serves to capture the full range of law's normative vocabulary of 
rights, duties, permissions, obligations and so on. Moreover, as Teubner 
has shown, it offers little insight into law as a proto-social science interested 
in understanding and regulating and not only evaluating the social world 
(Teubner, 1985 a). 
It is possible that some of these difficulties reflect the cultural divide 
between common law and civilian legal traditions and practices. But even 
if that is true it limits the wider applicability of Luhmann's approach. A 
more generous assessment of Luhmann's contribution would be that these 

Changing Paradigms in the Sociology of Law 
215 
problems arise because of the effort to provide a sociological understanding 
of law's self-understanding. In any event it is proper to end on a positive 
note. For it would certainly count as sufficient evidence of paradigm change 
if theoretical debates in the sociology of law were now to be conducted 
within Luhmann's framework and around Luhmann's questions even if his 
own formulations and answers were to be subjected to criticism and 
revision. 
This is a considerably extended version of the paper of the same title presented at the 
Colloquium on Autopoiesis in Law and Society held at the European University Institute, 
Firenze, December 12 — 15, 1985. It attempts to take into account the revisions which 
Richard Lempert incorporated into his paper, partly as a result of the questions raised 
in mine (Nelken, infra), and I am grateful to him for allowing me to see the revised 
version of his paper in preparing my own.

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
GUNTHER TEUBNER 
Bremen/Firenze 
I. Evolution versus Regulation? 
Recently, the most striking change of direction in politics, social science 
and law has been the tendency to replace the concept of regulation by that 
of evolution. It is not only within the "de-regulation" movement that 
concepts of active guidance of society (Etzioni, 1968) are being renounced 
as constructivist interventionism and are being replaced by evolutionist 
concepts (Hayek, 1973; 1976; 1979). The legalization/delegalization debate 
calls into question the regulatory effectiveness of politically instrumenta-
lized law and tends to favor autonomous processes of social evolution (see 
Voigt 1980, 1983, 1984). And one of the most fascinating theoretical 
innovations in systems theory — self-reference and autopoiesis — is con-
siderably involved in this change of direction. From the outset, critics of 
ideology, as shown by their critical enquiries concerning legal concepts 
inspired by systems theory, emphasized the political instrumentability of 
such concepts (Reich, 1984; Nocke, 1986; Bercusson, 1987; Nahamowitz, 
1987). And the protagonists themselves seem to confirm this. For instance, 
Varela and Luhmann have both stated that the paradigm change from the 
theory of open systems to the theory of autopoietic systems provokes a 
change of emphasis from design and control to autonomy and environmen-
tal sensibility, from allonomy, external law, input/output, definition from 
the outside, to autonomy, internal regulation, closure, definition from the 
inside — in short, from planning to evolution (Varela, 1981 a: 14; 1981 b: 
36; Luhmann, 1984 b: 27). 
I am disputing these practical consequences of a theory. According to 
my dissenting view, autopoiesis does not necessitate the replacement of 
regulation by evolution, but it does however necessitate a definite reformu-
lation of both concepts. I will develop this reformulation in three stages. 
Using an outline of the paradigmatic alterations which the concept of 
autopoiesis necessarily brings to conceptions of systems theory, I have first 
of all to clarify what evolutionary results must be reached so that the legal 
system is not only differentiated as an independent system, but so that it 

218 
Gunther Teubner 
also gains its autonomy in the sense of autopoietic self-reproduction. In 
other words, what does the concept of autopoiesis add to the theory of 
functional differentiation of the legal system? With regard to this point I 
intend to make use of the idea of the "hypercycle" (Eigen and Schuster, 
1979). For legal autopoiesis, it is not sufficient that the legal system 
constitute legal acts as emergent elements. Instead, the concept of legal 
autonomy needs to be gradualized. Autonomization of law means the 
cumulation of self-referential relations in various legal dimensions. Only 
after the cyclical self-constitution of all components of the legal system — 
elements, structures, processes, boundaries, etc. — can those components 
be linked up in a hypercycle. It is the constitution of such a hypercycle 
that produces autopoietic closure. As a result, the cycle of legal communica-
tion — legal structure — legal communication is set into motion and 
becomes independent from the general societal cycle of communication. 
In the second stage I will ask: how does autopoietic closure affect the 
evolution of the law? If we regard law as being autopoietically organized, 
how then must we revise the present theory of legal evolution? My 
tentative answer is that the essential consequence of legal autopoiesis is the 
internalization of the evolutionary mechanisms. 
The third stage leads finally from evolution to regulation — to the 
problem of regulation of society by law. The historical relationship of "law 
and society" must, in my view, be defined as a co-evolution of structurally 
coupled autopoietic systems. Concepts of guidance must build upon such 
co-evolutive structural changes in order to be realistic. This leads us to a 
concept of guidance by law which is defined as the controlled structural change 
of autopoietic systems. 
II. Autopoiesis in Society and Law 
1. Innovations in Systems Theory 
Systems theory owes a great deal of its success and dynamics to the fact 
that it viewed systems as open to the environment and adaptive (Buckley, 
1967; 1968). In overcoming the former conception of systems as closed, 
windowless monads, systems theory made it possible to bring into the 
foreground the interaction between systems and their environments and in 
particular the dependence of systems on their environments. From neo-
Darwinism in the theory of evolution to the contingency theory in soci-
ology of organization (Lawrence and Lorsch, 1967 a; 1967 b; 1969), a 
paradigm was established whereby the environment sets the conditions 
according to which systems orient themselves and to which they have to 
adapt themselves as well as possible in order to be "successful", i. e., to 
survive. Viewed within the framework of open, adaptive systems, it was a 
matter of fact that systems could be changed, regulated and even determined 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
219 
by environmental influences. Flexibility and adaptability were necessary 
features of systems in order to conform to altered environmental condi-
tions — by internal changes in the system processes or even by qualitative 
changes in the functional regime in ultra-stable systems. This meant the 
following, regarding the possibility of regulating social systems: on the 
one hand, it involved building a high level of flexibility into the systems 
which had to be regulated, and on the other hand, it involved giving the 
regulating actors (leadership, management, government) the possibility of 
direct intervention by defining environmental constraints. 
Now it is important first of all to see that this paradigm of environmen-
tally open, adaptive systems is clearly a cognitive progress. That the 
environment has an effect on systems — whether these be organisms or 
organizations — is indisputable. It is obvious that politics and administra-
tion — by means of law — affect nearly all areas of society. This, however, 
in the meantime has also led to increased criticism of the "juridification" 
not only of all societal subsystems, but also of the "life-world" (Voigt, 
1983, 1984; Habermas 1984; Kübler, 1984; Teubner, 1987 b). 
The paradigm of open systems, the difference between system and 
environment, orients thinking to a great degree towards ideas and concepts 
such as input-output relations, adaptation to the environment, structural 
changes as a rudimentary process of system transformation, reinstatement 
of a disturbed equilibrium by control and regulation, or the "rational" 
system organization achieving results in the environment. Instrumental 
rationality, control, management, structural change and system equilibrium 
became the guiding concepts of political strategies of reform which were 
intended to produce definite changes in various social areas by means of 
law. This was based on an understanding of law as a means of direct 
intervention in social systems, comparable with an analogous understanding 
of other social media — power, knowledge, technology, etc. — as a means 
for purposeful intervention in adaptive, open systems. 
While interventions of this kind do produce effects, it became increas-
ingly clear that these effects in the social systems concerned were different 
from those which were expected: sometimes too slight, sometimes too 
strong, sometimes only effective for a short period, sometimes counter-
productive and frequently somehow "swallowed" by the system (see Teub-
ner, 1984a; 1985b; 1987b). Guilty parties were quickly found: too much 
policy or too little policy, too much law or too little law, deficiencies in 
implementation and overreactions, the wrong instruments and processes 
which were no longer adequate — until finally the main guilty party 
remained; that is, traditional reform policy and traditional direct purpose-
oriented intervention (see Görlitz and Voigt, 1985). 
It is perhaps not pure chance that a theoretical paradigm attracted 
increasing attention in this situation, at the center of which was the 
concept of self-organisation (Jantsch, 1980). The further development of this 

220 
Gunther Teubner 
paradigm as far as the theory of autopoietic systems (Maturana and Varela, 
1975; 1980; Varela, 1979; Zeleny, 1980; 1981 b; Roth and Schwegler, 1981) 
in this respect initially seems absurd, when the model of a closed system, 
which was thought to be a thing of the past, seems to celebrate a comeback. 
For the theory of self-referential systems assumes that systems with a certain 
level of complexity gain their identity through the fact that they refer to 
themselves in all their operations and processes. This means that systems 
can only bring about their continuous self-reproduction by having recourse 
to themselves, i. e., only in a form in which the operations of the system 
reproduce in a circular way the elements of the system, its structures and 
processes, its boundary and the overall unity of the system. 
This conception of self-referential systems presupposes that systems do 
not seek the fixed points of their mode of operation in the environmental 
conditions, to which they adapt themselves as best as possible (as in the 
paradigm of open systems), but in themselves; more precisely, in a self-
description which, as an internal regulation program, organizes the system 
processes in such a way that it corresponds to this self-description in its 
operations and consequently produces itself continuously by means of its 
operations. This interplay of self-description and operation presupposes 
that the basic molecular and biochemical structures of these capacities 
appear explicable at least in outline (Zeleny, 1981 a: 91 ff.). However, finding 
their equivalents in systems of meaning is by no means a simple process. 
However, it does at least seem to be clear that self-referentiality always 
occurs when complex processes revert to the production of their initial 
conditions hyper-cyclically (Eigen and Schuster, 1979) or ultra-cyclically 
(Ballmer and von Weizsäcker, 1974) and as a result become independent of 
their environment in this process. In this sense, self-referentiality leads to 
"organizational closure" (Varela, 1981 b: 37), to recursive, self-reproductive 
processes in a system. 
The question then, of course, is: what evolutionary advantage or stabiliz-
ing effect could self-referentiality have in comparison with the alternative 
of open systems? There is one possible answer in quite fundamental 
terms; namely, that without self-referentiality, without "basic circularity" 
(Maturana and Varela, 1980: 9) and organizational isolation the stabilization 
of self-containing systems is not possible. Only the recursive closure of a 
process which refers exclusively to itself in its operations makes possible 
the independent reconstruction of this total process according to inherent 
rules of regulation. A self-referential system appears dependent and free of 
influence from its environment in these rules, and must be so, because 
otherwise its own continual maintenance and reproduction would be de-
pendent on the environment and consequently on chance, rather than on the 
necessities of recursively organized systematic operations. (The overview of 
historical development given by Zeleny, 1981 a: 91 ff. is informative on 
this point.) Only the systemically organized connection and selection of 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
221 
operations (drawn up into a program of regulation as self-description) can 
stabilize that highly improbable complex process, which as autopoiesis 
(Maturana and Varela, 1980) forms the basis of living systems. 
2. Legal Autopoiesis? 
The difficulties of transferring the paradigm of self-referential systems to 
social phenomena are considerable (Beer, 1975; Zeleny and Pierre, 1976; 
Luhmann, 1981; 1984 b; 1985 a; 1987; Hejl, 1982 a; 1982 b; 1985; Zolo,1987; 
Teubner and Willke, 1984; Ulrich and Probst, 1984; Teubner, 1985 a; 1987 c; 
Haferkamp and Schmid, 1987). The problems arise in particular from the 
uncertainty as to whether one should think from the point of view of the 
autopoiesis of life (Hejl, 1982 a; 1982 b) and therefore consider societies as 
biological "systems of coupled human beings" (Maturana, 1980: 118), or 
not, and how strictly one conceptualizes the term of production (Varela, 
1981 b: 38). In this respect I am following Luhmann's highly sophisticated 
attempt to conceptualize societies as autopoietically organized systems of 
communication (Luhmann, 1984 b), and pose the question which follows 
from this idea: whether one can consider the differentiated functional 
system of law as being autopoietically organized within the autopoietic 
system of society (cf. Luhmann, 1984 a; supra: 12; Teubner and Willke, 
1984; Ladeur, 1984; infra). Alongside social autopoiesis, and building itself 
upon this, can one conceive of an independent legal autopoiesis? 
In the general theory of autopoiesis, Maturana has examined in greater 
detail this question of how autopoietic systems are intertwined in various 
levels of order and has made some interesting distinctions (Maturana 1980: 
107 ff.). In my opinion, however, it is necessary to make a crucial correction 
to his views. On the basis of an autopoietic system, a second-order 
autopoietic system can only develop if and when it produces its own 
components itself in the strictest sense; whereby — and this is the guiding 
factor — these self-produced components are not identical to the first-
order autopoietic system itself nor to the components of that system. In 
other words: higher order autopoiesis necessitates emergent phenomena. 
There must be new and different self-referential circles that form the basis 
for a higher order autopoietic system. In the case of the law that means 
that an autopoietic closure can only occur when a legal system which is 
already autonomous to a certain degree constitutes its own elements — the 
legal acts — which trigger off legal changes and hence initiate the auto-
poietic circulation of: legal act — legal change — legal act (Luhmann, 
supra: 16). Somewhat overstated, only the legal "invention" of legal action 
establishes the autonomy of law. However, this is only a necessary, not yet 
a sufficient condition of legal autopoiesis. Not only legal acts as elements 
of the legal system must be self-constituted, but every component of the 
legal system. For this purpose it is necessary to distinguish between self-

222 
Gunther Teubner 
constitution of system components by the system and their 
self-reproduction. 
It is one thing when a system constitutes its components, i. e., when it 
defines self-referentially its elements, structures and processes as units and 
uses them operatively. It is another thing if the system reproduces itself in 
the sense that elements produce structures and vice versa. We can think of 
systems which constitute their components without having those compo-
nents produce each other recursively. In order to make a self-reproductive 
cycle possible, the components must be compatibilized with each other. In 
other words, apart from the elements, also structures, processes, boundaries, 
and environments need to be cyclically self-constituted in such a congruent 
manner that they can be coupled to each other in a hypercycle. 
In this relation between self-constitution and self-reproduction lies the 
key for an adequate understanding of legal autonomy. When legal communi-
cations specialize in relation to general social communications, they inevit-
ably will have to be applied to themselves: legal communication thematizes 
legal communication in legal terms. This leads to emergent phenomena of 
self-reference, to "vicious circles" and "virtuous circles", to tautologies, 
contradictions, infinite regresses and paradoxes (Varela, 1979; 1981a: 19). 
The most important consequence, however, is that law begins to describe 
its own components in legal categories. It is the legal system and not its 
political, economic, and social environment that defines the premises for 
the validity of a legal act, or a legal rule. The law regulates its own 
operations, structures, processes, boundaries, and identity reflexively. Thus, 
legal acts, legal rules, legal procedures, and legal doctrines emerge as self-
referential phenomena. Their self-referentiality is the very foundation of 
legal autonomy. 
In order to grasp the full meaning of legal autonomy, one needs to give 
up the idea of "all or nothing" (Luhmann, 1987). Of course, circularity 
exists or does not exist — there is no such thing as half-circularity. Yet 
autonomy can be seen as a gradualized concept. It increases with the 
cumulation of self-referential circular relations within a system. Under 
certain conditions this cumulation leads to the circular reproduction of the 
whole system. 
I will assume the following stages of legal autonomization: (1) The 
starting point is social conflict. Not every institutionalized conflict solution 
should be identified with law. In particular, the ending of conflict by 
oppression, assertion on the basis of sheer power, mediation, arbitration, 
pure compromise, etc., are still non-legal forms of solving conflict. (2) 
Law — however socially diffuse — only appears when three conditions 
are fulfilled: when (a) social conflicts are defined as differences between 
expectations which require a decision; (b) conflicts are solved when one of 
the diverging expectations is defined as socially "valid"; and therefore (c) 
a definite mode of behavior is declared to be "correct". Such a law is, 
however, still produced allopoietically, i. e., by processes external to the 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
223 
law. For the production of an expectation relies upon mechanisms outside 
the law, be they socially diffuse communications in which social norms are 
produced; power processes, when the expectations of the superior are 
declared to be binding; religion, when norms are declared to be willed by 
God; morals, when norms are valid because they are considered to be 
"good"; or truth, when cognition produces law. (3) A certain functional 
differentiation of the law occurs at the point when legal communications 
specialize thematically; that is, when the distinction between legal right 
and wrong becomes independent from other distinctions and gradually 
becomes universal. However even this does not yet signify the self-referen-
tial production of law and the autopoietic closure of the legal system. (4) 
Self-referentiality only emerges when the legal system itself constitutes anew its 
own components (i.e., elements, structures, processes, boundaries, environ-
ments) which are different from general societal system components. (5) 
Autopoiesis in the strict sense emerges when those cyclically constituted 
components are constituted congruently so that they are linked up to a 
hypercycle. The result is a self-reproductive circle of act-norm-act. The 
concept of autogenesis has been introduced to describe this transition to 
autopoiesis (Zeleny, 1981 b). The concept is so important because it deals 
with the problem of how self-reproductive processes come into being in 
the first place. Zeleny deals with this problem using the example of life, 
but his thoughts are applicable to the emergence of other autopoietic 
systems, also in particular to the emergence of the legal system as an 
autonomous system. 
It is important to see that the products of an autopoietic system and 
even the processes of production can exist initially without a full-fledged 
autopoietic organization. Both of them can be constituted self-referentially, 
however, without producing each other. Only when these products and 
producing processes are organized in a certain complementary way does 
autopoiesis emerge; namely at the point when the processes of production 
produce the product and the product produces the processes of production. 
With regard to law, this means that law as an ordering of expectations, as 
well as a legal system as communications concerning law, can exist without 
the process of the production of law already being organized autopoietically. 
Law can be produced from many possible societal communications and 
communications about law are possible without them producing new law. 
Specialization in a function (conflict solution, formation of expectations, 
behavioral regulation) or the formation of a code of media (the distinction 
between legal right and wrong) are necessary but insufficient conditions 
for the autopoietic organization of the legal system. In addition, there must 
evolve a hypercyclical structure, the products must produce such a network 
of conditions that a new legal production emerges from it. The point is 
that this circularity can only come about when legal acts, legal norms, 
legal procedures and legal doctrine are self-referentially constituted in a 

224 
Gunther Teubner 
congruent manner. The premise for the self-reproduction of the whole 
legal system is the self-referential constitution of the components. For legal 
norms this is nothing new. H. L. A. Hart's "secondary norms" (1961: 
77 ff.) is a famous example for such a self-referential constitution. Via 
secondary norms the law produces an internal self-description. By constitut-
ing rules for the identification and creation of norms, the law creates its 
own norm-creating structures. It does not matter if secondary norms refer 
to internal legal processes or refer to social norms or religious revelation. 
What is decisive in all these cases is the autonomous "self-indication". 
However, secondary norms are only one among many instances of legal 
self-constitution of its components. The same holds true for legal acts. 
Whatever criteria the legal discourse is using for the definition of the legal 
act, the important thing is that it is nothing but legal communication that 
selects legal acts from the variety of social acts and events. One needs to 
extend this idea to legal procedure and legal doctrine. Both become self-
referential when the legal discourse selects certain procedures and certain 
reality constructs as legal ones. 
But even if legal systems in part or entirely self-constitute their system 
components, they are not yet autopoietic in Maturana's sense. Self-repro-
duction of law emerges only when legal rules produce legal acts and vice 
versa and legal procedure and legal doctrine reproduce each other mutually. 
It is only once self-description and self-constitution of the law's components 
have in this way created the necessary pre-conditions for hypercyclical 
coupling that the actual production of legal communication from legal 
communication via the network of legal expectations, controlled by doctrine 
and procedure, can begin. 
One special case of self-constitution is of interest for our purposes: when 
the rules of recognition refer no longer to extra-legal sources but to other 
internal components of the legal system. Only once legal rules are no 
longer defined by religious revelation or as resulting from the nature of 
man, but as products of legal acts (contract, legislation) they become part 
of an internal self-reproductive cycle. Vice versa, when legal acts are defined 
as the product of legal rules, the cyclical relation between rule and act is 
completed. Likewise, only once legal procedures are defined as internal 
processes of rule-production and legal doctrine as the system of relations 
between rules and acts, then the legal system as a whole takes on a self-
reproductive character. 
The circularity of the production process therefore plays a decisive role. 
In an allopoietic legal system, legal communications would have to be 
produced in the context of general societal communications just as legal 
norms would have to develop in general societal processes of communica-
tion. Legal autopoiesis occurs only at the point when both mutually 
produce each other. 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
225 
III. Autopoiesis and the Evolution of Law 
If we understand the autonomy of law as its autopoietic self-closure, what 
does this signify for the evolution of law? In particular, how do we interpret 
the development of law dependent on societal conditions, if changes in 
law now only proceed on a circular, self-referential and closed basis? 
1. Legal Evolution Today 
Before we attempt to answer these questions, we should clear up some 
misunderstandings concerning a concept of legal evolution which is sup-
portable today. In recent years, evolutionary concepts have been used 
increasingly to explain legal developments (Luhmann; 1970; 1985 a; 1985 b; 
Eder, 1976; 1978; 1985; 1986; Habermas, 1979; 1985; Unger, 1976; Rubin, 
1977; Priest, 1977; Nonet and Selznick, 1978; Brüggemeier, 1980; 1982; 
Tugendhat, 
1980; Hirshleifer, 
1982; Teubner, 
1983; Zemen, 
1983; 
Rottleuthner, 1985; 1986; Watson, 1985; Wesel, 1985). This has triggered 
criticism and provoked misunderstandings which stand in the way of a 
fruitful application of the concept of evolution to legal phenomena (Fried-
man, 1975: 279 ff.; Gordon, 1984; Blankenburg, 1984). The misunderstand-
ings are essentially founded on the burdens which have riddled the concept 
of evolution since the 19th century and which affect its normative-analytical 
status, its range of explanations and the model elements contained within. 
I propose that the burdens can be removed only by withdrawing claims 
which are too far-reaching in all these dimensions. 
The criticism is greatest where it is certain — in the criticism of normative 
implications of legal evolution. The "spectre of evolution" is conjured up 
in developmental logic and phase models which threaten the neat separation 
between empirically-based theory and normative projections (Blankenburg, 
1984: 273). Nevertheless one should not adhere to the wrongly-posed 
alternatives of description versus prescription. My answer to the question 
of practical orientation of action versus theoretical explanation is: both 
are acceptable, not concurrently, but according to system context, be it 
sociological analysis or reflection in legal theory. 
In any case the compact syndrome of the old evolutionist concept must 
be broken up. Progress and natural causation, necessity, irreversibility, 
unilinearity and directionality must be separated from the analytical core 
of evolution theory. The distinction between "evolutionist" and "evolution-
ary" makes the problem clear (Toulmin, 1972: 321 ff.; van Parijs, 1981: 
51 f.; Bühl, 1984: 302). Evolutionist concepts, in which a certain direction 
is attributed to processes of change (e. g., progress, stages of development, 
perfection) are not under discussion. With regard to such evolutionist 
concepts well-founded doubts arise, especially in view of their unexplained 
normative-analytical status (see Friedman, 1975: 287 ff.). This becomes 

226 
Gunther Teubner 
more difficult however with regard to evolutionary concepts which are not 
based on the direction of development but on mechanisms of development. 
I am referring in particular here to filter mechanisms and trial and error 
mechanisms (e. g., Nozick, 1974: 314 ff.). What we are discussing therefore 
is not evolutionist models of law which are directed by a mysterious 
normative logic, but evolutionary models of law in which certain identifi-
able mechanisms regulate legal development by means of their filter effect. 
It would be relatively difficult to identify normative projections in such 
models (Blankenburg, 1984: 284). 
This conceptual limitation makes it possible to clarify the theoretical and 
practical application of legal evolution. In the sociological discourse and 
in the legal discourse, legal evolution can be applied differently. Such a 
refined concept of evolution can be used in a legal sociological sense as a 
pattern of explanation for major trends of development in the law. At the 
same time, however, a concept of evolution as "more or less empirical 
theory with a practical purpose" (Rottleuthner, 1986: 222) can become of 
practical importance in law if it is taken up in legal theory in "strategic 
legal concepts" (Teubner, 1985 a: 301). I would like to question whether this 
strengthens the normative projections. Conceptions of "blind" interaction 
between legal evolutionary mechanisms clearly tend to put a damper on 
hopes for legal progress. 
I think that a theory of legal evolution has great analytical and practical 
power if it withdraws its extensive explanatory claims and returns to pure 
pattern predictions (Hayek, 1967: 22; Luhmann, 1975: 152; 1983: 193). 
Evolution theory is concerned with the question — and should be limited 
to it — of how systems develop filter mechanisms which guarantee the 
stabilization of structural patterns selected from blind variations and conse-
quently regulate the development of systems. Structural patterns, however, 
are not sufficient to predict individual events. Here explanations must be 
added which represent "chances" from the standpoint of evolution theory. 
Causal analyses of another kind must take place. A theory of legal evolution 
will therefore only be in the position to explain general structural patterns 
of the legal system, but not individual legal events, court verdicts, laws 
and acts of administration. The current reproach against theories of legal 
evolution that they can contribute nothing to the explanation of concrete 
legal phenomena (Gordon, 1984: 81; Rottleuthner, 1986: 217) misunder-
stands evolutionary explanations two-fold, by simultaneously overestimat-
ing and underestimating them. Structural predictions are no less important 
than predictions of events, so far as their explanatory usefulness is concerned 
as well as their practical relevance. At the same time, such a withdrawal of 
extensive explanatory claims clearly relativizes the criticism of "evolutionary 
functionalism" in law, like for instance that recently and impressively 
formulated by Gordon (1984). 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
227 
The main point of Gordon's criticism is that actual developments are 
reinterpreted as functional necessities. Legal forms are the necessary answer 
to societal requirements. Here there must be a fundamental misunderstand-
ing. The thing about neo-evolutionism is particularly that it reconstructs 
reality from the perspective of functional equivalents, from non-necessary, 
contingent alternatives. It is modern equivalence functionalism especially 
which produces contingency consciousness, the consciousness of historical 
alternatives which Gordon so urgently demands (cf. Luhmann, 1982; 
Teubner, 1983). Gordon's perspective is to point to the submerged "human" 
progressive alternatives in order to make them available again for political 
action. That is a commendable normative perspective. The question is 
only whether equivalence functionalism makes available better analytical 
instruments than good political intentions. An elaborated system of con-
cepts which permits comparisons and judgments on various alternatives 
relating to solutions of problems, resultant problems and side effects seems 
to me to be more fruitful than the critical complaint concerning submerged 
or repressed discourses. 
In fact, the idea of submerged discourses must be generalized by dissolv-
ing the causal relationship between society and law into contingent require-
ments and contingent solutions of problems. This was exactly the starting-
point for modern equivalence functionalism and in this it has proved 
itself — functional equivalence of solutions to a problem and multi-
functionality of problem solutions. Furthermore it must be made clear that 
every functional solution of a problem for its part can be defined as a 
problem again and that the choice of problems is contingent. All this, 
however, is not criticism of evolutionary functionalism, but rather forms 
the basis of it. 
Gordon also criticizes the fact, concerning customary causal models of 
law and society, that comparative studies have continually shown that 
societal causes and societal effects of law vary considerably despite similar 
conditions at the beginning. Whether one can criticize evolutionary func-
tionalism as a result — as Gordon does — seems questionable in view 
of the contingency consciousness of equivalence functionalism. Certainly, 
however, this should be taken as an argument for the relative autonomy 
of the legal system and even more so as an argument for uncontrolled 
mutual effects of self-reproductive social systems. 
In conclusion Gordon poses the important question whether it is not 
more appropriate to replace broad functionalist explanations by concrete 
explanations of developments by interests and strategies of interest groups. 
The system's theoretical answer to this is: do not replace, but supplement. 
Two different levels of societal differentiation are involved, as well as two 
levels of analysis. On the level of concrete interactions, particularly in the 
political system, legal norms can adequately be explained as the result of 
processes of power and decision-making by various interests and interest 

228 
Gunther Teubner 
groups. Concerning these findings, the question arises as to whether and 
how far these legal norms represent functional solutions to social problems. 
At the same time, important interactions between these modes of explana-
tion can be assumed. In particular, an analysis should be made of how far 
social structures and functions affect and delimit political strategies. 
2. Mechanisms of Legal and Societal Evolution 
What does the seed of evolution theory consist of — a seed which even 
today carries responsibility? The following three conceptions of this seed 
should be released from the fruitless shells of legal progress, normative 
developmental logic, universal history of law, etc.: (1) the "blind" interac-
tion of the evolutionary mechanisms: variation, selection and retention; (2) 
the combination of ontogenetic and phylogenetic development; (3) the co-
evolution of the law, society, and other social subsystems. If this seed of 
evolution is planted in the field of autopoiesis — and this is where I see 
my task — then we have some hopes for a good harvest. 
It is thanks to Campbell that biological analogies of evolution have 
become fruitful for social science. Socio-cultural evolution is possible when 
within socio-cultural units definite social mechanisms can be identified 
which guarantee the separation and the interaction of three universal 
functions of evolution: variation, selection and retention (Campbell, 1969; 
1970; 1974; 1975; 1980). These thoughts have been continued by Luhmann. 
With regard to the evolution of law, he suggested that the functions of 
evolution be carried out by clearly defined legal mechanisms (Luhmann, 
1970; 1983). In the legal system, normative structures take over variation, 
institutional structures (especially procedures) take over selection, and 
doctrinal structures take over retention. 
This is a decisive step to get rid of the legacy of social Darwinism which 
has discredited evolutionary thought for a long time. Apart from normative 
hypostatization of evolution, the main difference between a renewed evolu-
tionism and social Darwinism concerns the unit of evolution. Evolving 
units are not, as social Darwinism has it, human individuals and their 
aggregates, groups, organizations, nations, races, but socio-cultural phe-
nomena. Ideas, customs, organizational forms form the material which is 
produced and transformed by socio-cultural evolutionary filter mechanisms. 
Furthermore, the selection mechanism for social evolution is by no means 
the survival of the fittest in a merciless struggle for life. Rather, this is an 
extreme and improbable borderline case. Evolutionary normality is the co-
existence of a rich variety of viable socio-cultural phenomena. 
It is likewise the evolving unit which defines the main difference between 
socio-cultural theories of evolution and sociobiology. One of the main 
contributions of sociobiology was to redefine the evolving unit. Neither 
the individual nor the group but the "selfish" gene has been identified as 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
229 
the evolutionary material. On this basis, otherwise inexplicable patterns of 
social behavior, especially altruistic behavior, could be explained in an 
evolutionary framework (Wilson, 1978; Dawkins, 1976; Hamilton, 1978; 
Meyer, 1982). The main problem is that sociobiology short-circuits biologi-
cal and social evolution and thus fails to take account of the autonomy of 
social systems and their evolution. Social autopoiesis insists on the emergent 
property of social and legal communication systems. To be sure, they can 
exist only on the basis of an organic and psychic materiality continuum, but 
in their operations they are self-referentially closed. Accordingly biological 
mechanisms of evolution cannot determine social and legal development. 
Evolution in the social and legal sphere can occur only once the mechanisms 
of variation, selection and retention emerge as communicative mechanisms. 
The unit of social evolution which is shaped through evolutionary filter 
mechanisms is thus neither the human individual, nor a social aggregate 
of human individuals, nor the "selfish" gene, but society and law as systems 
of social communication. This is not to exclude mutual influences between 
social evolution and biological evolution. However, they are conceivable 
only as interactions between autonomously and self-referentially evolving 
systems and not as an integrated "bio-cultural" evolution, as a co-determina-
tion by biological and social forces (e. g., Bühl, 1984: 305). Co-evolution 
of organic and social systems means first of all autonomy and closure. And 
it is only "structural coupling" (Maturana and Varela, 1980) that allows for 
an indirect mutual influence. 
However, as promising a theory of socio-cultural evolution seems it to 
be, it has to cope with one major problem: how to determine social identity 
in continual social change stimulated by the dynamics of evolution. This 
problem appears in three different versions. First, the phenomenon of 
"stasis" is a permanent challenge to evolution theory (Wake et al., 1983). 
If cultural phenomena like the law are exposed to the permanent pressure 
of environmental selection, how can one account for the undeniable fact 
that certain structures of the law remain stable for centuries? A similar 
point has always been raised against evolutionary functionalism. How can 
social systems maintain their "identity" despite evolutionary transformation 
(Habermas, 1973: 11)? Related to this is the question: how does one explain 
that the relation between social developments and legal developments is 
under-determined? Gordon (1984: 100 ff.) backs his critique of evolutionism 
with the statement: "... that comparable social conditions ... have generated 
contrary legal responses, and comparative legal forms have produced con-
trary social effects". And "legal forms and practices don't shift with every 
realignment of the balance of political forces". How can a post-Darwinian 
evolutionism cope with these problems? 
Obviously, evolving social systems must have a higher potential of 
autonomy from external influences than the theory of selective environmen-
tal pressures suggests. Evolution must be more than a "meandering process 

230 
Gunther Teubner 
almost entirely shaped by environmental contingencies, rather than insu-
lated from them" (Campbell, 1969: 70). But how can one account for this 
evolutionary autonomy? Campbell considers solutions according to which 
the internal process of organization — the "organizational 'reality'" — 
itself is the selector for stability or change. However, its "undesirable 
circularity" is his reason to abandon this solution. It is thus the taboo of 
circularity which blocks the view to the most promising solutions of stasis 
and identity: the solution of self-referentiality. 
It is the very autonomy of normative phenomena which induces Ha-
bermas (1979; 1984) to develop a combination of two evolution models. 
The identity of the moral-normative sphere in society and its autonomous 
evolution, Habermas maintains, cannot be sufficiently analyzed by post-
Darwinian evolution models which use the interplay of variation, selection 
and retention. Thus Habermas supplements the system/environment model 
of evolutionary functionalism with a model of "rational reconstruction" 
which describes autonomous learning processes in the cultural-normative 
sphere. He uses theories of moral ego development in the tradition of Piaget 
and Kohlberg and translates them from individual into social context. 
The "evolutionary dynamics" of basic social structures is exposed to an 
"evolutionary logic" of normative structures, the law being one among 
them. From this interplay of two diverse processes of evolution follows a 
sequence of "social organization principles" which are characterized by 
irreversibility, structured hierarchy and evolutionary directedness. 
Admittedly the autonomous logics of legal development would resolve 
the above-mentioned problems of "stasis", social identity and evolutionary 
autonomy. However, the model of normative eigenlogics gives up the 
advantages of modern evolutionism described above. Habermas' rational 
reconstruction is basically a new variant of an embryological developmental 
model: "the evolution from an 'indefinite incoherent homogeneity to a 
definite coherent heterogeneity' takes place as a result of internal dynamics, 
... as an orderly, progressive, goal-directed unfolding" (Campbell, 1969: 
70). And the question what mechanisms achieve the transfer from individual 
ego development to the development of social morality remains unanswered 
(cf. Bühl, 1984: 319 ff.). 
The "early" Luhmann (1970; 1983) came up with another attempt to 
solve the problem of evolutionary autonomy of law. He multiplies the 
interplay of evolutionary mechanisms by introducing various system refer-
ences. Evolutionary mechanisms work "endogenously" as well as "exogen-
ously". They work in the interplay of rules, institutions and doctrine within 
the law and their determination by analogue mechanisms in other social 
subsystems. 
Societal-legal evolution is therefore hallmarked by the interaction be-
tween these "endogenous" mechanisms of legal evolution on the one hand, 
and the "exogenous" evolution of the societal environment on the other. 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
231 
And in fact the endogenous evolution of the law is influenced systemically 
by exogenous developments in such a way that definite organizational 
principles of the whole society variably increase and decrease the relative 
weight of the endogenous mechanisms (norms, procedures, dogmatics) and 
therefore externally influence the inner dynamics of the legal system. The 
law is adapted to various developmental stages of societal differentiation 
in such a way that the dominant organizational principle of society (segmen-
tation, stratification, functional differentiation) creates typical configur-
ations in the legal system and at the same time specific "bottlenecks" of 
legal evolution. 
In segmented societies, which distinguish themselves by a lack of alterna-
tives, the evolutionary challenge to "archaic law" is to produce a sufficient 
variety of normative structures. This problem of variety is only solved in 
stratified societies with a differentiated hierarchical order. While they are 
in the position to create a greater wealth of norms, however, the law of 
highly cultivated, pre-modern societies is exposed to problems of selection. 
In the end, functionally differentiated societies are hallmarked by a huge 
over-production of norms. "Positive law" may have for its part overcome 
the selection problem with the institutionalization of highly developed 
legal proceedings, adjudication and legislation, yet it only has insufficient 
stabilization mechanisms at its disposal in the conventional dogmatic-
conceptual structures. 
The problem with this model is that it still works with the assumptions 
of open systems theory. Environmental evolution in this view is directly 
influencing legal evolution, even if filtered through the internal mecha-
nisms. Thus, it cannot cope with the problems of stasis, system identity 
and evolutionary autonomy. 
3. The Turn Toward Autopoiesis 
Is the theory of autopoiesis in a position to solve these problems? This is 
what autopoieticists maintain for the general theory of evolution (Roth, 
1982; 1984; Wake et al., 1984). The autopoiesis of a system is a limit to 
evolution. Autopoiesis defines the functional limits for any evolutionary 
change. "Stasis", system identity, and evolutionary autonomy can be ex-
plained by the autopoietic closure of a system: the system can undergo any 
change, provided the circular organization is not interrupted. 
It has been pointed out in the general discussion on autopoiesis that it is 
necessary to revise the concept of evolution under conditions of autopoietic 
reproduction (Maturana, 1980: 11 f.; Roth, 1982; 1984). These authors 
criticize an orthodox neo-Darwinism which understands the process of 
development as if a system open to information willingly follows the 
instructions, i.e., the selective pressures of the environment. In the face of 
this, autopoietic organization is significant for selection. A self-reproductive 

232 
Gunther Teubner 
system defines tolerance limits for structural change by its organization of 
cyclical self-preservation. "The actual primacy of evolution ... is therefore 
the maintenance of internal cyclicity, not adaptation to the environment" 
(Roth, 1984: 5). 
I will take up this argument and intend to generalize it at the same time. 
What is being said here with regard to function and mechanism of 
selection 
should be extended to the corresponding contexts of variation 
and 
retention. 
My thesis: the emergence of autopoiesis signifies for the legal system a 
dynamic shift of the functions of evolution inwards; an internalization of 
the mechanisms for variation, selection and retention. More precisely, a 
central shift from "external" societal mechanisms of evolution to "internal" 
legal mechanisms is involved, in the sense that external 
mechanisms 
can only 
have a "modulating' 
e f f e c t on legal developments while the evolutionary 
primacy 
passes over to internal structural 
determination. 
In other words: only once the legal system reaches autopoietic closure 
can it become capable of autonomous evolution. It is precisely this point 
of autopoietic closure which marks the difference in regard to recent 
economic models of legal evolution. There are at least two versions. 
According to Hayek (1967: 32; 1979: 167) the interplay of cultural variation 
and selection creates spontaneous orders in which adequate legal rules 
emerge, in contrast to political processes that arbitrarily select rules and 
impose them on social order via a contructivist interventionism. The second 
version was developed in the context of the non-normative, positive version 
of Posner's question: "Is common law efficient?" Common law tends to 
produce (Pareto-) efficient legal rules due to processes of relitigation. As 
long as the legal system formulates a non-efficient distribution of property 
rights, it produces permanent incentives for religitation. This process comes 
to a standstill only once efficiency has been achieved (see for this discussion 
Rubin, 1977; Priest, 1977; Hirshleifer, 1982: 46 ff.). 
Both versions of an economic theory of legal evolution neglect systemati-
cally the autonomous role of the legal system evolving internally via diverse 
evolutionary filters. In both views, legal rules appear only as the selection 
product of genuinely economic processes without taking into account the 
autonomous potential of the legal process for variation of normative 
content, for selection via legal institutions according to their criteria and 
for stabilization by the legal culture. In Hayek's version this leads to an 
absurd over-evaluation of customary law and similar "spontaneous" orders 
and an under-evaluation of political legislation. And in Posner's version 
the result is that legal selectivity (access to justice) is not taken into account 
at all. 
In any case, autopoietic closure of the law makes it impossible to see 
legal evolution as the sheer product of social evolution or to localize the 
effective evolutionary mechanisms outside the law. Evolutionary models 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
233 
that tend to fuse social and legal development have a limited plausibility 
only for the pre-autopoietic stage of the legal system. 
If autopoiesis signifies the internalization of the three functions of 
evolution: variation, selection and retention, then this means that in a 
pre-autopoietic condition of law, all three functions are fixed in societal 
institutions and therefore are external to the legal system. The variation of 
law is singled out from the variation of general societal structures, especially 
from the social norm structures originating here. Social norms directly 
determine the variation potential of legal norms. The selection of legal 
norms is carried out in societal processes, that is, by societal approval of 
norms or in other words their recognition by society. Retention — that is, 
the passing on of law — is achieved by means of societal myths, doctrines, 
philosophies and ideologies. And as long as quasi-autonomous legal dogma-
tics develop, they must be anchored in natural law conceptions of society 
at large. 
After the emergence of autopoiesis, according to my thesis, these 
functions of evolution are internalized, i. e., taken over by internal mecha-
nisms. Evolution can then only be "triggered off' from outside, but no 
longer directly "caused". Henceforth it only follows one inner developmen-
tal logic — the logic of autopoiesis. 
Variation 
within an autopoietic subsystem can now only succeed when 
it is structurally determined within the subsystem. When the legal system 
is autopoietically closed then Maturana's formulation also applies to the 
possibilities for variation in the law: 
... that at any instant of its operation the structure of an autopoietic system specifies 
into what structural configuration it goes as a result of structural transition, regardless 
of whether this results from its internal dynamics or from its interaction with the 
medium. 
Social norms can then no longer be adopted directly into law. Processes 
outside the law can now only have a "modulating" effect on the production 
of legal variety (Willke, 1987). Societal conflicts trigger off internal legal 
processes; they modulate the legal formulation of norm conflicts, which in 
the end are responsible for legal innovations, but which have little in 
common with the social norm conflicts of the disputing parties. Hence the 
protest against "expropriation of conflicts" (Christie, 1976). Hence the 
motive for an idealistic de-legalization movement (Abel, 1982) and for 
"alternatives to law" (Blankenburg and Rottleuthner, 1980). Likewise in 
the law-making process it is not social interests which trigger off legal 
changes but only such social pressures as appear on the internal screens of 
the legal system which can have an innovative effect. The same is true for 
inventions in jurisprudence. Innovations in science in general can only 
become indirectly relevant to law when they can be formulated in the 
relevance criteria of legal dogmatics (see Heller, 1985: 183; Wiethölter, 
1986: 53 f.). 

234 
Gunther Teubner 
Similarly, legal selection is now carried out internally. Social approval of 
the norm is no longer the factor governing selection. The inner approval 
of the autopoiesis of law takes over this role. Out of the diverse expectations 
which are created within the legal system, the only expectations which can 
be fed into the internal legal circulation are those which are selected by 
legal actions — which are defined as being legally internal — as a change 
of the legal situation. The legal system itself defines the preconditions of 
a legal action and therefore its legal change as well. 
As regards the stabilizing function of retention, it is in the end true 
that in autopoietic systems system-internal mechanisms must be ready to 
guarantee retention. Its establishment in societal contexts — in moral, 
religious and political contexts — is increasingly being phased out in favor 
of internal references in the law: references to other conflict rulings, sets 
of norms, legal arguments, systematic concepts and autonomous dogmatics. 
4. Ontogeny and Phylogeny 
It seems to me important, particularly in the context of evolutionary 
stabilization, to introduce into the theory of legal evolution in addition the 
distinction between ontogenetic learning and phylogenetic evolution. I 
consider this distinction in a theory of the evolution of norms — as 
introduced by Habermas (Habermas, 1976: 12 ff., 63 ff.; 1979) - 
to be 
fruitful, but I believe that the ontogenetic unity should be defined dif-
ferently. It is not the moral development of the child, not the concrete 
human being which forms the ontogenetic counterpart of societal develop-
ment. Rather, the concrete interaction is the laboratory in which the experi-
ments of society take place. The problem posed by Habermas, to relate 
stages of child development to the development of social norms, would 
however in systems theory be a problem of the co-evolution of two 
interpenetrating systems, a problem which must be separated from the 
context of phylogeny and ontogeny. 
The interplay of phylogeny and ontogeny is therefore adopted, not 
however in the relationship of man and society, but in the relationship of 
individual interaction to the whole society (as well as to societal subsys-
tems). Stated in concrete terms it is found in the relationship of concrete 
legal proceedings to the whole legal system. Ontogenetic learning takes 
place in the interaction of the proceedings of adjudication, legislation, 
administration. In the proceedings there is sufficient variation and selection; 
retention is however limited to the "memory" of the interaction itself, that 
is, to the history of the concrete proceeding. Phylogenetic development — 
and consequently evolution — only occurs when mechanisms of retention 
intervene on the level of society as a whole or on the level of functional 
subsystems, and "bequeath" learning successes which have taken place in 
the laboratory experiment of the interaction. The difficult transitional 

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
235 
mechanism must first of all be constructed to make it possible, for instance, 
that insight gained in legal proceedings is adopted into legal doctrine and 
consequently into the "memory" of law. 
The mechanism at work can be called "coupling of episodes" (for details 
see Teubner, 1987 a). This mechanism is responsible for the evolutionary 
capacity of law, since it makes possible that legal selections can be stabilized 
beyond the particular legal episode. It is via this mechanism that learning 
within legal episodes becomes evolution of the legal system. 
Each single legal episode is in itself an autonomous social system. The 
particular legal proceeding uses the legal code, has a particular history, 
forms its peculiar structures. However, legal episodes are transitory, they 
need to be related to each other if a permanent legal system is to emerge. 
Coupling of episodes means that structures which have been built up within 
one legal episode can be utilized in future episodes. Rather primitive forms 
of this coupling use only the individual memory of the judge or the 
collective memory of the court, while highly developed forms of episode 
coupling are in themselves autonomous legal discourses that thematize the 
relation between cases, the validity and consistency of legal rules, the 
establishment of principles and the construction of legal concepts. Coupling 
of episodes makes two things possible. The particular legal episode is 
furnished with elaborate structures. At the same time it produces via 
conflict resolution through rules a normative "surplus" which can be 
exploited in future legal episodes. 
Thus, the interplay of phylogenetic and ontogenetic development in law 
can be conceived as the linkage of two communicative cycles. The particular 
legal proceeding is in a sense the laboratory of law in which variations are 
produced and selection tried out. This is linked to the second communica-
tive cycle which decides about the stabilization of legal selections in legal 
culture and legal tradition. The concept of legal validity refers to the 
circular relationship between these two cycles. Legal decisions in concrete 
proceedings make reference to recursively culturally stabilized legal rules 
which have been shaped by recursive reference to other concrete proceed-
ings. On the other hand, we have the initial starting point for new legal 
developments within the sphere of legal culture. 
5. Coevolution and Regulation 
Until now, autopoiesis has led to the impression of a total internalization 
and isolation of subsystems in their evolution. Of course, it would be 
misleading to exclude the environment from the evolutionary processes. 
The environmental reference in evolution however is produced not in the 
direct, causal production of legal developments, but in processes of co-
evolution. The thesis is as follows: In co-evolutionary processes it is not only 
the autopoiesis of the legal system which has a selective effect on the 

236 
Gunther Teubner 
development of its own structures; the autopoiesis of other subsystems and that 
of society also a f f e c t s — in any case in a much more mediatory and indirect 
way — the selection of legal changes. 
Again the relationship of phylogenetic and ontogenetic development is 
crucial for this "process symbiosis" (Jantsch, 1980). The concrete interac-
tion (in law — the legal proceedings) forms the strategic hinge of coevolu-
tion. Societal interactions as a rule do not participate only in the autopoietic 
circulation of a subsystem, but are 
mostly bound in to various system 
circulations. It is the individual legal proceeding, the individual decision-
making process in a company, the confrontation in the family, in which 
the expectations of various subsystems converge, complement each other, 
supplement each other and conflict with each other. In the individual 
interaction it is, as it were, negotiated which expectations establish the 
direction and can be combined into practical clusters of roles. The individual 
interaction also rules on the compatibility of various subsystem structures. 
For here it must be concretely shown whether communication can still be 
achieved under various pressures of expectation and how they proceed 
under these pressures. 
The regulatory trilemma which I have analyzed elsewhere (Teubner, 
1985 a) only becomes clear in the individual interaction. It poses the choice: 
disintegration of the elements of the one subsystem or of the other, or 
finally, indifference and a lack of structural coupling. Where expectations 
totally diverge, either the interaction as a whole disintegrates or does not 
even materialize, or individual elements of expectation are ruled out as 
incompatible and irrelevant. A real disintegration can correspondingly not 
occur on the phylogenetic level or is only conceivable as an extreme 
borderline case. It can occur however on the ontogenetic level. The result 
is an interesting change of emphasis. What leads to disintegration on the 
ontogenetic level leads to a lack of structural coupling on the phylogenetic 
level. 
Coevolution by de-differentiated interaction can therefore be conceptual-
ized as follows. Variation is triggered off by impetuses to variation from 
the different subsystems. These must pass through the "needle's eye" of 
the interaction and can then, as mutual influences of the systems, produce 
pressure for change on each other. Selection happens in such a way that 
the structures which crystallize out of the concrete interaction form by 
exposure to the selection of the different autopoietic systems. Finally, 
retention happens in such a way that the expectation which has been singled 
out in the interaction must be adapted to the various philosophies and 
dogmatics. This can in the long term lead to a mutual influencing of the 
different subsystems by philosophies and dogmatics. These do not align 
themselves to each other by direct philosophical comparison and cognitive 
exchange, but by the requirement of compatibility with structures of 
expectation in the concrete interaction. This may then mean that philoso-

Evolution of Autopoietic Law 
237 
phies in different subsystems are incompatible as regards their cognitive 
preconditions, but nevertheless that they produce compatibility in their 
consequences of expectation for individual interactions. An example is on 
the one hand the idealistic image of a legal subject which chooses its 
relationships in freedom, and on the other hand the image of an economy 
regulated by the market. Both do not necessarily agree in their cognitive 
conditions but in their consequences of expectation, for instance in the 
emphasis on contractual freedom, contractual compliance, etc. 
In this coevolution, processes of coordination between the different 
subsystems take place on the level of concrete processes of interaction, in 
which the requirements of the different subsystems collide with each other. 
If the problems of coordination become critical, this may be an occasion 
to deploy systems of interaction between the systems — as it were, 
artificially, consciously and controlled — which drive on this coevolution 
purposefully. This is the sphere of intersystem systems of negotiation, in 
which the coordination of philosophies and of expectations is consciously 
and purposefully practiced. This would be an occasion to speak of regulated 
coevolution (on this see Teubner, 1987 c).
