Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law: A 
Critique of Niklas Luhmann, "The Unity of the 
Legal System" 
K A R L - H E I N Z LADEUR 
Bremen 
I. Competition and Substitution of Theories in Public Law 
1. "Argumentation Theory" vs. "New Dogmatics" — the Current 
Debate on Legal Methods 
It is with good reason that Krawietz in a critique of modern analytical 
theories of legal documentation called for a theory of "theory-substitution" 
(1979: 128; 1981; 1983 a: 354; 1984 a; 1984 b). He defines theory substitution 
as the "processes of severance and gradual replacement of 'old' theories of 
argumentation by 'new' ways of thinking". Krawietz understands the 
present interest and value-oriented jurisprudence (Interessen- und Wertungsju-
risprudenas 
a practical discipline, which is supported not only by common 
sense but by social theory, especially in its empirical knowledge (Krawietz, 
1983 a: 379). If this is correct, then one would not search for the "rules" 
of theory substitution in a metasystem of theory comparison, which in its 
turn would be in need of justification. Even the proponents of "rational 
argumentation" (Alexy, 1978; Peczenik, 1982; Aarnio et al., 1981; Aarnio, 
1981; for constitutional law, cf. Schlink, 1980; Ladeur 1982) refer their 
theory to the "groundlessness" of "forms of life" (Aarnio et al., 1981), that 
is, on historical contingencies.1 What is meant by "forms of life" is vaguely 
defined in the theory of rational argumentation, while the opposing theory 
gains access to them by its very pragmatism, which encompasses both 
normative and empirical levels. 
1 This reading implies the assumption of a quasi-spatial limit to rational understanding, 
the presupposition of minimal meanings. As opposed to this, a reading is to be 
preferred which sees the language game as being anchored in a "general agonistic", 
played as a competition (Lyotard, 1979: 23; Gondek, 1986). The public of the language 
game is not a fraction of a "universal auditorium" but the substrate of an historical 
consensus of praxis (Perelman and L. Olbrechts-Tyteka, 1969: 31). 

Perspectives on a Post-Modem Theory of Law 
243 
If one changes the question about theory substitution a little and asks 
about the conditions of the competition of theories — the replacement of 
theories by other theories can probably only be investigated over a longer 
period of time — then the "theory of argumentation" with its reliance on 
the relative autonomy and self-transparency of language (Broekman, 1983: 
105) as well as the possibility of gain of legal rationality through discursive 
experiences before an "auditorium" which is as comprehensive as possible 
is better associated with a social epoch or, more exactly, a trend of 
development which transcends the limits of the classical state, both in its 
"essence" as well as with regard to the personal substratum, in the direction 
of a "stronger plurality" (new social state agendas, the incorporation of 
groups into political and administrative processes, etc.). In constitutional 
law, that legal field in which political conjunctures show themselves most 
clearly, Häberle (1975) and Müller (1984) could be said to stand for this 
direction, Häberle for a more "personal" / group-oriented variant of the 
theory of argumentation with an orientation on "consensus" and the 
conditions of its maintenance in social state-induced change, and Müller 
for a more "factual" method insofar as he sees the rational "concretization 
of law" which goes beyond the classical concept of interpretation as 
being based in the "concrete dependency of normativity on factuality" 
(Sachbestimmtheit) and, therefore, designates the explanation of " 'basic' facts 
selected with the help of the program of norms" as the task of legal work 
(Müller, 1984: 253; Κ. Hesse, 1985: 16). For that other vein in the discussion 
of method which is of a dogmatically practical orientation, Böckenförde 
could be named in the area of constitutional law: Böckenförde (1983; also 
Krawietz, 1983 a; Schlink, 1984) stresses programmatically the dogmatic 
character of the "science of the law of the state" (Staatsrecht) which is 
oriented on the classical theory of interpretation. The employment of this 
term rather than "constitutional law" is, in itself, symptomatic. It would 
be wrong, however, to imagine nothing other than a backward-looking 
state-centeredness lies behind this — of course, that is valid for the other 
side of the controversy too: premature political estimations of the "theory 
of argumentation" are neither helpful nor intended here. It is much more 
a matter of describing social fields of perception. Especially practice-
oriented methods and those sciences understood as practical are particularly 
adjusted to the de- and re-structuring of those social fields of perception. 
This is accomplished through receptive (internal) assimilation and reactive 
(external) accommodation. Böckenförde's contribution contrasts remark-
ably with the context of the discussion of methods in the science of 
constitutional law in so far as, after the lively controversies of the seventies, 
stagnation is more readily to be observed. It would certainly not be correct 
to presume that in the discussion about constitutional law a "theory 
substitution" is announcing itself to the detriment of the theory of argumen-
tation: it has neither been predominant in constitutional law in the past 

244 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
nor will it disappear in the future, but it is certainly not misguided to 
suppose that dogmatic thinking in constitutional law at present and in the 
near future is likely to strengthen. This is the more so since the discussion 
of methods cannot be regarded as being independent from that criticism 
of the social state and of an instrumental understanding of law ("legaliza-
tion") which has been articulated both scientifically and politically in the 
last few years. A superficial generalization would certainly be misplaced 
but the method controversy and the political controversy run parallel to 
the extent that an important objection exists both to the practice of the 
social state and to the theory of argumentation in the accusation of disregard 
for or overburdening of the specific rationality and regulative capacity of 
the state and the law. Böckenförde emphasizes therefore — coupled with 
a sharp attack on Häberle in particular (Böckenförde 1983: 330; also 
1982) — the dogmatic character of the science of the law of the state which 
should orient itself much more strongly on the constitution as a prescribed 
order, that is, an order to be interpreted, and not a "still to be created" order, 
which is to be made concrete. The "uniform will" of the maker of the 
constitution, he says, is to be reconstructed and the science of the law of 
the state, as a dogmatic science, demands the adherence to a proven "method 
which [proceeds] according to rational, inter-subjectively conveyed and 
testable, and, therefore, objective criteria and standards" and is "thus not 
[open to] subjective preference or case by case pre-conceptions". He says, 
between the science of the law of the state and constitutional jurisdiction 
a methodically-conducted context of argumentation is to be maintained or 
established which "marks out and fixes the area of what can be said, 
dogmatized and criticized in the domain of the law of the state with a 
view to feedback and, thus, preserves the law of the state from political 
institutionalization". This approach is directed against the "anarchist plural-
ism of methods" which is characteristic of the so-called "open society of the 
interpreters of the constitution" (Häberle) and which sees the constitution as 
being constituted as a (group) process. As a consequence of the opposing 
position, the constitution would again become more strongly a citizens' 
constitution, as it is called elsewhere in Böckenförde. In representation, 
the immediate plurality of individuals finds a unity in which the "real self" 
of the citizen is brought to "public presentation". Groups would then 
again be more strongly reduced to their function as "mediating links" 
between state and citizen; they would forfeit the privileged position which 
the topical-open argumentative method of making concrete the constitu-
tion — even if not reflected in this consequence — has assigned them. 
The antithesis can be carried to the point that, according to Böckenförde's 
conception, the "privatized" and de-professionalized interpretation of the 
constitution accompanying the personal and technical extension of the 
state's duties should be concentrated, through the introduction of a "Nu-
merus clausus" for interpreters of the constitution in the profession of 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
245 
the specialists in state law and should be made more uniform through 
revitalization of classical methods of interpretation. 
On a higher level of abstraction, outside the doctrine of public law, 
Krawietz also holds this position: a teleological ordering of law is a specific 
type of legal systematization which allows the selection of aims and means 
and their hierarchization of intended results and unintended secondary 
effects. Its specific character can be found in the "area of aims and purposes 
of law which are empirically fruitful, sharply outlined in content, precisely 
circumscribed or, at least, circumscribable" (Krawietz, 1981: 335). This 
achievement in systematizing is neither purely linguistically based through 
the structuring of arguments or the analysis of "fields" of human experience 
and action, nor does it presuppose like the classical German legal positiv-
ism — often misunderstood, namely, by being reduced to a blind executive 
automatism — a pyramid shaped structure (Losano, 1984: 648), a "compre-
hensive idea rising in steps to the last rallying point" (Gerber, 1863: V). 
German legal positivism was, in accordance with classical, analytical scien-
tific thinking, based on the assumption of a hierarchical system of acts of 
volition, legal maxims and legal institutions, rising from the particular to 
the general. And the independence of positivistic legal dogma in particular, 
independent of the legislation of the legislator, was compatible with "blind" 
submission to the law to the extent that the middle level of the system-
structure (the level of legal maxims), did, in fact, leave a relatively large 
amount of room for maneuver between a constructively-modelled character 
of acts of volition by private and public body corporates and legal institu-
tions as the highest rules of legal action; but it saw its possiblities of 
development as being limited through already-existing structures of the 
"society of individuals" and through connection-constraints "from below" 
and "from above". The building of society on the basis of the will of the 
individual, the separation of state and society, the limitation of the state's 
duties which this entails, a linear, static model of equilibrium based upon 
this — these were the essential elements of construction which the specific 
rationality of the legal system laid down in a structure limiting the variabil-
ity of possibilities. The classical method of interpretation — in the form 
which already pointed beyond Savigny (1840: 260) and his primarily histor-
ical way of thinking — was also oriented on this: the hermeneutic systema-
tizing of legal texts sought in the change of perspective of "external" 
volition (variation) and "internal" grammatical combination (structure) to 
refer the new to connection possibilities which were to guarantee the 
continuity of the system in charge. 
2. From Orientation on Text-Structure 
to Situative 
Functionalization 
The crisis of the structure-oriented model of interpretation was unavoidable 
as the tasks of the state increased such that the relatively simple basic 

246 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
assumptions on which the system-construction of jurisprudence and the 
practice of law was built proved themselves to be too narrow because they 
allowed too few possibilities. The law which was applied (above all) to the 
social state, reflecting the transformation of the "society of individuals" 
into the "society of organizations" had, for its part, become fragmentary 
as a result of the change to the strategic handling of situations and the 
complex arenas of activity having plurally-bequeathed power, along with 
the interest-constellations particular to each. The structural unifying of law 
in a hierarchy of legal texts which were built pyramidically from the 
particular to the general proved itself to be too rigid. Even that canon of 
teleological explication of texts which seemed to be most flexible with 
regard to a future orientation by means of a "further consideration" of the 
aims pursued by the legislator and which, interestingly enough, is not to 
be found in Savigny could, on its own, not provide the concept of the 
application of laws with the necessary regulative capacity because of the 
fragmented decisional situations which could only be reflected upon in 
retrospect and no longer be reconstructed according to an already-existing 
model. This is, in my opinion, the reason for the appearance of methods 
of interpretation which give flexibility to the legal structure through 
proceduralizing, that is, through the generating of legal decisions ex post, 
through moulding the situation to be settled (and no longer only through 
subsumptive application of the general model to the concrete circumstances) 
(Ladeur, 1982: 393). This happened — as indicated above — in different 
directions through the widening of the circle of "interpreters"; through 
the involvement of the "auditorium" before which the situation has to be 
argumentatively constructed; through the greater gaining in autonomy of 
the "case area" whose development-dynamic is, at least partially, equipped 
with a carte-blanche, so to speak, in normativity; through "orientation on 
consequences" (Teubner, 1975; cf. also Liibbe-Wolff, 1981), etc. 
The "new dogmatics" represents a counter-movement in the old direction 
but one, informed through the theory of argumentation, on a higher level 
of complexity: today it should be agreed that a juridical methodology can 
no longer unconditionally revert to the re-building of the hierarchy of legal 
texts and the rule of the general over the particular. In this respect, a 
characteristic feature of an evolutionary development of theory — which 
will be examined more thoroughly below — asserts itself here: under the 
pressure of new problems, the old theory is initially maintained and shored 
up for a time through extensions and through an ever greater lengthening 
of the bond between legislative intention and teleological, situative interpre-
tation, only then to collapse. This collapse makes room for a new construc-
tion (Kuhn, 1962; Loeck, 1983) which, however, severs the bond in so far 
as it opens the legal formulation of judgements wider to criteria of rational-
ity drawn from the situation or from an argumentation proceeding. 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
247 
Simultaneously, it is typical, however, that the historical character of this 
evolutionary step is generally not taken notice of. It does not appear 
compatible with the dignity of a theory claiming to be true when it is 
confirmed that its conditions of possibility correlate with the conditions 
of the development of a field of social action and perception, and that, 
therefore, between the origin and the understanding of phenomena, "iso-
morphy" rules (Riedl, 1985; cf. also Allen, 1980; 1982). The excluding of 
the observer from the field of observation, the freeing of the internal 
"establishment context" of a theory from the heteronymous dross of the 
"discovery context" is still widely regarded in social and cultural sciences 
as an almost incontestable command. Accordingly, a decided tendency exists 
to de-historicize a theory to such an extent that its historical "conditions of 
discovery" (Schlink, 1980) are only brought up to explain that the theory 
in itself had always been valid but had not been recognized earlier. Conver-
sely, there is also a widespread tendency to detach the "old" theories from 
the context of establishment in which they were "discovered" and to 
measure their "context of establishment" using the criterion of the "new" 
theory which has, so to speak, raised itself to the level of a meta-theory, 
and to discard it as ideological. German constitutional potivism in particular 
has been a privileged victim of such a procedure (Oertzen, 1974; generally 
Feyerabend, 1976; M. Hesse, 1980; Lyotard, 1979: 42; Rorty, 1981; 1984: 
180). 
In this respect, Krawietz's question about the conditions of theory-
substitution, which have also to be analyzed historically, is the more 
remarkable in a legal dogma, however, which sees itself as a "practical 
science", and is also the more urgent (Krawietz, 1976). (The justification 
for such an isomorphy — which could have been regarded as an ideology 
in the traditional discussion context polarized by materialistic and idealistic 
reductionism — can be explained in newer approaches to an evolutionary 
theory of cognition.) 
The counter-movement of the "new dogmatics" maintains its thrust in 
that, while recognizing the context-dependency of the application of legal 
norms which changes the interpretation to a "concretization" (Krawietz, 
1981: 332), it insists on the rationality of a specific-legal form which has, to 
say the least, been neglected by the different variants of the "argumentation 
theory" in their search for a rationality presenting 
(Broekman, 1983: 96) 
itself directly in the discourse procedure of the people involved or in the 
reconstruction of the "nature of the case area" (as Müller, 1984, puts it). 
Juridical rationality has been — as Broekman (1983: 100) justly accepts — 
transferred from the theory of argumentation to a general social purpose-
rationality. With the discarding of the structural prescriptions of the pyra-
mid-shaped hierarchy of legal texts and of those formalistic rules necessary 
for application, the discursiveness of legal activities as language activities 
seemed to gain direct access to natural language as a medium of social 

248 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
communication and self-enlightenment, a possibility which the structure 
of the governing rules of deduction and the close reference to certain 
canonized texts of the classical legal method had obviously tended to 
impede (Broekman, 1982; 1983; 1984). Against this, the form-exactitude, 
thus the rationality specific to the law, is, in the view of the new dogmatics, 
to be distanced from substantial aims of justice and general demands 
for consistency and universalizability of social discourses: even if legal 
argumentation is not primarily restricted through particular (textual) struc-
tural prescriptions, there emerges a new, more flexible, but, nonetheless, 
specific selectivity from specific functional demands of the legal system 
(Krawietz, 1981: 333; see also Kitschelt, 1980). The reconstruction of 
system-thinking in jurisprudence vis-ä-vis procedure-oriented argumenta-
tion theory thus does not proceed ahistorically but transposes the orienta-
tion of selectivity from the structure to the function. This function consists 
above all in "absorbing", through the respective juridical decision-making, 
that uncertainty occurring in the legal system as a consequence of the 
structural imprecision of legal rules referring to the correctness of the 
normative result of the decision. Herewith, the function takes over the 
regulation of the aspect of cognition, which does not restrict itself to being 
a general, social self-enlightenment but is also adjusted to order "the 
experience and action of all people ... through the law according to particular 
aims" (Krawietz, 1981: 333). The absorption of uncertainty through the 
process of structure formation is made flexible through the linking to 
function because no longer is only one structure possible. A rather horizontal, 
variable structure formation is demanded which pays heed to the con-
nection-capability of decisions produced "with new information content" to 
former and to later decisions (Krawietz, 1983 a: 333). Initially, the function 
admits many possibilities but their fulfilment in time does not allow a new 
beginning either with regard to the matter or the person concerned; 
possibilities are always being excluded through earlier experience/knowl-
edge and activity as well as through decisions, which possibilities can only 
be newly thematicized at a high political and legal cost. Therewith, the 
"really effective relationships between legal norm-structure and human 
experience and action" (Luhmann, 1972) are admitted in a new form which 
distinguishes itself markedly from the structure-defined unity of traditional 
system-concept. The linking to the function of absorption of uncertainty 
also admits the demand — pointing beyond the old style of norm applica-
tion — to carry on legal system-formation only in the area of possibility 
where both the function and the limitation of law are clearly outlined and 
defined. This corresponds with the demand to build this legal realism into 
a theory of society founded on an empirical-scientific basis (Krawietz, 
1983 a: 383). Only thus can the fulfilment of the orientation-function of 
law, its normative stabilization of expectations and, thus, simultaneously 
the enabling of the "relief of consciousness" (Krawietz, 1981: 307; Schelsky, 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
249 
1972), be guaranteed. The further development of the connection-con-
straints, to which the new decisions are to be adjusted, is controlled through 
the stronger emphasis on professional self-control of the legal interpreters 
(educated in the science of law), which is irreconcilable with an "open 
society" of all those interested and, thus, with the search for as big an 
"auditorium" as possible. 
The relationship of the classical hierarchy model to the theory of argu-
mentation and to the "new dogmatics" can — by greatly simplifying a 
complex development — be reduced to a succession of granting privileges 
to different factors in the system-formation: the system-formation is 
changed over from structure (classical method) to process (the theory of 
argumentation) and, finally, in the "new dogmatics", to function. In the 
next intermediary step, an attempt shall be made to shore up the evolution 
of juridical system-elements, as it has first been demonstrated in one area, 
through a recourse to the element of time in more recent evolutionist 
theories of cognition in order then to examine Luhmann's concept of "self-
referential systems" in regard to its aptitude for the lasting stabilization of 
a function-oriented concept of the legal system. 
3. Time and Theory: The Concept of Autopoiesis as the Basis of a 
Self-Reflexive Theory of Evolution? 
A theory of the "unity of the legal system" which overcomes the old 
structure-oriented ideas of a system-construction based on the "ordering 
of perceptions according to a unified point of view" (Coing, 1954: 191) 
has recently been outlined by Luhmann (Luhmann, infra; see also Hejl, 
1982 a; 1982 b). This concept attempts to integrate the dimension of time 
into a theory which — not least sensitized through the change of theory-
concepts and theory-systems — places itself as a "theory of the system in 
the system" and, thereby, abandons the claim of classical subject-thinking 
to constitute unity as a synthesis of all appearances through concepts (rules) 
in the identity of consciousness as the subject of itself and, through the 
difference of the subject from the appearances, to make objectivity finally 
possible. Such a theory, which does not take the formation of identity and 
difference as a transcendental basis of "timeless cognition" (von Weizsäcker, 
1981: 19) but, on the other hand, does not evade the legitimation problem 
through a plea for pragmatic "social engineering", must be of interest 
regarding the question of the rules of competition and substitution of 
theories in legal dogmatics. The question concerning the theory of cogni-
tion in general and in legal dogmatics in particular was always due to a 
"need for restriction", the search for a "foundation" beyond which one 
cannot return (Rorty, 1981: 343). This is especially valid paradigmatically 
for "legal cognition": Kelsen ultimately hypothesized the foundation of law 
in the postulate of a "basic norm". Von Weizsäcker has pointed out that a 

250 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
greater sensitizing to historical change in social knowledge, to the relation 
between matter and movement as the alternation between two "roles in 
the game of knowledge" does not significantly make it appear reasonable 
to expect "an unending succession of ever more general theories. One 
would more readily expect a final theory to be the fulfilment of the 
paradigm 'theory'. ... A theory of theoretical knowledge itself" which can 
"hold a reflexion on itself insofar as this reflexion can receive the form of 
theoretical knowledge" (von Weizsäcker, 1981: 28). 
Thus, a position is reached which in classic philosophical thinking is 
furnished with the warning, "hie sunt leones". The tenet of the excluded 
third, namely, that something cannot simultaneously be and not be is 
demonstrated through shocking examples of the different paradoxes which 
"pedagogically" accompany occidental thinking, beginning with the tenet 
of Epimenides ("all Cretans lie"). It is precisely this paradoxical thinking, 
however, which Luhmann tries, in the wake of more recent theories of 
evolution, to make productive for a legal theory of the "unity of the legal 
system", which can self-referentially co-thematicize structural changes in 
its object and, simultaneously, in itself in the "form of imperceptible 
evolution" or "planned structural change". An evolutionist theory of 
cognition, in which context Luhmann's new system-thinking is also to be 
placed, transforms the classic subject as the "beginning" of knowledge into 
a series of observer-positions which are interchangeable and mutually 
detachable and "mark" (Spencer Brown, 1969: 26) a difference from which 
relations are possible. Indeed, this concept assumes that the observer is, in 
the end, identical to the difference, to the drawing of boundaries (Weinert, 
1984). The differences, the boundary-drawings are products of the interac-
tion between reality and the logical nature of the human mind. Cognition 
is therewith no longer understood simply as the empirical "application" of 
terms but, even from its origins, that is, from the concepts themselves, is 
placed in the movement of time (Costa de Beauregard, 1963: 90; 1967; von 
Foerster, 1981a). As a process, it is not reversible and cannot be traced 
back to the beginning but presupposes irreversible proceedings in the 
formation of "memory" (von Weizsäcker, 1981: 28; von Foerster, 1969) 
and systems (Atlan, 1984; 1979: 205; 1983 a; de Rosnay, 1981) which 
transform the linear time of reversible trajectories through irreversible 
incisions into a differential, evolutionary "sequence of levels and crises" 
(von Weizsäcker, 1981: 28). With the recognition of the autonomous 
existence of time, which makes possible the change not only of appearances, 
the new, the indeterminate, uncertainty itself is accepted which first gives 
time a direction: complete cognition would suppress time and place all 
elements in a succession which is only apparent but, in truth, however, 
would make them happen simultaneously. (This is precisely the basis for 
the autonomy of the subject of cognition which is postulated against the 
object: cognition becomes timeless, the new cognition has "actually" also 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
251 
been possible earlier (Atlan, 1985 b; 1979: 177; Prigogine, 1984).) Several 
theoretical fundamentals of the evolutionist cognition-theory will be further 
dealt with below. Before discussing the change of Luhmann's concept of 
a self-referential legal system which assumes evolution (time) and which 
constitutes itself as an autonomous system with its own criteria of self-
reproduction through the drawing of boundaries (Luhmann, 1987; generally 
1984; Teubner, 1983; Teubner and Willke, 1984) and henceforth observes 
reality only on its own "screen",2 (though this is linked to other "observa-
tion points"), a further intermediary step is necessary which joins the 
concept of self-referential systems with the fundamentals of the biological 
theory of self-organizing (living) systems and should examine their fruitful-
ness for the formation of social and legal scientific theory analogies. 
System-formation informed by the concept of "autopoiesis" is "no longer 
merely a matter of 'existence' or 'preservation of existence' nor merely of 
problems of self-organization which relate only to the structural level" 
which can change living systems on the basis of experience; it is much 
more a matter "of the elements of which the system consists" (Luhmann, 
supra: 14). The biological theory of autopoiesis is a decisive progress in 
cognition insofar as it reversed the classical adaptation model of "open 
systems" which develop through exchange of energy with their environ-
ment, point-blank into a model of closed systems: biological systems have, 
accordingly, no direct contact with their environment, all external impulses/ 
items of information are, so to speak, "digitalized" and only decoded in 
the system, in particular in the neuronal network of the brain through the 
"culling structures" which are produced and reproduced there. Emphasis 
thereby displaces itself from the input to the internal structure which needs 
external stimuli only in order to activate and preserve itself. The brain 
behaves self-referentially and in circular fashion insofar as it is both operator 
and operated upon — contrary to the tenet of the "excluded third" — a 
paradox which has now become thinkable or tolerable through the reflec-
tion on the irreversibility of time (Varela, 1981; also Scudder, 1975). The 
physiological view of living systems was characterized by the hierarchiza-
tion of single cells into larger function-units (organs) while the newer view 
(Varela, 1978: 78) already considers the individual cell as a circular chain 
of chemical processes which draw and maintain their own boundary and 
also form and reproduce a "higher" unity as an organ also through a 
circular interaction of the "endless repetition of the always identical" 
(Varela, 1981: 302). The two sides of reductionism, the fixation on the 
elements or, conversely, the fixation on the "organic" context, are aban-
2 But the boundary of a social system is not a distinction drawn between an inner and 
an outer space; it is rather to be viewed as the impact of the productive matrices of 
the "dissipative structure" of the system which are the preconditions of emergent 
new meaning (Ceruti, 1985: 34). 

252 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
doned, the search for the beginning proves itself to be in vain. The brain 
and its components produce nothing other than themselves. Maturana has 
formulated this peculiarity of autonomy and self-reference in a general 
form as follows (Maturana, 1981: 21): "We maintain that there are systems 
that are defined as unities, as networks of productions of components that: 
(1) recursively, through their interactions, generate and realize the network 
that produces them; and (2) constitute, in the space in which they exist, 
the boundaries of this network as components that participate in the 
realization of the network." 
This necessarily simplified description may be interrupted at this point 
as we are here chiefly concerned with the discussion of "secondary model-
ling" of this concept for juridical system-formation and with the conse-
quences resulting for the self-observation of the legal system and its "theory 
substitution". Details will be returned to during the presentation and 
criticism of this concept. 
II. Luhmann's Theory of "Self-Referential Systems'* — 
a Complex Model of the Self-Reflexion of Legal Systems? 
1. The Possibility of a Theory of the System in System 
Following Maturana's system-concept for living systems, Luhmann formu-
lated the following thesis for the legal system: "The indissoluble unity of an 
element for the system can be constituted only by the system; it follows from 
its capacity to associate which is produced within the system. An autopoietic 
system therefore constitutes the elements of which it consists through the 
elements of which it consists. In doing so it sets limits which do not exist in 
the substructure complexity of the environment of the system" (Luhmann, 
supra: 14). Thereby, what matters primarily to him is the unity of the element 
(Luhmann, supra: 16). Into the self-reproducing social system a "self-descrip-
tion of the system by itself must therefore be introduced" so that points 
of connection for further elements can be created again and again for the 
"continuous self-constituting". "The function of formation of unity — al-
ways presupposing differentiation — lies in the autopoiesis of the system". 
This means that the self-reproduction of law takes the form of change of 
law, of the transference of the quality of normative validity to partially new 
expectations (Luhmann, supra: 17 — 18). The legal system is closed to the 
extent that only the legal system can grant its elements legal-normative quality 
and, thereby, can constitute them as units. 
Normativity has no "purpose" which lies outside itself but has, rather, 
the function of "continually rendering the self possible from moment to 
moment, from event to event, from case to case". Thereby, naturally, 
adjustments to the environment are not excluded but the normativity of 
events can only be produced through the system itself. To enable demarca-

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
253 
tion from other normative systems (moral) and therewith to specify its 
own system, the law requires a function: "To the theory of the self-
referential completeness of systems there consequently belongs a theory of 
the function of law." This is — in the further development of the concept 
developed in Rechtsso^iologie — seen in the "exploitation of conflict perspect-
ives for the formation and reproduction of congruently (temporally/objec-
tively/socially) generalized behavioral expectations" (Luhmann, supra: 27). 
For the initial question, some important assumptions emerge from this: 
dogmatics is, thereby, more strongly required to take into account the self-
reference of the legal system on the level of the elements (in particular, of 
the individual decisions), because one element supports the other 
(Luhmann, 1987). For this purpose, the law no longer requires a hierarchy 
of norms but, rather, a "binary structure" (legal/illegal) upon which condi-
tional schemes can be built. Legal theory and legal dogma are, thereby, 
considerably relativized in that the "communications" through which the 
autopoietic reproduction of the legal system ensues — which, therefore, 
transfer the normative validity to other communications — do not seem 
able to be planned or regulated, whether vertically through recourse to 
universal principles or horizontally through the selection function and 
filter function of certain argumentation procedures (Luhmann, 1987). The 
instrumentalizing of law for social state regulative processes, which are 
aimed at inducing positive and avoiding negative conditions, is no more 
reconcileable with the self-referential, circular self-reproduction of the law 
than would be a dogmatic which did not understand itself as a continuance 
of the evolutionary process of the continual adaptation of arguments to 
a problematical relationship of redundancy and justification, autopoietic 
recursiveness and asymmetrical structure (Luhmann, 1987). 
The theory cannot, thereby, have as its task the replacing of an old 
through a new and better one; rather it must illuminate the context in 
which juridical argumentation takes place. This thesis makes one see the 
consequential renewal of the status of theory: theory and, still more, 
dogmatics are themselves built into an evolutionary process of the reproduc-
tion of law, as a theory of the system in the system. Dogmatics and legal 
theory produce, thus, terms and constructions whose aggregation-state is 
to be settled between "crystal and smoke" (Atlan, 1979); that is, they 
operate with the redundancy of the law, which — as follows from what is 
to be stated below — is no deficiency of the law but, rather, constitutes 
its possibility and necessity to develop. This is partly removed, partly used, 
but always employed in an asymmetrical way (Luhmann, 1987), that is, for 
the formation of structure, in particular through the justification of a 
decision. With its self-referential circularity, the law can activate events 
(actions, decisions) (Luhmann, 1985) within its system by exploiting the 
binary scheme legal/illegal — differentiated through evolution — in its 
privileged technique of conditional programming (if/then), if, and only if, 

254 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
events occur. With this procedure, "long event-chains" can be built up in 
which every step depends on the other, previously-accomplished steps and 
all depend on the normative validity of themselves and the others. The 
infinite regression is interrupted in this conception in that it sees the 
theory anchored in a network of references-contexts between origin and 
understanding, between "proven expectation" and "confirmed experience", 
in that it accepts the non-arbitrary combination-ability of connection-
restraints created through evolution in "levels and crises" (von Weizsäcker, 
1981: 28) but sees simultaneously in this redundancy the pre-condition for 
a self-reflexion of corrtl&tion-possibilities 
of the autonomous, autopoietic 
system. The introduction of the dimension of time, thus, in particular, the 
renunciation of the consciousness-centered philosophical establishment of 
the "beginning" of conceptual thinking, makes the theory, rather, into one 
of many forms of asymmetrical refraction with symmetrical interrelations 
through (understanding) recombination of possibilities, which is iso-
morphic to their origin. The concept avoids the fatal dilemma of the 
paradox: it neither solves the relationship between action and perception 
(observation) in the direction of a, finally, transcendental consciousness nor 
does it reduce perception simply to a reflection-relationship. It therefore 
prescribes, to neither one side nor the other, an external measure of 
"optimization" (Varela, 1984 a: 219), rather, the concept upholds this 
relationship as such in that it conceives perception, theory formation, 
dogmatics, etc., as a dynamic process of "cobbling together", accomplished 
in time, using the "materials" for structure-formation (its transformation 
and re-structuring, secondary modelling) created through the redundancy 
of possibilities of a self-referential system. But everything takes place on 
the "screen" of the self-referential system on which specific forms of 
"computing a reality" (von Foerster, 1981 a: 39) happen. Through feedback, 
new ramifications of avenues of possibility appear which, however, always 
presuppose those possibilities realized — with the exception of others — 
earlier in time. From this there emerges (as Varela and Maturana, in 
particular, have formulated for biological systems) a kind of "drift" of the 
history of internal options, examinations of interactions and ramifications 
through an autonomous autopoietic unity (Varela, 1984 a: 219; Maturana, 
1984) in a "dynamic landscape" (Gould and Lewontin, 1979), its field of 
possibility, in which it must maintain its unity. 
2. Self-Reproduction of the System and Self-Reproduction of its 
Elements 
The self-referential nature of the legal system is primarily related by 
Luhmann — in so far, displaying a certain difference from Maturana and 
Varela — to the reproduction of the individual elements (Luhmann, 1985: 
119): "The indissoluble unity of an element for the system can be constituted 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
255 
only by the system ... An autopoietic system therefore constitutes the 
elements of which it consists through the elements of which it consists" 
(Luhmann, supra: 14), because it is they which, through their transference-
achievement, through the linking from moment to moment, (re-)generate 
the reproduction of the system. 
But how does the element of movement, of change, of learning present 
itself now in this theory of the self-referential legal system? Firstly, it cannot 
be too clearly emphasized that the self-containment of self-reference cannot 
be regarded as synonymous with the condition of entropy of energetic 
systems, which have no relationship of exchange with their environment. 
Self-referential systems learn throughout and maintain interaction-relation-
ships to their environment but their specific openness is conveyed through 
self-reference and its translation achievements (Luhmann, 1985: 119). There 
emerges in this way a characteristic coupling of openness and self-contain-
ment. The closure interrupts indiscriminate exchange through boundary 
drawing in order to no longer only exchange energy/information, but with 
every operation to simultaneously activate the code of its possibilities for 
self-reproduction (Luhmann, supra: 15 — 16). 
In Luhmann, the concept of self-reference which is based on the elements 
presents itself thus: the legal system, with the help of legal codes (legal/ 
illegal) controls its "own negation-possibilities", that is, constructs its own, 
above all, counter-factual reality. "Items of information" from the environ-
ment are selected through the conditional mechanism (if/then) and make 
possible a connection between non-learning and learning: on the normative 
level, the system does not permit any purposes, compulsions or categories 
to obtrude. Normativity is not gained from the environment. It "remains 
... dependent on the self-generating context of legal elements and their 
boundaries" and reproduces the system-environment-boundary. The general-
ising of the conditional mechanism fixes the possibilities of reaction in its 
own selectivity for items of information, the norm anticipating even deviant 
behavior, and builds up, in contrast to this, its own (normative) reality, 
which does not mean that programs cannot also be changed "under the 
pressure of acts". But even the change can only ensue through transforma-
tion into normativity (Luhmann, supra: 20). It must, therefore, continue the 
interruption of the complex reciprocal actions through system-formation in 
a new form. In this respect, cognitive processes, and thus, learning pro-
cesses, keep the system open: the employment of the program presupposes 
the processing of items of information from the environment and the 
examination whether certain presuppositions are realized or not. The nor-
mativity (self-containment) which is self-referentially oriented on its own 
model is meant to absorb uncertainty and risk but makes the activating of 
the program itself dependent on facts (Luhmann, 1985: 119; supra: 20). 
This combination of general non-learning (with reference to normativity) 
and specified learning (fact-related), constitutes the legal function to which 

256 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
the exceptions, not ignored by Luhmann — which should, in fact, prove 
the rule — are to be related. The legal system should be sensitized, in fact, 
to particular situations. Through legal doctrine, learning processes are made 
possible which surpass specified "learning"-learning channelled through the 
conditional mechanism. It makes changes possible through a kind of 
reflected trial action because terms and constructions are not normatively-
binding decisions (Luhmann, 1974: 49; 1985: 120). The unity of the legal 
system which has been differentiated through evolution and which is 
reproduced through autopoiesis demands, however, that changes on the 
level of court practice and of dogmatics should be integrated. New dogma 
must be adjusted to suitable cases and new standardizations of practice 
depend on terminological developments. All this requires time, according 
to Luhmann, because normative and cognitive, general and specific levels 
must be co-ordinated. Luhmann sees a disturbance of the balance in favor 
of the cognitive level in the primacy of the legislator, whose activities 
ensure that, through the statutes, the law is adapted to society: a process 
whose acceleration can impair the self-referential character of the law. At 
this point, convergences and divergences of system-formations which are 
built on structure or on function become clear: the horizontal restrictions 
of function-orientation take the place of those restrictions written into the 
structure of the pyramid shaped legal arrangement. 
The legal system can certainly transpose coincidences to a new normativ-
ity because no structure can process any longer all the problems in the 
relationship of system and environment. A danger of overstrain can, 
however, be seen if result-oriented jurisdiction and legislation produce a 
complexity which by-passes the self-reproduction ability of normativity 
because "states" aspired to can, indeed, be a subject of opinion but cannot 
guarantee, in the form of "balanced" decisions without adhesion to norms, 
connectibility for new decisions. In new conference papers, Luhmann 
considers it possible, though he does not declare it as being necessarily 
so, that through functionally-unsuitable legislation and jurisdiction an 
irreversible state has, in the meantime, set in. Perhaps doctrine is, according 
to Luhmann, only possible as a form of self-observation and self-description 
of the system (Luhmann, 1985: 119, 121, 125). 
3. Contribution of the "New System Theory" to the Self-
Thematicizing of the Legal System 
The decisive, qualitatively new step in Luhmann's reading of system theory 
consists — as has already been emphasized — in a new function-definition 
of the law as a self-referential system which is no longer simply fixated on 
the problem of reproduction of a given state of society but situates the 
theory of normativity within the legal system itself. It does not, therefore, 
appear as a social scientific theory beside a normative theory of law which 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
257 
adheres to the highest norms, methods and legal principles, but, as a theory 
of self-referential systems, it is simultaneously a theory of self-observation 
and self-substitution of theory and dogmatics within the evolutionary 
process of the differentiation and self-reproduction of the law. It gains its 
impetus from a global paradigm change: understanding proves itself to be, 
within the context of the evolutionist theory of cognition, a time-dependent 
self-reference to the functioning of systems. To be sure many elements of 
the concept are not new: they have been, as references to the above so-
called new dogmatics indicate, part of a practice-oriented dogmatics. The 
newness consists much more in connecting the reference context of theory, 
method, dogmatics and practice circularly in a reproduction process which 
can thematicize the conditions of self-change in various avenues of possibil-
ity. Thereby, a theoretical level is attained from which a theory of the self-
substitution of competing theoretical and methodological starting points 
can become thinkable, a concept which reflects the fact that the historical 
consumption of theories has discredited claims of validity which cannot 
connect understanding circularly with the origin of the understood. It thus 
contributes to a new relativism which co-thematicizes its own conditions 
of possibility. 
Luhmann's new reading of system theories in general and their differen-
tiation for the legal system in particular is impressively stringent. Precisely 
because of this, however, the question must be raised whether this 
stringency is compatible with the concept of self-organization/self-reference 
and — related to this — whether this very stringency of self-reference does 
not block the explanation-potentialities contained in the concept of self-
organisation jautopoie sis. In the first instance, doubts exist concerning the 
very self-willed separation of the self-organization of the system from the 
self-reference of the elements (actions). In Luhmann's view, self-organiza-
tion becomes a form of self-reference of structures through the possibility 
of self-alteration, while self-reference on the level of the elements consists 
in the ability of elements produced in the system to connect to other 
elements. Thus, self-reference means that the legal system as a system of 
actions consists only of elements "which, through the operations of the 
elements of the systems, are themselves built". Here, however, there arises 
a fundamental problem: the system is not simply made up of actions. This 
would more truly be a traditional, analytical view through which reality 
would be mistaken as which the system produces and reproduces itself 
(Luhmann, supra: 14). In order to clarify further the relationship between 
system and element, a further intermediary step is now necessary by means 
of which the difference between communication and action has to be 
introduced: a social system consists of communications which establish a 
synthesis out of information (environmental reference), communication 
(system reference) and understanding (interpenetration between system and 
environment). Social systems reproduce themselves through communica-

258 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
tions (Luhmann, 1982: 368; 1984 b: 191; supra: 17) and that means through 
the "mutual accentuation of meaning". Actions introduce into this system 
of communication an asymmetry and a temporalization in that, through 
selectivity and through the apportioning of responsibilities, the building 
up of communication-chains is made possible. Action is the reduction 
which effects the transmission of meaning in that it creates connections on 
which depends who can further communicate what and to whom. "Every 
meaning, even the meaning of purely factual events, can become legally 
relevant, i.e., can enter into the self-reproduction of the legal system ... 
But within this sphere of relevance there exists the core of legally valid 
action which ... makes possible new normative expectations which would 
not have acquired legal quality without this action of engendering ... The 
constitution of these elements is an autonomous achievement of the legal 
system" (Luhmann, supra: 17). The action side of communication makes 
possible the self-perpetuation of the system which only by means of a 
"strongly simplifying self-observation" is enabled to reach the aim of 
establishing, "sufficiently quickly, simplified connections (partners, themes, 
items of information, messages) for the formation of further elements". 
The system communicates about itself in that it evidences its own boundary: 
through self-observation, the system uses its difference (from something 
else) in its operations in order — through interruption of communication, 
so to speak — to portray itself as a chain of defined and definable actions 
which it simultaneously "credits" as its own and, in so far, cuts off the 
interrelation of communication. 
This "self-simplification" through self-observational modelling of chains 
of action, proves itself to be the prerequisite for autonomy as communica-
tion about communication and possibility of the selection of basic elements 
through whose reproduction the system reproduces itself as a whole. Only 
in this way can it also develop and change (autopoietic) structures as 
consolidated action-expectations for the formation of future actions. The 
drawing of boundaries between system/environment repeats itself on the 
basis of the elements as the difference between event/situation. The term 
"event" is meant to indicate that the stability of the system rests on 
instability: the situation as the "horizon of the event" refers to the system, 
its environment and the latter's difference, but does so selectively in that 
it refers to the limited possibilities of production of the next event 
(Luhmann, 1985: 119, 122). Here the recursive circle closes: the difference 
between system and environment is, so to speak, "processed" in the 
system, in that the system uses for self-reproduction the distinction between 
"information" as (hetero-)reference to the environment and the "communi-
cation" as self-reference to the ^/^»-possibilities of the system. In this 
way, the system continually activates the relationship between closure and 
openness as a means for the selection and conveyance of meaning. 
Every element is thus, as an action, a selection which is under the 
compulsion to produce the next element and the next action. 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
259 
III. A Critique of Luhmann's Reading of the Theory of 
Self-Referential Systems 
1. The Theoretical Status of the "System" — the Relationship 
Between System and Element 
The last statement above all makes plain that the autopoiesis of the legal 
system is seen in terms of the element and not so very much from the 
reproduction of the system as a whole. In my view, this point can best be 
explained if one compares Luhmann's concept of evolution and of the 
differentiation of the function of the legal system applied in this process 
with the different readings of the autonomy of biological systems (es-
pecially, of the brain) and the construction of the concept of system in 
general systems theory: in both fields, there is the tendency to consider 
systems ontologically as a holistic complex of relations whose autonomy 
is relatively stably constituted in an evolutionary step of development (if 
this is demonstrated by using brain research as a model, this means 
approximately that the neuronal connection-possibilities have already been 
inborn and the environment is more or less reduced to the "animation" 
and stabilization of the activated connections) (cf. Hubel and Wiesel, 1984). 
In general systems theory, this accords approximately with Bertalanffy's 
(1969) approach. The other conception stresses — in research on the 
brain — more or less strongly the instructive character of the environment, 
a character which specifies neuronal connections without, however, aban-
doning the concept of self-organization (Bourguignon, 1981: 452) — on 
the contrary. In general systems theory, this variable concept stresses 
evolution less than a quasi-ontological prefixing of system and function. 
It allots to these terms a much more conventional status, dependent upon 
the observer. The observer has, therefore, in this reading of system theory 
a far more significant status than in the other view: according to this 
reading, the system is constituted as a kind of modelling, as a "picture" of 
a particular complex of relationships to the environment which, as such, 
that is, as a model, can be used in "self-regulation" through the actualization 
of further possible relations which, with the previous "distinctions" (of the 
system), have become visible. Systems theory in this sense is, in a consider-
ably more pointed form, a "logic of the possible" within which the 
observer — who is not simply the subject but a variable point of reflexion — 
construes "pictures"/conceptions and is itself simultaneously construed as 
a point. This second variation thus connects action and observation more 
strongly, while for the former the system precedes its actualization in the 
elements (Lacroix, 1980: 43; von Foerster, 1981 a; Pardi, 1983: 570). 
In my opinion, Luhmann's concept belongs to the first variant: the 
strong emphasis on the self-reference of the system on the level of the 
reproduction of the "elements" is only possible if the system and its 

260 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
function can be seen as stabilized in such a way that the reproduction is, 
in the end, nothing other than a process of self-application in the process 
of the reproduction of elements: the function itself cannot be transcended. 
Rather, the function has originated in the process of differentiating the 
social system's "society" and cannot be varied with the other sub-systems 
through adjustment. In contrast to this, the second system concept would 
define the function, rather, in the relation to other sub-systems (that is, in 
the relation which Luhmann himself sees as an achievement of the function 
differentiated on the level of society), which gives the variation greater room 
for maneuver (a point which will be returned to later). This scientific-
theoretical difference is not, despite all the differentiation of terminology-
formation in other respects, clearly expressed in Luhmann's works. It is, 
however, of great significance, not only for the conception but also for the 
question of the possibilities of legal-theoretical reception. In my view, 
those possibilities of the autopoiesis-concept which are fascinating precisely 
because of the prospect emerging of a new, inter-disciplinary, integrative 
theory-construction, are not exhausted in Luhmann's reading. It seems to 
me that the second variant of system-theory, rather, makes possible a 
system-theory of the "second generation" which can also be made fruitful 
for jurisprudence. Its difference when compared with the first variant 
would consist primarily in its connecting much more closely than is the 
case in Luhmann the level of self-organization as self-change of the structu-
res and self-reference on the level of the elements. Precisely that mutual, 
interactive establishment of elements which in Luhmann becomes an actual-
ization of the system through a sense-conveying chain of actions (Luhmann, 
1981), forces the various levels to be united operationally more closely. 
The autonomy of systems originates precisely at the intersections of the 
levels, that is, at the "inter-twining" which, with the formation of logical 
statement-systems, leads to paradoxes (Varela, 1981: 294). This means that 
the self-reproduction of the legal system does not proceed primarily from 
element to element but is to be explained thus: that the function of the 
system can at first be varied and. above all, differentiated imperceptibly 
but then also self-reflexively. If one bears this in mind, the rigid linking 
of the concepts themselves — which is scarcely reconcilable with the 
concept of autopoiesis — can be slackened and opened to non-directed 
historical learning and differentiation processes. The "self-description", as 
a system of action which is self-prescribed for the system for the reproduc-
tion of the elements is, from the start, limited in Luhmann to self-
thematicizing as a chain of attributable actions. Therein, the thought is 
contained that the construction of a reality is inseparably connected with 
an action (Lacroix, 1980: 43; Motulsky, 1980; Varela, 1983: 160). Through 
the perception/construction of an event through a system, the modus operandi 
of the construction is always simultaneously co-thematicized. 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
261 
Luhmann's concept of the function of social systems in general and of 
the legal system in particular carries the comparison of biological and 
social-scientific evolutionary theory too far: the relation between element 
and system — by chance or intentionally — matches the relation between 
epigenesis and cell/neuron of biological system theories. These start from 
the premise that the "basic plan" for the formation of organisms, but also 
for mental objects in the brain, is contained not in the single elements but 
in the functional system of the combination of cells, or synapses "between" 
these (Riedl, 1985: 146; Changeux, 1983: 277, 327). Epigenesis ensures the 
reproducibility of the function in the autopoietic process of fluctuations 
which proceed with the construction and activity of the (constructed) 
"apparatus". The "basic plan" determines the construction and activity, 
simultaneously, however, the "hyper-cycle" (Eigen and Winkler, 1983: 257) 
enters into the organization again, as essential characteristics, the elements 
formed through identical replication. The internal reproduction of the 
function "gradually copies its own practice": "decision and event form a 
circle of action, a unity" (Riedl, 1985: 146, 155). The "memory" stores, so 
to speak, the structure-forming capacity of the events. 
This achievement in selection in living systems consists in that they 
realize a previously "tested" and proven basic plan and, for the rest 
permanently test limited possibilities of adaptation, that is, survival of a 
total population (van Parijs, 1981: 53) (thereby, human behavior should be 
initially left out of consideration). Its evolutionary "attractor" is a local 
optimum. The evolution of social systems, however, knows no natural 
selection but only the reinforcement of permanent patterns of reaction (van 
Parijs, 1981: 96) which must be processed within an organized system and 
are not optimized through variations of the individuals of a population 
(van Parijs, 1981: 50; generally Hadley, 1983). This processing is carried 
out in "social memories" in complex interference-relationships between 
processes which generate information and processes which block this 
information and, thereby, form organization. In social systems the internal 
reproduction of functions, therefore, is circular in a more comprehensive 
way than in living systems. Therefore, also the unambiguous relationship 
between learning and non-learning as the exhaustion and elimination of 
possibilities is only possible in living systems (Changeux, 1983: 326, 328). 
The mental objects of the memory and the associative capacity of its 
individual and collective forms (Green, 1983: 356; Pascot and Le Moigne, 
1980) which have been processed through the "intertwining" of levels 
(here, for example, the blocking and generating of information ) — enabled 
a virtuality of language (Fornari, 1979: 112) which is characteristic of the 
evolution of social systems. The knowledge of autonomous systems is, 
especially through the more complex intertwining of its levels in a more 
problematical way identical with itself because it can vary its own reproduc-
tion of functions (Dupuy, 1982 a: 120, 137; 1982 b). The relevant regularities 
are to be found in the evolving network of actions and interactions, a 

262 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
context in which meaningfulness cannot follow on a priori connectivity set 
by a given function of a system (Winograd, 1980: 227). The system itself 
becomes an evolving network whose "progams" are probabilistic and not 
deterministic in as much as it not only needs the products of its own 
readings (Pattee, 1977: 262) (a new version of the hermeneutic circle) but 
also develops functional redundancy for "perturbations" (which can to 
some extent be protected against error). It modifies its own rules not by 
meta-rules but by its random construction as a "pattern recognizer", where 
"the pattern to be recognized is the outcome of the functioning of the 
system itself. A posteriori this pattern can be analyzed and the functioning of 
the recognition system can be understood as the behavior of a complicated 
dynamic system evolving towards one of its many attractors" (Atlan, 1985 a; 
Milgram and Atlan, 1983 a: 525, 538; see also Dupuy, 1985; Dupuy and 
Dumouchel, 1984; Fischer, 1981). (The random component which is in-
accessible to control provides an explanation of the system's ability to 
extract "order from noise".) 
The self-(re-)production of the legal system does not consist in the 
transfer of a sort of "trait" (validity of social expectations) from the 
elements of the system to new elements. Crucial for the closure of the 
system is the interconnectivity of the components (Varela, 1985: 146; 
Probst, 1981: 291) and their mutual definition. The stabilization of a 
network-like "landscape of internal coherences" (Varela, 1984 b: 26) requires 
a capability of self-observation and self-description which is distributed 
over the whole process of the (re-)production of the system (but of course 
not in equal "portions"). That is why the system has not got complete 
mastery of its meaning (Dupuy, 1985: 28). 
A legal action may include a plurality of future possibilities and so induce 
an auto-catalytic process of fluctuations moving toward the stabilization of 
a new form of eigenbehavior (see Varela, 1984 b: 27; Fischer, 1977: 65). 
There is not either "insensible evolution" or "planned change of structure" 
(as Luhmann, 1983: 136 puts it). The theory of autonomous systems must 
be primarily concerned with what lies in between: the "succession of 
catastrophes" and stabilities resulting in unintended "dissipative structures" 
of intentional acts. 
It is especially the infinite succession of "computation of computation" 
(von Foerster) Luhmann is referring to (1983: 136) which characterizes the 
systemic recursivity of a program reading the results of its own lecture. 
That is why the system cannot be said to consist of elements. The system 
is in a paradoxical way made of ... systems! "Le systeme est toujours plus 
grand que lui-meme" (Barel, 1979: 169, 186). 
2. Autopoiesis — Time — Memory: System-Function and the Status 
of the Observer 
The mechanism of self-indication of social systems can avoid a collapse 
into chaos only in that it stabilizes its own states or complexes of internal 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
263 
relations. This cannot — as with living systems — occur through a quasi-
ontological function but only through the training of a specific memory 
(von Foerster, 1969: 44). In this memory, not only would events not be 
preserved but neither would their structure-forming power (as Luhmann, 
1984 a: 16, puts it). Precisely this may be assumed only of living systems. 
The structure of the memory of social systems, however, is to be constructed 
as stochastic: this means that memory has its "own" internal culling-
structures which are reproduced through recursive self-indication, through 
"blocking" of information, but this structure represents, as a kind of 
"convergent" organizing principle, only one side of a "dissipative structure" 
of a non-linear equilibrium model whose other side is represented by a 
divergent distribution of internal items of information which, within the 
complex network of junctions and tracks of the structure, carry out a kind 
of game of chance with intruding external disturbances ("noise") (von 
Foerster, 1984; 1960; Atlan, 1979; 1983 a: 115; 1984 a: 109; Prigogine, 1984; 
1979; Prigogine and Stengers, 1981) and try out "new things" (Paillard, 
1983; Tabary, 1983; Le Moigne, 1983; 1984). This means that the possibility 
of change does not necessarily correlate with the function which has been 
stabilized through "blocking". The redundancy of the culling-structure 
includes an element of chance which makes possible a continual change 
between organizing elements and thereby also opens to change the function-
modulation with the other subsystems. The culling-structure itself can, for 
example, be maintained in that smaller "fluctuations" are ignored and 
others encapsulated as "exceptions", etc., or differentiated in alternative 
structures for particular special fields. A fluctuation can, however, reinforce 
itself to such an extent that the system arrives at a "bifurcation" at which 
it must take a new form (Allen: 1980: 21). Thereby, the history 
of the 
fluctuations and bifurcations becomes a part of the evolution of the system 
(Prigogine, 1984: 44); simultaneously, it is also recognizable why a change 
of the legal system, as of all other systems, is difficult to anticipate. The 
evaluation-structure always "converges" with the maintenance of the system 
and can, only with difficulty, check whether a self-transcendency is indicated 
concerning the divergent disturbances (Atlan, Salomon, Fogelman, and 
Weisbuch, 1982: 193; Atlan, 1976). This depends simultaneously on the 
internal differentiation of the social memory and on the degree of connect-
edness between the different parts of the evolutionary network, the "mem-
ory" (Atlan, 1976: 125). The memory of an autopoietic system must contain 
a certain chance component, without which self-organization is not possible. 
Therewith, simultaneously, time is no longer a horizon of the connectibility 
of actions but an element of creativity of the experiment (Prigogine, 1984: 
44). The structure of the memory as an evolutive network changes in time 
and thereby not only the (internal) structure but also the external function 
of the system can change (Atlan, 1983 a: 115; Le Moigne, 1982; Varela, 
1979: 125). The single "elements" change the rules governing how they 

264 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
can be combined and precisely this, the paradoxical inter-twining of dif-
ferent levels (system, structure, element), constitutes what is new in the 
concept of autopoiesis. The recognition of temporality makes possible the 
construction of a "cascade", of iterative change of organization — action — 
organization — action, etc., in which there is no linear stability regulated 
through a unified legal parameter but only a non-linear process of equilibra-
tion. In this way, the memory of a social system acquires a paradoxical 
character typical of autonomy in so far as the perception of an event 
exhibits either the actualization of other events or, better,, of the traces left 
behind by them, or it induces a virtualization in which the event is initially 
only processed through the different parts of the evolutive network-
memory and then taken into "reserve" (Le Moigne, 1983: 155). Thus, one 
can, on the other hand, also imagine the origin of new "pictures": the 
memory contains, so to speak, traces of the events which, beside the stable 
culling-structures, continually rotate through a kind of chance-generator 
and produce something more or less useful. This is a further consequence 
of the construction of social systems as networks of relations with emergent 
characteristics which are not characteristics of the structure or the elements 
(Jantsch, 1979: 51, 54; Riedl, 1985: 146; Prigogine, 1979: 67; Prigogine and 
Stengers, 1981; see also Haken, 1981). In so far, the memory is also in no 
way — as Luhmann assumes — geared to the storing of structure-forming 
characteristics of events. 
In this way, one could even speak of several time-levels on which the 
system operates and, therewith, simultaneously construct the plurality of 
the observer-positions within the system: the system observes itself and it 
registers on a higher level that also alternative possibilities of self-observa-
tion are possible from other points. This, of course, presupposes that the 
connectivity of the structure-elements is not too rigid and, in fact, a 
potential for (limited) self-transcendency is built-in and the system under-
takes in the memory, rather, a kind of equilibration of different perspectives 
of modelling rather than enforcing one "correct" culling structure (Le 
Moigne, 1983: 149). 
In the point of view just presented, the origin of system theory itself 
can be co-thematicized as an evolutionary step: system theory as a science 
of "modelling" is the reflexion of an evolutionary development in which 
the observer — as already indicated at the beginning — no longer stands 
outside the "re-presented" object and the object is no longer analytically 
reduced but variable distinctions and relations are thematicized which 
incorporate the observer and the consequences of this action. It is, simulta-
neously, a recursive result of (self-)observation in that the observed is ever 
more strongly permeated by the "artificial" created by the observer and, 
therefore, can be constructed, rather, in functional 
relations and no longer 
in static-parametric causalities 
(Simon, 1969: 6). These are, it is true, no 
longer analyzed through systematic simultation, construction of scenarios, 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
265 
etc., but are flexibly modelled and operationalized in a form which is no 
longer without alternatives. The circularity of self-reference/autopoiesis 
originates from the fact that the observer can observe his observation and, 
therewith, the observation of the first level becomes, quasi-independently 
of the observation of the second level, the object, but remains "self-
dependent" on the mode of observation (Varela, 1981 a: 16). 
From this, a new view of regulation may be gained for social systems: 
the concern is no longer with the regulation of behavior within the model 
of homeostasis — a linear equilibrium-model in which the individuals were 
only abstract components of the equilibrium-function of the market and 
other "normalities" (Pizzorno, 1974: 17) — but with a model of homeo-
rhesis according to which the functional conditions of a non-linear equili-
brium is constructed of inter-active action-networks (Pascot and Le Moigne, 
1980: 230), for which a more complex memory and a suitably more complex 
modelling are necessary. For theoretical system models, this means that 
there can also be no linear equilibrium between reality and thought-
structure but that the unity of science and cognition must be replaced 
through a construction-model of a sequence of equilibrations, disequilibra-
tions and re-equilibrations which evolves in non-linear fashion and ensues 
in a never-ending process between observer and observed (see generally 
Piaget, 1980; Kesselring, 1981). The observation/modelling itself becomes 
a form of equilibration and not of the image of an object. 
In the theory of science an evolutionary thought-model, is thereby 
emerging that considers itself no longer as parametric (oriented on object-
independent variables) but as strategic, i. e., that is built on thinking 
in functional alternatives and "enters" in circular-reactive manner the 
consequences of its operations into the thought-model again (van Parijs, 
1981: 196). 
3. The Internal Differentiation of the Legal System — the Possibility 
of Variation of Functions 
One can, following Paillard (1983: 156), distinguish the following levels 
in autopoietic systems on the analogy of a model drawn from neuro-
physiology: 
(I) The organized level (structure in the classical meaning of an executive 
model); 
(II) the level of the "organizing function" (which controls and regulates 
the transformations on level I through activating the function which 
remains latent on level I); 
(III) the level of the "virtualizing" of structure and function. 
On this level, a potential of the de-stabilization of the memory is made 
possible and those divergences of level I excluded or bracketed through 

266 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
level II are experimentally processed and varied. On this level of experimen-
tation, there is, so to speak, no hierarchy but rather "strange loops" (of 
levels) which lead, among other things, to a fluctuation which has appeared 
on level I being mitigated on level II, strengthened on level III and leading 
to a change of function on level II. In this way, in an autonomous system 
different levels are, indeed, connected to each other. This highly conditional 
modelling presumes an evolutionary step which leads social systems not to 
strive any longer for certainty but, on the basis of learning processes about 
the de- and re-structuring of systems in time, to operate with uncertainty, 
thus not to operate with only one reality but with a plurality of possibilities.3 
In the future, new interactive technologies will perhaps make possible a 
more comprehensive strategy for the replacement of the central "distribu-
tion media" through a pluralization of norm-systems (Wersig, 1985: 137). 
This concept permits a fruitful criticism of Luhmann's understanding of 
self-reference on the transactional level (level I): transactions of the (legal) 
system are, in Luhmann's system-concept, selections which make asymmet-
rical the symmetrical communications between the legal system and personal 
as well as other social systems in that they no longer admit "everything" 
but create connection-possibilities for other future transactions and, thereby, 
enable the actualization of the function of the (legal) system, namely, to 
generalize "congruent behavioral expectations" and, thereby, to guarantee, 
through the reduction of complexity, the transferability of meaning. A 
language theory is associated with this concept, as indicated by a reference 
to Bühler (Luhmann, 1985: 114; Bühler, 1965: 34), in which language acts 
primarily as a "sign system" (see also Hjelmslev, 1968), as a medium of 
transfer. The stable sign which is maintained as a unit in different situations 
of use and in the conflict-perspective even against the deviant perception 
of the addressee, enables a pre-notion of meaning which changes the 
internal processing of meaning which is carried out through the different 
levels of the legal system and its culling structure into a "term" that is 
transferable to others (Eco, 1984: 51). 
Luhmann makes the homogenizing function of the sign-concept fruitful 
for the concept of the "symbolic generalizing of the self-reference of 
meaning", through which the reference-structure of every meaning is 
condensed into "expectations" which "indicate what a given meaning-
situation proposes" (Luhmann, 1984 a: 137,139). The system makes possible 
the generalizing of meaning through self-simplification, by which the

within the text, see the examples of Calvino, 1983; Kundera, 1984, cf. hereto Sato/ 
Nielsen, 1984.

process 
of 
(re-) activation 
and
