(Luhmann, 1984a: 97, 100). 
"Vibration" of the foundation of reality is "eliminated through emergent 
self-referential systems". Indeed, the paradox which Luhmann places within 
the system itself (the system reproduces the elements which maintain its 
unity) repeats itself in the relationship, system-environment4: the construc-
tion of the system is itself dependent upon an external standpoint of the 
observer who, thereby, anticipates a metasystem and is thus referred to the 
historical possibilities, experiences and contingencies of operating with 
system-constructions (Lanzara and Pardi, 1980: 128). The historically 
diagnosed loss of the center is also valid for the observer of the system 
who finds no solid, unified assumptions of the system-construction (see 
Barel, 1984: 187; 193). Complexity has a relative, topological character 
which points to the historical realm of possibility of the system-construction 
(Lanzara and Pardi, 1980: 125). Precisely that emphasizing of the condition-
ing of meaning-process through differentiated systems which are based on 
generalizing imposes narrow limits on the historical perception of the 
possibility of "local", plural, non-generalizable meaning which demands a 
different system-construction. If, however, one does not define evolution 
only in terms of differentiation, and regards systems as constructs for the 
processing of information and the orientation of actions, (Crozier and 
Friedberg, 1977: 25), one must accept that systems which originate through 
strategic games are also circularly changed through them again and again; 
that is, that the process of change is not continually assimilated through 
the generalizing-possibilities of the system. Meaning-systems, therefore, 
have, rather, a "dissipative structure" whose fluctuations in dependency on 
time lead to phase-transitions in which the relationship between order and 
disorder is determined in a new way. 
Through an action, which is simultaneously an object (of the transfer-
ence) and a self-referential operation (Varela, 1975; Schwartz, 1981; Schne-
ider 1983; generally Maturana and Varela, 1980: 191), the system undertakes 
permanently, so to speak, a self-fulfilling prophecy: the problem to be dealt 
with cannot be perceived "objectively" but just as it is observed from the 
system in an action-perspective. The perception is self-referential (Motulsky, 
1980: 103) in that it breaks down the problem in a (language) model which 
is itself based on distinctions and relations which the observing system has 
constructed on the basis of interactions with the environment. But, finally, 
the systemic perception results from the "original act of severance" (Spencer 
Brown, 1969: 26; Motulsky, 1980: 108; Costa de Beauregard, 1963: 90). 
The artificial (originally, arbitary) element of distinction remains permanent, 
4 As for the relationship of system and (natural) environment cf. Godard (1984). 
Luhmann (1984 a: 36) rejects the concept of "eco-system" because "eco-complexes" 
have no boundary.

Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
while the postulation of the (language) action means also an incision in a 
processing, evolutive network of connectivities. The language-action is 
constituted through a productive element of temporality: time does not 
continue a chronology of "action-points"; it is much more the horizon of 
an irreversible projection of internal operations which are externalized as 
action-terms (Schneider, 1983: 5). 
In Luhmann, the replacement of the hierarchic-structural subsumption of 
acting under the law through the strategic-situative, functional processing 
of connection-constraints does not seem to be carried out consistently. In 
particular, the construction of meaning-transference in language theory 
shows that the loss of the traditional (ideal type) unity of the state as 
macro-subject, which through the unity of the hierarchical-structural code 
of the "signs" of law simultaneously gives unity to the individual subjects 
(Eco, 1984: 53), cannot be compensated for by the postulate of the unity 
of the legal system (and its function). The strategic acting of the subjects 
which undermines the presuppositions of the classical "subsumption" model 
itself and which anticipates a more complex model has not only affected 
their own unity — a phenomenon which leads Luhmann as a consequence 
not to build his system any more on the unified subject — but has also 
turned the unity of the symbolic generalizing of meaning into a problem.5 
Adherence to the unity of the legal system enables the decomposition of 
the subjects to be intercepted in the construction of the unity of the 
(sub-)systems and the "permeability" and plurality of the subjects to be 
processed in the blank reference to the no longer systemically conveyed 
transference of meaning (Rositi, 1983: 19). 
5 The "dissemination", the "dissipative structure" of meaning cannot be interrupted 
through the functional differentiation of specific systems, in particular, the separation 
of individual and society as a psychic and a social system. The self-referential iteration 
of the identity and difference of meaning cannot "de-layer" specification as an 
irrevocable evolutionary step, as a pre-condition of the further processing of transfer-
ence and connection possibilities. (Cf. in general Derrida, 1977: 24; 1972). Precisely 
this assumption is based on an indeterminate concept of language (cf. Habermas, 
1985: 441). In Luhmann, language exhausts itself in symbolic generalizing, in the 
"segmenting, abstracting and generalizing" of meaning (cf. Habermas, 1985: 439) 
through the substitute of the sign. A "structuralist" language concept, on the contrary, 
will assert the "emergence of the significant of the linguistic as an always differential, 
articulated order but order which is open and which is grasped as displacement" 
(Gondek, 1986) and will, thereby, open a persepctive in which the other (and, 
therewith, the otherness of the language) is never simply the alter ego. Language 
retains the circle of self-reference in that it binds cognition reticularly into the "trace" 
of experience of the world. This "trace" indicates nothing other than uncertainty 
which the language games (and their rules) refer back to the characteristics of play 
and makes linguistically-conveyed rationality dependent upon language-transaction. 
The unity and rationality of language is always made possible through a practical 
incision (consensus) in the non-reversible plurality and temporality of language-
transaction (Murphy, 1984: 136; 139; Derrida, see Waldenfels, 1983: 543).

269 
As an adjunct to the model outlined above the question must, however, 
also be raised about the possibility and necessity of a unit of normative 
meaning systemically and functionally brought about by the self-referential 
reproduction of connectable performance-elements. The transfer to a more 
complex, non-linear model of equilibrium oriented upon new phase-trans-
fers and self-transformation which sets in with the loss of the subject's 
unity can only be construed in a temporal, plural logic of negotiation and 
equilibration of heterogeneous values. The new function of law, which co-
thematicizes its own conditions of evolution, could consist precisely in 
making possible an abundance of alternatives, openness, flexibility and the 
examination of the dimensionalizing of time-perspectives for such a logic of 
bargaining and compatibilization instead of the generalizing of expectations 
(Donzelot, 1984: 259). 
Individuals and organizations as addressees of (legal) transactions are no 
longer completely dependent on meaning-transference to the same extent 
as in the time of the old-style equilibrium model for which they were 
basically only abstract components of a linear equilibrium. For this time, 
one can introduce Luhmann's function-concept into the system (on level 
II) in order to test how it "processes". In the modelling, however, it then 
becomes evident that the conflict-perspective which signals the sensitivity 
of the more flexible yet still unified legal parameter towards deviations 
from equilibrium, is evaded by strategic co-ordination and, similarly, by the 
fragmented harmonizing of behavioral expectations in different political 
and administrative arenas (Pizzorno, 1974: 10). Thereby the identity of the 
personal and organized systems as addressees of legal decisions also becomes 
a problem. The conditions of possibility for legal decisions are considerably 
changed if in organizationally-controlled fields of action, specified transac-
tion networks which can no longer be a meaningful object of congruent 
generalised behavioral expectations are "installed". The transference of mean-
ing, as an activation of generalizable meaning, which in conflict perspective 
results in making possible single, individual actions, would then possibly 
prove to be insufficient. The situation-specific methods of "consequence-
consideration", etc., which Luhmann criticizes spring not only from the 
search for function-alien aim-orientation but result from changes in the 
conditions of interaction between the legal system and its environment (for 
the economic system see Luhmann, 1984 c)6. 
4. The Transition from the Parametric to the Strategic Orientation of 
the Legal System — Consequences for Function and Autonomy 
The selective transference of meaning through decisions, in Luhmann's 
sense, assumes that the connections are clear for further actions: for 
6 In former epochs of evolution this remained primarily in a state of latency to be 
activated only in "exceptional" states of crisis and transition. 

270 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
large organizations and groups, however, unlike for individuals or smaller 
organizations, particular selections are — for different reasons — not the 
"last word", and this without their disregarding decisions. Here only 
processes of negotiation and adjustment are possible. This, however, has 
decisive repercussions on the action-perspective, particularly of the legal 
system. Problems become of necessity insoluble on level I. In many fields 
of action, the legal system must vary its own function-adjustment with 
the other sub-systems through the building of "consensual domains" for 
interactive networking. This does not mean the end of autopoiesis through 
the opening for exchange with other systems. The legal system remains 
restricted to its own homeorhesis, to operating with constraints, produced 
by its closure, which cannot be assimilated through a mere adaptation to 
standards set externally (Varela, 1983: 158) and which impose limits on its 
own transformation-possibility. In connection with the thesis expounded 
above, that an observer does not have an ontological or subject-character 
but is a variable which is bound to a system, one can accomplish a further 
conceptual step regarding the domain of the function-adjustment of the 
legal system here problematicized: as a social system, the legal system, 
unlike living systems, has neither in a literal nor in a figurative sense 
topological (spatial) limits; much more are they self-constituted through 
its own operations (Varela 1981 a: 14; 1976). It is therefore possible, on the 
basis of the de-stabilization potential of level III (see above), to add to 
level I a level F, which is partially constituted together with the actors in 
a specific arena. This means that a combination is created (Motulsky, 1980: 
116; for the concept of consensual domain see Maturana, 1978: 41; 1975: 
323) in which a field of action is modelled together with the actors and a 
common "observer" is created. The autonomy of the legal system does not 
disappear, not even partially, in this "consensual domain" but remains 
conveyed through a separate evaluation level, II', and is also retained in 
the "consensual domain" though the common level III. The strategic acting 
of the legal system remains bound to the horizon of the production of 
action-orientations in other systems, but instead of orienting itself on the 
equilibrium-parameter of behavior-regulation, the law orients itself on the 
possibility of the (re-)equilibrizing and compatibilizing of values and action-
perspectives for complex action-Ätf/wör&r. This presupposes a broader per-
spective on structural coupling of systems which "takes place as a process 
of reciprocal selection of congruent paths of structural changes in the 
interacting systems which result in continuous selection in them of con-
gruent dynamics of state" (Maturana and Guiloff, 1980: 139). The legal 
system activates and accelerates its virtualization potential in order to 
maintain and broaden the range of possibilities in other systems.7 As such 
7 It should not be forgotten that level 1 does not disappear.

it generalizes a flexible procedural modal (and not substantial) rationality 
accompanying the evolving interaction-networks by (re-)constructing, eval-

inherent in their connectivity (see 
Teubner, 1983; Teubner and Willke, 1984). (This is, for example, characteris-
tic of the field of proceduralization of planning through "interest weighing" 
{Abwägung), the field, in constitutional law, of decisions by the constitutional 
courts of justice on basic problems of the harmonization of essential 
conditions of competition and co-operation, in particular in decisions on 
the reversibility or irreversibility of particular options and, therewith, on 
the narrowness or breadth of the connectivity of system-elements (for 
example, party prohibitions, problems with radicals, educational policy 
decisions, abortion, co-determination of workers, the structure of the 
media, etc.) (Ladeur, 1980; Schulze-Fielitz, 1984). In this area, the separation 
of cognitive learning ability and normative non-learning can no longer 
hold out. The actual enforceability of decisions and their consequences 
must also be reflected in this context as the concern here is not with actions 
but with making action-networks compatible. This, also, does not mean that 
the law should not pursue its own ends and should henceforth adapt 
to the production of justice or similar complex aims which cannot be 
operationalized. Rather, the law should, in this area in which there can 
only be a non-linear equilibrium, orient its perspectives on the 
maintenance 
of uncertainty 
against the building of large strategies which exclude alterna-
tives and should assert the plurality of the realms of possibility — which 
have become conceivable through evolution — against conformity and 
thus function as a kind of interruptor of trivialization within the "consen-
sual domain" constituted by the history of structural coupling with other 
systems. From this could come a new perspective for the control of 
irreversible political and administrative "large projects" which could ex-
clude variable, reversible options in the future. Where irreversibilities are 
to be feared, the maintenance of learning capability could be compelled 
through new proceduralizations (this is particularly valid for the area of 
the strategic use of the environment where irreversibilities threaten to a 
high degree). A new perspective could confront the law in the wake of 
the successful spread of new technologies: if it turns out that, in fact, a 
large part of humanity will be excluded from the production process in 
post-industrial society, the question arises concerning the necessity of 
making possible plural and also alternative life styles outside the area of 
high productivity and the large organizations oriented thereon as, so to 
speak, a necessity of compensation in order to maintain a dynamic equilib-
rium which can no longer be realized in a unified model and which is, 
thus, non-linear. Also in the field of communication technology, there arises 
for the law the problem concerning the maintenance of the possibilities of 
learning, of difference and divergence from the building of control strat-

272 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
egies in a plural space which, simultaneously, becomes ever larger. This 
should suffice for the moment as a description of an alternative perspective. 
The change of perspective here indicated or, better, the pluralization of 
perspectives, must still be specified historically: the first social state phase of 
the "society of organizations" can be seen as a continuation of the linear 
equilibrium model with other (collective) means of distributing resources and 
creating parity of opportunities and groups instead of contractual freedom, 
etc. The new phase of the "society of organizations" is characterized by the 
loss of a linear development trajectory, the entry into a dynamic development 
of non-linear equilibrium, of dissipative structures, of uncertainty, but an un-
certainty which should not be regarded as a product of the decomposition of 
certainty and, therefore, to be converted as soon as possible into a state of 
new (or old) certainty. This uncertainty is an uncertainty of many possibilities, 
of plurality of developments and scenarios, which can and must be accepted. 
To this extent, the social system has, in general, to change from the stability 
of one reality to the mode of plural possibilities. 
IV. Outlines of an Alternative Model 
1. Operating with Uncertainty — a New Challenge for the Legal 
System 
This flexible operating within uncertainty could also be a new paradigm for 
the law. Against the background of the model of temporalized, autopoietic 
systems, this could mean for the law that it does no longer primarily pursue 
behavior-orientation or behavior-regulation but engages in adjustment with 
other autopoietic systems. The role of the law would be to facilitate and 
evaluate interactive networks, which means in some cases to interrupt them 
or to reconstruct them. Instead of a simple goal orientation which Luhmann 
ascribes to the materialization of law, the law would have to seek new forms 
of self-referentialprocedurali^ing. In so doing, the concern is not at all primarily 
to achieve henceforth "correct" methods instead of achieving "correct" re-
sults through making possible the interaction of those concerned. Rather, the 
relativistic perspective which is contained in the insoluble combination of 
observer/system and action, of descriptive and prescriptive elements of law, 
has to be radicalized for the evolution of the legal system as an autopoietic 
system (see Locker and Coulter, 1977). This means, the concern is no longer 
to transfer the old demand for objectivity to a new pluralistic context which 
is found through processes of argumentation or of "analysis of the field of 
norms". What is decisive is that with the increasing complexity of problems, 
particularly as regards the shaping of the future (for the limits of majority 
rule see Preuss, 1984), present social knowledge is more and more devalued 
(Masuch, 1984:137) and this cannot be without consequences for the function 
of law, above all, of constitutional law, but also of the law of the planning 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
273 
administration. For law making which is to be integrated into a self-reflexive 
concept of the autopoietic legal system which thematicizes its own historical 
possibilities, this means an orientation on an experimental, flexible norm-
model which, above all, is working with the mechanism of proceduralizing 
and is "non-linear" and would have to operate with iterative forms of the 
bringing about of action- and negotiation-networks, of the introduction of 
self-observing evaluation. Also, as regards evaluation, the point would no 
longer be to establish anew old illusions of a self-explanation of "reality" 
conveyed through social sciences; the concern is, rather, with the opening 
and maintenance of realms of possibility in which paths of development are 
drafted, compared, corrected and operationalized. This perspective could be 
supported in the near future by the integration of computer models into the 
decision-making process (see Haefner, 1984). The greater the time-horizon 
of a project is, the less the value of present knowledge and the quality of a 
political/legal decision (Masuch, 1984: 137). It cannot be too clearly pointed 
out that such models should not be used to produce new certainties but, on 
the contrary, to project trajectories of possibility — their ramifications, their 
connection-possibilities, their risks and prospects — and to allow options 
which are not to be referred to certain rigid "supreme values" (individualism, 
progress, industrial growth), but instead co-reflect variably and flexibly their 
own self-transcendence in time and, therefore, simultaneously try out exper-
imentally alternative possibilities (Krippendorff, 1984). What is required is a 
model for regulation of complex Action-tie (works and cause-networks instead 
of action-chains, that is, a legal culture of uncertainty (for experimental law 
see Stock, 1981; Hoffmann-Riem, 1980). 
The classical liberal action and society model was based upon the 
deliberation of the individual about his own needs; the socialist alternative 
rested upon planning the satisfaction (and development) of needs and, 
thereby, also proceeded from a certainty which can be called into question 
(because there is no procedure for its establishment) (Allen, 1982: 95; also 
Morin, 1984; 1977; 1980; Atias and Le Moigne, 1984). In liberal society, 
the law executed an abstraction, an incision, which established the "man 
within" instead of concrete local bonds as the point of orientation, a project 
which aimed at the assimilation and comparison of the Marktburger through 
self-observation in the "looking glass" of the others (A. Smith) (Costa, 
1974: 236).8 A new thought-model for the politico-legal regulation of

society must be erected above all on the institutionalizing of the permanent 
capacity to learn the design of a complex non-linear system whose reference 
points are neither the element (liberalism) nor a whole (socialism) but 
relational, recursively linked autopoietic networks of networks of networks 
. . . A counter-movement can, for example, be seen in that in environmental 
law "science and technology" as sub-systems are to guarantee certainty 
which previously was reproduced from all social sub-systems through, so 
to speak, interpenetration and through the formation of the classical rule-
models. With this in mind, the hypothesis might be tentatively advanced 
that it is precisely the lack of a new political and legal culture based on 
uncertainty which favors sub-cultural compensations for uncertainty which 
can only be personally experienced in pseudo-religious, political, therapeutic 
and other sub-cultural invocations of identity. 
2. An Alternative Orientation of Legal Doctrine? 
A prefatory remark must be made to the outline of the consequences arising 
from the model presented here for doctrine and legal theory which have 
changed with respect to operating with uncertainty: dogmatics receives a 
different status merely in that also the law, as a system of distinctions/ 
incisions in previous practice, does not represent a beginning from which 
something is to be derived but constitutes a self-referential unit of operation 
and "term" (legal norm). Dogmatics continues this self-referential game in 
that it constructs in time further operations/terms which allows connections 
in concrete situations of cases and decisions for other cases. That the textual 
reference of dogmatics has been so strongly emphasized lies not least in 
the fact that the law makes a distinction regarding local, fragmented 
practices and does not only make possible the changeability of the law 
positivistically but, above all and decisively, bases the construction of the 
law on the universality of the individual, which can behave towards itself 
as towards a[n] (changeable, exchangeable) object. 
Texts, through whose reading the self-awareness of the individual since 
the earliest modern times had, in particular, developed, were actually the 
privileged medium in which the self-references of different individuals 
could be made compatible with one another because, through the mouth 
of the judge, they brought to expression, so to speak, the "man within". 
Dogmatics referred the uncertainties of behavioral expectations which arose 
in the fluctuations in actions around the point of equlibrium (of the 
market and of the law) again and again to the "form of 'centralized inter-
dependence' " in that "the similarity of cases is reflected upon and is made 
the criterion of relationing" (Luhmann, 1974: 18). Dogmatics represented 
through retaining viewpoints centrally, the equilibrium that could not be 
regulated by individuals themselves but which produced itself as a cross-
section of the actions which were oriented on abstract parameters (money, 

Perspectives on a Post-Modern Theory of Law 
275 
justice). The portrayal of the uncertainty of individuals in action-situations 
as uncertainties of the text is, in the face of the dependence on model-
formation and action, neither objectionable as ideological, "false" con-
sciousness, nor in any other way. 
If one accepts this self-reference of the legal system which, historically, has 
only become possible as a consequence of the operations of the legal system 
itself, it is taken into account that the identity of the legal text, the unity of 
the law as a system, has always been borne by the unity of the state to which 
the individual subject stood in a hetero-referential relation and which first 
made possible the self-reference of the subjects (Varela, 1975; 1976; 65). Thus, 
the pluralization of dogmatic and methodological concepts which has arisen 
in the meantime is hardly surprising. A dogmatics for legal action in frag-
mented arenas with non-linear equilibrium can no longer generate "inter-
dependencies centralized" (Luhmann, 1974:18) through the processing of one 
text (Legendre, 1983: 524). Together with Touraine, (1979: 410), one could 
even ask whether — at least as regards society's organizationally dominated 
fields of action — an identitarian concept of the state as reference point for 
the self-reference of persons can still be adhered to and whether instead it is 
not necessary, rather, to proceed from plural, differential, evolutive action 
and negotiation networks (Masuch, 1984: 137). 
For legal doctrine, this means the transition from a central logic to a 
local logic of inter-dependencies (Rosenstiehl and Petitot, 1974). A doctrine 
which is no longer oriented on individual uncertainties and, correspond-
ingly, on a parametrically determined model of equilibrium, but is oriented 
on a non-linear, dynamic model of equilibrium based on plural networks, 
should, for its part, develop a new, non-individual plural method of making 
compatible and equilibrating organizational action-networks. Such a doc-
trine must, with reference to the network,9 structure inter-dependencies 
from case to case, however in a horizontal and de-centralized way. Such a 
doctrine can, therefore, only be developed with reference to specific areas; 
a starting point of a successful, even if not developed, doctrinal construct 
9 Cf. Ladeur, 1983; 1984; the problem of new approaches to the reconstruction of a 
general understanding of constitutional law independent from situative-strategical 
valuations consists precisely in the fact that the loss of the structure-forming function 
of the equilibrium model of the society of individuals is not sufficiently reflected 
upon — the "reconstruction of the classical function of fundamental law" by Schlink 
(1984) is, insofar, theoretically insufficiently founded and, therefore, rather, leads up 
to the pragmatic plea to leave the legislator greater scope in valuation; in the face of 
the difficulty of formulating in law a public interest comprising the private, this 
postulate can only be made plausible through specification according to areas of 
activity; also Suhr's (1984) concept of "freedom through sociability" lacks, in contrast 
to classical individualism (in its time), the structure-forming power of a paradigm 
which cannot be won alone through the antithetical fixation on the metaphor of the 
"homo 
negatorius". 

276 
Karl-Heinz Ladeur 
for the regulation of strategic, evolutive networks is — as indicated 
above — the method of "interest weighing" (Abwägung) in planning law 
(Ladeur, 1983). This cannot be worked out here in detail. 
Finally, however, the initial question shall at least be briefly taken up 
again: the claim of the above so-called new dogmatics also holds good 
tested against the conception developed here, insofar as dogmatics — and 
legal theory — as one form of evolutionary self-regulation of practice, can 
be established against the background of an evolutionist theory of model-
ling. The limitation also of the new dogmatics, however, lies in the fact 
that it is too little sensitized to problems which, through the appearance 
of the different variants of the argumentation-theory, have been signalized 
rather than mastered — namely, the necessity for the development of 
procedure-oriented dogmatic constructions for the equilibration of evolu-
tive action- and negotiation-networks which are no longer referable to 
"congruently generalized behavioral expectations". Argumentation-theory 
does, indeed, signalize the problem but tries through recourse to generalized 
discourse-procedures to develop a solution for which there can be no 
abstract solution. The reference-context of argumentation-theory, reason 
and life-form also only leads back to the necessity of institutionalising 
and, 
thereby, of specifiying in a plurality of life-forms. 
The historical assumptions of the "grand theories" which dissect their 
object into concepts, according to the pattern of classical cognition-theory, 
are no longer valid. The concept suggested here has the advantage of 
situating the temporal differentiation of fields of practice in a theory 
which sees itself as a self-observation of the system. It makes possible a 
systematization of evolutionary steps — observable in practice itself — 
towards the development of new, procedural dogmatic concepts. Further-
more, the concept shares recent tendencies to overcome the "cleavage in 
the worldview" (Spaltung des Weltbildes) (Riedel, 1985) between natural 
sciences and the humanities. In the perspective of a new relativism, it aims 
at constructing a horizontal logic of multiplicity. To be sure, its success 
depends not only on conceptual precision but also on the practical question 
of how much complexity the legal system can assimilate.
