Accounting for Law 
THOMAS C . HELLER 
Stanford 
Since the mid-1960s in the United States, there has existed a protracted, often 
bitter, somewhat confused debate about bilingual or bicultural education. 
There have always been outlying examples of private schools which attempted 
to preserve the linguistic and cultural integrity of national or religious groups 
that had emigrated to the United States. However, it is generally true that 
public school systems have insisted upon the dominance of English language 
instruction and expected immigrant children to struggle with classes not 
taught in their native languages until such point as they could manage in 
English or leave schooling behind them. This policy came under challenge 
both in the legislatures and the courts during the past two decades. Bilingual 
education acts were enacted in the United States Congress and a number of 
state assemblies in response principally to pressure brought by the increas-
ingly self-conscious Spanish speaking community concentrated in the region 
from Texas to California and expanding due to the legal and illegal influx of 
workers from Mexico. In addition, the United States Supreme Court in 1975 
ruled that under federal civil rights statutes, non-English speaking children 
had a right to some sort of special educational programming that recognized 
their linguistic difficulties in traditional schools. Neither the bilingual educa-
tion legislation nor the judicial constitution of linguistic rights were highly 
specific with regard to the details of implementation of new educational 
structures or legal obligations. A process of interpretation by both adminis-
trative and lower court rulings on the meaning of these acts became the focal 
point of a conflict over educational and, ultimately, a broader cultural politics 
that has led to a particular evolution of the character of bilingual or bicultural 
schooling in the United States. 
This essay will first examine two contending representations of what was 
at stake in this conflict and why the issue was resolved in the predominant 
form that has now emerged. These representations may be basically associated 
with, on the one hand, mainstream institutions and interests demanding a 
continuity with established educational practice because such practice is con-
sistent with the orthodox construction of American social organization. On 
the other hand, a contending interpretation of the controversy was put for-

284 
Thomas C. Heller 
ward by a coalition of oppositional groups centered around alternative images 
of national identity and socialization thereto that were described as more 
authentically Hispanic. If I can broadly classify the orthodox account of the 
events as liberal and the Hispanic as structural, I would then propose to 
consider how the representation of this history might be reformed by a post-
structuralist discourse that is built around the analysis of autopoietic systems. 
One possible benefit of this very brief sketch of a third, disparate account of 
the bilingualism conflict is to generate a previously unexplored space for 
pragmatic solutions to continuing political and economic difficulties in this 
area currently not well resolved. More generally, the introduction of exotic 
and unsettled theoretical terminology allows us the opportunity to reflect 
upon the definition of central terms and figures in this unfamiliar set of 
categories and concepts that must be clarified if we are to employ it coherently. 
Consequently, the essay is a speculation about what commitments we make 
when we speak of the world in the grammar of autopoiesis, about some 
immediate methodological puzzles that attend this usage, and finally, about 
the politics, intellectual and industrial, in which this linguistic practice makes 
sense. 
I. Representations of the Controversy: American Liberalism 
The standard response of American legal authorities to the demand for in-
struction in Spanish and schooling attuned to the normative organization of 
local Hispanic communities has been to understand those claims in terms of 
a more general liberal discourse of education and language. I have argued 
previously that the central figure of liberal discourse is the autonomous 
individual subject (see Heller, 1984). This subject has direct access, through 
empirical and logical processes, to knowledge of the external environment 
and, through immediate perception of its own consciousness, to knowledge 
of normative evaluations. Social organization is designed to maximize the 
ability of such autonomous individuals to carry forward their self-defining 
projects through some appropriate combination of market and public institu-
tions. Conversely, government is prohibited from imposing any collectively 
established, normative standard of human welfare since such a standard could 
only be based on substantive interpretations of human history or being that 
have no objective epistemological grounding. 
Within such a configuration of experience, the roles of education and lan-
guage are constrained. Since the goal of social institutions is to facilitate the 
likelihood that individuals can satisfy their own normative preferences, the 
purpose of education cannot easily include the shaping of those evaluative 
structures. In the absence of any theory of the public good that may go beyond 
the aggregation of individual welfare, the notion of education to a collective 
moral ideal is displayed from the central place it occupied in traditional sys-

Accounting for Law 
285 
tems. Instead, the function of liberal education is twofold. First, it is a form 
of technical empowering that equips the individual with empirical knowledge 
and logical skills that will permit him or her to coherently define, order, and 
subsequently implement a coherent set of projects and constitute, over time, 
one's self-identity. Second, education provides an odd sort of holding station 
where immature subjects can be controlled and entertained while their onto-
genetic passage to full autonomy progresses. Since, until this genetic matura-
tion has been completed, children are less than full legal or moral subjects, 
schooling provides a paternalistic discipline for beings whose normative 
choices do not yet merit social respect. The culture of the liberal classroom is 
in theory at once individualistic, morally anarchic, competitive, and techni-
cally oriented. However, the reality of hierarchical control, especially in the 
early years, imposes a constant counterpoint to the Utopian end point of 
subjective autonomy. 
Similarly, language in liberal discourse has a practical character. Because 
the access of true subjects to the objective world and to their mental processes 
is unmediated by conceptual representations, the world is in no way con-
structed by or contained in discursive orders. For classical liberalism, a word 
either corresponded to an unchanging aspect of the objective world or repre-
sented a self-evident idea or intention. Language was not understood to create 
meaning, but rather to operate as a tool to uncover and manipulate a con-
cealed, but already known or knowable, order. The content of this order was 
neither altered by, nor contingent upon, the mediation of the encounter with 
language itself. Rather, language ought to be seen, in this view, as a tool of 
action in that it allows our will, cognizant of the consequences of its action, 
to become effective in the world. Like all cultural institutions, it implements 
individual intentions. Both its development and adequacy must be under-
stood and appraised with reference to the voluntarist projects that motivate 
its use. Finally, translation, too, is ultimately only a technical exercise made 
possible by the shared extralinguistic referents of speech. To translate, one 
must locate the object or idea being associated with expressions in different 
languages. The commonality of the non-linguistic world of material and ideal 
forms should always permit the persistent and competent translator to make 
this discovery. 
Given these core images of subjectivity, education, and language, Ameri-
can legal authorities reworked demands from the Mexican community for 
bilingual/bicultural education into familiar patterns. Since American liberal 
education did not imagine itself to socialize children into any collective moral-
ity or cultural structure, no demand that it reform its pedagogy or classroom 
organization to reproduce any particular cultural order or series of orders 
could be recognized as legitimate. Moreover, in as much as speakers of dif-
ferent languages had access to a single reality, the use of one language or 
another in school carried no serious epistemological or ontological conse-
quences. Instead, there was only a technical question of how to most effi-

286 
Thomas C. Heller 
ciently bring a Spanish speaking child as rapidly as possible to employ the 
English representation for the common referent. This technical problem re-
sulted in a widely shared agreement that there was a need for special programs 
during the period in which children became proficient translators — a con-
sensus converted into a legal right to some form of exceptional remedial 
attention. Additionally, research funds were made available to study which of 
several different methods of teaching English and managing the transitional 
period was pedagogically superior. In effect, any radical implications of the 
demands for bilingual/bicultural education that might arise in a non-liberal 
discourse were themselves translated or re-represented in liberal images of 
education, language, and identity. At the close of the legislative, administra-
tive and judicial process in which what might have been deviant were assimi-
lated claims into a well understood set of established representations, newly 
established legal rights responded to the abnormal educational requirements 
of peculiar individuals in a fashion consistent with liberal images of subjective 
capabilities and repressed any implicit reference to an alien discourse that 
privileged not the subject, but the culture that constituted it. 
II. Representations of the Controversy: Latin Structuralism 
Hispanic proponents of the movement for bilingual/bicultural education ac-
counted differently for both the origins and the resolution of the controversy. 
However, like their American counterparts, they grounded their arguments 
about education and the place of language within it in more abstract represen-
tations of identity and social organization. In contemporary American liberal-
ism identity is associated with the existential self-definition of the autonomous 
will, social contract with the voluntary assent of such wills to public coopera-
tion, and modernity with the supercession of collective institutions that im-
posed culturally ascribed roles and definitions of character. At the same time, 
there continues to exist in Latin American thought a vital tradition of inter-
pretation of self in which culture is not seen as a stage in human evolution, 
but as a permanent attribute of human existence. Political norms of organiza-
tion are not determined by the pre-social consent of individuals, but are 
derived directly from the defining principles of the social structure that pro-
duces identity of the participants in the system. Similarly, authority does not 
flow from the voluntaristic adherence to contractual relations as it does in the 
deculturalized liberal image of modernity. The authority of culture is located 
in its organic origins in charismatic revelations (Catholicism) or immutable 
tradition (Meso-American views of world order). The continuing practice of 
an objectivist discourse that imagines culture structures to reproduce themsel-
ves through both language and other institutions of socialization transforms 
the question of the (bi)cultural education from an issue of technique to a 
matter of ontology. 

Accounting for Law 
287 
To illustrate the potential connection between current political discourse 
in Mexico and biculturalist accounts of culture and education, I will refer to 
Octavio Paz's Labyrinth of Solitude — a classic of the genre of essays defining 
Latin culture by negative reference to North American society. In his poetic 
elaboration of organic discourse, Paz gives complete primacy to the Meso-
American and Catholic heritage of Mexico. He describes the Mexican as fa-
talistic and non-instrumental. Aztec culture fully determined man's lot and 
life. Freedom was assigned to the Gods alone. There was no sense of personal 
salvation in Indian religious images or activities. All activities, including 
human sacrifice, had no individual or subjective meaning, but were directed 
to the preservation of the social and universal order. In turn, Latin Catholi-
cism stresses the blood and suffering of Christ, the indelibility of original sin, 
and the free gift of the condition of grace. The patroness Virgin of Guadelupe 
represents pure receptivity to fallen man seeking only a return from his pain 
and a passive absorption to his salvation. 
For Paz' Mexico, the world is not a mirror of man's creative efforts. Man's 
constitution of social forms mirrors the world as a determining and dangerous 
reality, which is stable and unmoving. For example, male and female are 
understood as natural characteristics of universal order played out as machismo 
and submissiveness. Paz dwells on the Mexican obsession with death, the 
final determinism, and the quest for transparency and disappearance. He ar-
gues that unremitting conflict, both with other men and external reality, has 
been the dominant attribute of Mexican psychological history. This conflict 
reflects the centrality in our nature of a minetic and rivalrous combat for non-
material forms of the desirable (status, power) which are necessarily in limited 
supply. At the same time, Mexico aspires to community in ritual and ideology 
in order to struggle against the loneliness created by increasing confrontra-
tions with the inevitable. Human tragedy is at the core of a being both alie-
nated from and in constant need of other men. There is an indissolvable 
contradiction of actuality and ideality to which is traced the pessimistic tone 
of Paz' Mexico. His claim is that the opposition between the natural sense of 
solitude and the communal effort to overcome the separations imposed by 
time and space produces Mexico's quest for a unity of being in a fixed present. 
It is the illusory expulsion from timelessness into time which establishes 
the unnatural nature of individual human life. It is a return from narrative 
diachrony to synchronic order toward which Mexico strives. 
Paz' definition of the culture which is Mexico may be grasped by its structu-
ral opposition to North American history. The United States is optimistic, 
activist, reformist; Mexico pessimistic, quietist, without illusions. [North] 
Americans eliminate death, Mexicans are obsessed with it. Americans are 
incredulous, Mexicans believers. Americans love fairy tales and detective 
stories; Mexicans myths and legends. Americans want to understand, Mex-
icans contemplate. Americans consider the world something to be perfected; 
Mexicans consider it something to be redeemed. "We enjoy our wounds and 

288 
Thomas C. Heller 
they enjoy their inventions." Even the two central events of the history of 
Mexico are to be understood as symbolic of her cultural identity. Mexico, for 
Paz, is born not in self-proclaimed revolt but in the collective pain of the 
externally imposed conquest of the accepting Aztec. The quest for communal 
fulfillment, Mexico's Revolution, is not an instrumental program, but rather 
a repudiation of foreign intrusions of liberalism. The Revolution is no more 
than a desire to purify and recapture Mexican cultural origins. It has no ideas. 
It is only "a sudden immersion of Mexico in her own being," "an explosion 
of reality," "a return and a communion." The posited relationship between 
North and Latin America (Mexico) is both semiological and political. The 
two entities are defined by the negative of the other and evaluate their own 
merit by depreciating the quality of that which they are not. 
Commitment to such a structuralist form of discourse that privileges 
culture as an unanalyzed term logically alters the understanding of the 
relation of meaning, language, and schooling. At the core of the American 
liberal account of language are fundamental propositions about both the 
particularity of meaning and the agency of the subject. The former specifies 
the correspondential relation between linguistic units, the internal mental, 
and the external physical worlds. The latter defines the character of language 
as instrumental and renders concrete the history of linguistic evolution. 
Structural theories of language displace both of these propositions. Initial 
formulations of structuralist linguistics relocated the production of meaning 
within the network of relations that was language itself. Structuralism 
argued that the systematic form of language, rather than the particular 
linguistic elements of actual spoken words, gave rise to intelligibility. 
Similarly, since meaning was contained in the intralinguistic system, the 
role of the speaker as agent was displaced. The speaker was now dependent 
on language itself to engage in meaningful activities. The meaning available 
to a subject was that opened up by the conceptual ordering his or her 
language afforded. The subject was better understood as a product of 
culture, an identity created in language, a potentiality limited by the 
language that defined the conventions of a world. 
To a linguistic structuralist to abandon a particular language is to abandon 
a discrete universe of meanings and the representations of personal existence 
it alone makes possible. Acquiring English — understood in an instrumental 
theory of language — is neither an excessively difficult or disruptive task. 
Learning English — understood in a structuralist theory of language — is 
another matter. To learn a new language will be understood to be a metaphor 
for entering a new world. We do not learn English so much as we learn how 
to see or reconstruct ourselves. There is an unspoken shift in the meaning we 
attribute to the campaign to defend the dominant use of English, or of any 
one language, as our theory about the meaning of language shifts from liberal 
instrumentalism to structuralist representation. The anger and repression 
associated with the defense against biculturalist education results from the 

Accounting for Law 
289 
reinterpretation of its text to mean that the rejection of English is the rejection 
of the way the liberal world is constructed. 
Similarly, in a structuralist representation of social order, the role of the 
school in the reproduction of the individual assumes a greater importance 
than it can have in a liberal theory of education. It is essential for an analyst 
speaking a discourse of culture to integrate an account of the activity of 
all socializing institutions that transmit the formative structure of the code. 
Hispanic advocates of educational reform insisted upon a program of cultural 
maintenance that required predominant and continued teaching in the Span-
ish language because it imagined a particular construction of reality, and 
upon the reorganization of the American classroom form that reflected liberal 
understandings of schooling. Bilingual/bicultural ideologies (see, e. g., Rami-
rez and Cardenas, Cultural Democracy, 
Biocognitive 
Development 
and Education) 
argue that liberal education rewards universalism, secularism, rationality and 
competitive individualism. Conversely, it illegitimately disparages the attri-
butes of Latin order — traditionalism, ritual, community and interdependent 
learning. Bicultural education attempts to improve the relatively poor educa-
tional performance of Latin children in American schools by creating a conti-
nuity and concordance between the culture of the Mexican home and family 
and that of the school. 
There are four value clusters, familiar elements of the Latin organicist dis-
course, which at once define Mexican-American culture and distinguish it 
from the dominant Anglo culture. The Latino's primary self-identification is 
particularistic with reference to family, community, and ethnic group. Social 
relations are personalized rather than conceived as universalizations of the 
abstracted capacities of dehistoricized subjects. Status acquisition and role 
definition are ascribed through family and local community. Finally, there is 
a general world construction associated with fatalistic Catholic ideology. In 
describing the family, in both its nuclear and its extended form (La Raza), as 
the fundamental unit of social analysis, biculturalists speak of the cultural 
tendencies to subordinate individual to collective need, to render time less 
narrative through the sense of the repetitive continuity of family reproduc-
tion, and to contrast Hispanic communality to the liberal understanding of a 
predominantly personal identity. Communalization implies mutual depend-
ence rather than independence, cooperative achievement rather than indivi-
dual competitive projects, and a desire for guidance, direction and support 
from authority figures. Cultural ascription rather than individual definition 
of status and role produces both an emphasis on conformity to prescribed age 
and sex roles and a valued recognition of traditional internal hierarchies. As 
in Mexico, religion reinforces, by the constant presence of ritual, the cultural 
production of the individual as a determined aspect of the collective. 
The biculturalist case for educational reform centers on a hypothetical 
reconstruction of educational institutions in such a way that they would 
mirror, rather than undercut, Latin cultural attributes. At the least, schools 
must not produce a type of cultural schizophrenia by socializing children with 

290 
Thomas C. Heller 
a double-binded message about appropriate identity formations. Bicultural 
education requires first an alteration of the incentive-motivation style of 
schools. There must be less stress on individual achievement and competition, 
and more on cooperative and collective effort, to cause Mexican-American 
children to participate. Human relations between student and teacher must 
shift toward nurturing, creating social affiliation within the group, providing 
need succorance, and diminishing the remoteness of authority figures. Differ-
ences in valued intellectual attributes would produce a redirection of learning 
toward the transmission of skills that related to being sensitive to the social 
environment rather than to abstracted analytic reasoning. Most importantly, 
educators must recognize that the cognitive abilities of Chicano children are 
field dependent rather than field independent. Field dependent children learn 
better with materials that are social rather than impersonal, with tasks that are 
more verbal than purely logical, with authority figures who express approval, 
with situations in which fantasy, humor and socialibility are present. 
The judicial and administrative decisions which denied the biculturalist 
arguments that the Hispanic community had a legal right to particular restruc-
tured educational programs must be characterized within a structuralist repre-
sentation of politics as acts of repression. Those who articulate the discourse 
of Latin culture employ a grammar that deconstructs the dominant American 
discourse of universal subjectivity by translating it into a regional discourse 
of Anglo culture. Heaving asserted the equality of discourses by reducing all 
conceptual orderings to limited cultural practices, Hispanic educators claim 
that school environments should be adjusted with respect to their modes 
of communication, human relations, motivational techniques and learning 
theory so that discordant fits between institutional design and the organiza-
tion of alternative cultural forms are eliminated. The heart of this biculturalist 
thesis is that the dominant self-understanding of the American educational 
theory is a form of false consciousness. The notion that schools can be profi-
cient transmitters of factual (empirical) and technical (logical) information or 
could be neutral with respect to cultural (normative) content is treated as 
ideology. With the deconstruction of liberalism's grammatical denial of its 
own status as a culture, biculturalism seeks to expose the parochial and con-
tingent context in which subjectivity is spoken. It is implied that the delegiti-
mation of the dominant theory must at least open a space for localized institu-
tional reform. To biculturalists the refusal of the legal system in the United 
States to incorporate these alternative images into its doctrinal representa-
tions of identity, language and education was evidence only of its ideological 
role in the reproduction of an existing, exclusive social order. 
III. Metastructural Oppositions 
The opposition of two contradictory characterizations of the result of the 
legal process that settled the contested practices of bicultural education 

Accounting for Law 
291 
may be described as the outcome of the encounter of two structurally 
disjunctive discourses. Both the translation of the claims into legal terms 
compatible with the predominant American liberal discourse and the conse-
quent repression in the legal system of the alternative representations that 
pictured education as an artifact of cultural reproduction are expectable 
phenomena in what we might call a metastructural analysis. Metastructural-
ism treats discursive formations as mediating structures that organize 
experience: (1) by taking as primitive some selected aspects of that experi-
ence and (2) explaining all other phenomena in accounts privileging or 
refusing to reduce to prior explanatory sequences those central terms. 
However, when two such discourses are placed in active contention with 
one another, there is necessarily an incompatibility between their simultane-
ous expression. Since each privileges central terms that the other treats as 
explainable in terms of its own irreducible categories, to speak the two 
discourses together undercuts whatever semblance of order the other pur-
ports to permit. Where conflict between mutually deconstructive discourses 
comes to our attention, it would seem appropriate to have recourse to a 
procedure for the resettlement of disturbed practices that would permit us 
to go on without dehabilitating confusion or the adoption of ironic attitude 
about the contingency of our claims to knowledge that most of us seem 
incapable of sustaining for long. Either one discourse must be shown to 
be wrongly used or distinguishable from other inconsistent linguistic 
practices, or, alternatively, the boundaries must be reinstitutionalized that 
previously served to prevent the direct confrontation of these opposed 
representations of events. 
The reciprocal deprivileging of the essential terms of the opposing liberal 
and structural discourses involved in the biculturalism controversy can illus-
trate the broader argument. Within liberal accounts the central image is the 
existential account of the passage of subjectivity across narrative time. This 
passage is demarcated with respect both to the lives of individuals and the 
progressive evolution of social organization. The autonomy of the subject 
is represented in the phenomenology of the indeterminacy of action, the 
experience of the openness of the future, and the need to construct through 
choice normative projects that can constitute a self. From this perspective, the 
unanalyzed categories within a discourse of culture are reduced to elements of 
an earlier, pre-modern stage. Just as the liberal interpretation of the genetic 
psychology of Piaget and Kohlberg shows that the individual subject follows 
a natural teleology from dependent childhood to a mature and responsible 
adulthood, so liberal political economy argues that societies progress from 
a pre-modern or undeveloped condition toward a particular form of self-
governance. To be pre-modern is to see individual roles and identity as as-
cribed by a static and traditional reproduction of culture. To be undeveloped 
is to fatalistically accept such ascriptions, to see social differentiation as the 
outcome of luck and not individual effort, to understand economic processes 

292 
Thomas C. Heller 
as the partition of a restricted quantity of the good and not as a cooperative 
game of indefinite expansion. 
Modernity is precisely the obliteration of the limits on individual expres-
sion and the end of ideology and other collective discursive categories such 
as culture. These terms are reduced by liberalism to the political instruments 
of those who would continue to disempower the subject. The figure of culture 
is translated into an ideological mechanism of oppression in the pre-modern 
world and into a chosen attribute of self such as ethnicity or lifestyle in the 
developed sphere. The undeveloped are condemned to cultural determinism; 
the modern may put it on or shed it like a costume for weekend food festivals. 
Consequently, the liberal analyst can easily explain in causal terms the ongoing 
predominance of pre-individualist discourse in Latin America as a defensive 
reaction to the North American overcoming of the barriers that delayed the 
emergence of the subject. A non-evolutionary and fatalistic perspective on 
human history is more to be expected from those who have less reason to feel 
satisfaction with their current historical condition. 
From the perspective of liberal theory, it is apparent that the purported 
virtues of Hispanic culture are not original characteristics of the attributes 
of communal society. Instead, they are simply nostalgic inversions of the 
several components of the familiar critique of pre-modern society put 
forward by American economists, educators, and anthropologists in the 
post-war period. In this Latin transformation of the liberal developmentalist 
account of pre-modern culture, immaturity is revalued as realism, adherence 
to tradition rendered into the recognition of universal forms. Fatalism 
becomes resignation. Ineffectiveness becomes communion. The limited 
good is no longer a reflection of a relatively primitive epoch of the history 
of production. It is a permanent condition which makes the distribution 
of immaterial rather than material goods into the meaningful core of human 
relations. Similarly, in educational discourse the return to a theory of field 
dependence is a nostalgic movement analogous to the shift in general 
political discourse. Field independence was initially produced as a genetic 
development to which modern education could aspire. Field dependence 
and reliance on authority relations were originally conceived as pathological 
or immature conditions to be superseded by progression toward a healthy, 
independent state. In its advocacy of a permanent, rather than a remedial, 
restructuring of educational environments toward field dependence, bicul-
turalism both accepts the validity of the categorical distinctions of liberal 
education theory and attempts to revalue the discourse of culture by 
derogating the universalistic pretensions of field independence as the condi-
tion of psychological normality. 
In translating the imagery of culture into (1) an attribute of a more primitive 
stage of the human teleology, (2) an instrument for ongoing political oppres-
sion, and (3) a nostalgic but pathological defense mechanism of a collective 
psychology, liberal theorists assimilate the contradictory grammar to their 

Accounting for Law 
293 
own familiar categories and delegitimate its usage. However, the opposite 
deconstruction and translation is no more difficult to manage. All structuralist 
discourses begin in our ability and our need to account for the past as meaning-
ful and to discover a determinate order of events that supercedes the vagaries 
of our immediate experience. The unprogrammed evolution of time and the 
autonomy of the subject — the unanalyzed figures of liberal discourse — 
must be re-presented if such objective accounts are to be possible. To speak of 
the continuing presence of a meaningful ordering of experience is to relegate 
historical change to the exceptional or the ephemeral. To understand the 
mechanisms by which this order is reproduced is to see the artifactuality of 
the institutional forms and personal identities in which the structure becomes 
manifest. The reduction of all particular phenomena, including human indivi-
duals, to the artifacts of a cultural structure, transposes liberalism into one 
culture among many. However, the effects of this translation associated with 
biculturalism are especially critical for American society because it so contra-
dicts the dominant legal modes of speech. It is not simply that the authority 
of one recognized understanding of the world is challenged by another. Ra-
ther the crisis is grave and anxiety-creating precisely because it identifies 
liberals as having a culture which may be a proper object for challenge. The 
individualist terms in which one speaks of one's actions are translated from 
what seem now to be universal categories to one historically contingent ar-
rangement of, or cutting up of, experience. The primacy of the subject is 
reduced from the journey's end of the evolutionary narrative to no more than 
one discourse among others. 
When biculturalism exposes liberalism as a discrete culture, it threatens to 
expose much that has been with effort forgotten. One is thrown back from 
the hard won present where culture has been left behind, into the pre-modern 
past. According to the evolutionary liberal metaphors of modernity one is 
cast out of adulthood to childhood, from health to pathology. The meaning 
of progress from past to future and of the growth of the self-constituting 
subject that supercedes the immaturity of culturally-constituted object be-
comes illusory. The sudden and total recharacterization of the individual 
subject as no more than an element of a local discourse is the loss of phenome-
nological freedom. The application of the discourse of culture to deconstruct 
liberal practice recreates individuals as objects of knowledge and, thereby, of 
power. The superior position assumed by the knower to that which is known 
is now to be shared equally with others who previously were denied the 
capacity to name the modern. The shift of discourse may be both psychologi-
cally disruptive and politically revolutionary. To the extent that a (meta)struc-
turalist theory of law associates the operation of legal institutions with the 
reproduction of the established discourse, the theory should predict the devel-
opment of mechanisms to repress or marginalize the use of representations 
that contradict discourse or alter the meaning of its practice. 

294 
Thomas C. Heller 
IV. Post-Structural Elements 
Autopoiesis is a post-structural discourse in both a chronological and a prag-
matic sense. It need not deny that a legal controversy, such as biculturalism, 
can be analyzed as a struggle over the reproduction of differentiated discursive 
orders (one of which, liberalism, has the grammatical property that it denies 
the primacy of discourse). It can accept the view that among contemporary 
institutions, the legal system is a principal arena of ideological representation 
where this struggle is likely to manifest itself. At the same time, however, 
autopoiesis must rework what have now become excessive simplifications of 
pure structuralist accounts. It must resituate the understanding of historical 
time and individuality, representations which are reduced to derivative arti-
facts of structure in the discourse of the collective, in order to open up new 
space for innovative approaches to political conflicts that are not being re-
solved as currently imagined within the field of alternative discourses now 
deployed. Dissatisfactions with the (meta)structural account may revolve 
around the following points: 
1. An accurate mapping of the theoretical and practical discourses actually 
in place in any set of institutions shows that there is never reference to only 
one representation of events. Instead of structural unity, any functioning 
system displays a complex topography of partial accounts that very often 
contradict one another when brought close together. In the liberal legal sys-
tem there are wide areas of practice organized around a series of determinist 
discourses whose fundamental grammar would deconstruct the liberal indivi-
dualism that dominates the system. The behavior of the insane, of children, 
formerly of women or slaves, of immigrants and primitives has been charac-
terized as the product of objective social and genetic mechanisms. Its perpetra-
tors have thus been absolved of legal responsibility and control. In some 
restricted domains collective entities such as families and even nations have 
been ascribed the status of phenomenological subjects normally reserved for 
individuals. However, such well established differences in legal categorization 
do not stand up to close analysis that examines the coherence between such 
practices and the operative terms of the liberal discourse that ought to deter-
mine legal practices in a structurally integrated legal system. In fact, the 
presence of outlying and contradictory practices in every complex representa-
tional order suggests that one essential attribute of legal institutions is to keep 
firm boundaries between conceptually indistinguishable areas of practice that 
at once coexist and threaten one another within a legal system. 
2. An account given in a discourse built upon the figure of autopoietic sys-
tems may move beyond the imagery of opposed, untranslatable, and mutually 
deconstructive structures by emphasizing the hierarchical organization of 
information systems and relations among multiple levels of representation. 
In a sense, the liberal and cultural representations of the world never touch 

Accounting for Law 
295 
one another since they aggregate information about experience at quite dif-
ferent levels of abstraction. Like computer languages in which there may be 
more or less detailed or compiled descriptions of available information, the 
discursive ordering of information may cut into the set of innumerable pos-
sible representations of events by means of wholly disparate and logically 
discrete characterizations. A liberal discourse that privileges an existential 
phenomenology imagines and describes all reality from the standpoint of 
an individual subject. It aggregates the multiple physical subsystems that 
compose the individual into one unitary entity while disaggregating all more 
complex social orders into collections of individual wills. Since this stand-
point or mode of organizing information is exclusive, it is not coherent to 
describe experience from other locations within the complex topography of 
possible representations of information in the same voice that we use when 
we speak of ourselves as the elemental units we call subjects. However, it is 
easily possible to re-present events as more or less aggregated chunks of 
information so that individuality is only: (1) a product or sub-unit of a higher 
level system (e. g., cultural discourse), or (2) a composite field of interactions 
among more reduced physiological or psychological entities. 
To see the endless range of possible systems into which information can be 
differentiated displaces the impression that any single arrangement is natural 
or teleologically privileged. All arrangements of information must suppress 
other imaginable systematizations in order to create meaning. Because the 
production of significance from chaos (information from noise), demands 
repression of some information available in discarded representations, the 
total information content of all particular systems approaches constancy. At 
the same time that autopoiesis deprivileges any single discourse in the hierar-
chy of multiple orderings, it poses questions about the historical deployment 
of discourses. Although discrete arrangements of information are epistemo-
logically necessary to permit the emergence of meaning, it is not evident how 
such systems are to be defined, how they institutionalize the reproduction of 
their elements, or how they evolve and are superceded. Since it is possible 
to use alternative discourses sequentially to describe the same domain of 
experience or simultaneously to describe differentiated domains of experi-
ence, it is not necessary to assume that the evolution of discourse must involve 
transformative eclipse of, or epistemological break with, existing practices. 
Instead, a post-structural discourse may involve a pastiche of rearranged 
practices taken from established linguistic orderings, partially replicated and 
innovatively juxtaposed, to create a reworked image of the identity of self-
organizing systems. Similarly, autopoietic time should be reimagined as a 
forking, uncertain passage through a labyrinth of equally probable accounts 
of events rather than as either a continuous narrative of individual lives or as 
a succession of disjunctive structural periodizations of history. 
3. Although pure structural accounts described the production of practice 
by theory as determinate, a poststructuralist grammar can emphasize the 

296 
Thomas C. Heller 
openness and interpretative ambiguity of this relationship. Practice ought 
to be seen as discontinuous from theory to emphasize that all theory 
undetermines the production of more concrete operations and each practice 
has overdetermined explanations. Autopoiesis must posit a discursive sys-
tem in which the linkage of practice to theory, at each level of abstraction 
of information, is historical rather than logical and the nature of authority 
to establish both theory and practice is not formally rational or exclusively 
objective. 
In addition to the indeterminacy that characterizes the internal arrangement 
of the elements of meaning systems, autopoiesis can be distinguished from 
structuralism or earlier systems theories by its focus on the instability of 
discourse. There is a dynamic tendency in all autopoietic systems of order to 
break down. Given (1) that there exist multiple possibilities for the representa-
tion of information, (2) that the repression of alternative representations must 
attend the emergence of any particular order, (3) that the indeterminacy of 
the process by which practice is settled within a discursive order will repeat-
edly recall our attention to the contingency of representations, and (4) that 
every discursive order contains contradictory references to alternative ar-
rangements of information within it, it is most plausible that any meaning 
system will have a limited capacity for self-reproduction. Instead of structural 
fixity and equilibrated systems, autopoiesis expects the death of systems and 
exposes the unexplored field of far-from-equilibrium events. 
4. Autopoiesis and all post-structural discourse is fundamentally local and 
not global. Discursive practices, both of theory and differently institutional-
ized forms of expression, are not consistent across all sub-systems of a wider 
interactive system. The complex and local normal state of discursive orders 
can be observed by examining the contradictory accounts of events given by 
the same actors in different institutional arenas. For example, Hispanics who, 
when confronting North Americans, argue that Mexican culture produces an 
identity rooted in community and a recognition of a wider structural order, 
will, when engaged in domestic Mexican politics, castigate their Indian popu-
lations as non-individualistic and resigned to perpetual poverty. Similarly, 
North Americans, who formulate an educational policy vis-ä-vis Latinos in 
a liberal discourse, will invoke all forms of psychoanalytic, sociological, or 
geopolitical determinisms in internal regional struggles situated in other pol-
itical institutions. Identity, like discursive practices more generally, is de-
ployed within and derived from local political confrontation. Since the outco-
mes of institutional processes that establish the evolution of discourse within 
a specific domain are indeterminate, it is logical that discrete but interactive 
sub-systems will develop incompatible practices over time. This dispersion 
of representations may lead to dissonance and intrasystemic conflict that redu-
ces the stability of any established ordering of events. The interactions among 
locally evolving institutions that concurrently reproduce highly selective, 

Accounting for Law 
297 
differentially systematized information will emerge as an originary or genetic 
style in post-structural accounts. 
5. An autopoietic discourse will be post-liberal in that it characterizes indivi-
dual self-consciousness as a non-privileged standpoint from which to view a 
complex hierarchy of representations. It shares with structuralist accounts an 
acceptance of social discourse that operates at a higher level of aggregation 
than the individual actor. However, it is post-structural in that it opens a 
new discursive space for politics by generating accounts that emphasize the 
contradictory, multi-storied, unstable and local nature of systems of meaning. 
Additionally, a coherent autopoietic discourse must be closed in form so that 
it may offer an autopoietic account of its own genetic, local, and transitory 
character. A post-structuralist representation must both rearrange the con-
figuration of images to expose fresh grounds for semiotic expression and, 
given the circular movement of an autopoietic logic, be self-conscious of its 
status as one discourse among many in a more complex information system. 
Autopoietic discourse must account for the genetic politics of its evolution 
and be content with the indeterminate nature of its own self-definition. By its 
own terms, autopoiesis cannot be an unsituated meta-account of experience. 
Rather, it must be located within a particular history of evolving institutional 
practices in order to clarify, convey, and reformulate the world in which those 
practices will compete for survival. 
V. An Autopoietic Sketch of the Biculturalism Controversy 
An autopoietic account of bilingualism would be too lengthy to attempt in 
this essay. Instead, I will simply begin to elaborate the kind of narrative that 
one might employ, outline some of the major points that a full account would 
have to discuss, and conclude by speculating about the political meaning of 
the invocation of a discourse of this type. 
1. Intersystemic Origins of Perturbations of the Legal System 
In the initial half of this century, the American economic and legal systems 
underwent substantial change. The rise of mass production industries based 
upon technologies that increased the ratio of capital to labor and encouraged 
enlarged economies of scale brought about a reorganization of corporate 
enterprise. The growing need for semi-skilled laborers, trained in shop-spe-
cific tasks and amenable to the industrial pace necessary for uninterrupted 
long production runs influenced the reform of industrial organization. Indus-
trial relations in the advanced sector stabilized around shared administration 
of the workplace between management and worker representatives and a 
splitting of the economic rents between capital and organized labor. At the 

298 
Thomas C. Heller 
same time, the legal system evolved from a relatively laissez-faire liberal order 
to a neo-liberal order featuring a variety of new interventionary practices. 
The period from 1917 to the Second World War saw the institutionalization 
of rights of labor to bargain over economic surplus and administer the shop 
floor, the establishment of macro-economic controls to uphold the level of 
aggregate demand required by capital intensive production, the passage of 
limited transfer systems of social security and unemployment compensation 
aimed principally at the modern element of the workforce, immigration re-
strictions targeted upon the European populations that had always supplied 
the unskilled labor pool in America, and a vast expansion of regulatory 
authority to alter market structure and the relative prices of productive activi-
ties. These changes in the law were not conceived to be aberrations from 
the pre-existing liberal order. Rather, they were represented as corrective 
procedures needed to permit the implementation of the projects of autono-
mous subjects in markets that did not correspond to technically ideal condi-
tions. 
The evolution of institutional practice in the national economic and legal 
systems was matched by corresponding shifts in the political and cultural 
domains. Politically, the dominant trends involved the growth of bureaucra-
tization and planning in various administrative authorities and a movement 
of legislative power toward a coalition composed of organized labor, 
corporate capital and state bureaucrats. At the same time the task of 
completing the incorporation of marginal groups, most importantly Blacks 
and women, to the status of full participation as autonomous individuals 
became a central focus of the increasingly prominent state apparatus. In 
cultural matters, the reaffirmation of traditional images of American identity 
to create the appearance of the continuity of American history was an 
overwhelming concern. The discontinuities and contingencies in the Ameri-
can liberal self-presentation occasioned by the strong flirtations with social-
ism and a kind of technological utopianism of a corporatist form in the 
1919 — 37 period were overtly repressed in the post-War II years. Economic 
unionism as the natural order of industrial relations, immigration as a 
process of individual investment in human capital and flight from pre-
modernity, regulation as the perfection of liberal market processes — all 
represented a Whiggish reconstruction of the recent past to banish its 
deconstructive implications. 
After 1945, the transformation of the national system penetrated the 
order of international relations as well. The international economic system, 
in which the national state as an aggregate unit was represented as an 
autonomous actor, had been characterized in the interwar era as an unco-
ordinated realm marked by conflicting, autarchic national domestic policies. 
However, given the preponderant force of the United States in the non-
socialist world after the Second War, it was possible for American interests 
to impose new international institutions more consistent with the American 

Accounting for Law 
299 
political economy. The creation of largely integrated markets for trade in 
goods (GATT), the stabilization of currencies (IMF), the increased world 
wide demand (IBRD and Marshall Plan), and the opening of borders to 
multinational capital flows met the demands both of the American military 
attempting to rebind the West and the intact American mass industrial sector 
seeking to avoid potential unemployment by exporting its unimpaired high 
levels of production. The reform of the international order allowed the 
continued institutionalization in the United States of the economic system 
that had been developed before the war under conditions of relative 
isolation from external economic competition. As a consequence, prosperity 
in the unionized or advanced production sector sustained a socio-psycho-
logical shift in which it came to be expected by Americans that they should 
have stable, organized, well paying, semi-skilled or skilled jobs connected 
to job ladders that promised a career of advancement. Dead end, unskilled 
jobs outside the advanced sector were rejected as demeaning. This rejection 
was supported by a system of compensating public transfer payments 
supported by the government share of the economic surplus produced in 
modern industry. 
This configuration of the American national system has proven to be 
unstable since 1970. The spread of American capital and technology to 
other nations, combined with recovery of Western Europe and Japan, 
began to compete away the economic rents on which the system depended. 
Competition drove American capital in the advanced sectors to seek lower 
cost labor and productive conditions by investment in facilities overseas 
and by the introduction of labor saving technologies at home. In addition, 
in the agricultural, small service, and traditional manufacturing sectors 
where good jobs on the industrial model had never been plentiful, relatively 
low profit margins created a growing demand for low wage, high quality 
labor that American workers were relatively unwilling to provide. In 
expanding regions like the Southwest and West, this sectoral labor shortage 
was made up principally by importing Latin workers illegally from Mexico 
across frontiers where the immigration laws had never been focused or 
functioned. The increasing Hispanic population, although initially com-
posed principally of temporary-stay young males, has always deposited a 
percentage of its members as a permanent residence community and has 
recently shifted toward greater employment of young women with aptitude 
in light assembly and manufacturing. Moreover, as the migration grew, it 
spawned communities that replicated the institutions of Mexican daily life 
and diminished the cultural exile that a temporary worker necessarily 
suffered in the United States. The gradual reproduction of a cultural 
system that linked areas of origin in central Mexico with communities of 
destination in California and Texas has produced a social order that is 
situated in extended geographical space. At the level of the working class, 
the normalization of migratory networks has produced an adjustment 

300 
Thomas C. Heller 
toward a binational or a transnational cultural system that has evolved 
along a trajectory consistent with that of the transnationalized economic 
system. However, the contemporary frontiers of the economic and cultural 
orders no longer coincide with the boundaries of the American political 
and legal systems. 
Just as the American domestic economy responded to effects generated 
in the restructured internal economic order, the Mexican domestic system 
evolved in relation to those broader economic operations. Mexican post-
war development strategies were imagined in terms of their relation to an 
integrated global order. In spite of abundant supplies of labor, the basic 
drive has been to retrace the industrial history of more advanced societies 
through a strategy of building import substituting industries that were 
relatively capital intensive. These industries were often initially financed 
by direct multinational investment and later through borrowing of portfolio 
capital from the North. In addition, the subsistence or rain-fed agricultural 
sector received little state attention or investment. Agricultural capital was 
channeled into capital heavy, irrigated corporate farms aimed at export 
production. As a result, Mexico, like most semi-peripheral economies, made 
available large pools of surplus labor as an export good to the labor short 
sectors of the American market. The Mexican role in the integrated world 
economy depended on the obliteration of economic frontiers between the 
two increasingly interdependent domestic systems. The presence of a mas-
sive, relatively stabilized Mexican labor force in the United States remains 
wholly consistent with a Mexican development policy whose unchanged 
basic form is still encouraged by the institutions of the post-war inter-
national system. 
In accounting for the intersystemic origins of the biculturalism issue, it 
is necessary to point to multiple levels of interaction. National evolutionary 
trends in the United States penetrated the international system that in turn 
fed back consequences to the national level of various systems. The particu-
lar form of the institutions that emerged in the national and international 
systems were not inevitable and each could be analyzed separately to show 
much more complex histories about the nature of their constitution. Why 
technology, social psychology, legal theory, and international economics 
interacted to yield the specific conjunction of sub-system evolutionary paths 
that existed until quite recently is a part of some larger project. Moreover, 
the current situation is unstable and non-predictable in a number of 
dimensions. The economic system itself functions in a manner which does 
not correspond to the interests of the political coalition that set it in place. 
The open global economy was established to protect and expand the 
American share of world rents on behalf of a state/labor/capital coalition 
in the advanced industrial sector. It ought, therefore, to be expected that 
there will be strong initiatives to close off American economy from the 
effects of integration and to alter the existing terms of competition to limit 

Accounting for Law 
301 
the ability of other nations to exploit their relative advantages in low wages 
or lack of regulation. The recurrent legislative efforts to cut off Mexican 
migration are misguided in their focus on economic activities beyond the 
mass industrial sectors where the political crisis lies. However, they may 
symbolize a return to autarchic national policies that escape the unintended 
and dysfunctional consequence of earlier integrative strategies. 
A spillover from the reshaping of economic boundaries also is manifest 
in the biculturalism controversy in the legal system. It is the presence 
of a permanent Latino community culturally linked to an alternative 
representation of identity, language, and education, that set up the 
possibility of perturbation of established legal practice. It is problematic 
whether the legal system has the capacity to reproduce itself as an 
autonomous system in the face of a refiguration of concrete practices 
in both the economic and cultural subsystems discordant with existing 
legal representations. Schematically, that historical evidence suggests that 
beginning from a state in which there was a convergence of representa-
tions (statei) between the national American subsystems of law, economy, 
culture and politics in the 1945 to 1960 period, the penetration of the 
American economy into the international economic system led to an 
unforeseen evolution (state2) of the penetrating subsystem itself and a 
secondary shift in the operation of cultural institutions. The uneven 
development of subsystems that figure in each other's representations 
of events gives rise to an inquiry about the nature of the linkage of 
autopoietic systems and the possible paths of behavior of American 
legal and political institutions in such circumstances. 
More reduced or less aggregated units of analysis 

302 
Thomas C. Heller 
2. Elements of an Autopoietic Analysis 
Autopoietic meaning systems are distinguished from prior representa-
tions of social systems by their internal complexity, system closure, instabil-
ity, and locality. Grammatically, if we are to speak coherently of their 
behavior in particular historical circumstances, we must: (1) define with 
care which information must be reproduced for systemic continuity within 
an ordering that normally contains multiple and contradictory representa-
tions of experience; (2) describe the interactive effects among coexistent 
systems, each of which autonomously represents the other to itself and in 
so doing may originate instability between themselves; (3) explain the 
internal dynamics of self-reproduction within a single autopoietic system 
given the epistemological and political contingencies associated with the 
generation and maintenance of any specific construction of order. Stylisti-
cally, if autopoietic analysis is to be interesting, the content of the self-
organizing systems of meaning must be defined in such a way that its death 
or inability to continue reproduction is a possibility under imaginable 
circumstances. The sources of variation within the system must illustrate 
the complicated sense in which autopoietic systems must be both closed 
to the environment if they are to be autonomous and open to cognitive 
adjustment and response if they are to endure. An evolutionary account in 
which selective response to system variation functions as an operative 
term should be described with fractile cybernetic models that allow for 
catastrophic solutions. By fragmenting the representation of space into 
multiple coexisting domains and of time into discontinuous histories, the 
figure of locality recalls our attention to the contingency of order and the 
costs of avoiding chaos.

lined points and diagrams below.

3. The Politics of Autopoiesis 
The politics of the use of a post-structuralist discourse, such as autopoiesis, 
remain as yet obscure. On the one hand, the account is overtly deconstruct-
ive and seeks to define a reformed theoretical space that escapes the 
historical difficulties attendant upon both determinist discourses and narrat-
ives of free consciousness. On the other hand, autopoiesis must not be 
critique alone and cannot define itself as only an affirmation of the absence 
of those representations with which we have become familiar. At the level 
of theory, in order to close its own circle and give a self-reflective account 
of itself, autopoiesis must explain its own evolutionary appearance in terms 
of the particular historical possibilities allowed by the disruption of accepted 
theoretical practices in epistemology and the philosophy of science. In 
addition, however, according to its own discursive terms, the politics of 

306 
Thomas C. Heller 
autopoiesis must be equally manifest in concrete institutional practices of 
wider scope than a dialectics of knowledge alone would suggest. Because 
autopoiesis does not distinguish qualitatively between levels of representa-
tion, there is no logical hierarchical relationship between practices at 
different levels of aggregation of information. Consequently, to evaluate 
the emergence of post-structural discourse, we should move beyond the 
evolution of theory to examine the development of the economic and 
cultural institutions in which the discourse is commonly spoken. This final 
element of the essay will focus on the deconstructive implications of post-
structuralist imagery for existing political traditions and the potential 
interests for which autopoiesis may become the dominant ideology. 
/W-structural discourse has been read as a«//-structuralist. Since auto-
poiesis emphasizes the complex, the local, the closed or self-referential, and 
the unstable, it evidently assaults structuralist accounts that center upon 
the operations of global, coherent, artificing and equilibrating mechanisms, 
whether physical, biological or cultural. In particular, the force of post-
structuralist analysis has been directed against the unitary and continuous 
philosophy of history explicit in Marxism and the institutional embodiment 
of centralized power in the contemporary welfare state. Post-structuralism 
has been castigated by sophisticated progressive critics as a reactionary form 
of late capitalism precisely because it disrupts this last great emancipatory 
narrative of the Enlightenment Tradition and delegitimates the modern 
advances of the social democracy linked to that narrative. 
The post-structuralist polemic was originally directed against the ideal 
of the disciplinary and totalitarian state that reproduces its own image in 
every niche of social life. Its analysis has more recently spilled over into a 
more generalized critique of existing regulatory institutions, their ability 
to control a complex, interactive social network, and the stability of the 
coalition of capital, labor, and bureaucratic interests that sustain them. 
However, it is a misjudgment to fold post-structuralist discourse back into 
either an amended Marxist stage theory or into a revived libertarian 
argument against the collective per se. Once it is accepted that continuous 
histories like that of humanistic Marxism have been effectively de-
constructed theoretically, to call for their reaffirmation as effective mass 
myths brings the left close to a politics of fascism. The argument that 
autopoiesis is the ideology produced by late capitalist corporations seeking 
to disempower their regulators is a more potentially interesting line of 
analysis that too often flounders in highly simplistic accounts that ignore 
the changing political economy of both governmental and corporate organi-
zations for the sake of narrative continuity. Nevertheless, it is correct to 
see that the political evaluation of autopoiesis is concretely linked to a 
judgment about the desirability of the newly emergent institutions and 
disciplines which express themselves autopoietically. On the other hand, 
to suggest that post-structuralism is a resuscitation of liberal individualism 

Accounting for Law 
307 
is to lose sight of the displacement of the figure of the autonomous subject 
within the core representations of autopoietic discourse and to forget the 
fundamental anti-humanism that carries over from structuralism to the 
images emerging from it. If we understand autopoiesis as the beginning 
of an answer to structuralism's suppression of temporality and its oblitera-
tion of the experience of subjectivity, we must not forget how much 
structuralism has altered us. 
The non-humanist or non-liberal character of autopoiesis can be high-
lighted in several ways. Liberal humanism arose in conjunction with a 
bifurcated epistemology. Normative knowledge was available in the direct 
examination of subjective inner discourse. Moral judgment was necessarily 
individual, available publicly only when confessed by the evaluator, unveri-
fiable and uncriticizable by collective standards. Factual and logical know-
ledge was not a matter for interpretation, but for immediate apperception. 
The domain of the objective — positive science and mathematics — was 
not in need of mediation by representational structures whose very nature 
was to construct order rather than discover it. This division of the ways 
of knowing was reified into a bifurcation of types of being and the creation 
of an image of a separable realm of the human with its own intellectual 
disciplines and activities. Structuralist anti-humanism struggled to empty 
this differentiated realm by reducing its contents to the artifacts of one 
objective mechanism or another. Autopoietic scientific practice rejects both 
this extension of positive science to the status of a universal discourse and 
the bifurcation that preceded it. Instead, if we examine the biology of self-
organizing systems, the anti-classical mechanics of dissipative structures in 
physical chemistry, catastrophe theory in mathematics, or the principles of 
system formation and reproduction in cybernetics and information theory, 
it is apparent that the production of scientific knowledge involves represen-
tation, selective repression of information, indeterminate behavior of sys-
tems and other attributes formerly reserved for the discourse of the human. 
However, if for autopoiesis technique is hermeneutic, so is interpretation 
technical. To point out that contemporary science depends on the recogni-
tion of the value of terms originating in phenomenological discourse does 
not consent to the general primacy of that discourse as historically practiced. 
To speak of the representational character of all knowledge and the indeter-
minacy in the evolutionary history of every system is consistent with the 
proposition that each discourse occupies only a local standpoint in the 
hierarchy of possible representational orders. Indeterminacy does not arise 
because the standpoint of the human individual is in some way privileged 
or central. Rather, indeterminacy is an element of the grammar of complex 
systems or a feature of the observation/system relationship. Von Neumann 
writes in his description of quantum mechanics: "The state of a [physical] 
system evolved perfectly deterministically; it was the observation that 
introduced an element of absolute randomness. But if the process of 

308 
Thomas C. Heller 
observation were itself observed from outside, it could be regarded as 
deterministic. There was no way of saying where the indeterminacy was; 
it was not localized in any particular place." 
In a systems discourse, indeterminacy, consciousness and the other 
elements of phenomenological discourse do not imply a specialness to 
human experience. They arise in the task of creating order through differen-
tiation. Because observation or the entry of information into a system is 
necessarily selective and requires an imposition of order by the observing 
system, indeterminacy is an artifact of the process in which alternative 
characterizations of what is received are rejected. From the standpoint of 
the human individual, systems are the creation of autonomous authors. 
Yet, reflecting upon the experience of an author who selectively organizes 
the elements that define a system out of a number of plausible accounts, 
it is incorrect to conclude that systems have a fictional character or that 
the liberal discourse which expresses this experience is in some way more 
real. In a systems grammar that emphasizes a hierarchy of levels of represen-
tation, the indeterminacy of system definition may be expressed as the 
overdetermination of all explanatory structures relative to the event to be 
explained. Indeterminacy is an attendant consequence to every shift among 
levels of representation. In a subjectivist discourse that privileges the 
individual author's phenomenology, indeterminacy names the experience 
of constructing a text that moves among discourses.
