Alternatively, the shift of levels can be expressed as the underdetermina-
tion of practices by any single theory. Within an objectivist representation, 
this will be labelled the probabilistic nature of scientific cause. From this 
higher level, or more aggregated standpoint, human identity is only an 
output of system activity. Each discourse reports the problem of informa-
tion organization at different levels of aggregation distinctly and in its own 
terms. No discourse has preeminent claims against the other. All must be 
evaluated in conjunction with the historical institutions and practices in 
which they are articulated. 
The question of the relationship between the politics of individualism 
and those of autopoiesis is posed again in the apparent contradiction 
between the concept of system autonomy and the role of the analyst in 

Accounting for Law 
309 
constructing systems. An autonomous system is one which defines and 
reproduces its own elements, boundaries, and processes. However, if the 
specification of its nature is left to the system itself, it is likely to describe 
and name its current composition as its identity or to define its content at 
such a high level of generality that no concrete transformation threatens 
its existence. For example, if we accept the legal system's account of its 
own identity to determine what constitutes the system, it may specify some 
particular form of property relations it manifests at the moment of the 
inquiry. Nevertheless, if at a subsequent date the practice of property law 
is greatly altered, an interrogation of the legal system at this later time will 
yield a revised account of itself that will identify the newer property rules 
as essential. Alternatively, if theorists of the legal system assert that its 
identity lies in having a set of rules which it describes as property rules, 
or institutions to generate such rules, or learning procedures to generate 
such institutions, then the act of self-definition is again emptied of analytic 
value. In either case self-specification seems to offer no firm ground upon 
which to develop an evolutionary systems grammar. 
If we use a biological analogy, the differentiation of the genetic identity 
of species seems to require an analyst who stands outside the evolutionary 
history. We might imagine a process in which genome yields a phenome 
that is subject to selection and reproduces itself as genome2. There must 
be some pragmatically nominalist definition of how much maintenance of 
the information content of the linked genomes must be constant in order 
to constitute a single species. Over an extended period of time, as genetic 
information patterns are altered, only the continuity of the evolutionary 
history may link two individuals. Yet the very fact of that historical 
connection may be named by those individuals as the essence of their joint 
identity. To escape the methodological problems of self-definition we may 
invoke the figure of the observer/analyst/author to specify how species, 
systems, or any categories used to organize information are to be deployed. 
However, this tactic seems to involve the loss of system autonomy to 
whichever other being defines the system as an object. 
System autonomy and the activity of authorship are made compatible 
with one another by post-structuralist image of complex hierarchies of 
multiple discourses of meaning systems that are closed to one another. 
Closure, or the qualitative discontinuity between the levels of aggregation 
of information within autopoietic and liberal discourses, segregates self-
referential definition and analytical objectification. In a liberal representa-
tion, an author/analyst with an already specified identity constructs the 
figure of the system as his existential project. In a discourse of autopoietic 
systems, the identity of the individual author is defined only within the 
process of system formation and is stabilized only by the mechanisms of 
system reproduction. There is no self-identity that pre-exists that which 

310 
Thomas C. Heller 
emerges in the political conflicts that simultaneously define subjective 
character and system content. 
For autopoiesis, neither the identity of the analyst nor the nature of the 
system precedes the other. Both are elements of a coherent story or account 
of experience in which they figure concurrently with a variety of other 
technical, institutional and theoretical practices. These story elements are 
unified neither by theoretical logic nor authorial intent, but by their 
association in constituting a praxis in the world. To insist that the intention-
ality of the author is prior to the autonomy of the system is to abandon 
post-structural discourse. The grammar of autopoiesis requires that repre-
sentations at multiple levels of aggregation emerge and function conjointly 
to differentiate experience meaningfully. Which particular discourse will be 
spoken depends neither upon choice nor theory, but upon the politics of 
the practical activities wherein these various accounts are retold. 
We must distinguish autopoietic histories from both an author's creation 
of texts and a theorist's sociology of knowledge. Autopoiesis is rooted in 
a series of innovative projects in science and politics that is ongoing and 
likely to expand. These activities include making computers, doing biologi-
cal engineering, and struggling against centralized concentrations of power 
that impede the development of new forms of organizing and transmitting 
information. The evolution of systems discourse is tied to its convergence 
with historically specific changes in technology and the organization of 
production. The claim of autopoiesis to authority is essentially Heideg-
gerian. It will be recognized along with the activities in which it is grounded 
and whose self-expression it represents. Autopoiesis is appropriate to and 
facilitates the emergence of a world where these endeavors play an impor-
tant part. 
An autopoietic account of the recent evolution of post-structuralist 
discourse would be rooted in the local politics of theoretical and other 
productive institutions. Since there are in autopoietic discourse no qualita-
tive distinctions or hierarchial relationships between theoretical and more 
concrete practices at any level of representation, within each autonomous 
system the production of theory and practice will be organized according 
to the same semiotic referents. If theory and practice are one, then all levels 
of theory, including the meta-theory that is autopoietic discourse, are 
part of the post-structural political project. This as yet ill-defined project 
recognizes that contemporary changes in the organization of science and 
technology, communication, and production economics could have exten-
sive implications for the reorganization of social life. The possibility of a 
qualitative shift in the underlying basis of social relations calls into question 
the dominant images of liberal capitalism, social democracy, and an inter-
national order founded on the interaction of national states. Autopoiesis 
represents an impetus to reform both cultural and political institutions so 
that the current boundaries between technique and culture, science and 

Accounting for Law 
311 
production, collectivity and individual, state and enterprise, capital and 
labor become problematic. The potential outlines of these reforms should 
not be discussed as developments within the logic of the abstracted social 
theories or narratives that now empower the modern national state and the 
political coalitions which are committed to the continuation of its program. 
Rather they should be examined in the contingent institutional experiments 
that are evolving at the margins of advanced industrial societies. 
Post-structuralism does not criticize the contemporary national state in 
order to justify a return to pre-regulatory capitalism on behalf of multi-
national capital. The orthodox left cannot replace the shift in discourse 
within the familiar Enlightenment meta-story of social democracy or wel-
fare liberalism unless it asserts a continuity in the nature of productive 
relations between capital, labor, and the state that is denied by the technical 
practices of the institutions where autopoiesis is expressed. At the same 
time, post-structuralism does not criticize the expansion of state power in 
order to celebrate the end of ideology and institute an anarchism of 
unrestricted individual desire freed of the mythic narratives of real history. 
Instead, autopoiesis insists that meaning is an artifact of local systems 
contained within limited, but collectively generated and reproduced, do-
mains. The claim that post-structuralism is an invitation to the barbarism 
of unreason in the wake of the disruption of the positivist/Cartesian 
tradition is not to be purely judged at the level of theory, but against the 
emerging practice in which these revised accounts of authority, institutions, 
theory, and technique are grounded. Critical phenomena including the 
reorganization of work and social relations in information based industries 
and research facilities, the restructuring of communication and educational 
institutions around differentiations other than the humanistic/scientific 
dualism, the political repositioning of a superskilled technical/management 
class and an unskilled working class whose productive lives are played out 
in networks and enterprises that are transnational in character must consti-
tute the practices on which the representations of autopoiesis will spread 
or recede. It is the evolution of practice in the reformulated processes of 
production, distribution, communication and coordination that attend the 
institutionalization of the discourses of information science whose potential 
for progressive politics must be evaluated.

Considering the theory of autopoiesis in its application to law, we propose 
to examine in this paper the notion of autonomy in law. In so doing, we 
do not wish to reproduce the major flaws that any confirmed theory in 
general has, consisting in taking only one more or less central aspect and 
specifically regarding it to the point of equating it with the theory as a 
whole. Take for instance the concept of autopoiesis, which recently has 
gained so much attention. It seems to be overlooked that it is only one 
part of a much more general question of the systems theory built around 
the notions of "structure", "element", "information", "communication", 
etc. We shall not forget that, but this theory covers so many questions and 
deals with them in sometimes such a new way that it would be impossible 
for us to approach them all in the context of this article. Accordingly, we 
shall confine ourselves to one aspect only. 
When it is said that the law can be regarded as an autopoietic system, 
what that essentially means is (and this is the major departure from 
traditional systemics or cybernetics) that it is the law itself, regarded as a 
system, that says what is law and what is not, with the theory defining the 
way in which that statement is made. Let us note immediately that we shall 
refrain from speaking about boundaries or limits between the legal system 
and other social systems, especially since that separation is, as a general 
rule, used as a methodological distinction intended to be explanatory for 
law, a thing we shall eventually refute. 
The source of law as lying within law itself: that is one of the major 
points of Luhmann's transposition of the theories of Maturana and Varela 
The title may seem to indicate that we are speaking about facts in law in general; in 
reality, we would tend to say that each particular legal area constructs its own facts. 
It would thus be more accurate, in conformity with our thinking, to speak of the 
fact in public law, economic law, etc. We have kept this general title because we shall 
throughout this article endeavor to think about how a fact is constructed in law, not 
to identify the type of reality that each particular legal field has to deal with. We shall, 
however, draw on specific examples taken essentially from private law.

into legal science. The relation of an object to its context comes to be seen 
in terms of the capacity that this particular object may have to organize 
itself, to reproduce itself. The major idea of this transposition thus consists 
in positing that the law presupposes 
and reproduces 
itself \ that it is the result 
of a self-referential process. Put another way, a law becomes legal through 
the interplay of mechanisms internal to the legal system itself; it is not 
merely determined by the environment. 
Using the language of systems theory, we shall say that the legal system 
is an autonomous system because it is the only one able to assign to its 
elements a legal (normative) quality, and thus to constitute its elements as 
unity of the system. Normativity can be produced only through the legal 
system, in a self-referential process.1 
To describe this mechanism, systems theory traditionally uses the terms 
"closure" and "openness", in general in contraposition: a system is said to 
be either closed or open. In the theory of autopoiesis, this distinction or 
opposition does not exist; the two concepts are instead inseparable, cannot 
be seen as alternatives, and are articulated in a mechanism reflected in the 
idea of organizational closure. 
To say that the legal system is autopoietic, then, is to say that it is 
"normatively closed". The "information" (various events) coming from 
the environment is selected through mechanisms intrinsic to the legal 
system (idea of closure), but the functioning of the system as a whole 
depends on "facts" (idea of openness). The system's self-reference we 
mentioned above consists, at the level of system elements, in the empower-
ment of elements produced within the system to deal with other elements, 
that is, to give them a specific meaning, to "transform information into 
communication", in Luhmann's terms. 
Coming to the question of the autonomy of the legal system expressed 
through the concept of "operational closure",2 we would note that the 
debate on the issue has always taken place on an extremely abstract level; 
we would even tend to say extra-legal, within theories about systems. 
In our own treatment of this question, we shall instead endeavor to 
bring out what the notion implies when applied to law, and hence what 
new it may bring for the analysis of legal practice. We thus take up 
Teubner's idea (Teubner, 1984: 292) when he says for instance: "To use it 
[this theory] as a strictly heuristic device. What follows for the problematic 
law and society relation if it is formulated in terms of self-referentiality".

Enquiring into legal practice in order to strengthen the notion of 
"normative closure" inevitably leads in our view to posing once again the 
traditional problem of the distinction between fact and law.3 In doing so, 
we go to the point where the law realizes itself in practice, at the very core 
of legal life, to what was for Ihering "the life and truth of law". 
Our thoughts on the practical realization of law will, then, consist in an 
enquiry into the way the law apprehends the facts,4 on the basis of the 
idea of self-reproduction. In doing so, we shall reuse a number of the 
established tools of social science, which if they no longer today have the 
charm of total novelty that the theory of autopoiesis may have, still remain 
extremely rich, especially when reintegrated into this new legal theory. 
Thus, we are brought to develop a critique of the positive conception 
of legal dogmatics, whereby a theory is deduced from facts, as for instance 
mathematical theorems are deduced from axioms. Contemporary epistemol-
ogy has amply shown that none of the endeavors made to show that there 
is "a valid mode of inductive inference thanks to which theories could be 
deduced from facts" have ever succeded (O'Neil, 1969: 278). 
From fact to idea, the circuit posited by positivism, is too short: every 
fact is interpreted, and unless this is done, a fact is nothing. Bachelard has 
shown that even before authenticating a fact, one explains it (Bachelard, 
1983: 43).5 Through this idea of self-reproduction of law, we shall seek to 
imagine a possible trajectory there might be between fact and rule; to 
understand its "intrigue", in Veyne's terms (Veyne, 1978: 203). The two 
guiding points of our discussion will be: 1) the concept of fact in positive 
legal philosophy; and 2) legal science and the nature of things. 
I. The Fact in Positive Legal Philosophy 
Legal dogmatics systematically treats the logical question of the distinction 
between fact and law as a purely technical question: the extent of control 
by appellate jurisdictions on the one hand, and that of the sytematization 
of rules on the other, carried out on the basis of the notion of legal fact, 
most frequently contraposed to that of legal act; or else on the basis of a 
determination of the role of the judge and the parties in the judicial process, 
where the latter are supposed to bring out the facts for the judge to lay 
down the law (Dialectica, 1961).

Take, for instance, the question of the extent of control over lower 
courts by the Appeals Court. Since the Appeals Court is to exercise control 
over the legality of judicial decisions, doctrine has thought that it could 
consider a limit to this control as being laid down scientifically by appealing 
to the distinction between fact and law: errors of law would be referred 
to the Appeals Court, but not errors of fact. This dichotomy, which has 
the virtue of simplicity and clarity, has a relatively recent history in doctrine. 
From the Enlightenment, the revolutionaries had retained two principles: 
that of national sovereignty and that of the separation of powers. The 
Declaration of the Rights of Man stated that the freedom of individuals 
could be restricted only by the law as an expression of the general will; 
and (recalling the Ancien Regime) that the judiciary power could not limit 
that freedom, or in other words, take part in making law. The position of 
exegesis was that the law was a set of abstract general rules, and an order, 
the keystone of which was the written law. However, the enlargement 
of control by the Appeals Court from formal breach of the law to its 
misinterpretation and its application (made necessary by the elimination of 
summary legislative procedure — a cumbersome and technically inefficient 
method), as well as the power conferred on it to impose its assessment 
over resistance by the trial judges, with an eye to the unification of positive 
law, led to the opposite result from what was sought: the setting up of a 
case law, the extent of which, it had been claimed, would be limited by 
positing this distinction between fact and law. 
A study could be done on this: this procedure, presented as a purely 
technical question, involves another aspect not without interest as being 
intended as the basis of a major political organization, that aimed at warding 
off "government by judges". This distinction would thus invite us to 
inquire into the legal practices whereby power is organized and to pursue 
the historical evolution of that organization (Marty, 1929). However, such 
research could not be done before undertaking a preliminary study of 
another underlying issue, without which an inquiry into what that legal 
practice represents would be much impoverished. The previous question 
is whether this distinction between fact and law is as simple as is claimed, 
and above all, what it actually says. 
Rational legal systems — such as for instance Roman law — are all 
organized around a fundamental distinction between what is supposed to 
be, in a terminology widespread today, the order of the "given" and the 
order of the "constructed". A new legal epistemology was worked out in 
the 16th and 17th centuries (Villey, 1975: 347): the law exists in the 
consciousness of man (and is therefore no longer the object of knowledge); 
it is constructed artificially by individuals. The law became an operational 
system of rules (the predominant idea being that of conceiving definitions, 
of classified types of law — Grotius) held to express laws of nature (positive 
law as based on natural law), a nature that was getting steadily farther 

316 
Patrick Nerhot 
away from the classical conception, the new conception being increasingly 
mechanistic. The sole mode of apprehending it was to be expressed by the 
notion of "fact"; this relationship to nature thus led to society's being 
objectivized in the way a fact is. 
As long as one seeks to set up abstract scientific systems, such notions 
as "law" or "fact" seem easy to define. The real difficulty appears when 
this relationship has to be qualified, when these concepts have to be handled 
in a practical way (Kuhn, 1962). Thus Dalloz's general jurisprudence of 
1847 says, in his article on the Court of Cassation: "The distinction between 
fact and law seems easy in theory, but in application gives rise to the most 
embarrassing doubts and raises the most metaphysical questions". 
Legal dogmatics approaches these difficulties by splitting up the opera-
tion of the application of the law into three periods: the substantive 
finding of the facts, their subsumption by a legal concept, and the legal 
consequences deduced from these two operations; the first being a "judg-
ment in fact",6 and the second two "judgments in law", and subject as 
such to appeal. 
However, this method has never been totally satisfactory, for the simple 
reason that it is based on too many ambiguities, particularly because the 
situation that gives rise to application of a rule is constituted by a set of 
acts, circumstances, etc., that have to be picked out of an often complex 
and obscure context. At bottom, what this method tends principally to 
ignore is the way in which it proceeds in order to know, to apprehend, 
the context submitted to it. 
Reducing this problem to a purely technical question is perhaps a bit 
hasty. Our way of knowing the law, which posits in particular that it is 
abstract and general, while the facts are concrete and particular, does 
permit the development of a legal argument (and the subsequent technical 
statements); but first of all it expresses a theory of legal knowledge. Legally, 
when we oppose fact and law, we argue as if the facts were all given, as 
if at bottom the difficulty consisted only in finding them (the function of 
legal science). The legal rule and the finding of a fact are supposed to be 
presented, fully elaborated, to an interpreter, who has only to fit them 
together in order to be able to lay down the law. 
"The epistemological obstacle" is that, as Atias well points out (Atias, 
1985: 154), it often happens that the jurist allows himself to be caught in 
the trap of realism, being always tempted to believe that the quality of a 
legal concept can be measured very exactly by its capacity to express reality. 
Regrettable as this confusion is, it is very widespread today, with all the

instance the law on proof: there is a question of law (which therefore leads to a 
judgment in law), which is raised during establishment of the facts (and leads to a 
judgment in fact). The distinction is, then, hardly operational in this case.

harping on about how law should espouse only the facts (not just some

The ultimate goal of law should indeed be to embrace, as exactly as 
possible, all the forms of facts and their solution.7 This means that there 
are the world of facts (equated with reality) and the world of law, i. e., 
what has been worked at by reason in order to organize that reality. A 
perfect society would be one that rejected any misfit between reality and 
its legal organization, in other words one that could" always juridically 
reflect any social novelty, immediately representable by the notion of facts. 
In the traditional positivist conception, the law is perceived only as a 
condensation of the facts, and making law means reflecting reality (Hayek, 
1983: 137): making the law means picking out from the raw materials of 
social relations the normative principle which, once crystallized, has in 
future to govern those relations. By constituting itself on the pattern of 
the methods employed in science, legal positivism thought it could assert 
the objectivity of its findings. Legal rationality would then be based on 
the capacity our legal system has to reflect reality, a reality knowledge of 
which is supposed to be immediate and complete. To bring this out a little 
more, we shall take a detour through the notion of legal fiction. 
The legal fiction is presented as a concept that fails to recognize reality; 
it is considered that it is not concerned with inquiring into likelihood, but 
instead denies what is generally regarded as the reality of things. Let us 
quote Geny: "instead of contemplating things as they are, in the whole 
splendor of their truth, to reproduce their most varied aspects or penetrate 
their hidden arrangements, man takes pleasure in imagining ways of being 
that nature does not offer him" (Geny, 1930: III, 361). It is enough to 
introduce an element manifestly alien to the "strictly natural" representation 
of things into a classical concept in order for us to be in the presence of 
fiction. 
It is at the cost of this illusion8 that legal statements are worked out. 
The most important thing for us to keep to here is that the notion of 
fiction implies the idea of a natural concept, in order to oppose to it a 
more or less arbitrarily manufactured concept. The legal fiction states 
explicitly that facts are denatured, but also implicitly, and principally, that 
there are concepts that are "real" as being the very expression of reality. 
Using Geny's vocabulary, there is a "given", reality, which jurists have to 
reflect scientifically. 
The fiction is supposed to be an unscientific elaboration of law, as being 
a deformation of reality, an open denial of the real; some authors do not

even hesitate to speak in terms of "conflict between the idea and the reality"

to consist in the observation, knowledge and then understanding of reality; 
a legal structure is supposed to be nothing more or less than a raw social 
fact put into legal form, and the fiction to be a procedure representing a 
grave anomaly vis-ä-vis the truth of things. 
The law would, then, be a general, abstract construction emerging from 
a natural order, from a "given", that is immediately perceptible, and the 
norm would be a pure product of that given, deriving completely therefrom. 
The idea is rejected that the law relates to situations or institutions whose 
elements are linked by teleological links and that, if one can in fact speak 
of a "given", a common denominator of all societies, namely the mental 
and physical structure of our species, then the legislator must inevitably 
be conditioned by it — for the simple reason that he is not directly 
confronted with it (Atias, 1985: 177). 
This distinction will be used to justify another distinction, between 
"positive law" and "legal science", the latter being aimed at raising positive 
law to the highest stage, to the point of coinciding with reality. What we 
shall however be led to find is that positive law and legal science, far 
from being separate, on the contrary express a unity, as abstractions that 
unceasingly refer to each other. 
Far from positing this dichotomy between the given and the construct, 
the theory of autopoietic systems instead compels reconsideration of this 
idea of given, by asking how we know the facts that claim to express 
reality and seem to be adequately represented by the theoretical model. Let 
us, moreover, note with interest that however obvious the notion of fact 
might seem to be, we find a multiplicity of methods of gathering (O'Neil, 
1969: 124). 
We know that in science experiment is identified with the facts, since 
regarding an experiment as a fact amounts to asserting its objectivity; in 
other words, any observer whatever may carry it out. For Comte (1974: 
31), "only facts need be considered, since they do not depend on who is 
observing them. Fidelity to reality, without which there could be no science, 
is itself possible only by confining the sciences to the determination of 
laws". The latter are held to be derived from the observation of facts. 
Objectivity, as guarantor of the success of the sciences, assumes that 
propositions can be the object of experimental verification; that facts 
(reality) can be symbolized directly. 
Returning, then, to our field, the rational realization of law implies the 
possibility of conceiving of reality; the rational legal order is possible only 
if the natural is itself regarded as a rational order. Motulsky (1948: 26) 
before expounding his method, states that "the jurist conceives of the legal 
community as the juxtaposition 
of individual spheres (our emphasis) in which 
the law shuts up the members of the collectivity ... these spheres by 

The Fact of Law 
319 
definition fill the whole space of the collectivity's legal life; no one can 
emerge from their own circle without entering someone else's area ...". 
Nominalism is at the very basis of the method. It is still more interesting 
to observe how the faithful reflection of nature by legal science is asserted 
conceptually: nature is made up of individual beings, and man is the center 
of nature, sovereign of his territory. The whole legal system is supposed 
to be built up on this original truth; which leads Motulsky to the following 
remark, in the passage already cited: "... physical persons and legal persons, 
so improperly called moral persons ..."; we shall come back later to this 
legal perception of reality and the way that perception is handled.9 
Positive legal philosophy refers back to the philosophy of nature offered 
us by the classical philosophy of science. Physics, from the 17th century 
onward, solely sought laws. Reality was made subject to the "atomistic" 
logic of scientific thought, and split up into non-complex isolated frag-
ments. Motulsky's text just cited is a striking illustration of this passage 
of the method of natural science into legal science. Logic has thus to 
operate perfectly on propositions isolated from each other; to develop 
"particular argumentations" about the real (Morin, 1980: II, 195), fragment 
by fragment. The real becomes a logical idea. The elaboration of a rational 
legal order and the perception of nature constitute the same operation, 
within which it is impossible to distinguish what is supposed to be the 
order of the "given" and what is that of the construct. The "given", as 
we shall see, is the "given of a construct". 
What seems to us the most fundamental thing to bear in mind here is 
that, in its process of rationalization, the rule can be abstract and general 
only because the facts it is intended to regulate can be reduced to a common type. 
In other words, the distinction drawn between nature and science is the 
very essence of the rationalist method; far from imposing itself naturally 
on scientific method, it is the outcome of it. For primitive law or magical 
law, etc., questions of fact do not exist; nor do those of law in their 
technical or rational aspects. The distinction between fact and law can 
appear only once primitive legal systems give way to rational legal systems 
(Max Weber). 
The distinction between fact and law is the very product of legal 
rationality, which means that the norm is most certainly not, as positivist 
doctrine regards it, the product of the actual situation; this distinction is 
at the heart of legal rationality. The fact is not external to that rationality, 
but internal to it. For this reason, we shall say that the delimitation of the 
legal sphere is definitely not posited in terms of "frontiers" laid down from 
outside which objectively circumscribe the legal sphere. To say that facts 
can be independent of a theory underlying them, that a limit can objectively 
9 On these distinctions, see e.g., Amselek, 1964: 86. 

320 
Patrick Nerhot 
be set to the legal sphere, would amount to saying that the method of 
reasoning was objective in itself. Finally, we shall say that the foundation 
of law is the law itself and therefore that law presupposes law. Here we 
come to Niklas Luhmann's major statement in transposing the theory of 
self-reproduction to the law regarded as a system. 
Legal thought, when it claims to be positive, posits facts as all given, 
as "always already" present, constituted, independent of the discipline that 
claims to found them. This really is a fiction. As we shall see, a fact is the 
result of a conceptualization that puts together a set of elements separated 
from their context. 
II. Legal Science and the Nature of Things 
Let us first of all note that the term "finding the facts", used to describe 
the operation carried out by the judge when he works out his judgment 
on the basis of situations brought before him, is an unfortunate one. The 
term, a pure product of positive philosophy, is a rather poor representation, 
in our view, of the operation carried out by the judge. He does not "find" 
anything in the sense that the expression "finding of fact" would suggest; 
the judge decides. He decides on the basis of situations as put before him 
by the parties and brought by them into relationship with legal statements. 
He thus decides on the basis of the relationship of identity felt by the 
parties between their situation and what they regard as being covered by 
the legal text they have adopted, and he decides as to the legal consequence 
argued for by the parties of the identity relationship that they have 
previously posited. He intervenes, thus, in respect of an identity relationship 
and of a causality relationship; if he is brought to find anything, he does 
so at the very center of the intellectual operation whereby he assesses these 
relationships brought before him by the parties. 
We are here at the very heart of the life of the law; the legal mechanisms 
whereby the identity and causality relationships are assessed is part of a 
constantly changing story, in which Clause 2 of Art. 12 of the French New 
Code of Civil Procedure is the latest outcome.10 Legal positivism is not 
right in stating that this provision means that the law is deduced from 
facts since, as the text itself states, the facts in question are qualified 
ones: 
the nature of this operation is passed over in silence. 
The judge's decision is not a pure and simple application of the rules it 
refers to, but an assessment of the situations presented by the parties. This 
10 Art. 12.2 of the New French Code of Civil Procedure says that the judge "must 
supply or restore the proper designation of the facts and acts at dispute, without 
being bound by the description given by the parties". 

The Fact of Law 
321 
is, quite obviously, within the framework that these rules set forth, and in 
that sense the decision is bound up with facts, but, and this is an important 
point, the latter cannot be regarded as either a fragment of reality or even 
as the manifestation of something underlying it (Goodman, 1982: 18). The 
object of the human sciences in general and of legal science in particular 
is a representation covering a diversity of experience with a view to "putting 
it in order" and thus providing and organizing a rational knowledge of 
reality. 
This object is manifested only indirectly through knowledge, through 
language, through practices (Kuhn, 1962) which are only one aspect of 
reality, and cannot be recognized as such except by someone who already 
knows reality in a particular way. The reading of all these signs thus 
presupposes prior knowledge and an interpretation of the "given" in its 
light (Watzlawick, 1976). 
We were already able to say that the situation that gives rise to the 
application of a legal rule was constituted by a set of acts or circumstances 
extracted from a most often complicated context. We may now look at the 
way this extraction takes place: how are the facts gathered in legal science? 
Let us remain with the example of the judge. 
This basis on which the judge builds up his judgment, far from imposing 
itself by itself, is on the contrary determined by the rule under which the facts 
have to be brought (Husson, 1974: 125). It is in fact such rules that supply 
the grid whereby on the one hand the facts are chosen and on the other 
their meaning(s) are read. 
The organization of facts that allows the application of a rule is supported 
by a prior interpretation, without which these facts have no sense whatever. 
This prior interpretation is supplied by the legal rule itself, and is in no 
way an objective datum, a pure reflection of reality. It is a commonplace 
today to say that the fact is a pure creation; that the "raw" fact does not 
exist. The choice of givens in a particular situation made by the judge is 
determined by the norm in terms of which they are judged. 
Husson (1974: 259) reminds us that "a single system of positive law will 
offer those concerned a choice of various grids, and a single fact may 
display opposite characteristics, of lawfulness or unlawfulness, depending 
on the grid applied to it". The advocate's skill consists, after all, in a 
particular choice of elements, of "facts", to make one rule applicable rather 
than another. The judge in fact decides within limits traced out for him 
by the conclusions exchanged between the parties; Motulsky even consid-
ered that the judge has no right to regard as false what both parties declare 
as true.11 
The legal rule enters in not merely in order to decide which treatment 
to apply to establish facts, but first of all to trace out the background 
11 Motulsky, 1948: 81. The new Article 12 we cited above has now settled this question. 

322 
Patrick Nerhot 
against which these facts have to be defined and analyzed, in order for it 
to be applied. The argumentation underlying the constitution of the parties' 
cases and the judgment that the judge delivers is teleological. Thinking 
about the goal they wish to attain, the parties pick out the legal rules 
necessary to attain that goal (at least, those they imagine to be so) and seek 
to present facts liable to make these rules operational. For his part, the 
judge picks out the rules necessary to secure the goal desired by the parties, 
and then decides whether the facts presented to him are indeed compatible 
with the rules chosen. 
In his Pure Theory of Law, Kelsen had already shown that no norm could 
be deduced from a "raw" fact (Kelsen, 1967). Speaking legally, no fact can 
be stated without reference to a rule. The fact, as legal science understands 
it, is in no way a given that imposes itself by itself, external to legal science. 
Quite the contrary, legal science in fact speaks of "conclusive" facts (i. e., 
those able to convince the judge), of "pertinent" facts (useful in the matter, 
but no more), and conversely of "inconclusive" or "non-pertinent" facts, 
i. e., facts which do not exist for the law "having regard to the circumstances 
of the case". Frustra probatur quod probatum non relevat. 
This barrier alleged to exist between fact and law can evidently not 
appear other than as badly traced, fugitive, "raising problems of a meta-
physical nature". By definition and in consequence of what we have just 
said, the law takes a grip on the fact and, far from being separate, facts of 
law constitute a unity, or better, a totality. 
They constitute a totality because the law is in no way attached to the 
"materiality" of the facts, acts, and various events that it considers, but to 
the meaning they have within the legal system itself. This meaning is in 
no way bound up with the elementary events, taken in isolation, that 
constitute them (which would mean joining with the "atomism" of the 
natural sciences to which we alluded); it results from the whole of them 
as a construct under the rules. 
In saying this, we are doing no more than describing daily legal practice, 
as may be illustrated by repeating an example from Husson (1974: 220): 
"When case law and doctrine have to evaluate the causal link required by 
Art. 1382 in connection with damage and the fact to which it is attributed, 
they do not take into consideration all the relations that may substantively 
be established between the bringing about of this damage and the very 
varied factors that have had to concur in order for it to be produced; they 
consider only those which in their eyes imply non-observance of a duty". 
Let us go on to say that this duty is itself defined by a set of rules. 
We have said (at the beginning of this second section) why in our view 
the expression "finding the facts" used to describe the judge's function is 
an unfortunate one. The fact is not meaningful in itself, but only when 
bound up with and integrated into a set of practices that give it meaning. 
To reject this expression amounts to rendering the legal epistemology it 

The Fact of Law 
323 
emerged from suspect. The term "finding the facts" is in fact located within 
a general conception of law where the judge is regarded as finding a reality 
(and therefore that nature is "given"), that he goes on to determine its 
legal nature (and thus that the jurist's scientific work consists in reflecting 
the statements of nature as faithfully as possible) in order finally to give 
these facts legal effect (hence the idea, here too, that the norm is a pure 
product of the factual situation). 
Far from finding the facts in the first place, the judge, as we said, first 
seeks the conclusion he wishes to reach (Motulsky, 1948: 155/6). Legal 
reasoning is, in this sense, teleological. Once the goal is identified (and 
hence the possible legal rule identified), the judge must think what typical 
situation justifies the application of this rule. Here, the legal apparatus may 
become extremely complex. 
The appeal to experts, for instance, has the goal of conceiving of this 
situation. Thus, the scientific process whereby legal science reflects reality 
is accomplished by a detour through other social sciences (organized by 
legal science). We are thinking here, for instance, of .the role of economic 
science in the drawing up of an economic law. What is being worked out 
in this phase is the very meaning to be attributed to a legal rule. But the 
mechanism that we describe for legal science, the relationship between 
norm and society, will clearly be repeated in the same way for the other 
social sciences. The theoretical model posited by, for instance, economics 
refers to ideal facts. The "openness" of the legal system thus refers to the 
process of "informational closure" of economics. 
Motulsky spoke here of "presupposition" (1948: 156). This would be 
the model worked out on the basis of the rule but not yet on that of the 
various events argued by the parties. The facts adopted by the judge will 
be those that seem to him to be similar to those in the model derived from 
the rule (and here we again find the notions of conclusive, pertinent, etc., 
facts). The "informational closure", the mechanism of openness, in other 
words, of the legal system, thus organizes a series of detours in order to 
grasp reality. 
Reality is like the horizon, which one continually approaches but never 
reaches. Once this operation in accomplished, the judge then proceeds to 
a comparison between the type situation model and the facts of the case 
presented by the parties; in so doing the notions of conclusive, pertinent, 
etc., facts are thus created. The mechanism of openness of the legal system 
would, then, be located in this exchange between a judge abstractly positing 
facts once the rule that might be applied to the case has been determined, 
and the parties who, on the basis of different events, have imagined the 
rule that legitimates their acts and subsequently picked out facts that can 
support their claim to the expected right. In all this there is no question 
of "finding facts". The point is to compare two types of facts, which are 
the resultant of a priori knowledge of legal rules. This, we feel, constitutes 

324 
Patrick Nerhot 
the operation that brings about the articulation between what Luhmann 
calls "information" and "communication" in the legal system. 
The operation that consists in "finding facts" does indeed exist, but has 
in our view a quite different meaning from the one traditionally attributed 
to it. In the parties' allegations, since the applicable rule (and hence the 
law, consecutive to it) is justified 
by a set of elements (called facts), it is up 
to a party that wishes to deny its opponent's claim to dispute the elements 
justifying the application of the rule. And it is because facts justifying 
application of a rule will be disputed that the judge has to find the facts 
raised in the case (Motulsky, 1948: 155). 
Perhaps an objection might be raised here that a number of social 
practices have preceded the existence of legal rules; that in other words 
facts preceded law (and therefore that law emerged from fact). This 
hypothesis ought not to seem to contradict what we are trying to show; 
only the conclusion is disputable. We would even say that regarding this 
hypothesis as inoperative would amount to saying no less than that the 
law is a "closed" system. That would be a pure absurdity; by definition, a 
system in the social sciences has to be "open". It would perhaps be 
appropriate to distinguish the "facts" on the basis of which the legislator 
works from "facts" brought out in the context of litigation. 
Take for instance penal law. By the principle of the legality of offenses 
and penalties, we have a sort of "discontinuity" of criminal law, since the 
law, through this principle, is posited as the exception, and the absence of 
legal relations as being the rule. But clearly nothing prevents a particular 
social situation not apprehended by the penal law at a particular moment 
from being so later. But in this case is it not more accurate to say that a 
new penalty has created a new type of crime, and that therefore it is indeed 
law that creates the facts and that the foundation of law is the law itself? 
Man is not a thief by nature; he is a thief in the light of the law. 
A number of social practices do not, by definition and in consequence 
of what we have said, constitute the object of any involvement by the law. 
Only those events are taken into consideration that allow the demanding 
of a right or the operation of rules. Carbonnier (1976: 26) had already 
noted this phenomenon when he spoke of the "self-neutralization" of law. 
It is in fact through its own needs that the law manages to annihilate itself. 
The need for proof, for instance, puts outside the law everything that 
cannot be proved (1976: 28). 
Just as legal rules can be the source of new social practices, as we observe 
daily, and this is the very goal of law, so social practices can be the origin 
of new legal rules. But saying that social practices are at the origin of new 
legal rules (as was the case for labor law, environmental law, economic 
law, etc.), it does not imply that the law emerged from the fact. It means 
in our view that situations devoid of legal effect had such effect attributed 

The Fact of Law 
325 
to them; and therefore that situations regarded as simple facts, non-existent 
for legal science, thenceforth came to form part of the legal order. 
There is no opposition between fact and law, but an opposition between 
social practices that are non-existent in the eyes of the law and a situation 
for which legal effect has been imagined. We have seen how social practices 
were not purely and simply the situations that the law constitutes. This 
distinction consists in counterposing to the unqualified fact those facts 
which through being treated as legal become bound up with legal effects; 
these facts are themselves a "legal situation" (Rigaux, 1966: 85). We here 
agree with Luhmann on the point of the "autonomous" element of the 
legal system. 
The object of legal rationality is the relationship between these two 
situations, and to positive legal thinking that says that this relationship is 
in part a function of the facts and in part immediate, we shall say first of 
all that the relationship is mediated, and secondly that it is not directly a 
function of the facts. Positive thought says that the meaning of the 
relationship is immanent within the facts themselves. Dilthey has shown 
that "lack of skill in posing methodological questions is due to the fact 
that an abstract scheme has been arbitrarily borrowed from the natural 
sciences" (Dilthey, 1957: 320). 
In the physical sciences, in fact, far from demonstrating the existence of 
the natural order, one constantly verifies through facts the partial orders 
expressed by the law and theories (Kuhn, 1962). The facts are therefore 
inseparable from the theories; and this relationship should be the same in 
the social sciences. 
While for the natural sciences the interpretation of data consists in fitting 
them in with other data of the same order (Parain-Vial, 1966: 11), for the 
human sciences, on the contrary, interpreting data consists in linking them 
to a "reality" of a different order. We have seen this notion of reality 
worked out by the law, and we have shown that the notion of fact, which 
seems to be identified with that of the real, is twofold. The fact is sometimes 
what is gathered, sometimes the reality of which it is the manifestation and 
to which interpretation allows us to ascend. 
Let us once again cite Motulsky. The phrase "the defendant is the 
employer of the plaintiff' has a twofold content; on the one hand, it closes 
the analysis of the circumstances of the case and has the nature of a finding 
of facts; "... but at the same time it implies the conclusion that if a 
comparison is made between facts and the elements that generate the law 
invoked, it does appear that the legal notion of employer is reflected in 
the circumstances of the case: this conclusion is part of law" (Motulsky, 
1948: 157). 
What a discipline has to do is to set up concepts specific to it; but this 
is equally true of the data it selects through these concepts. Since they do 
not have the same concepts, the jurist's facts are not those of the sociologist, 

326 
Patrick Nerhot 
for instance (O'Neil, 1969: 177). We may likewise say that within a discipline 
subdisciplines (others might say systems and subsystems) arise, using dif-
ferent concepts. For legal science, for instance, let us think of the birth of 
labor law which, from its beginning, has been marked off from the other 
subdiscipline of civil law, by forging its own concepts and consequently 
its own "reality".12 
In his remarkable study on the Welfare State, an analysis of the transition 
from "liberal" State to "social" State, Ewald (1986: 41) shows that any 
judgment expresses a type of rationality, and that facts will be taken into 
consideration or not as a function of it: "What changes in the 1830s is that 
facts till then excluded from law come to have a place in it, to be recognized 
in it and to be associated with a sanction" (Ewald, 1986: 103). Nothing 
authorizes idealism, for which reality amounts to the sum of the facts, to 
regard givens as determined in the same way as things, with both equally 
able to be relied on by the laws, because before they take on meaning they 
must, as we have seen, be interpreted. 
This primary operation, interpretation, has to do in legal science with 
what is termed description: the operation that defines reality. As we know, 
the role of the judge, who has not been a witness to the situation he has 
to define, consists in interpreting legal rules. He therefore arrives at 
cognizance of the facts through rules, or in other words takes cognizance 
of the situation brought before him using methods authorized by the law. 
We have seen that the judges' investigation into the facts is organized, 
limited by principles of procedure; moreover, the burden of proof, the 
hierarchy of means of proof set down by the law, the degree of probative 
force of the elements invoked, etc., are questions of law raised by the law 
itself, that is, by the legal treatment of the facts. We were thus able to say 
that a fact can be noted only in terms of a goal that is sought; that a fact 
is the result of an operation whereby a particular element is taken out, 
isolated from a context of its own, to be placed in another context that 
gives it a particular meaning. 
At the same time, however, as Husson has noted (Husson, 1974: 167), 
this goal appears only "in the presence of facts and to an extent that it 
guides their analysis". We can see why it is not appropriate to speak in 
terms of "boundaries" of the legal system, for that would be to suppose 
that the law is kept within limits that are objective to itself. 
A legal solution is the outcome of a twofold pressure, of an event and 
of the goal sought for in terms of the representation we historically have 
of each. History, as Duby tells us, is "a constrained dream"; we could use 
this formula for the operation of description carried out by the judge, and 
12 Passage from one to the other, far from being impossible, is used very frequently, 
because by changing discipline and hence concepts, one secures other facts, (another 
reality) more pertinent to the goal one is seeking. 

The Fact of Law 
327 
call the fact the outcome of a "plot" (Veyne, 1978: 33). In the same way, 
the goal sought takes form only "by being reflected in a rule, and the 
action of that rule, with its manifold implications, transforms the situation 
that posits it, poses new problems and raises new claims" (Husson, 1974: 
168). 
Having shown that the norm was produced by the legal system itself, 
we shall now posit that this production results from a circular, self-
referential process in which the factors react indefinitely on each other. But 
in positing this, we have to consider that it is by definition not possible 
to pick out external ahistorical notions used by the law, any more, by the 
way, than it is possible to conceive of the law comprehensively as a system 
of purely logical relationships. 
Legal description contributes to both creating 
and modifying 
a reality 
that 
it is its object to found. For a fact to be used in objective knowledge, we 
have seen that it must be interpreted, and have shown that it is the legal 
rule itself that supplies the keys for this conceptual interpretation. The 
finding of facts to which legal reasoning is applied is not independent of 
the evaluation that motivates and orients the intervention of the law. For 
this reason, legal truth is neither absolute not objective; it consists only in 
the judge's belief, formed according to legal bases (Motulsky, 1948: 85). 
Along the same lines, it would in our view be erroneous to conceive of 
legal proof as the specification of a particular situation for which an 
explanation is supplied. Legal proof is the justification 
brought to an 
argument within which the rules were chosen and facts, acts, and various 
events selected with a view to attaining a particular goal. All that can be 
the object of proof, then, we said, is the circumstances, which are to be 
regarded in the same way as the judge does in applying the chosen rule 
with an eye to the goal being pursued. 
If doctrine runs into blind alleys in its theory of description, this is 
because it posits that there exist a priori 
natural frontiers between the 
marking of law and social reality, which are no longer there when it comes 
to appeals in positive law. Here, far from being separate, fact and law are 
organically united, constituting what legal science calls "grounds". Since 
there is no room for the concrete in legal argumentation, the question of 
the legal description raises the problem of supplying and giving the nature 
of the "grounds" that a judge has invoked in his argumentation. Let us 
now set up a few landmarks. 
The grounds may have three types of defect: they may be non-existent 
(when Art. 7 of the law of 21 April 1810 would apply, for "lack of 
grounds"); inexact (when there would be "breach of the statute" 
on the 
basis of the same text); or insufficient (an opening worked out in case law; 
here there would be "lack of legal basis"). 
We said at the outset that before approaching the question of the 
distinction between fact and law in order to determine the extent of 

328 
Patrick Nerhot 
competence of the highest court, we would first have to think about the 
very principle of that distinction. We may now, perhaps, say something on 
this criterion of competence. 
The hypothesis of the self-reproduction of law has enabled us to show 
in what way it is wrong to say that the highest court is competent only 
for questions of law; more exactly, if by the criterion of the distinction 
between fact and law it is intended to demonstrate that the highest court 
can only deal with law, then we would say that this demonstration can 
never be given. In fact, we have shown at length that any description raises 
a legal problem, and therefore that the highest court of appeal ought to 
be competent for any decision given by lower courts. What, then, would 
be the criterion? 
Art. 7 of the law of 20 April 1810 states explicitly that the Court of 
Cassation is entirely competent to assess the facts, which is in line with 
what we have endeavored to show throughout this study. What we have 
said is that the investigation carried out by the judge is a question of law 
raised by the legal treatment of the fact, but also that the goal sought 
appeared only in the presence of facts, to the extent that it guided their 
analysis. In other words, the informational closure (openness) of the legal 
system brings ideal facts, regarded a priori 
as necessary by the judge in 
order for such-and-such a rule to be actuated, into contact with a set of 
elements put forward by the parties with a view to having the right that 
that rule confers recognized. The whole of this operation is essentially that 
of law, and law alone, and the Supreme Court is therefore competent to 
exercise control over all its aspects. In exercising this control, it will talk 
about inexact, non-existent or insufficient facts. This is part of what we 
have called the informational closure. 
By contrast, the area where the Supreme Court regards itself as incompe-
tent is where one party disputes the veracity of facts alleged by the other. 
This dispute obliges the lower court judge to verify the veracity before 
proceeding to the operation of description. Here we are no longer at the 
level of the process of informational closure; we are outside it. Exclusive 
competence is given over to the trial judges. The Supreme Court intervenes 
only in the comparison phase we described above, in which (legal) meaning 
is manufactured out of (legal) meaninglessness. 
Conclusion 
The theory of autopoiesis applied to the legal system abandons the classical 
methodology positing the rule of general before particular, which amounts 
to positing the dependence of the concrete (the fact) on the abstract (the 
rule). This theory, in our view, gets out of the impasses of positivist legal 
dogmatics, and to do so posits that the norm is engendered by the norm; 

The Fact of Law 
329 
that law constitutes the elements that constitute it. The idea of autopoiesis 
implies that organizational rules are internal to the system regarded as 
"informationally closed"; cognitive interactions with the environment are 
valid only for it. 
The question of autonomy becomes central because it expresses the idea 
that the legal character of a situation can be produced only by the system 
itself; that it is dependent on its "self-generation". "The recursive closure 
of the production of the elements by the elements is, from a logical point 
of view, equivalent to the self-indication of the system. This is its autonomy, 
its unity" (Luhmann, 1987). 
Luhmann conceives the idea of the system's self-reproduction on the 
basis of the distinction he draws between information, which is in some 
sense a hetero-reference to the environment, and communication, which is 
the self-reference of the system's possibilities of action (Varela, 1979: 211). 
We have sought to develop this point by trying it out on the basis of a 
critique of the distinction between fact and law, and in so doing we have 
found that the idea of autopoiesis might prove to be a very rich one. 
Going back to the example of the legal fiction, which allowed us to 
highlight the ontology of the real underlying the distinction between fact 
and law: in consequence of what we have said throughout this article on 
this distinction, the fiction is not be to perceived as a negation of reality; 
it is in no way "an anomaly with regard to the truth of things". At bottom, 
if the legal system produces legal reality, it would be more correct to regard 
the legal system as a whole as a fiction from the viewpoint of the other 
social sciences. 
The legal procedures traditionally meant in speaking of legal fictions do 
not express a relationship between the legal system and something outside 
("reality", say); what these procedures express is non-knowledge, let us 
say, of legal reality, or putting it differently, a non-logical relationship 
inside the legal system itself, to allow internal communication in the system 
to continue to function. Take for instance the legal notion of "moral 
person": there the fiction is not in relation to reality external to the legal 
system, such as the physical reality of an individual, but in relation to the 
legal reality, which is that of the legal notion of personality of individuals. 
Geny, for whom it is for the jurist to "bring social reality into law", 
gave the question why the fiction the following answer: "this is a why that 
really seems to me unfathomable" (Geny, 1930: 378). This procedure, 
generally perceived as among the most shocking and condemned by the 
"given" (Geny, 1930: III, 396), must inevitably disappear.13 
The "natural person", which was, and still is for some tendencies in 
legal thought, the "sovereign and conscious" individual, had, and has, as 
13 See Association Henri Capitant, 1948: 247, Fuller, 1967. 

330 
Patrick Nerhot 
long as the natural law represented by the idea of legal subject lasts, 
autonomy of will; for the school of jus naturalis, jus gentium, legal rules are 
the work of individual wills (or of the general will) and sovereignly 
translate into contracts or law the a priori requirements of Universal Reason. 
This natural person was spectacularly denied by the idea of moral 
personality. In our view, however, it will take a lot for this procedure ever 
to disappear. The error consists in calling what is construct "given",14 and 
moral personality is nothing but a deepening of the notions of law contained 
in the legal notion of personality; we reply thereby to the question that 
Geny, in his initial hypothesis, regarded as inconceivable. 
Throughout this article we have been able to claim to transcend the 
distinction between fact and law posited by legal science by making use of 
the idea of autopoiesis; but that does not mean we have worked out the 
actual model proposed by the theory of autopoiesis applied to the law 
regarded as a system. This is not simply due to the fact that, by dealing 
with only one aspect of that matter, namely autonomy, we were not able 
to claim to speak about all of it. We have deliberately maintained a certain 
reserve. The question that applies to all theories and is obviously essential 
is to know the goal they are pursuing. Thought about law that wants to 
be theoretical is also, and above all, an analysis of practices, or the adoption 
of a stance on the matters at stake in the law at a given historical moment. 
Without that, it is nothing but pure rhetoric, not worth even a minute's 
effort. What, then, is the goal that this theory is pursuing? 
It is not easy to answer that question, for many reasons,15 and the reply 
has to be a very qualified one. If, to give a beginning of an answer, we 
stay with the distinction between fact and law, the question that should be 
put to this theory is whether it intends to rethink the notion of fact. Legal 
science calls itself positive because it sees itself as conceiving a rationality 
on the basis of objects that impose themselves by themselves — facts — 
and with this rationalization being a conceptualization of those facts. Is 
the autopoiesis theory put forward by Luhmann a break with this method? 
Is the abusive use of "fact" in the human sciences put into question by 
this method? 
In regard to that author's writings that we have been able to read (and 
such understanding as we may have been able to arrive at), we posit that 
there is in fact a shift. If we take as an example the classical distinction we 
mentioned above between positive law and legal science, then the novelty 
14 Geny, 1930: III, 418, note 4 had another notion of what is "natural" and said in 
connection with the will, "by nature autonomous": "I believe that it is the attitude 
that is necessary in regard to fictions of the will, which under the pretext of applying 
it, falsify the legitimate action of the principle of autonomy". 
15 One of the most essential being that autopoiesis is not yet definitely a new "paradigm". 
For a contrary view, see Zolo, 1986: 129/173. 

The Fact of Law 
331 
in Luhmann is not so much to go back on the basis of that distinction, 
but to rethink the relationship. Thus, the question of the distinction 
between fact and law is not a primary question in him: but because the 
question of the sources of law become central, the problem of fact will 
arise. 
If in the natural sciences experiment has to be identified with the facts, 
because the objectivity of the experiment lies in regarding it as a fact that 
can be arrived at by any observer whatever. That is the very basis of 
positivist philosophy, and Luhmann posits it as a theoretician endeavoring 
to conceive of a possibility of this kind of interchangeability between 
observers/operators. This endeavor may however make the "fact", as 
expression of nature, become substantially different. 
In conceiving a systems theory within the system, Luhmann in fact 
abandons the classical idea of the thinking subject (conscious and autono-
mous) and seeks, through the notion of system unity, to set up a sort of 
synthesis. The classical subject is transformed into a series of positions of 
interchangeable observers. 
The idea of autopoiesis thus becomes a radically new method for inter-
preting and thinking about the sources of law. For Geny, for instance, 
legal science was the scientific interpretation that the jurist had to give of 
reality; an interpretation that would subsequently be given a technical 
translation into legal language. In Luhmann the idea remains, but these 
two operations that bring about legal rationality no longer express a 
situation external/internal to the law; everything becomes internal. It is 
here that we come to the terms "information" (a construct already able to 
be translated by the legal system) and "communication" (the internal 
mechanisms of the legal system; its techniques, as Geny would have said). 
Luhmann abandons the model of the autonomous, conscious, voluntary 
subject as the foundation of law, as well as any idea of exteriority that 
founds the legal system. The "natural" that imposed itself with axiomatic 
force was the basis of law for the jus naturalis, jus gentium 
school. The 
rational method of the natural-law school posited the distinction between 
fact and law and stated the nature of their realtionship. With the so-called 
positivist school, it was the nature of this relationship that was changed. 
In that school's view, nature was, no doubt, the source of law, and laying 
down the law perhaps meant interpreting nature, but the law was the result 
of a scientific elaboration: interpreting nature is not laying down law. 
Luhmann's theory is an accentuation of positivist thought. Legal positiv-
ism does not in fact deny that the foundation of positive law may be 
natural law; with this author, on the contrary, the foundation of law cannot 
be anything but law itself. The law is a scientific construction, but the 
"given" disappears; nature disappears as an entity outside law. Nature and 
reality are no longer obstacles to a rationality that no longer has anything 

332 
Patrick Nerhot 
to do with processes and relationships among processes brought about 
through elements themselves determined by those processes. 
When Varela (1979: 6) put forward the idea of autopoiesis, he stated that 
his problem was "the living organization, and therefore our interest will 
not be in properties of components but in processes and relations between 
processes realized through components". This "therefore", far from being 
obvious, nevertheless very clearly expresses the mechanistic nature of this 
method, and the author even goes on to clarify (Yarela, 1979: 7, note 4) 
that "'machines' and 'systems' are used interchangeably".16 This metaphor, 
consisting here in regarding living organization in the way one does a 
machine, is also prevalent in the human sciences. 
One cannot, however, confine a metaphor to a single realm of application 
as easily as one may pretend to. Whether we want them to or not, 
"metaphors seduce the reason" (Bachelard, 1983: 78). Nor did this escape 
Varela, who writes: "The understanding of life becomes a mirror of our 
epistemological choices, which carry over to human actions" (Varela, 1979: 
46). For thirty years Jacques Ellul has been teaching us that nothing would 
be able to dominate technique. What this theory shows is the infiltration 
of technique into the epistemology of our society, in the sense that it is 
the logic of artificial machines that is increasingly applied in our lives and 
in our society. 
With society being regarded as a machine, the body politic becomes 
more than ever the object of experimentation, but with an essential novelty 
brought by this method, by comparison with instrumentalism. Here there is 
nothing "determined", transcending social practice;17 there is no "invisible 
hand", any more than there is any goal to be reached; this theory functions 
on the indeterminate. 
From being external to legal practice, purpose becomes internal to it; it 
is an aspect of the (dynamic) legal system. The evolution of the legal system 
is perceived as a blind mechanism. 
Teubner writes in this connection: "An 
autopoietic closure occurs when a legal system which is already autonomous 
to a certain degree constitutes its own elements — the legal acts — which 
trigger off legal changes and hence initiate the autopoietic circulation of 
legal act — legal change — legal act" (Teubner, supra). The object of law 
would then consist in dealing with any social practice, any conflict (pro-
cessed in the form of "information"), and its function lies in the formation 
and reproduction of generalized conforming expectations of behavior. A 
theory of communication becomes central.18 
16 There follows the definition that the author gives us of an autopoietic system, Varela, 
1979: 13. 
17 A major difference from classical liberal thought, even though the theory has many 
points in common with it. 
18 "The legal system is seen as a system of actions comprising not only legal discourse 
about norms or organized actions like court decisions and legislation, but human 
communication which has reference to legal expectations." (Teubner, 1984: 294). 

The Fact of Law 
333 
A total impasse is reached regarding the underlying stakes of the legal 
question, what Ewald calls "the rule of judgment", i. e., that whereby one 
judges "about the way in which at a particular time, in a particular society, 
it is thought that behavior ought to be judged" (Ewald, 1986: 37). 
This theory is positive, indeed hyper-positive, a "formalism" in the sense 
meant by Fassö (1970: 217), and it leaves the central questions of legal 
theory on one side. Even if the "epistemological conjuncture" constrains 
us to be positivist, as one author feels (Ewald, 1986: 39), a theory of law 
claiming to discard the problem of justice would be merely a theory of 
legality — a formalism.
