Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
Peter Kennealy 
Firenze 
A religion and a drug were two of the metaphors used to describe the 
concept of autopoiesis at the Florence conference where many of the 
chapters of this book were first presented as papers. However, not all of 
those present were either devotees or addicts and some, as it emerged, 
were highly critical of the attempt to transfer the idea of autopoiesis 
and related concepts of self-reference from their initial application in the 
biological and cognitive sciences to social and legal studies. One of the 
avowed autopoieticists had only to say something like "when I say 'open' 
I mean 'open' in a closed sort of way" (G. Teubner — Day II) to send 
looks of consternation — not to say apoplexy — across the faces of the 
unbelievers. 
Indeed, the religious metaphor is the most apt for classifying the partici-
pants of the conference. In the role of prophet was Niklas Luhmann, 
progenitor of the most sophisticated attempt yet to achieve a full-scale 
implementation of autopoietic concepts in social theory. Next to him — 
on the right hand side so to speak — were the disciples who, with indecent 
haste and under the stern eye of the magus, seek to make theoretical 
adjustments that would remove some of the uncongenially purist implica-
tions of the original (particularly those concerned with the closure of 
systems and their mutual incommunicability). However, compared to the 
next group the disciples had not fallen completely from the state of grace; 
for these were the Doubting Thomases of modern social theory, the 
empiricists, who will believe once they have seen that the theory can 
perform adequately at a mundane level. Finally there were the critics, some 
of whom belonged to well-established rival sects (such as the Anglo-
American theory of law), others who were trying to get their own sect off 
the ground (IPSES, law as a game), the remainder being, of course, the 
natural skeptics that belong to any age. 
Membership of these tendencies was not exclusive. Many of the disciples 
were keen to make theoretical advances because of what they saw as 
empirical difficulties while the critics based their dissent on a mixture of 
immanent criticism and methodological inadequacy. Still, there is no doubt 

350 
Peter Kennealy 
that the discussion at the conference tended to follow the pattern of an 
attack by a critic, a statement/defense from the prophet, the suggestion of 
a possible development from a disciple and a plea from the empiricists for 
the theory to take into account certain obvious facts of the real world. 
The issues on which these temperaments were brought to bear also fall 
into four groups: 
Firstly, there were those to do with the status of the theory. Was the 
whole elaborate construction just a sophisticated biological metaphor or 
was it a fully-fledged scientific theory rigorously applied to social phenome-
non? Were social systems analyzed as autopoietic really like that or was it 
just that we chose to see them in that way? Was the autopoietic standpoint 
one among many which we could use pragmatically when and as we wished 
or were we compelled of necessity to adopt it when dealing with this sort 
of object domain? 
The second set of issues had to do with the applicability of the theory. 
Why was the law (legal subsystem) suitable for treatment in an autopoietic 
manner? What were the advantages of applying such an approach to the 
legal system? What elements of the legal system corresponded to the already 
given categories of this theory? Did there exist a "surplus of significance" 
where the theory failed to accommodate self-evidently important aspects 
of law and society? What was to be hoped for from such a theoretical 
analysis of the legal system? 
A third set of issues was concerned with the testing and evaluation of 
the approach. Once we have erected the theoretical apparatus, what happens 
when we set it in motion? Is it coherent? Does it yield valuable results? 
Does it make sense of phenomena previously obscure and, if so, does it 
pay a price in rendering opaque and problematic what was once taken for 
granted? What sort of evidence would prove the theory wrong? Is the 
theory a complete and adequate characterization of the legal system and its 
relations with other social systems — particularly the political and 
economic? Does it help identify features of law that had previously gone 
unnoticed? 
The last set of issues was about the development of the theory — about 
extending its range and explanatory power and clarifying its practical 
implications. In this report I have treated these together with the third 
group of questions. 
These questions are not logically separate and remarks made during 
discussion did not fall rigidly into any one of these categories. But they 
are the sorts of issues one would expect to be raised in the course of a 
conference about the implementation of a new theory in social science so 
it was not surprising that in three days of argument the same questions 
cropped up again and again. Naturally, practitioners from the more settled 
areas of the discipline wanted to be alerted to exactly what sort of theory 
they were being asked to take on board, whether it had even plausible 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
351 
initial applicability and, moreover, some sweetener in the form of interesting 
insights or theoretical power; and whether its evident shortcomings were 
such as to eliminate it from consideration or whether potential develop-
ments were likely to repair these. 
I. The Status of the Theory 
1. Metaphor? 
It is possibly only because of the vestigial power of the organicist metaphor 
that we can entertain readily enough the idea of transferring a theory used 
in the natural science of biology (and even there considered to be exotic 
although it is only fair to point out that autopoiesis is held, by its adherents 
to be a feature of all living systems including cognitive ones) to the 
sociological study of the legal system? Without doubt any suggestion that 
social sub-systems should be characterized in the same manner as sub-
atomic systems would, I suppose, be greeted with derision. Yet why should 
the principle of organization governing, among other things, the most 
basic of living entities be any more applicable to collectivities containing 
millions of people than the relations between quarks, charms and neutrinos. 
Surely, it was suggested many times, the whole thing is a metaphor. 
Apart from size, too many all-too-obvious differences exist between a 
cell and a social system, the most glaring of which is that a cell is primarily 
a physical entity and a social system is not. Consequently a cell is separated 
from its environment by a physical boundary behind which it organizes its 
self-reproduction through deterministic chemico-physical processes — us-
ing its elements to produce its elements. Viewing this as a metaphor for 
the social system would have several advantages: it allows us to be flex-
ible — cavalier even — in deploying the terms of the theory so that they 
are no longer tied to their strictly delimited use in the original field. After 
all metaphors are designed to be illuminating and provocative rather than 
explanatory and the metaphorical use of a biological concept is likely to 
be more imaginative and wide-ranging than a strictly theoretical one. 
Moreover, the lower level of committment in treating the approach meta-
phorically enables us, in the face of a bad fit between construct and reality, 
merely to switch metaphor. 
Many of the critics, not surprisingly, were attached to this view of 
things. Seeing the law as if it were an autopoietic system allows us better 
to understand some of its features such as its unity and its autonomy and 
even its difficulty in regulating other social sub-systems. But taken too 
seriously the results were seen by some as less palatable (see below) so why 
not abandon the metaphor at the limit of its usefulness and switch to seeing 
law as if it were a game (Ost), a metaphor apt for highlighting the strategic 
behavior of actors within a system of rules and constraints; or as an input-

352 
Peter Kennealy 
output machine — a metaphor that immediately suggests itself for the 
relations between law and society? 
However, there was no gainsaying Luhmann's radical intentions of 
autopoiesis, although a feature of certain biological and cognitive systems, 
is not held to be peculiar to to these areas. Any system is a possible 
candidate. A theory of autopoietic systems is itself quite formal and 
independent of the media involved; if this is true then the non-physical 
nature of a social system is not of its own an impediment to the employment 
of the theory. Clearly Luhmann was engaged upon a radically committed 
use of autopoietic terms within the sociology of law notwithstanding — 
but not ignoring either — the difference of media. In fact, the difference 
of substrata does enjoin at least one significant alteration: in the physical 
world of the cell-system autopoiesis refers to the network of elements 
reproducing themselves by replacing themselves with identical elements, 
that is elements distinguishable from each other only temporally. In the 
social system a different basic element has been chosen — that of a single 
communication — which if it were to reproduce itself identically would 
lead to absurdity (imagine the foreman of the jury replying to the question 
'do you find the prisoner guilty or not guilty?' with the identical phrase). 
In social systems, then, it is not the same element that is reproduced but 
an another one — in the form of an appropriate response to the original 
communication (in the example, when the foreman delivers the verdict, 
the judge pronounces sentence, the defendant launches an appeal and so 
on.) 
2. Realism or Constructivism? 
So a reasonably clean start had been made. Autopoiesis was a theory and 
not a metaphor — which seemed to put us onto the home stretch: set up 
your theory, make hypotheses, match them against the facts and with a 
nod in the direction of paradigms draw the relevant conclusions. Whatever 
the sophisticated state of the philosophy of science today, most social 
scientists operatively subscribe to some sort of naive realism about facts 
and testability about theories. If autopoiesis was a bona fide scientific 
theory, considered by some to be well corrobborated in the biological and 
cognitive sciences, what about putting it through its legal-system steps? 
Straightforward enough, one would have thought, but an obstacle immedi-
ately presented itself: was the theory of autopoietic systems that kind of 
theory at all? 
The question arose when it was pointed out that there existed in 
Luhmann's work a tension between realist and constructivist emphases. 
On the one hand "system" and "self-reference" are not analytic constructs; 
they seem to be the sort of concepts that have empirical criteria for their 
proper use. That is to say, if certain sorts of things were not happening 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
353 
or were not present in the law we would not be entitled to describe it as 
either a system or self-referential. On the other hand systems are said to 
construct their environments through certain internal operations — and 
that means that the worlds created are system-relative. 
A possible origin of this tension was indicated in the differing approaches 
of the originators of the theory, Maturana and Varela. Where the first had 
an essentialist view of the position of autopoiesis in the world of systems, 
Varela adhered to a variety of perspectivism in which autopoiesis is consid-
ered to be a characteristic of the description of systems. The implication 
of this is that other types of descriptions of systems are possible and 
Luhmann assented to this when he said that an autopoietic description 
does not preclude an input-output description merely that the "closure 
perspective was more interesting". 
This lands us right back in the realm of metaphors and analogies: we 
choose the perspective that is most interesting and illuminating, switching 
metaphors as any one of them approaches redundancy. Luhmann's remark 
that there is no privileged grasp on reality certainly appears to radicalize 
his constructivism — but not in the sense of reality being some realm of 
ineffable essences Protean against our attempts to capture them in a net of 
incompatible metaphors. There is no privileged grasp on reality because 
not only are law, politics and the economy autopoietic with their system-
relative and system-created environments but so is the science system itself! 
This certainly launches us into a pluralist world because it prevents us 
from saying that any particular environment is more real than another. To 
the extent that we may assign degrees of reality to system environments 
committment to the autopoietic viewpoint only allows to say that the 
environment of the science system is just as real — and no more real — 
than the environment of any other system (which rather removes the point 
of using the word "real" at all). This unexpected turn also has the slightly 
fazing effect of making us realize that, like Moliere's Monsieur Jourdain, 
we have been speaking autopoietically all our lives without knowing it. 
The implications of this double autopoietic twist are not to be lightly 
dismissed. For a start, the very distinction "realist-constructivist" is not a 
description on the part of a subject of how certain theories deal with reality 
but "the result of a self-description of the scientific system" (Luhmann — 
Day I). And science, like any other system, autopoietically reproduces itself 
on the basis of its code (true/false) and in accordance with its function — 
in the manner of any other autopoietic system. It would also be a mistake 
to think that there is a difference between the science system and the other 
systems along the following lines, viz., that all social systems except for 
science are closed and self-referential, creating an environment that can be 
dealt with in terms of the system's code and its operations, while the 
science system is somehow open. It is not about itself but about the other 
systems which form an objective reality against which the hypotheses of 
the science system can be tested. To be good autopoieticists we must accept 

354 
Peter Kennealy 
that the environment of the science system is equally a product of the 
system as the environment of law or economics. (There does remain, 
however, one difference between science and the other social systems which 
has to do with the code. The legal code (right/wrong) and the economic 
code (paid/not paid) we can both accept as arbitrary: which is to say that 
it is a matter of various constitutive rules belonging to the system that 
determine whether a legal or illegal act has occurred or whether a proper 
payment has taken place. But it is difficult to accept that in science, truth 
or falsity is a matter of accordance with some internal rule of the 
system. 
Whatever our notion of truth it is not easy to get away from the idea that 
the truth of a proposition is independent of our asserting it. So if the 
environment of the science system is a creation of the system itself, what 
are the independent constraints on the application of the code "true/false"?) 
A second implication of this autopoietic double-bind is that we are not 
engaged in legal theory but in the sociological theory of law. Legal theory 
can be taken to be something like the conceptual analysis of law (Hart, 
Raz, Kelsen et al.) and within the autopoietic theory of social sub-systems 
counts as a self-description of the legal system. But the sociological theory 
of law as an autopoietic system stands outside the legal system and its 
environment and can see things about the system that the system cannot 
see about itself: the arbitrariness of its code, the partiality of its functional 
orientation, the interrelationship of its openness and closure ("open" in a 
closed sort of way). This, in turn, raises the important question of what 
would happen if the autopoietic viewpoint became the operative self-
description of the legal system. What would happen if the legal system 
came not only to see itself as autopoietic but as one autopoietic system in 
a world of such systems? 
This brings to mind an apparently odd statement made during the 
conference — that an account of autopoiesis should itself be autopoietic 
(Heller) but not quite in the way the speaker intended. The claim that the 
science system is autopoietic and, therefore, that the descriptions of the 
legal system as autopoietic are themselves the product of an autopoietic 
system should be distinguished from Heller's demand that any account of 
autopoiesis should itself be autopoietic. Luhmann's claim is that an account 
of systems as autopoietic is itself the product of an autopoietic system. 
Now it is one thing to say that a statement shares the same characteristics 
as the thing it is describing for this is merely the demand that the 
statement be autological — as when the word "short" is short and the word 
"polysyllabic" is polysyllabic (rather an arbitrary demand, I should have 
thought) — and another that the description of the legal system as auto-
poietic is the product of another system that is itself autopoietic. 
So we have come some way to appreciating the all embracing way of 
looking at things that autopoiesis is and which made it appropriate to liken 
the theory to a drug or a religion. But does it work? Will it lead to 
epistemological salvation or will it just blow our minds? 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
355 
II. The Categories of Autopoietic Theory and their Application 
to the Legal System 
If the legal system is to be described successfully as an autopoietic system 
then it must be the case that there are some minimal criteria for the 
application of the term "autopoietic" which, if the term is to be useful, are 
not met by some systems. Thus a car, considered as a system of elements, 
structures, and organization is not autopoietic but allopoietic because a car 
does not meet the essential criterion of autopoietic systems, viz., that they 
use their elements to produce their elements. A car produces motion (and 
exhaust-fumes and injuries to pedestrians) and consumes petrol and metal 
and rubber all of which have to be replaced if the car is to continue as a 
viable system adequately performing its function. By contrast, an auto-
poietic system reproduces itself by using its elements to produce its ele-
ments. 
So why is the law best considered as an autopoietic system rather than 
as an input-output system. To some of the participants at the conference, 
if they had to adopt the language of systems theory at all, the second 
perspective seemed more natural — after all, law is in continual interaction 
with society at large: where would law be without politicians legislating? 
Where would society be without the law settling conflicts? How could the 
economy function without legal definitions of money and property and 
contract? On the face of it, society looks like a series of complex, interlock-
ing and symbiotically related input-output systems. But is it? 
An autopoietic system has been defined by Maturana as: 
a dynamic system that is defined as a network of production of components that: a) 
through their interactions recursively regenerate the network of productions that 
produced them; and b) realize their network as a unity by constituting and specifying 
its boundaries in the sphere in which they exist (1980: 52 — 53). 
The central idea is that of self-production and it is as well to be aware 
from the beginning that this is a notion quite foreign to our more usual 
ways of thinking. Typically, a production process produces something other 
than itself: capital and labor produce output; grapes and fermentation 
produce wine and not more grapes and fermentation; and so the primary 
meaning of production appears to belong to an input-output way of 
thinking. 
We should not attempt to interpret self-production along these lines; it 
makes no sense to think — outside of the religious system anyway — of 
creatio ex nihilo, the making of something tangible where nothing tangible 
previously existed. Evidently the medium of the system is not its object 
and systems are not described as autopoietic in virtue of any medium in 
which they subsist. The self-production referred to in autopoiesis is the 
self-production of the organization of the system. 

356 
Peter Kennealy 
Maturana (1980: 48) defines organization as "the relations among compo-
nents, whether static or dynamic, that constitute a composite unity as a 
unity of a particular kind". The organization of a system determines its 
class identity — or more simply what sort of thing it is. Thus a car is a 
set of relationships between its engine (whether diesel or petrol, internal 
combustion or steam) its steering mechanism (stick or wheel), its contact 
with the road surface (three-wheel, four-wheel, tracks). In spite of the 
possible variety any number of things count as cars because of their 
organization. Organization is to be differentiated from the actual structure 
of the system which is the concrete instantiation of its organization — 
what we might call the particular conception of the thing. It follows that 
many different structures can instantiate the same organization (a Fiat 500 
and a Rolls Royce are both cars but that is about all they have in common). 
The system is the unity of its organization and its structure and for the 
system to count as autopoietic they must both be reproduced. Obviously, 
we are dealing with dynamic processes and not with a static system as a 
table or a house. Such a system is subject to a decay of structure that 
ultimately entails a loss of organization (for example, the loss of its 
"tableness"). Many dynamic systems like cars also suffer from the decay of 
their components which, being in no position to replace them, brings about 
the same loss of structure and organization. But in an autopoietic system 
the elements are organized in such a way that their very turnover creates 
the conditions for their replacement by identical elements in the same 
structure. Such a system can properly be called self-reproductive. 
This ceaseless material turnover of components and yet continuity of 
pattern means that the autopoietic system acquires the material to replace 
its components from somewhere outside the system. For example, a cell is 
constantly absorbing heat, water and nutrition from its environment and 
expelling waste matter. Its own organization, however, remains unchanged 
by this process and this allows us to say that the system is organizationally 
closed with respect to its environment but open in terms of energy and 
matter. In the case of physical systems this is ensured by a physical boundary 
that responds to certain aspects of the environment in order to ingest 
materials (and in this sense the system is open in a closed sort of way). 
Zeleny (1980 a: 4) sums it up concisely: 
an autopoietic system is a distinguishable complex of component-producing processes 
and their resulting components, bounded as an autonomous unity within its environ-
ment, and characterised by a particular kind of relations among its components and 
component-producing processes; the components through their interaction recursively 
regenerate, maintain and recover the same complex of processes that produced them. 
1. Advantages? 
It sometimes seemed to the critics and skeptics at the conference that the 
advantages of applying autopoietic theory to the legal system could only 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
357 
be appreciated by one already committed to that viewpoint. Yet in many 
ways the advantages claimed by the autopoieticists for their approach were 
quite conventional in their scope: that it enabled us to reach a more refined 
and differentiated view of the law; that it highlighted important legal 
characteristics obscured or neglected by other approaches; and that it had 
greater explanatory power with respect to certain outstanding problems. 
In the course of discussion at least some of the following were mentioned 
as factors in favor of seeing the law as an autopoietic sub-system. 
1. One of the advantages claimed by the autopoieticists for their approach 
is that it is capable of taking account of the legal system's self-description 
without being bound to it. There is, of course, necessarily a tension 
between these perspectives — the law's view of itself, its operative self-
understanding, is bound to clash with the external viewpoint of a sociologi-
cal theory of law. The legal system tends to see itself in terms of legal 
norms, institutions and acts, operating within a definite hierarchy; insofar 
as it thinks in terms of system and environment, it works in terms of an 
input-output model: the law receives inputs in the form of demands for 
legal solutions to problems and processes these as best it can. Autopoietic 
theory accepts the importance of this self-description especially for the self-
reproduction of the system. On certain points there is a measure of 
convergence between the two perspectives — on the question of normative 
closure, for instance. However, a systems theory approach is bound to 
focus on other aspects and thus depart from the internal point of view: it 
is not so much interested in the operation of law as law but in the operation 
of law as a system. Where the law sees the rules of the system as the basic 
elements out of which its other structures are constituted, systems theory 
concentrates on the basic binary code of the system and construes its 
elements as communications which use that code. Moreover, unlike the 
norms of the system legal communications are not part of any hierarchy. 
2. The autopoieticists believe that the systems theory approach can make 
sense of certain features of the legal system that might otherwise be puzzling 
or heighten those that might be obscured. Just two may be mentioned 
here — circularity and paradox. The question of autonomy on which 
autopoieticists place special emphasis is dealt with in a later section. 
The concentration of autopoietic systems theory on self-referentiality is 
not merely an academic exercise but points to the presence of circularity 
as a real phenomenon in law. Legal communications refer to other legal 
communications, to legal structures and to legal acts. This is not a specifi-
cally new discovery on the part of systems theory — one has only to think 
of Hart's secondary rules, for example, which deal with the production 
and validation of other rules. However, autopoietically speaking, self-
referentiality is seen not in terms of the production and validation of norms 

358 
Peter Kennealy 
by norms but as part of the self-reproduction of the system's elements and 
organization over time. 
Another feature of the law to which systems theory pays particular 
attention is the possibility of the emergence of paradox. This occurs 
when the code, according to which the communications of the system are 
thematized, is applied to itself. In the case of the legal system it happens 
when the question is asked whether the code of the legal system, "right/ 
wrong" is itself right or wrong. This might seem a fairly remote possibility 
but instances of it can be found as, for example, the right, found in some 
constitutions, of civil disobedience. Perhaps a more common example is 
that of equity law where the legal system contains a program for overriding 
its own statute law in the interests of fairness. 
3. An autopoietic approach enables us to deploy a theoretically sophisti-
cated apparatus in dealing with problems insufficiently analyzed by less 
exalted versions of legal theory. Part of this power stems from the fact 
that the sociological theory of law as an autopoietic sub-system is part 
of a wider theory of functionally differentiated social sub-systems and, 
consequently, the theory supplies interesting perspectives on the inter-
relationships of the legal and other systems — on the interactions of law 
and society. Why does legal regulation often fail to achieve its intended 
results? Why does it occasionally work? What are the conditions for the 
successful interaction of functionally differentiated, autopoietic social sub-
systems? 
2. Fortuitous fit? 
Two sorts of problems can be expected in applying to the law a model as 
precisely articulated as the autopoietic one. In the first instance, it is 
possible that the law might not contain enough components to fill out the 
model in a non-trivial manner (what we might call the problem of paucity). 
Secondly, there is the possibility already mentioned, that the law might 
contain a surplus of significant components above and beyond what the 
theory is capable of dealing with. It is even possible that both problems 
might occur together: there could be such a bad fit that not only would 
some objectively important autopoietic categories remain empty but there 
would also remain self-evidently important legal phenomena with no place 
in the theory whatsoever. 
It is not being claimed here that there must exist some pre-determined 
fortuitous symmetry of parts between the theory and its object. One of 
the hopes in adopting any new theory is that it will alter our conception 
of law, enabling us to identify hitherto passed-over areas of significance 
and to re-assess traditional ideas of the self-evident importance of other 
parts (which, of course, raises the question of where we acquire our 
standards of the significance of the various components of the legal sys-

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
359 
tem — are we talking about their functional significance, their normative 
significance or their social consequences?). 
This suggests that there are two sets of criteria for the application of 
autopoietic concepts: the theoretical set which requires that what is selected 
will perform the necessary role in the model; and the object set which 
stipulates that the elements do in fact exist in the legal system. Problems 
with either of these two sets of criteria are likely to arise from the same 
source: that even if law is an autopoietic system it is one that operates in 
a very different medium from other autopoietic systems. 
For a start, in a non-physical system, the notion of a boundary within 
which the elements are organized becomes a metaphor (or, at least, must 
be reinterpreted). But if this is so how do we distinguish between a system 
and its environment and how can we tell that the elements of the legal 
system are organized in such a manner that they are self-reproductive? 
Luhmann's first step to achieving this is to designate social systems, 
along with psychic systems, as meaning-processing. In psychic systems — such 
as the self — consciousness is the mode of meaning-based reproduction. 
But in the legal sub-system legal communications are indicated as filling 
the role of elements in the autopoietic model, as being the things that 
vanish and so need to be reproduced along with their organization. In the 
course of the conference there were some objections to this decision. Why 
legal communications (which are defined as communications intended to 
have legal effect and change legal expectations), it was asked. Why not 
legal acts, or legal actors, or legal rules or statutes or judgements? Legal 
actors were particularly suggested because of their central importance in 
the legal system — producing, observing and submitting to law. However, 
in Luhmann's conception, where the subject, if not entirely eliminated 
from the game, has certainly been sent off the pitch, legal actors are part 
of the environment because everything is environment except communication. 
And it is through looking at this idea that we discover the nature of the 
boundary between a system and the environment. 
Legal communications are a subset of general social communications 
that have been thematized according to the legal code which is the binary 
normative code of right and wrong. This is not to be understood as right 
and wrong in any wider normative sense but right and wrong according 
to legal norms. Evidently, legal communications would not exist if legal 
actors did not exist — obviously nothing "social" would exist if there were 
not any human beings — but though they are necessary to the existence 
of the legal system they are not part of it. What is distinctive about placing 
legal communications in the role of elements within the model is that while 
elements must still be produced by elements the replacement of one 
communication by another only makes sense if the produced communica-
tion is different. 

360 
Peter Kennealy 
Legal communications have both normative and a cognitive quality. 
Normatively speaking, they refer to the code of the system, legal/illegal, 
and some points were raised about this during discussion. One difficulty 
was whether the legal system could correctly be said to possess only one 
binary code. After all, many norms of the system were not directly con-
cerned with prescribing or forbidding types of behavior but in making 
possible types of behavior which would not exist without the norm. In 
other words, some legal rules are constitutive rather than regulative — for 
instance, marriages, wills and divorces are neither prescribed or forbidden 
by law but made possible and in the circumstances it is not correct to 
speak of a marriage being right or wrong but valid or invalid. 
It is interesting to see why this reasonable criticism misses the mark. At 
one level, it could be pointed out that the code right/wrong is not of itself 
intrinsically regulative but only requires that relevant behavior be in 
accordance with the norm, whether that norm is regulative or constitutive 
in scope. Going a little deeper, we can see that this is not just a verbal 
gloss but demonstrates the close connection between the code of a system 
and the function of the legal sub-system. Law, as a functionally differenti-
ated sub-system is specialized in the maintenance of the stability of expecta-
tions which it achieves through normative closure. By normative closure 
is meant that in the face of a disappointed expectation about behavior the 
system does not react by changing its attribution "right" or "wrong". For 
example, if someone is caught evading income tax the legal system does 
not just change its norms concerning the duty of everyone to pay income 
tax but goes ahead and enforces the norm thereby maintaining everyone's 
expectation that they will have to pay income tax. Now unless a legal 
system is completely moribund it will not preserve rigidly and indefinitely 
the same set of expectations. The creation of new norms and the replacement 
of outdated or completely ignored norms is going to change the profile of 
the set of expectations. Constitutive norms act in a private fashion in this 
manner allowing the individual to change the profile of his own particular 
portfolio of expectations. Constitutive norms once invoked soon lead to 
new regulations being applied to the invoker and consequently to new 
expectations about his behaviour on his own part and on the part of others. 
However, still on the question of the code, a more serious problem was 
raised. What happens in case of undecidability or where the system self-
referentially negates its own code? The first issue is surely linked to the 
problem much discussed in Anglo-American jurisprudence of whether there 
is always a right answer and lies outside the scope of this report. The 
second issue is potentially more problematic for the autopoietic view of 
things. An example — if self-referential negation seems too abstract — 
would be where a Supreme Court allows for a right of civil disobedience 
because the implication is that the requirement of submission to norms 
depends on some extra-systemic factor — some higher code. 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
361 
The closure of the system clearly refers to its norms; but for the norms 
to operate the system must be in some sense open — cognitively open. 
There is no point in having norms if the system doesn't know what is 
going on in its environment, that is whether the norms are being respected 
or not. Yet it should be made clear that when it is said that the system is 
open to information it is not meant that it perceives everything going on 
around it. The environment exists for the system, for the most part, as 
meaningless noise which the system refuses to take into account in its 
operations. Still, some events in the environment are of relevance to the 
law because they have been conditioned by legal norms and it these sort 
of events that count as information for the system. In a sense then, the 
information is purely internal: "it" is not created by the system but the 
system creates the possibility of its becoming information. 
One way of putting this is to say that the system has two environments: 
one which we as observers can point to and includes everything outside 
the system including other funtionally differentiated sub-systems with their 
own operative codes. The other is the system-relative environment created 
by the system's unique network of distinctions and indications and which 
are closely tied to the system's code. According to the theory, the inhibition 
placed on the system's sensors is a severe one because of the mutual 
untranslatability of the codes precludes the possibility of any system becom-
ing part of the accessible environment of another. Each system is completely 
separate and autonomous even where some element seems to be common 
to each. Take the example of money — vital to the economic system and 
unimaginable in its present form without either the legal system or the 
political system. Yet the theory of autopoiesis holds that this is not a case 
of the interaction or even of the overlapping of systems and refers to the 
phenomenon as dual membership — rather like a man who belongs to two 
clubs and behaves differently in each. But this is only a metaphor and it 
is not clear that it works. What counts as money is a product of the legal 
system; the supply of money and, therefore, part of its value is controlled 
by the political system. So how can we say that the economic system is 
autonomous? Why does autopoietic theory not accept this as part of the 
mutual dependence of the functionally differentiated sub-systems? 
III. The Interaction and Autonomy of Autopoietic 
Sub-Systems 
This section includes the last two sets of issues that were raised at the 
conference — those to do with the testing and the development of the 
theory. Many of the critics and the empiricists felt that this is where the 
theory flew most unreasonably in the face of reality and reached the limits 
of their toleration. But what was a stumbling block to the unfaithful 

362 
Peter Kennealy 
appeared to the disciples as a springboard to future developments in which 
not only the theoretical problems would be cleared up but also in their 
wake the practical implications of the theory would become evident. 
These questions can be dealt with in two sections: 
1. What do we mean by equating the autonomy of law to the autonomy 
of an autopoietic system? 
2. How can we theoretically conceive of the interaction of autopoietic 
systems? 
1. Autonomy 
It is on the question of the autonomy of law that the greatest contrast 
emerged between our everyday, common-sense conception of law and the 
autopoietic vision. The discussion of Lempert's paper by Nelken brought 
out the main points of contrast. 
On Nelken's reading, everyday folk use the notion of autonomy as an 
empirically ascertainable, scalar concept that functions both as an ideal and 
an ideal type. As such it is not a theory but a central concept in our way 
of looking at the law — and not with the aspects of law that haunt the 
autopoieticists: its unity, its identity and its self-reproduction but with the 
undeniable relations that exist between law and society. From this point of 
view, legislation as carried out in parliaments is very definitely a political 
activity that centrally affects the law whereas in autopoietic terms only law 
can make law and so is autonomous by definition. 
It cannot be hoped that an illuminating argument will emerge between 
two parties who, using radically different approaches, claim to be talking 
about the same phenomenon of autonomy. There is no disagreement that 
the word "autonomy" means autonomy in anybody's world. However, an 
apparent difference of opinion emerged because the unspecified autonomy 
being spoken of was the autonomy of two different things: very simply, 
Lempert's legal system was not congruent with Luhmann's legal system. 
Lempert speaks of a legal system because he is dealing with a whole whose 
parts are not only in constant interaction with each other but with things 
that are not part of the system. This is both the strength of law — 
systematic and hierarchical interaction between its parts — and its purpose, 
viz., to interfere in a systematic manner in the operation of other parts of 
society through the direction of human behavior. 
Autopoietic theory, on the other hand, is focused not on interaction but 
on self-production. And as by definition only the law can make law we 
have a condition of complete autonomy. In a legislature an autopoieticist 
does not see politicians representing various points of view, interests, 
parties, etc. He only sees legal communications occurring within a structure 
of legal norms that refer to other legal communications and norms. 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
363 
These differences are made possible by what is probably the single most 
important characteristic of the autopoietic discourse: it is entirely formal. 
It has little interest in the content of a legal norm. Therefore, the criteria 
for the application of the autopoietic concept are quite entirely different 
than those to be found in a viewpoint that is heavily concerned with the 
substance of laws. The occurrence of events which to the Anglo-American 
point of view make all the difference to our assessment of the degree of 
autonomy of law have no bearing whatsoever on the autonomy in the 
mind of the autopoieticist. 
To take an example: a moral pressure group decides that the law on 
abortion should be tightened up because in their view it constitutes legalized 
murder. In order to achieve this they mount a publicity campaign, lobby 
legislators, hold demonstrations to display the strength of their support 
and commitment, make contributions to political parties that support their 
viewpoint and generally maintain pressure until the law has been changed 
in accordance with their values. From the point of view of people like 
Lempert the autonomy of law has been diminished and the legal system 
shown to be vulnerable to the pressure that small, determined groups can 
exercise on the political system. Not so for the autopoieticist. For him, the 
law has changed; but the law is always changing and in changing reproduces 
itself. The only conditions under which a loss of the autonomy of the law 
could possibly be imagined in an autopoietic world would be if moral 
communications directly brought about a change in legal norms. And if 
this were to happen there would no longer exist the legal system as we 
know it (and could not happen by definition if we accept Hart's definition 
of law as the union of primary and secondary norms). The relative autono-
mist is interested in how moral norms influence legal norms. The autopoie-
ticist is only keen to show that it was legal communications and legal acts 
that brought about legal change. For him, there is no minimum content 
of natural law in the legal system: it is irrelevant whether theft is legal or 
illegal because either conditioning is a successful instance of the binary 
code at work. Even the attributed function of the system — the maintenance 
of the stability of expectations — is indifferent between which sets of 
expectations are stabilized. 
This contrast was brought out clearly by Luhmann in his reply to 
Lempert. According to Lempert, autonomy was like a zero-sum game 
between the system and the environment: the more the environment 
influences law, the less autonomous law becomes. In Luhmann's view there 
can be a simultaneous increase of dependence and independence in system-
environment relations: the legal system can have more and varied relations 
with its environment — and to that degree become more dependent; 
however, to the extent that its organization has complexified and powers 
of self-reproduction increased the system has become more independent of 
its environment (i.e., becomes better able to deal with external perturba-

364 
Peter Kennealy 
tions). The two approaches can be contrasted as follows: for a relative 
autonomist, that a moral issue should bring about changes in legal commu-
nications that bring about changes in legal norms is a blow to legal 
autonomy; for the autopoieticist, it is a demonstration of legal autonomy 
because it shows that for anything to cross the boundary of law it must 
first become part of it. 
But here we come to a problem about the boundaries of the system. 
What is it that constitutes a communication as a legal communication? The 
standard definition is that a legal communication is one designed to have 
legal effect ("communicative actions that engender legal consequences") 
and it is by no means clear how strictly and unequivocally this separates 
legal from other social communications. Does it include any communication 
about law and the possibility of changing it including arguments about 
what the law should be? 
2. Interaction? 
The foregoing questions are relevant to the problem of the interaction of 
autopoietic systems. The problem can be formulated in the following 
manner: in an autopoietic account we can provide solid theoretical ground-
ing for the autonomy and unity of law. It also helps to account for the 
puzzling phenomenon of the failure of autopoietic systems to interact in 
the intended manner (the explanation being that the attempted interference 
by one system in the working of another fails to break through its filter 
mechanism and succeeds only in creating disturbing noise in the object 
system's environment — and with possible rebound effects on the active 
system). 
This has two undesirable consequences, one methodological and one 
practical. The practical one is that this means that systems are — as Teubner 
put it — like windowless monads, closed to and oblivious of each other with 
the result that any attempted communication between them is guaranteed 
misunderstanding. The scientific disadvantage is that this absoluteness of 
closure and guaranteed autonomy of autopoietic systems fails to make sense 
of those instances of the successful interaction of autopoietic systems. 
The question posed for the autopoieticist, then, is how to develop the 
vocabulary of autopoietic concepts in order to make sense of the diversity 
of interaction between systems. And resolving these questions will also 
help resolve the practical question of how to identify opportunities and 
means for the accurate manipulation of one system by another. 
Nearly all of the disciples were engaged upon this enterprise (not being 
the kind of social theorists who like to leave things alone). 
Hutter's suggestion was that systems can successfully interact by using 
conversation circles. His example was taken from the area of patent law — 
an area of obvious concern to the economy and which in this case was 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
365 
concerned with what could or could not be patented. The strategy for 
tackling the problem of mutual opacity is that on a particular issue represen-
tatives of the various sub-systems involved get together in a conversation 
circle and make each other aware of the problems that each would have 
in the light of any proposed solution. 
Unfortunately this idea of a sort of parliament of subsystems seemed to 
create as many problems theoretically as it appeared to have solved practi-
cally for the parties involved. Firstly, this approach involves conceptualizing 
the law and the economy as collective actors seeing them as psychic systems 
capable of intentionalistic actions. However, subsystems are not psychic 
systems and in autopoietic terms do not even interact with them. Secondly, 
it was pointed out, it is not legitimate to think of a firm in one of the 
conversation circles as representing the economic system. Firms tend to 
represent nobody but themselves and their own interests. Because of this 
it would be a matter of luck if a firm in a conversation circle was 
representative of the relevant conditions in the economic system. But perhaps 
the most difficult point for those interested in the theoretical issues was 
that the approach complicated unnecessarily the path of interaction between 
the two systems. Not only was another system placed between the law and 
the economy — with the possibility that it too might be autopoietic — 
but also between this and each of the subsystems there was postulated a 
specialized boundary position for the maintenance of contact. Again it was 
stressed that this was a problem of the conceptualisation of the interaction 
of systems seeing, as in this case at least, the procedure appeared to have 
overcome its theoretical deficiencies and worked in practice. 
Willke approached the autopoietic barrier to the interaction of systems 
with more respect. Reflecting on the paradox that in a modern functionally 
differentiated society social sub-systems simultaneously become more interde-
pendent — in the sense that the survival of each sub-system depends on 
the others performing their function for the overall society — and more 
independent of each other through their operative closure and increasing 
internal complexity. This creates the odd situation that although locked 
together into a wider whole to which each contributes its necessary function 
they are yet capable of creating negative externalities for each other because 
of their mutual blindness. Willke's concern was to discover ways of making 
each system sensitive to its environment in the sense of creating an 
awareness of its disturbing effects on other systems. Or, in other words, 
how might the self-guidance capacities of the various systems, including 
the legal system, be activated. (It was suggested by Braten that certain 
systems — if one could regard organized crime as an autopoietic subsys-
tem — might be prima facie resistant to the stimulation of their self-guidance 
capacities, if they had any.) 
Willke's term for this form of non-intrusive regulation was societal 
guidance. The precise mechanism involved was "a grammar of transforma-

366 
Peter Kennealy 
tional rules which allow for the transfer of external conditions into the 
internally determined operational cycles of an acting unit." In essence the 
role of law in this approach is "indirect rule" and, according to Willke, 
this suggested solution overcomes the paradox of interdependence and 
independence by strengthening "... the autonomy and operative closure of 
the guided system in order to increase its responsiveness and sensitivity to 
specific external conditions". 
There were some objections to this treatment of the problem. Ladeur 
found the conception of guidance too abstract while Clune was skeptical 
about the coaxing capacity of law and the potential for the sort of self-
guidance looked for being present in the sub-systems. Teubner objected that 
the strategy suggested was not in agreement with the central assumptions of 
self-referentiality which is that there is no direct contact with the environ-
ment and communication systems only interact with self-constructed real-
ities. 
For himself, Teubner's preferred line of development was to investigate 
the possibility of the self-identification of the law as one autopoietic system 
in a world of autopoietic systems. Law regulates society through regulating 
itself was the motto for this approach. But in view of the fact that in the 
autopoietic vision there is no output of law from the system, how is the 
control of others made possible through the control of self? 
The difficulty of this was illustrated with an autopoietically interpreted 
example of a price-freeze imposed by law on the economy. Autopoietically 
speaking, this is not an intervention by the law in the economy but a mere 
act of observation by the law — and, moreover, not even a direct observa-
tion of the economy but a self-observation: "through a price-control norm 
the law merely observes its own operation". The reason for this is that 
observation is "to be understood as a procedure strictly within the system 
that neither leads into reality 'out there' nor from the outside in. Observing 
means that a system introduces distinctions into internal operations and 
indicates something on the basis of these distinctions". Now the same 
holds for the economic system so that neither does it have any knowledge 
of a price-control "out there." If any observation does take place, it is 
in terms of the distinctions and indications intrinsic to the economy. 
Consequently, legal norms are not considered in virtue of their normative 
validity — as they are in the legal system — but as items in cost-
benefit calculations. Clearly, in this world, there is no possibility of direct 
intervention. (What is also clear is that the motto "law regulates the world 
through regulating itself' loses its pleasant and rather hazy aura of the 
harmony of the spheres because in the light of the view expressed above 
it no longer means that through ordering itself the law attunes the world 
to its order. It must now be interpreted as meaning that even if the law 
tries directly to regulate the world it will only succeed in regulating itself. 
Law, according to the autopoietic canon, only operates on law.) 

Talking About Autopoiesis — Order From Noise? 
367 
How then did Teubner think the harmony of the spheres might be 
attained? In contrast to linking up systems through conversation circles 
and boundary positions, or trying to connect the cognitive opennesses of 
the various systems using transformational grammers, Teubner advocated 
the interference of similar autopoietic systems at the level of communication. 
There were three reasons for this. In the first place, social sub-systems as 
social communication systems possess the same raw material of meaning; 
secondly, they each use communications, albeit thematized differently, as 
the elements of their systems; thirdly, any communication in any sub-system 
is at one and the same time sub-system and general societal communication. 
Taking communication as a synthesis of information, utterance and 
understanding it is clear that at the informational level a legal communica-
tion, for example, is thematized according to the legal code of right and 
wrong. However, not only is it possible for one legal communication to 
link up to other legal communications (as when a fine leads to an appeal) 
but also to wider social communication circuits; and this social communica-
tion can, in turn, link up to other specialized communicative circuits such 
as the economy or politics. In this manner interfering systems can make 
their complexity available for each other. However, a problem with these 
communicative links was the loss of motivation and information that they 
were considered to cause in the interacting systems. 
A mode of more direct interference lies in institutions like contract 
where the legal, moral and economic actions occur in the same single act 
(though with three different system perspectives). 
Finally, in the same genre there is the same possibility of communication 
through organization. This refers to the formal organizations that exist in 
social sub-systems (for instance, in the economy, firms and trades unions) 
and whose own system elements (organization decisions) can link. 
Teubner indicates some of the neo-corporatist negotiation systems as 
instances of this and one where the role of the law might be expanded. 
3. Conclusion 
Throughout the discussion of these and other suggestions for incorporating 
possible modes of system interaction into autopoietic theory, there regularly 
sounded a note of exasperation from the critics and the empiricists. Why 
suggest coaxing systems when we know how recalcitrant they are? Why 
say the law operates only on the law when we know that it operates on 
the economy? Why point to the economic code as one of the reasons for 
the flaunting of the law in the economic system when we know that it is 
due to acts of individual evasion caused by the profit motive? 
These and similar questions demonstrated just what a twist of perspective 
is involved in the autopoietic approach. Whether it is possible to speak in 
a pure autopoietic manner is itself debatable, so radically different is that 

368 
Peter Kennealy 
point of view from our normal ways of thinking. Even the committed 
autopoieticists' accounts of things are riddled with anthropomorphic and 
intentionalistic features though this is excused, they claim, by the fact that 
even a theory that tries to abandon the subject-object distinction must 
operate in a language into whose very structure that distinction is built. 
The veil of language is opaque and conceals from us the true order of 
things — despite the fact that systems, both observing and observed, are 
themselves linguistically constituted. It is not surprising that by the end 
of the conference there were few new converts prepared to make, as they 
saw it, a leap into faith. It seems, to this neutral observer at least, that the 
autopoieticists, if they are seriously interested in spreading the good news, 
must make the effort to be more accessible. It is not the case that their 
writings are obscure and, some would say, perverse; but it is true that, to 
the uninitiated outsider, they seem like this. On the other hand, appreciation 
of this unique point of view is an intellectual effort and, considering that 
the autopoietic approach is among the most interesting challenges in current 
legal theory, one worth making.
